name: Kairos / rusty_rtos_kernel (FreeRTOS kernel remade in Rust)
baseline: FreeRTOS V11.3.1 kernel (C), unmodified, with its first-party GCC RISC-V port, built with clang -O2
workload: Retired instructions per call on RV32IMAC under QEMU virt with -icount shift=0, same operations in both kernels (tick, scheduler selection, whole task switch, list operation), plus RAM per task and flash size; both kernels are first proven trace-identical on 22 conformance scenarios.
claimed_speedup: Kairos umbrella README table (headed rv32), retired instructions unless stated: tick 9 vs 15 (0.60x, bench/tick-work, runtime minstret count); scheduler selection 45 vs 27 (1.67x against Kairos); whole cooperative switch 75 vs 110 (0.68x) and whole preemptive switch 119 vs 110 (1.08x against). Both switch rows add the measured selection row to a static llvm-objdump count of the register half from bench/switch-cost (Kairos 30 cooperative and 74 preemptive against FreeRTOS portASM.S 83; the 83/30/74 constants are typed into tick-work/run.sh). List operation 18.47 vs 22.32 instructions per op (0.83x) is not an rv32 row: it is bench/list-cost, callgrind on an x86-64 host, rustc opt-level 3 plus LTO against gcc 15.2 -O2 list.c. The ledger gives gcc -O3 at 21.82 (about 0.85x, derived from page data) and a 32-bit row of 23.75 vs 33.42, and its latest 64-bit Rust figure is 18.80; 18.47 appears only in the README. RAM per task 176 B vs 596 B (0.30x); the C figure includes a 512 B task stack that stackless Kairos tasks do not own. Flash 19,484 B vs 13,924 B (1.40x against); the scorecard says 19,746 B (1.42x) and the kernel README says 22,396 B by default or 17,860 B with the small feature. The kernel README adds Cortex-M3 PendSV 19 vs 19 (parity) and an RV32 preemptive register half of 74 vs 83.
compiler_and_flags: tick-work (tick, selection): C arm clang -target riscv32-unknown-elf -march=rv32imac -mabi=ilp32 -O2 -ffreestanding -fno-builtin, compiled per translation unit and linked with ld.lld (bench/tick-work/run.sh). Rust arm firmware/riscv32-qemu-tick-work [profile.release] opt-level 2, lto false, codegen-units 1, panic abort, overflow-checks off. The script does not pin compiler versions. switch-cost (register half): static instruction counts with llvm-objdump; FreeRTOS portASM.S macros assembled by clang, so both sides of that half are hand-written assembly. list-cost: gcc -O2 and -O3 (gcc 15.2 per LEDGER.md) against Rust release opt-level 3, lto true, one codegen unit, counted under callgrind on an x86-64 WSL2 host.
hardware: QEMU virt -cpu rv32 (rv32imac) with -icount shift=0 for the tick and selection rows (retired instructions read from minstret, deterministic, independent of the host). The register half is a static disassembly count. The list row ran under callgrind on an x86-64 WSL2 host whose CPU is not stated. ESP32-S3 cycle figures (tick 54, switch 166 cycles) are Kairos-only and predate kernel 0.2.1.
stars_or_usage: 0 stars (kernel repo), 1 star (kairos umbrella repo); rusty_rtos_kernel crate about 424 crates.io downloads
tradeoffs: Flash is 1.40x larger (handle validation, stackless resume machinery, u16 list ids); queue items are at most 8 bytes; SMP only on two cores with no affinity; no MPU, no static allocation and no co-routines; no privilege separation between tasks; a C ABI crate (rusty_rtos-capi) lets unmodified FreeRTOS C demos link against it.
caveats: The metric is retired instructions under an emulator, not wall-clock time or cycles. The project says these are work rows, not cycle rows, and its only silicon cycle figures have no C arm. Both arms of the tick-work rows are matched at -O2 with no LTO, not -O3. The list row breaks the matching: Rust at opt-level 3 with LTO against gcc -O2, measured on an x86-64 host but shown under an rv32 heading. Against gcc -O3 (21.82) it is still about 0.85x (derived from page data). The headline cooperative-switch win (75 vs 110) is a composite of a runtime count and a static count of hand-written assembly. Its gap is structural, not Rust codegen: FreeRTOS's RISC-V portYIELD() is an ecall trap that saves all 28 GPRs, while a Kairos yield happens at a call site and saves 14. The project's own Cortex-M3 control shows parity (19 vs 19). The RAM-per-task win compares stackless state-machine tasks with FreeRTOS tasks that own a 512 B stack. The tick win came from a cached current_priority (one arena resolve removed) and a 32-bit compare fix (LEDGER 2026-09-28); neither the ledger nor the scorecard explains why 9 ends up below C's 15. Mixed result: preemptive switch, scheduler selection and flash are worse than C. Numbers drift between documents. bench/tick-work/README.md still prints the older 56 vs 15 tick and 79 selection. Flash appears as 19,484, 19,746 and 22,396 B. The README says thirteen rows have a C arm with three against Kairos, the scorecard says eleven with one loss. The ledger records two corrected harness defects (a hand-rolled NoTrace that inflated the silicon and selection rows 305 to 79, and a broken work-parity anchor) and a list-cost bench that once could not run. First-party only, no independent measurement, near-zero adoption (0 stars on the kernel repo, 1 on the umbrella, 424 crates.io downloads). An RTOS scheduler is a loose fit for concurrency-runtimes.
found_via: crates.io API harvest ('rtos', 'scheduler kernel' and concurrency queries), then a README grep for 'vs C' comparison tables; opened the kairos umbrella README, bench/tick-work/run.sh and README, docs/LEDGER.md, rusty_rtos_kernel README and rusty_rtos_core README, and the GitHub repo and commits pages.
why_faster: README: FreeRTOS pays 110 instructions for every RISC-V switch because its portYIELD() is a trap that saves everything an interrupt could clobber, while Kairos yields cooperatively for 75; the stackless task design removes the per-task stack (RAM); the project itself says the cooperative gain is about where the yield is taken, not about moving registers more cheaply.

verification.tier_reason: The tick and scheduler-selection rows are reproducible from public code (kairos bench/tick-work/run.sh building unmodified FreeRTOS V11.3.1 plus firmware/riscv32-qemu-tick-work) with the compiler, flags (-O2 both arms, no LTO) and machine (QEMU virt -cpu rv32, -icount shift=0, minstret) stated, so the A tier holds for those rows. The verdict is a downgrade of the claim, not the tier: the record overstated the list row, the composite switch rows and same_algorithm.
verification.notes: Tier A kept for bench/tick-work (tick 9 vs 15, selection 45 vs 27), which is public, deterministic and gated by PARITY and POISON checks against unmodified FreeRTOS V11.3.1 at matched -O2. Record shortcomings: the list row is mislabelled as rv32 and opt-mismatched, the switch rows are composites with typed-in register-half constants, the wins come from design (call-site yield vs ecall trap, stackless tasks, index arenas) rather than the language, the C baseline is -O2 rather than -O3, the result is mixed, and figures are stale across documents. Metadata checked: MIT OR Apache-2.0, 0 stars, 220 commits, last commit 2026-10-09, crate 424 downloads.

Against Kairos in the same table: preemptive switch 119 vs 110 (1.08x), scheduler selection alone 45 vs 27 (1.67x), flash 19,484 B vs 13,924 B (1.40x). name: Myelon / disruptor-mp (shared-memory ring-buffer IPC transport, Rust)
baseline: Boost.Interprocess message_queue ('Boost-MQ', C++) and an Open MPI shared-memory ping-pong (C, built with mpicc); the same chart also holds Rust and Java-ecosystem peers (iceoryx2, Aeron through rusteron, shmipc-rs, crossbeam, ZeroMQ).
workload: Two-process 1p1c ping-pong of 1 KB messages over shared memory or mmap, reported as messages per second, run by the project's competitive-bench harness (adapters for Boost message queue and Open MPI are small C++/C helper programs under third_party/).
claimed_speedup: Chart labels in assets/bench-pingpong-throughput-1kb.png (1 KB, 1p1c, msgs/sec, log scale): Myelon-Raw mmap 4.9M and shm 4.4M, plus the project's own Disruptor (disruptor-mp) baselines at 4.8M (mmap) and 4.6M (shm). Peers: Crossbeam 2.6M, Rusteron (Aeron) 2.6M, OpenMPI 2.0M, Iceoryx2 1.4M, Boost-MQ 164K, Shmipc 60K, ZeroMQ-IPC 25K, ZeroMQ-IPC-abs 20K, ZeroMQ-TCP 14K. Against Boost-MQ this is about 27x to 30x and against Open MPI about 2.2x to 2.5x (both derived from page data). Against Aeron IPC through rusteron it is about 1.7x to 1.9x (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Boost-MQ helper (crates/competitive-bench/third_party/boost_pingpong/Makefile): g++ -O3 -std=c++17 -pthread -march=native -flto -DNDEBUG on Linux. Open MPI helper (crates/competitive-bench/third_party/ompi_pingpong/Makefile, pingpong.c): mpicc -O3 -std=c11 -march=native -flto -DNDEBUG. Rust side: workspace profile 'competitive' with opt-level 3, fat LTO, codegen-units 1, panic abort, overflow-checks off and no target-cpu, so only the C/C++ helpers get -march=native. Compiler versions are not stated.
hardware: README headline tables: AMD Ryzen 7 5800X (8C/16T, 4.85 GHz boost), 64 GiB DDR4, Ubuntu 22.04, kernel 6.8, via crates/perf-bench; the chart's machine is not stated separately.
stars_or_usage: 20 stars, 1 fork; crates.io downloads: disruptor-mp about 358, myelon about 242
tradeoffs: Linux and macOS only. Fixed-size frames chosen at compile time (FixedFrame<N>), consumers busy-spin and burn a core each, and the crate does non-trivial unsafe work internally behind a safe API. Rust only: the README roadmap leaves 'C / C++' unchecked, so a C++ project would need FFI or a separate process. Framing, codecs and typed zero-copy cost throughput: the README's framed 1 KB ping-pong table gives 2.45M ops/s against the chart's 4.4M to 4.9M for the raw ring.
caveats: The win over the C++ peer is a wait-strategy gap, not a language gap. The Boost helper (main.cpp) uses blocking boost::interprocess::message_queue send and receive, which wait on an interprocess mutex and condition variable, while Myelon busy-spins on atomics. The 27x to 30x therefore measures spinning against blocking, and same_algorithm is false. Comparisons against busy-polling peers are smaller: Open MPI's vader shared-memory path is about 2.2x to 2.5x behind, and Aeron IPC, whose rusteron crate is a Rust wrapper over the Aeron C client (not checked here), is about 1.7x to 1.9x behind. The numbers exist only as PNG chart labels; the repo has no results table. Single run, no variance, and the chart's machine, compiler versions and run date are not stated (the README's Ryzen 7 5800X belongs to the perf-bench headline tables). The C/C++ helpers are built with -march=native and the Rust side is not, so flags do not handicap the baseline. The harness is first party. This is an IPC transport rather than a general concurrency runtime, so the category fit is loose. Alpha release (0.1.0-alpha.2), last commit 2026-05-21, 106 commits.
found_via: crates.io API harvest of concurrency keyword queries, then a grep of crate READMEs for C++ comparator names; the Myelon README listing 'Boost.MQ, OpenMPI' adapters surfaced it; opened README.md, the competitive-bench README, SETUP.md and Makefile, third_party/boost_pingpong/Makefile and main.cpp, third_party/ompi_pingpong/Makefile, Cargo.toml and the 1 KB ping-pong chart.
why_faster: README: LMAX Disruptor design extended to cross-process IPC with lock-free atomics, no syscalls in the hot path, cache-aligned cursors and busy-spin waiting; the Boost-MQ peer waits on a mutex and condition variable instead of spinning.

name: GHC Haskell lightweight threads (skynet 1M-spawn benchmark vs pthread/std::thread)
baseline: pthread_create and std::thread (C/C++ OS threads, 8 kB pthread stacks) running the skynet recursive spawn-and-sum benchmark
workload: skynet microbenchmark: a root unit spawns 10 children, each spawns 10 more, down to 1,000,000 leaves that return their ordinal; sums flow back up; time per spawned unit (GHC thread versus OS thread).
claimed_speedup: Haskell (stack-1.4.0/ghc-8.0.1): 0.05-0.06 us per unit (average over 1,000,000) versus pthread 54-73 us, std::thread 52-73 us and std::async 106-122 us per thread (average over 10,000, because 1,000,000 OS threads exhausted resources): about 870x-1,460x lower per-unit cost (derived from page data; sizes differ). The same page shows Boost.Fiber (C++, 16C/32T, work stealing, tcmalloc) at 0.05-0.09 us per fiber, so C++ user-space fibers match the Haskell row.
compiler_and_flags: C++ side (page): gcc-6.3.1, Boost.Build variant=release optimization=speed (-O3), pthreads created with 8 kB stacks, std::thread with the system default 1-2 MB stacks, glibc malloc or tcmalloc (-ltcmalloc). Haskell side (page): stack-1.4.0 / ghc-8.0.1 only. The skynet repo's haskell/skynet.cabal sets ghc-options -O2 -threaded -rtsopts and its README runs 'stack exec skynet +RTS -N', but the Boost page does not say which Haskell variant or RTS options it used.
hardware: dual Intel Xeon E5-2620 v4 2.2 GHz, 16C/32T, 64 GB RAM, Linux x86_64
stars_or_usage: 3.3k stars (github.com/ghc/ghc is a read-only mirror of gitlab.haskell.org/ghc/ghc, which was not opened)
tradeoffs: GHC threads are heap-allocated stack chunks scheduled by the GHC runtime (garbage-collected, optional -threaded and -N). Foreign calls and unsafe FFI interact with the scheduler differently from C.
caveats: Variant mismatch (main finding): atemerev/skynet haskell/src/Main.hs runs five implementations under criterion (Parallel, MVar, Chan, TBQueue, Unagi); its own comments give, on an i7-4930K with +RTS -N6, Parallel 0.017 s and MVar 1.7 s per 1,000,000-leaf run. The Boost row (0.05-0.06 us x 1,000,000 = 50-60 ms) matches the Parallel variant's order of magnitude, not the forkIO+MVar one (inference; the page does not name the variant). Parallel.hs computes a pure tree sum with parMap rpar: it creates sparks (work-stealing pool entries the parent may evaluate itself), no forkIO threads and no channel messages, whereas the C++ port (boostorg/fiber performance/thread/skynet_pthread.cpp) creates about 11,110 detached pthreads for its 10,000 leaves and passes every value through a mutex/condition-variable buffered_channel. So the comparison is sparks (or green threads) against kernel threads, not the same work, and the win is the runtime's, not Haskell codegen's. Scale differs (1,000,000 units for Haskell, 10,000 for pthread/std::thread). The skynet README's own Haskell (GHC 7.10.3) results range from 41-44 ms (i7-4771, Ubuntu) to 2820-6181 ms (Windows, OS X), consistent with different variants being run. Toolchains date from 2017 (go1.8.1, ghc-8.0.1, erts-8.3, gcc-6.3.1). The baseline is OS threads, not the idiomatic C++ answer for massive concurrency; Boost.Fiber on the same page reaches 0.05-0.09 us. No Haskell benchmark code lives in boostorg/fiber (performance/ holds only fiber/ and thread/). The repo_url is the GHC mirror (gitlab.haskell.org/ghc/ghc is upstream); the skynet sources are MIT, last commit 2023-11-10. GHC's licence file is the Glasgow Haskell Compiler License (BSD-3-Clause text).
found_via: WebSearch: 'lightweight threads comparison goroutines vs pthreads creation time Go faster than C pthreads paper evaluation' surfaced the Boost.Fiber performance page; the Haskell row is on the same page.
why_faster: Implied by the page rather than argued: GHC threads are runtime-scheduled green threads, pthreads are OS threads. No explicit mechanism is given.

verification.tier_reason: boostorg/fiber doc/performance.qbk (Boost.Fiber author, independent of GHC) shows Haskell 0.05-0.06 us per unit at 1,000,000 units against pthread 54-73 us and std::thread 52-73 us at 10,000 threads on a stated Xeon E5-2620 v4 with gcc-6.3.1 release/speed, but the Haskell build flags, RTS options and which of the five skynet Haskell variants ran are unstated, the gain is ~870-1,460x (cap at C for >50x with unstated flags), and the two sides run at different sizes and very likely different algorithms. Not A (no Haskell flags), not B (unequal workloads, unknown variant).
verification.notes: Downgrade B to C: numbers are on the Boost.Fiber page, but the Haskell row very likely measured the parMap/rpar spark variant (no threads, no channels) against one detached pthread per unit, at different sizes (1M vs 10k) and with Haskell flags unstated. Shortcomings to record: different algorithm (sparks vs kernel threads), unequal workload sizes, Haskell variant/flags/RTS options unstated, 2017 toolchains, C++ fibers on the same page match Haskell so no language-level win. baseline_stdlib set to libstdc++ (gcc-6.3.1 on Linux runs std::thread/std::async from libstdc++).

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: Haskell (stack-1.4.0/ghc-8.0.1): 0.05-0.06 us per thread (average over 1,000,000) versus pthread 54-73 us and std::thread 52-73 us per thread (average over 10,000): about 900x-1,460x lower cost per unit (derived from page data).
corrected_fields.compiler_and_flags: C++ side: gcc-6.3.1, Boost.Build variant=release optimization=speed (pthreads created with 8 kB stacks); Haskell side: stack-1.4.0 / ghc-8.0.1, flags not stated
corrected_fields.caveats: The baseline is OS threads (pthread_create, std::thread), not the idiomatic C++ answer for massive concurrency. The same page shows Boost.Fiber (C++ user-space fibers, work stealing, tcmalloc) at 0.05-0.09 us per fiber, which matches or beats Go and Erlang, so this is not a claim that the language beats well-tuned C++. Scale differs: the Go/Haskell/Erlang rows average over 1,000,000 spawned units while the pthread/std::thread rows average over only 10,000 threads because the 1,000,000-thread run exhausted resources (so the ratio compares per-unit cost at different sizes). The numbers come from the Boost.Fiber author's own documentation, ported skynet code for the C++ side (performance/thread/skynet_pthread.cpp: detached pthreads plus a mutex and condition-variable buffered channel) versus the upstream Go source's unbuffered channels; toolchains are from 2017 (go1.8.1, ghc-8.0.1, erts-8.3, gcc-6.3.1). Go/Haskell/Erlang compile flags and runtime options (for example GHC +RTS -N) are not stated on the page. The per-language skynet sources are in https://github.com/atemerev/skynet (MIT, last commit 2023-11-10). Tier B, not A, because the workload sizes differ and the non-C++ flags are unstated; rerunning at an equal unit count would settle it. The repo_url is the GHC compiler mirror because the claim is about the compiler/runtime; the skynet Haskell source is haskell/ in atemerev/skynet. The license file is the Glasgow Haskell Compiler License (BSD-3-Clause text).

name: Cynosure RingBuf (async-native SPSC ring buffer, Rust)
baseline: rigtorp::SPSCQueue (C++ single-producer single-consumer ring buffer). The same table also holds a hand-rolled C11 cached-index ring, which is faster than Cynosure.
workload: Single-thread push plus pop latency of an SPSC ring buffer, measured in a tight loop with LTO and DoNotOptimize against the C++ reference and a bare C11 ring; the same BENCHMARKS.md file also ranks the crate against Rust channels (rtrb, kanal, crossbeam, flume, tokio mpsc) on throughput and cross-thread latency.
claimed_speedup: BENCHMARKS.md, 'How it compares to the absolute fastest (C / C++)', 1-thread push+pop latency: hand-rolled C11 ring 0.79 ns, Cynosure 1.29 ns, rigtorp::SPSCQueue 2.46 ns, ringbuffer-spsc (Rust) 2.03 ns. Cynosure is about 1.9x lower than rigtorp, and the C11 ring is about 1.6x lower than Cynosure (both derived from page data). The same file's criterion spsc_compare table gives 2.2 ns per push+pop for Cynosure and 2.5 ns for rtrb.
compiler_and_flags: Rust stable, cargo bench with release plus LTO (README). The C++ and C comparison is described only as a 'maximally-tuned tight loop (LTO, DoNotOptimize)'; C++ compiler, version and flags are not stated.
hardware: Apple M4 Max (aarch64, macOS)
license: MIT (declared in Cargo.toml and the README; the repository has no LICENSE file)
stars_or_usage: 3 stars; cynosure crate has about 59.6k crates.io downloads
tradeoffs: Rust crate, so use from C++ needs FFI or a separate process. Tuned on AArch64: the benchmark file notes the SeqCst publish store is free on Apple silicon and a barrier on x86, and that numbers 'are very different on x86'. The async-native design pays about one atomic load and a branch per operation to check for a waiting task, which is why a bare synchronous C ring stays faster. Sibling primitives (LocalMutex, LocalSemaphore, triple_buffer, bip_buffer, oneshot, mpsc_light) are for thread-per-core executors such as monoio and glommio.
caveats: The C++ and C11 comparison code is not in the repository. benches/ holds only Rust criterion suites, and spsc_compare.rs and Cargo.toml mention neither rigtorp nor ringbuffer-spsc. The C/C++ rows therefore cannot be reproduced, and the C++ compiler, version and flags are unstated, which keeps the entry at tier C. The project's own table refutes a language-level win: a bare C11 cached-index ring beats Cynosure by about 1.6x on the same path. The win over rigtorp is single-thread push+pop latency only (producer and consumer on one thread, not two cores), and why rigtorp reads 2.46 ns in that harness is not explained. The 1.29 ns figure comes from a different harness than the 2.2 ns criterion figure for the same operation. Single representative run on one Apple M4 Max; the file warns that a back-to-back cargo bench run throttles later benches by about 15% and that x86 results differ (a SeqCst store is a barrier there). The repository has no LICENSE file; MIT is declared in Cargo.toml and the README. Young project: first commits July 2025, 3 stars, one author, 42 commits. Found through a README claim, not an independent measurement.
found_via: crates.io API harvest of about 100 concurrency keyword queries (spsc, channel, lock-free, thread-per-core and others), then a grep of about 5,600 crate READMEs for C++ comparator names (rigtorp, moodycamel, folly, boost, libuv, seastar); the Cynosure README line 'beating every async channel, and even rigtorp::SPSCQueue on latency' surfaced it; opened README.md, BENCHMARKS.md, benches/README.md, benches/spsc_compare.rs and the GitHub repo and commits pages.
why_faster: README and BENCHMARKS.md name the cached-index, cache-line-padded ring design (the same family as rtrb and rigtorp::SPSCQueue) and a waiter check that costs one atomic load and branch per call (free on AArch64 ldarb); neither says why 1.29 ns beats rigtorp's 2.46 ns.

name: Erlang/OTP processes on thread-ring (SCOOP/Qs paper, arXiv 1405.7153) vs C++/TBB
baseline: The paper's 'C++/TBB' column; for thread-ring the authors' public code (scottgw/quicksilver benchmarks/concurrent/cxx/threadring/main.cpp) is not TBB but the Computer Language Benchmarks Game C++ program by The Anh Tran: 503 OS pthreads (4 KB stacks) all blocked in one boost::asio::io_service::run() queue, each token pass a post() that wakes an OS thread; built with g++ -O3 -std=c++11 -pthread -lboost_system. No fiber, coroutine or single-threaded C++ ring was measured.
workload: thread-ring (Computer Language Benchmarks Game spec): 503 ring members pass a token 5,000,000 times (input in benchmarks/run_all.py); essentially single-threaded and bound by context-switch cost. Paper table reported for a 32-core machine (snippet).
claimed_speedup: Thread-ring on 32 cores (snippet only, paper Table 5): Erlang 3.30 s versus the paper's C++/TBB column 34.13 s, about 10.3x (derived from the snippet numbers); the C++ program is Boost.Asio over 503 OS threads.
compiler_and_flags: From the authors' Makefiles and run.sh in scottgw/quicksilver benchmarks/concurrent/*/threadring: C++ g++ -O3 -std=c++11 -pthread -lboost_system; Go 'go build' defaults, run with GOMAXPROCS set to the worker count; Erlang erlc -W (plain BEAM, no +native) run as erl -smp enable -noshell +t 8192 +P <n> +ec +K true +hms 4 +hmbs 1; Haskell ghc --make -O2 -threaded -rtsopts. Input 5,000,000 token passes for every language. Compiler and runtime versions not stated in the repo (code dates from 2014).
hardware: 32 cores (CPU model not seen)
tradeoffs: BEAM gives cheap processes and preemptive per-process scheduling with garbage-collected per-process heaps; a language runtime is required, and raw single-thread compute is slower than C++. Calling C needs NIFs or ports.
caveats: Paper numbers seen only through WebSearch result summaries (Table 5 of arXiv 1405.7153, 'Efficient and Reasonable Object-Oriented Concurrency', West, Nanz and Meyer, published at ESEC/FSE 2015): thread-ring on 32 cores Erlang 3.30 s, SCOOP/Qs 5.82 s, Go 13.98 s, C++/TBB 34.13 s, Haskell 57.44 s; arxiv.org is blocked here, so the table, CPU model and compiler versions were not opened. The benchmark code is public in https://github.com/scottgw/quicksilver/tree/master/benchmarks/concurrent (cxx, go, erlang, haskell, qs, java), and all thread-ring programs are Computer Language Benchmarks Game submissions. The C++ side is not TBB: it is the Benchmarks Game Boost.Asio program with 503 OS pthreads waiting on one shared io_service queue, so every token pass is an OS-level futex wake-up and context switch, while Erlang passes the token between BEAM processes inside a user-space scheduler. The win is green threads against OS threads (runtime, not codegen); a C++ ring on Boost.Fiber, Boost.Context or a single-threaded loop was not measured and would very likely beat both. The C++ build is -O3, so the baseline is not crippled by flags, but the comparison is of threading models. Timing asymmetry in benchmarks/run_all.py: Erlang's TotalTime is its own timer:tc figure printed to stderr (excludes VM boot and shutdown), while C++, Go and Haskell are wall-clock around Popen including process launch and, for C++, creating 503 pthreads; small against multi-second runs but it favours Erlang. The repo's run_all.py at HEAD runs the concurrent tasks with worker_range = [4], while the snippet says the paper table is for 32 cores, so the exact configuration of the published run is not certain. Toolchains date from about 2014 (BEAM without JIT). Lead for a paper-access retier.

name: evio (Go epoll/kqueue event loop; Redis clone vs real Redis)
baseline: Redis 4.0.2 (C, single-threaded ae event loop on epoll) answering PING_INLINE; the same table also holds Go net/http, fasthttp and a Go net echo server, which are Go baselines and not counted here
workload: redis-benchmark -t ping_inline -q -c 50 -n 1000000 with pipeline depth 1, 8 and 16 against the real redis-server and against the evio example Redis clone (examples/redis-server/main.go), both started with GOMAXPROCS=1 on localhost.
claimed_speedup: Requests per second, evio Redis clone vs real Redis 4.0.2 (benchmarks/out/redis{1,8,16}.txt, final redis-benchmark line): pipeline 1: 177,147.92 vs 176,991.14 (parity); pipeline 8: 1,285,347.00 vs 878,734.62 (about 1.46x, derived from page data); pipeline 16: 2,123,142.25 vs 879,507.50 (about 2.41x, derived from page data). The README itself only shows chart images and states the goal 'performs on par with Redis and Haproxy'.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated. Go version not recorded (2017 snapshot); bench-redis.sh builds the clone with plain 'go build' and starts both servers with GOMAXPROCS=1. Real Redis is whatever 'redis-server' was on PATH (Redis 4.0.2 per the log, commit=00000000), started with only '--port 6392' (no config file); its build flags are not stated. Redis 4.0.2's own src/Makefile defaults to OPTIMIZATION?=-O2 with jemalloc, so a default build was -O2, not -O3.
hardware: EC2 c4.xlarge instance (CPU model not named in the repo), client and server on localhost over IPv4; run on 2017-11-04 per the log timestamps
tradeoffs: Not a drop-in replacement for Go net or net/http (the README says so). Handlers run inside the event-loop goroutines and must not block. Linux epoll and BSD/macOS kqueue only, with a net-package fallback elsewhere. Calling it from C++ means a separate Go process.
caveats: The two servers do different amounts of work: the evio example is a tiny Redis-protocol clone (PING, ECHO, GET, SET, DEL, FLUSHDB, QUIT, SHUTDOWN, WAKE) over a Go map with a mutex, parsed by redcon.ReadNextCommand (so evio's clone reuses tidwall/redcon's parser), with no persistence, expiry, replication, statistics or full command table; PING is a string switch that appends +PONG. At pipeline depth 1 both are client-bound and equal (177,147.92 vs 176,991.14). Real Redis stays at about 878k-880k requests per second at depth 8 and 16 while the clone keeps climbing; the repo gives no explanation, and the most plausible one is Redis's per-command dispatch path rather than the language or event loop (verifier inference). Only PING_INLINE was benchmarked. One run per cell, no variance, and the redis-benchmark client shares the 4-vCPU instance with the server. Redis 4.0.2 is from 2017; its binary came from PATH with unstated build flags (Redis's Makefile default was -O2) and the log shows THP enabled and somaxconn 128 warnings. The README shows only chart PNGs for pipeline 1 and 8 and states the goal 'performs on par with Redis and Haproxy'; the depth-16 numbers come from benchmarks/out/redis16.txt. The clone at HEAD differs from the 2017 build that was measured (its 'redis server started' log line has since gained a loops field). Latest two commits are README edits (2026-05-12, 2026-05-19) and the one before is from 2022-05-14.

name: Go goroutines vs Intel TBB on a task-graph dynamic program (Comparison-Go-CppTBB)
baseline: Intel oneTBB (2017 Update 3) C++ task scheduler, MSVC v14 build, on the same static optimal binary search tree task graph
workload: Static optimal binary search tree (dynamic programming over a DAG of chunk tasks, problem sizes N=2048 and N=4096, chunking factor VP 1 to 2048, 1 to 8 processors) implemented as goroutines plus channels in Go and as TBB tasks with atomic reference counts in C++.
claimed_speedup: From docs/N4096.xlsx and docs/N2048.xlsx (d503e57, 5 runs per cell): Go faster than TBB in 14 of 96 N=4096 cells (1.003-1.149x) and in 0 of 96 at N=2048; best configuration against best at N=4096 Go 25,574.2 ms vs TBB 28,655.2 ms (1.12x, derived from page data). Paper: at N=4096 and 4 processors Go ran faster than TBB at VP=256 and VP=512 (TBB/Go 1.12 and 1.15); best speed-up over each language's own sequential code 6.53 (Go) vs 4.41 (TBB) at N=2048 and 6.28 vs 3.95 at N=4096.
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.7.4 (default go build, GOMAXPROCS set to NP); Intel TBB 2017 Update 3 prebuilt (tbb.lib/tbb.dll, vc14); C++ built with MSVC v14 in Visual Studio 2015 Update 3. The public TBB/TBB.vcxproj at release commit d503e57 sets Release|x64 to Optimization Full (/Ox), IntrinsicFunctions (/Oi), FavorSizeOrSpeed Speed (/Ot), WholeProgramOptimization (/GL), RuntimeLibrary MultiThreaded (/MT) and SDLCheck (/sdl); the Debug|x64 configuration is /Od with tbb_debug.lib. The paper does not say which configuration was measured; the README's run instructions require tbb.dll, which implies the Release build.
hardware: Intel Core i7-6700HQ (4 cores, 8 threads, 6 MB cache), Windows 10 Pro build 14393
tradeoffs: Goroutines come with a garbage-collected runtime and growable stacks; at the highest chunk counts (VP=2048, millions of goroutines) Go lost most of its time in the runtime (up to 84% of CPU time in the worst case, runs from 4.9 s to 66.6 s with 4 processors) while TBB degraded smoothly. Go code is much shorter than the TBB task-graph code.
caveats: Single small first-party experiment: one laptop CPU (i7-6700HQ, 4 cores/8 threads), Windows 10, 5 repetitions averaged, 2017 toolchains (Go 1.7.4, TBB 2017U3); raw timings are not in the repo, only figures. The paper's own wording is that TBB was faster in general and Go won only partially at the larger size (N=4096, VP=256 and VP=512, ratio 1.12 and 1.15; the paper does not label the ratio's direction, TBB time over Go time is implied). At N=2048 TBB was faster in every condition and best-vs-best TBB was 1.37x faster. Go's 'superlinear' self-speed-up (6.28 on N=4096, 6.53 in the conclusion) against TBB's 3.95 (4.41) implies a Go sequential run roughly 1.3-1.4x slower than TBB's (derived from page data, assuming the best cases coincide), so the speed-up figures say little about scheduler quality; the two sets of best speed-ups in section 5 and the conclusion also disagree. At VP=2048 Go collapsed (72-91 s at NP=1, 4.9-66.6 s at NP=4) with the Go runtime taking up to 84% of CPU time, attributed to millions of goroutines. The measured build configuration is not stated in the paper; the public vcxproj Release|x64 flags (/Ox /GL) are inferred to be the ones used. The C++ Matrix holds new T[] in a std::unique_ptr<T> (delete instead of delete[]; undefined behaviour at destruction, outside the timed region). The paper is a KIPS (Korea Information Processing Society) conference paper per the release README ('The paper's copyright is reserved by KIPS'); the PDF itself states no venue and peer review of the proceedings is not established. The repo is archived and the README says it is no longer updated; code is under CC-BY-4.0 (not an OSI software licence), so usability is reference. The 2012 Serfass and Tang paper that this repeats is behind a blocked ACM page. [retier] The tiled code on one thread already beats the sequential baseline (TBB 1.50x, Go 1.75x at N=2048), so Go's 'superlinear' speed-up is partly cache blocking; Equal/operator== is never called and is inverted, so the parallel output is never checked. 6255.4/12689.6 are sequential times (the sheet says 12698.6).
found_via: WebSearch: '"faster than Intel TBB" OR "faster than OpenMP" OR "faster than Taskflow" Rust OR Zig OR Go OR Nim task scheduler thread pool benchmark README' surfaced the repo; opened github.com/luncliff/Comparison-Go-CppTBB (README, tree, commits) and read the checked-in PDF through raw.githubusercontent.com (pdftotext) and docs/Draft.md.
why_faster: Paper's speculation: TBB's atomic reference-counter dependencies and depth-first execution give better locality overall, while Go's channel-based synchronization can trigger many more scheduling events; Go wins only at the larger problem size where its chunked tasks fit the cache better. No single mechanism is claimed for the Go win.

name: Go net TCP echo server (Boost.Redis echo benchmark, vs libuv)
baseline: libuv TCP echo server (C, epoll event loop, libuv docs tcp-echo-server example); the table also holds a Boost.Asio C++20 coroutine echo server that is faster than Go
workload: TCP echo server serving 1000 concurrent client connections on localhost (the Boost.Redis echo_server_client driver, benchmarks.tex comment 'time ./echo_server_client 1000 5000'); metric is the total wall-clock seconds the client run took against each server, one server per language/library, each written from that library's own docs example.
claimed_speedup: Go 35.6 s vs libuv 43.6 s wall time for 1000 connections x 5000 echoes (about 1.22x less wall time, derived from page data); Boost.Asio (C++) 29.5 s is about 1.21x faster than Go (derived from page data). Each value is a single run; the Go value was recorded on 2022-08-25 after the Go server was rewritten (it was 81.0 s before), the libuv value by 2022-07-15. Doc text: 'Go did surprise me: faster than nodejs and libuv!'
compiler_and_flags: libuv server: 'gcc echo_server_direct.c -luv -O2 -o echo_server_direct' (benchmarks/c/libuv/README.md), linked against an unstated system libuv build. Go server: version and build command not stated; runtime.GOMAXPROCS(1), one goroutine per connection, 1024-byte buffer. Asio server/client: CMake target with C++20 (benchmarks/CMakeLists.txt), compiler and optimisation level not stated.
stars_or_usage: 139.2k stars (golang/go); suite repo boostorg/redis has 282 stars
tradeoffs: Go brings a garbage-collected runtime and goroutine scheduler with its own netpoller; calling Go from C++ goes through cgo or a separate process.
caveats: Numbers are the pgfplots source (benchmarks.tex) of the chart on the Boost.Redis doc page 'Echo server benchmark' (doc/modules/ROOT/pages/benchmarks.adoc); the rendered PNG on boostorg.github.io was not viewed. The chart is a composite of single `time` runs recorded on different dates by the Boost.Redis (C++) author on 'my machine' (localhost latency 0.07 ms; no CPU model, OS, Go/Rust/compiler versions, no repetitions or variance): libuv 43.568 s was recorded by 2022-07-15 (commit 3fb018c) and never re-run; Tokio moved from 42.2 s/43.2 s to 30.7 s on 2022-07-16 after switching to a newer Tokio and the current_thread runtime; Go moved from 81.0 s to 35.6 s on 2022-08-25 (commit f11622e) after its server was rewritten from bufio ReadBytes line echo to a raw 1024-byte read loop with GOMAXPROCS(1); Asio was re-measured at 29.5 s on 2022-10-07. Unequal work: the libuv server is the unmodified libuv docs tcp-echo-server example, which mallocs a 64 KiB read buffer (libuv passes 64*1024 as suggested_size, src/unix/stream.c) on every read callback and a write_req_t per echo and frees both after each write, while the Go, Tokio and Asio servers reuse one 1 KiB buffer per connection; the Go server was revised between runs, the libuv one never was. The libuv server is built per benchmarks/c/libuv/README.md with 'gcc echo_server_direct.c -luv -O2' (not -O3; system libuv build flags unknown). The load generator is the single-threaded Boost.Asio echo_server_client (1000 sessions x 5000 13-byte ping-pong messages) on the same host, which may set a floor near the Asio/Tokio results. All servers are single-threaded (Asio io_context with BOOST_ASIO_CONCURRENCY_HINT_UNSAFE_IO, Tokio current_thread, Go GOMAXPROCS(1), one libuv loop). The C++ Boost.Asio coroutine server in the same table is the fastest entry (29.5 s), so this is not a win over the best C++ result. The author gives no explanation for the gap beyond 'I expected Libuv to have similar performance to Asio and Tokio'. The Go server ignores conn.Write's return value (its error check tests the stale read error), harmless for timing. Measured in 2022 (Go about 1.19); the doc page is unchanged since.

name: Lingua Franca (reactor language, C++ runtime) on the Savina actor benchmarks vs CAF
language: Lingua Franca (code generator targeting C++ and C)
baseline: CAF (C++ Actor Framework) running the same Savina benchmarks; Akka (JVM) is the second baseline
workload: Savina actor benchmark suite ported to Lingua Franca reactors (micro-benchmarks such as Ping Pong, Thread Ring, Counting, Fork Join, Big, Chameneos plus concurrency and parallelism benchmarks), execution time at a given number of worker threads.
claimed_speedup: Not on any page opened. From the abstract of the ACM TACO 2023 paper 'High-Performance Deterministic Concurrency using Lingua Franca', seen only as web search snippets (arXiv, ACM and mirrors were blocked): LF is about 1.42x faster than CAF and about 1.85-1.86x faster than Akka over the Savina suite at 20 threads, with LF behind CAF on Ping Pong and Thread Ring, ahead on Fork Join and Chameneos, and roughly on par on the parallelism benchmarks.
compiler_and_flags: Paper flags not seen. From the public build sources: the LF C++ benchmarks declare target Cpp { build-type: Release, no-runtime-validation: true, fast: true } (Cpp/Savina/src/micro/PingPong.lf), i.e. CMake Release (-O3 -DNDEBUG); the CAF baseline programs (lf-lang/savina CMakeLists.txt) and CAF 0.16.5 itself both default CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE to RelWithDebInfo (-O2 -g level) and the README build commands pass no build type, so a build that follows the README compares LF at -O3 against CAF at -O2. Compiler and version not stated.
stars_or_usage: 329 stars (lingua-franca); benchmark repo lf-lang/benchmarks-lingua-franca has 4 stars
tradeoffs: Programs are written in the LF language and compiled by a code generator, so adopting it means a new toolchain; the generated runtime is C or C++, so this is a coordination-language and scheduler claim, not a claim that non-C/C++ machine code is faster. Deterministic semantics restrict some actor patterns (logical time, reactors).
caveats: Numbers are snippet only: the TACO 2023 paper and its artifact data were not opened (arXiv, par.nsf.gov, cfaed.tu-dresden.de, ar5iv and deepai unreachable), so tier C; snippets agree on 1.86x over Akka and 1.42x over CAF but give no thread count, CPU or aggregation method, and the '20 threads' setting, CAF 0.17.6, Akka 2.6.17 and i9-10900K details could not be confirmed (the benchmark README names CAF 0.16.5). Snippets also say only 22 of the 30 Savina benchmarks were ported to the LF C++ target: benchmarks needing dynamic actor creation (Fork Join creation, Fibonacci, Quicksort and others), A*-Search and Logistic Map Series (whose CAF version uses a blocking call) are excluded, so the suite average covers only benchmarks LF can express with a static reactor graph. Same-opt-level problem in the public sources: LF benchmarks build with build-type Release (-O3) plus no-runtime-validation, while the lf-lang/savina CAF programs and CAF 0.16.5 default to RelWithDebInfo (-O2) and the README passes no build type; whether the paper overrode this is unknown. The LF ports restructure the Savina programs into reactors with fixed connections (PingPong breaks its causality loop with a logical action), so the work is equivalent but not line-for-line identical to the CAF and Akka versions. The paper's authors built both sides. Both sides are C++ (LF generates C++ against the reactor-cpp runtime), so the win is a runtime and programming-model result, not a code-generation one; the paper also reports LF behind CAF on Ping Pong and Thread Ring and behind Akka on Counting and Big (snippet). The benchmark repo has no LICENSE file; the lingua-franca repo is BSD-2-Clause.

name: NPB-Rust (NAS Parallel Benchmarks in Rust, sequential and Rayon)
baseline: NPB-CPP, the group's C++ port of NAS Parallel Benchmarks 3.4.1 (sequential NPB-SER, and OpenMP NPB-OMP for the parallel comparison), plus the original Fortran NPB
workload: NAS Parallel Benchmarks kernels EP, CG, MG, IS, FT and pseudo-applications BT, SP, LU in Rust (sequential NPB-RUST and Rayon-parallel NPB-RAYON), compared with the C++ and Fortran versions.
claimed_speedup: From the paper abstract as shown in a search snippet (snippet only): Rust sequential is 5.59% faster than C++ and 1.23% slower than Fortran; Rust with Rayon is slower than both the Fortran and the C++ OpenMP versions.
compiler_and_flags: Repo defaults (paper's actual compilers and flags not seen): Rust 1.85.0+, RUSTFLAGS='--cfg class="X"' cargo build --release with no [profile] section in NPB-RUST/Cargo.toml (opt-level 3, no LTO, no target-cpu); C++ NPB-CPP NPB-SER/config/make.def: g++ -std=c++14 with CFLAGS -O3 -mcmodel=medium; Fortran compiler and flags unknown.
tradeoffs: Rust port of NPB with a sequential variant (NPB-RUST) and a Rayon variant (NPB-RAYON); safety and ergonomics trade-offs are not discussed on the pages that were opened.
caveats: The arXiv page (2502.15536) is blocked in this environment and was not opened; the numbers come from WebSearch snippets of arxiv.org/html/2502.15536v1 (snippet only), so venue, peer-review status, hardware, compiler versions and per-kernel results are unconfirmed; a verifier with paper access should retier. The GitHub repo has no performance numbers. The only win over C++ is the sequential aggregate (5.59%, a small margin); Rayon is slower than C++ OpenMP and Fortran OpenMP, so the concurrency-runtimes category fits poorly (the win is sequential codegen, closer to numerics). The C++ baseline is the same group's NPB-CPP port (FGCS 2021, https://github.com/GMAP/NPB-CPP). Public build defaults are equivalent in optimisation level (-O3 against cargo --release opt-level 3, neither with -march=native), but the C++ default adds -mcmodel=medium; whether that or anything else explains the 5.59% is untested. The latest commit (2026-10-08, 3bb2455 'fix: adjusted tolrsd constants in LU') only assigns the 1.0e-08 tolrsd constants that were previously left at zero; with zero tolerances the early-exit residual check never fired, so the measured LU did the full iteration count and the fix does not inflate the published numbers. NPB-Rust has a --cfg safe="true" switch whose default (unset) reports UNSAFE=true; which mode the paper timed is not stated.

name: Pony actor mailbox performance (100,000,000 messages) vs CAF and Charm++
baseline: CAF 0.13 (C++ Actor Framework); Charm++ 6.6.1 (C++) is in the same chart
workload: Mailbox performance benchmark from the CAF benchmark suite: N sender actors each send M payload-free messages to one counting receiver, 100,000,000 messages in total (N/M split not stated). Pony side: examples/mailbox/main.pony (tag 0.1.7; now examples/actors/mailbox), Mailer actors each calling receiver.pong() M times; CAF side: src/caf/mailbox_performance.cpp in actor-framework/benchmarks. Plotted as speed relative to Erlang OTP 17 on 1 core against physical cores (1-32) and against 32 physical cores with hyper-threading (up to 64 threads).
claimed_speedup: Read off the charts (approximate, ratios derived from page data): at 1 core Pony 0.1.5 about 3.7 versus CAF 0.13 about 0.56 (about 6.6x) and Charm++ 6.6.1 about 0.9 (about 4x); at 16 physical cores Pony about 1.67 versus CAF about 0.27 (about 6x); at 32 physical cores Pony about 1.62 versus CAF about 0.2 (about 8x). Charm++ drops to about 0.15 at 2 cores and stays at or below about 0.13 after that; Erlang OTP 17 falls below 0.1 from about 15 cores; Scala/Akka stays near 0.02 at every core count. With hyper-threading (also Figure 8 of the AGERE! 2015 paper) Pony is about 1.48 against CAF about 0.15-0.2 at 64 threads (roughly 7-10x). Every system, Pony included, loses speed as cores are added (Pony falls from 3.7 at 1 core to about 1.8 at 4), since all senders target one mailbox.
tradeoffs: Pony is a separate language and runtime (actors with per-actor heaps, reference capabilities, no shared mutable state); using it from C++ means FFI or a separate process. Smaller ecosystem and a steeper learning curve than a C++ library such as CAF.
caveats: Charts only: the website PDF (6 pages, gnuplot, created 2015-07-06) and the AGERE! 2015 paper (HT chart only, Figure 8) have no tables, so all figures are read off the plots and are approximate. The paper says results are the average of 100 runs normalised to Erlang on one core, and that the benchmark implementations come from the CAF suite, written by programmers expert in each system (the CAF team for CAF). Neither source names the CPU (only '32 physical cores with HT'), compiler, optimisation flags or variance. The CAF-side build type used in 2015 could not be recovered: the suite's history before today is not browsable, and its current CMakeLists sets Erlang +native/hipe o3 and Charm++ -O3 but no C++ build type. The March 2015 tech-report version (fast-cheap-with-proof.pdf) ran an execution-time version on a 12-core 2.3 GHz Opteron 6338P; those are different runs. The versions are about a decade old (Pony 0.1.5, CAF 0.13, Charm++ 6.6.1, Erlang OTP 17, Scala 2.11.6 Akka; ponyc is now at 0.75.0 and CAF at 1.x), so the ratio may not hold today. CAF 0.13 at 1 core (about 0.56) is slower than both Erlang (1.0) and Charm++ (about 0.9) here, so the C++ baseline is a weak spot of CAF 0.13 under a contended mailbox, not tuned hand-written C++. Both papers are by the Pony authors (Causality and Imperial College). The same PDF and paper show a loss: on 'Creating 1,048,576 actors' CAF overtakes Pony beyond about 10 physical cores (about 17 versus 9 at 32 cores), so this is a per-benchmark win. The Pony runtime (libponyrt) is written in C. www.ponylang.io and a later Pony 0.26.0 versus CAF 0.16.3 run on doc.ic.ac.uk/~scb12/pony.html were blocked here and are not used.

name: Pony actor message ring plus factorisation vs CAF and Charm++
baseline: CAF 0.13 (C++ Actor Framework); Charm++ 6.6.1 (C++) is in the same chart
workload: Mixed case ('Message ring + factorisation') from the CAF benchmark suite: rings of actors pass a token while a worker factorises 86028157 x 329545133 by trial division on each repetition. Pony side: examples/mixed/main.pony (tag 0.1.7; now examples/actors/mixed) with defaults of 20 rings of 50 actors, 10,000 laps and 5 repetitions. CAF side: src/caf/mixed_case.cpp in actor-framework/benchmarks. The run parameters behind the charts are not stated. Plotted as speed relative to Erlang OTP 17 on 1 core against physical cores (1-32) and against 32 physical cores with hyper-threading (up to 64 threads).
claimed_speedup: Read off the charts (approximate, ratios derived from page data): at 1 core Pony 0.1.5 about 2.2 versus CAF 0.13 about 0.5 (about 4x); at 16 physical cores Pony about 29 versus CAF about 8 (about 3.6x); at 32 physical cores Pony about 48 versus CAF about 16 (about 3.0x), with Erlang OTP 17 about 19, Scala/Akka about 13.5 and Charm++ 6.6.1 about 9. With hyper-threading (also Figure 9 of the AGERE! 2015 paper) Pony is about 62 at 64 threads, against CAF at about 26-27 over 56-63 threads and about 30 at its final 64-thread point (about 2.1-2.4x), Erlang about 24 and Akka about 25.
tradeoffs: Pony is a separate language and runtime (actors with per-actor heaps, reference capabilities, no shared mutable state); using it from C++ means FFI or a separate process. Smaller ecosystem and a steeper learning curve than a C++ library such as CAF.
caveats: Unequal work between implementations: in the public Pony program (unchanged from tag 0.1.7 to today) each Ring master builds its ring once and reuses it across all repetitions, spawns a fresh Worker actor per repetition, and computes but never uses the factorisation result (the 'correct' flag is dropped; no message, no check). The CAF suite's mixed_case.cpp (current version; the 2015 CAF 0.13 version could not be retrieved) spawns a new ring of ring_size-1 actors on every repetition while the old links quit, factorises in one detached (own-thread) worker per ring, and sends every factor vector to a supervisor that checks it. Pony therefore skips ring re-creation and the result messages that CAF pays for. Charts only: the website PDF (gnuplot, created 2015-07-06) and the paper have no tables, so figures are approximate. The paper gives 100-run averages but no CPU model (only '32 physical cores with HT'), compiler, flags or variance, and the CAF build type is unknown. Versions are about a decade old (Pony 0.1.5, CAF 0.13, Charm++ 6.6.1, Erlang OTP 17, Scala 2.11.6 Akka). On the physical-core chart Erlang OTP 17 beats CAF at every core count (about 19 versus 16 at 32 cores); with HT, CAF passes Erlang at about 48 threads and ends ahead (about 30 versus 24 at 64). So CAF 0.13 is a weak baseline here, and the Pony gap says more about CAF's scaling and the unequal work than about the language. Both papers are by the Pony authors. The same sources show CAF beating Pony on actor creation beyond about 10 physical cores. The Pony runtime (libponyrt) is written in C. www.ponylang.io and doc.ic.ac.uk/~scb12/pony.html were blocked and are not used.

It stays C because the public Pony program does less work than the CAF suite's mixed_case: Pony builds each ring once and discards the factorisation result, while CAF rebuilds every ring on each repetition and sends checked results to a supervisor. verification.notes: Kept at C. The peer-reviewed AGERE! 2015 paper (Figure 9) carries the chart, but the Pony and CAF programs do unequal work: Pony skips ring re-creation per repetition and drops the factorisation result. The 64-thread figure was corrected: CAF is about 30 at its last point, so the gap is about 2.1x there, not 2.4x. Erlang does not merely reach parity; CAF overtakes it near 48 threads. Shortcomings: unequal work (same_algorithm false), flags and CPU unknown, decade-old versions, weak CAF 0.13 baseline, first-party authors.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: Read off the chart (approximate, ratios derived from page data): at 16 physical cores Pony 0.1.5 about 29 versus CAF 0.13 about 8 (about 3.6x); at 32 physical cores Pony about 48 versus CAF about 16 (about 3.0x), with Erlang OTP 17 about 19, Scala/Akka about 13.5 and Charm++ 6.6.1 about 8.7; with hyper-threading at 64 threads Pony about 62 versus CAF about 26 (about 2.4x) and Erlang about 25.
corrected_fields.workload: Message ring plus factorisation benchmark (chart title 'Message ring + factorisation'; exact ring size and numbers factorised are not stated), plotted as speed relative to Erlang OTP 17 on 1 core against physical cores (1-32) and against 32 physical cores with hyper-threading (up to 64 threads).
corrected_fields.caveats: Charts only: the PDF (6 pages, gnuplot output, file creation date 2015-07-06) has no tables, so every figure here is read off the plot and is approximate. The PDF states no CPU model, compiler, optimisation flags, run count or variance, and does not link the benchmark programs; the y axis is 'speed relative to Erlang OTP 17 on 1 core', so the ratio to CAF is derived from two plotted lines. The versions are about a decade old (Pony 0.1.5, CAF 0.13, Charm++ 6.6.1, Erlang OTP 17, Scala 2.11.6 Akka); current Pony is much newer and newer CAF releases exist, so the ratio may not hold today (the qb-vs-others README, opened, names CAF 1.1.0 as current). The charts are first-party material of the Pony project, hosted in the Pony website repository, so the competitor builds are not independently tuned. The same PDF shows a loss: on 'Creating 1,048,576 actors' CAF 0.13 overtakes Pony beyond roughly 10 physical cores (about 17x versus about 9x Erlang-on-1-core at 32 cores), so this is a per-benchmark win, not a general win over CAF. www.ponylang.io (which serves this PDF) was blocked here by the egress policy, so the copy in the ponylang-website repository was used; a later Pony 0.26.0 versus CAF 0.16.3 run on 2x Xeon E5-2690 v3 listed on a doc.ic.ac.uk page was seen only as a search snippet and could not be opened, so it is not used. On this chart Erlang OTP 17 also edges past CAF (about 19 versus 16 at 32 physical cores, about parity at 64 threads), so the ring result says more about CAF 0.13's scaling than about a Pony-only mechanism.

name: Rayon vs OpenMP (CMU 15-618 project)
baseline: C++ with OpenMP (and GNU parallel-mode sort) for Mandelbrot, matrix multiplication, sorting and reduction; C++ compiled with GCC per the report
workload: Four shared-memory benchmarks written in Rust+Rayon and C++/OpenMP: Mandelbrot (2048 to 8192 square images, 7 views), integer matrix multiplication (1024 and 2048 square, all-ones inputs), stable and unstable sort of 1M, 10M and 100M random elements (Rust: uniform random u64 via par_sort/par_sort_unstable; C++: std::vector<int> via GNU parallel mode, source not committed), and sum/sum-of-squares reduction over 500M, 1B and 2B f64; best of three runs, threads 1 to 16.
claimed_speedup: Mixed; absolute times from data/Data.xlsx (best of three). Matmul 2048x2048, Rayon par_chunks row-dot vs OpenMP: Rust faster at 1, 2, 4, 6, 12 and 16 threads (12 threads 2168.8 vs 2864.5 ms, about 1.32x; 16 threads 2149.1 vs 2264.2 ms, about 1.05x, derived from page data) but slower at 8 threads (2501.7 vs 2277.6 ms) and serially (16277.1 vs 15509.5 ms); the report's 'Rayon performs better for all cases of threads for size 2048' is contradicted by its own 8-thread row, and its 'C++ is faster for all cases of threads for size 1024' by the 12-thread (272.4 vs 362.1 ms) and 16-thread (265.2 vs 285.7 ms) rows. These matmul comparisons are invalid (see caveats). Stable parallel sort, 100M elements: Rayon par_sort 1380 ms vs GNU parallel stable sort 1534.1 ms at 12 threads and 1226 vs 1476.2 ms at 16 threads (about 1.11x and 1.20x, derived from page data); C++ faster at 1 to 8 threads (8 threads 1690.0 vs 1834 ms) and serially (8467.6 vs 10908 ms). Unstable sort: Rust pdqsort/par_sort_unstable is faster in absolute time at every thread count (100M serial 3611 vs 7851.1 ms; 16 threads 684 vs 975.4 ms) although the report says C++ scales better; this is pdqsort vs introsort/multiway mergesort, an algorithm difference. Mandelbrot: C++ faster serially and Rust within about 1% multithreaded; quoted serial view 1 (4096x4096): Rust 19319.043 ms vs C++ 18813.754 ms, Rust 18758.684 ms after removing the num::Complex32 overhead. Reduction: Rust marginally faster serially (500M sum 456.5 vs 460.5 ms), OpenMP faster at every thread count.
compiler_and_flags: C++: g++ -m64 -O3 -Wall -fopenmp (C++/mandelbrot, matrixmultiply, quicksort, reduction Makefiles; no -march); the committed C++ quicksort binary's .comment reads 'GCC: (GNU) 4.8.5 20150623 (Red Hat 4.8.5-36)'. Rust: Cargo.toml files have no [profile] section; build command (release or not) and rustc version not stated; Rayon 1.0.3.
tradeoffs: Rayon work stealing adapts to uneven work but pays split and steal overhead; the report finds OpenMP static scheduling faster on reductions and Mandelbrot. Rust refuses to compile unsafe sharing between threads.
caveats: Student course project (CMU 15-618, 2019): results are graphs inside a PDF plus raw timings in data/Data.xlsx; no hardware stated (threads swept to 16); no license file. Harness defects found in the committed code: (1) the C++ matmul kernels matmul_serial2 and matmul_par_row compute c += A[iOff + k] * B[RM(k, i, size)], indexing B by the row i instead of the column j, so C++ computes a different (wrong) product whose B working set is a single cache-resident column per row, while the Rust kernel correctly walks B[index][col]; the bug is masked because A and B are all ones and the C++ result is never verified, so the matmul comparison is not same-work; (2) the C++ 'par_outer' timing block calls matmul_par_row again and never resets minThread, so the par_outer rows duplicate par_row; (3) the C++ sort source (C++/quicksort/main.cpp) is not committed, only a prebuilt ELF binary whose symbols show std::vector<int> (32-bit keys) sorted with __gnu_parallel multiway mergesort, while the Rust benchmark sorts Vec<u64> (64-bit keys), so element widths differ (against Rust); (4) the committed Rust sort code times stable_sort_par in its 'unstable parallel' loop (unstable_sort_par, typed &mut [u32], is never called) and prints fractional milliseconds, whereas Data.xlsx holds integer-millisecond Rust sort times that differ between stable and unstable, so the Rust sort numbers came from an earlier, uncommitted code version; correctness asserts are commented out; (5) Data.xlsx has copy errors (Rust Mandelbrot view 1 row-parallel row duplicates view 0). The Rayon matmul advantage the report explains (Rust not vectorizing the inner loop and hitting the compute limit later, par_chunks avoiding fork-join overhead) rests on the invalid kernel comparison. Sort compares different library algorithms (Rust stable merge sort and pdqsort vs GNU parallel multiway mergesort and introsort). Old toolchains: GCC 4.8.5 (2015) vs Rayon 1.0.3-era rustc (2019).
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/rayon and github.com/topics/openmp?l=rust (repo description 'Comparison of Multi-threading between C++ and Rust (OpenMP vs Rayon)'); opened repo README, project_docs/15618-Project-Final.pdf and commits.
why_faster: Report: Rayon work stealing balances load and its merge sort was tuned (three merge variants benchmarked); for 2048x2048 matmul the unvectorized Rust inner loop keeps scaling longer and par_chunks avoids fork-join overhead.

verification.tier_reason: First-party student report (graphs; the only quoted timings, Mandelbrot view 1 Rust 19319.043 ms vs C++ 18813.754 ms and 18758.684 ms after the Complex32 fix, match) with raw timings in data/Data.xlsx and C++ Makefiles at g++ -m64 -O3 -fopenmp, but no CPU model, no Rust build flags or rustc version, the C++ sort source is not committed, and the matmul baseline kernel computes a different product; C at best.
verification.notes: Keep at tier C but the claim was overstated: the matmul win is invalid because the C++ kernel indexes B by row i (wrong, cache-friendlier product, masked by all-ones inputs), the report's 2048 'every thread count' claim fails at 8 threads, the C++ sort source is missing (binary only, 32-bit ints vs Rust u64), and the committed Rust sort code is not the version that produced the numbers. The only surviving Rayon-over-OpenMP result is stable parallel sort at 12-16 threads (about 1.11-1.20x at 100M, derived). Usability reference (no license), abandoned (last commit 2019-11-01).

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: Mixed result, graphs only. Report: Rayon faster than OpenMP for 2048x2048 matrix multiply at every thread count and for stable (merge) sort at higher thread counts; C++ faster for 1024x1024 matmul, for unstable sort at large sizes, for Mandelbrot (Rust within 1% in the multithreaded case) and for reduction. Only quoted timings: serial Mandelbrot 4096x4096 view 1, Rust 19319.043 ms vs C++ 18813.754 ms before the fix and 18758.684 ms after removing the Complex32 overhead.
corrected_fields.compiler_and_flags: Not stated (report mentions GCC for the C++ side and Clang/LLVM for the Rust side; no optimization flags or versions; Rayon 1.0.3).
corrected_fields.caveats: Student course project: results are graphs inside a PDF, no hardware or compiler flags stated, no license file. The Rayon matmul win comes from Rust not vectorizing the inner loop (C++ vectorized it and hit a compute limit at 8 threads) and from par_chunks removing fork-join overhead, so it is not evidence that Rayon is the better scheduler. The sort comparison pits Rust's merge sort and pdqsort-based sort against GNU parallel sort, so the algorithms differ. Rayon 1.0.3 era (2018-2019).
corrected_fields.workload: Four shared-memory benchmarks written in Rust+Rayon and C++/OpenMP: Mandelbrot (2048 to 8192 square images), matrix multiplication (1024 and 2048 square), stable and unstable sort of 1M, 10M and 100M random elements (Rayon par_sort vs GNU parallel sort), and sum/sum-of-squares reduction over 500M, 1B and 2B f64; best of three runs, thread counts swept.

name: Redcon (Go Redis-compatible server framework; clone vs real Redis)
baseline: Redis (C, single-threaded, started as 'redis-server --port 6379 --appendonly no'; version not stated)
workload: redis-benchmark -t set,get -n 10000000 -q -P 512 -c 512 against real Redis ('redis-server --port 6379 --appendonly no') and against example/clone.go (Go map with an RWMutex; PING, QUIT, SET, GET, SETNX, DEL, PUBLISH, SUBSCRIBE/PSUBSCRIBE, DETACH and a blank CONFIG stub that exists only so redis-benchmark runs), Redcon run with GOMAXPROCS=1 and GOMAXPROCS=0. No -r flag is passed, so redis-benchmark uses one fixed key for every SET and GET with its default 3-byte value.
claimed_speedup: Requests per second, README table: SET 2,018,570.88 (Redcon, one thread) vs 941,265.12 (Redis) = about 2.14x (derived from page data); GET 2,403,846.25 vs 1,189,909.50 = about 2.02x (derived from page data). Multi-threaded Redcon: SET 1,944,390.38 (about 2.07x, derived) and GET 3,993,610.25 (about 3.36x, derived).
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.7 via 'go run' (default flags); Redis version and build flags not stated (Redis's own Makefile defaulted to -O2, checked for 4.0.2).
hardware: MacBook Pro 15-inch, 2.8 GHz Intel Core i7 (README), client and server on one laptop
tradeoffs: Go library, so a C++ project would run it as a separate server or sidecar. The clone in the benchmark has none of Redis's persistence, expiry, data structures or replication. Each connection is served by Go's net package with goroutines.
caveats: First-party README numbers from the Go 1.7 era (2016) with no Redis version, no compiler, no run count and no variance. The Redis command disables the append-only file but not RDB snapshots; because redis-benchmark ran without -r, the dataset is a single key, so any snapshot fork during the 10M-command SET run would be cheap and this is a minor concern. The Go clone implements a handful of commands over a bare map behind an RWMutex, while Redis runs its full command dispatch, so the two servers do different work per command and the gap is mostly per-command overhead, not language (verifier inference). Client, server and OS share one laptop; 512 connections and pipeline depth 512 favour batch throughput over latency. Multi-threaded Redcon SET (1,944,390.38) is slower than single-threaded (2,018,570.88), consistent with every SET taking the global mutex. No latency numbers. The README names no mechanism. The redcon parser has changed since the measurement (it copies each command's raw bytes, and a 2026-07-22 commit reworked number parsing), so the numbers predate the current code. Redis-vs-Go comparison, not a runtime-level language claim. evio's Redis example reuses redcon's parser.
found_via: GitHub: grepped raw READMEs of Go server frameworks (tidwall/redcon, evio, gnet, nbio) for Redis/libuv/C++ comparisons; opened github.com/tidwall/redcon, its README benchmark section, example/clone.go and the commits page.

name: Rust std futex-based Mutex (rust-lang/rust PR 95035) vs the pthread_mutex-based std Mutex
baseline: glibc (and musl) pthread_mutex_t, as wrapped by the previous Rust std::sync::Mutex on Linux
workload: matklad/lock-bench: 32 threads, 10,000 lock/unlock operations per thread over 2 (extreme), 64 (heavy), 1,000 (light) or 1,000,000 (no contention) locks, 100 rounds, average time per round.
claimed_speedup: PR comment by m-ou-se on a 64C/128T AMD Threadripper (average per round): extreme contention new 27.65 ms vs old std (gnu pthread) 58.51 ms and old std (musl) 89.15 ms; heavy contention 1.82 ms vs 8.11 ms (gnu) and 7.08 ms (musl); light contention 0.784 ms vs 2.80 ms (gnu) and 2.90 ms (musl); no contention 1.19 ms vs 2.98 ms (gnu) and 2.79 ms (musl). About 2.1x, 4.4x, 3.6x and 2.5x faster than the glibc pthread-based version (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the PR comment; lock-bench is run with cargo run --release (rustc of March 2022, flags otherwise unstated); the glibc and musl pthread builds are distribution builds
hardware: 64-core / 128-thread AMD Threadripper (exact model not stated)
stars_or_usage: 119.7k stars, 18.3k forks (rust-lang/rust); part of the Rust standard library: PR 95035 merged by bors on 2022-04-05, milestone 1.62.0, listed in the 1.62.0 release notes
tradeoffs: A futex-based lock is Linux-specific (the PR targets Linux; other platforms keep their own implementations); one word of state with no heap allocation and a const constructor, but no priority inheritance or robust-mutex support that pthread mutex attributes offer.
caveats: The baseline is the earlier Rust std::sync::Mutex (library/std/src/sys/unix/mutex.rs in 1.60.0): a Box<Mutex> around a pthread_mutex_t initialised as PTHREAD_MUTEX_NORMAL and called through non-inlined libc calls, so part of the gap is the heap indirection rather than glibc's lock algorithm; a C program would normally embed pthread_mutex_t inline, and no standalone C program was benchmarked. glibc's normal mutex is itself a three-state futex lock without spinning, so the new lock's main algorithmic difference is a 100-iteration spin before futex_wait (background knowledge for glibc, not checked in this pass). The run used 32 threads on a 128-thread machine (no oversubscription), which favours spinning: in the same table even spin::Mutex (42.4 ms extreme, 2.13 ms heavy) and AmdSpinlock beat the old glibc-based std Mutex, and parking_lot::Mutex and spin::Mutex were faster than the new std Mutex under light and no contention (parking_lot 0.695 ms and 0.940 ms, spin 0.605 ms and 0.765 ms), while lock-bench's own README on a 4-core i7-7820HQ found spinlocks much worse than a good mutex. Under extreme contention parking_lot (313 ms) was about 11x slower than the new lock. In the 1,000,000-lock no-contention case the old version holds one separately heap-allocated pthread_mutex_t per lock, so its 2.5x gap is mostly memory footprint. Single author-posted run on one machine; the comment itself says 'Realistic benchmarks are very hard'; glibc and musl versions are not stated. rust-timer found no relevant compiler-performance change. lock-bench carries no licence file. Only the Mutex has numbers on the PR page; this PR also replaced Condvar, and the matching RwLock PR (95801) gives none.
found_via: GitHub: pthread-versus-Rust lock idea; opened github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/95035 (title 'Replace Linux Mutex and Condvar with futex based ones.', merged April 2022) and github.com/matklad/lock-bench.
why_faster: PR design: the lock is a single 32-bit futex word (0 unlocked, 1 locked, 2 contended) with a short spin before parking in the kernel and no heap-allocated pthread_mutex_t, so uncontended lock and unlock are one atomic operation each.

verification.tier_reason: The numbers are an author-posted lock-bench run in the PR conversation (m-ou-se, a Rust libs maintainer, so first-party) on an unnamed '64C/128T AMD Threadripper' with no rustc version or flags; lock-bench (matklad/lock-bench) is public and runs with cargo run --release, but the CPU model and compiler are not given, so it is not A, and nothing independent or peer-reviewed backs it.
verification.notes: All new-vs-old averages in claimed_speedup match the PR comment tables (27.645506 vs 58.506588/89.146548 ms; 1.822707 vs 8.10534/7.08335 ms; 784.189 us vs 2.802436/2.900143 ms; 1.189231 vs 2.97886/2.794938 ms) and the derived ratios 2.1x, 4.4x, 3.6x, 2.5x check out. Record shortcomings: baseline is glibc pthread_mutex boxed behind Rust std, not a C program; win is lock design (spin, inline futex word), not language; parking_lot and spin beat the new lock under light and no contention; one run, CPU model and compiler unstated.

corrected_fields.stars_or_usage: 119.7k stars (rust-lang/rust); part of the Rust standard library (merged April 2022; the companion RwLock PR 95801 is milestoned 1.62.0)
corrected_fields.caveats: The baseline is the earlier Rust std::sync::Mutex, which called pthread_mutex_t through a heap-allocated box, so part of the gap is Rust-side indirection and the Box allocation rather than glibc's lock algorithm alone; no standalone C program was benchmarked. Single author-posted run on one machine; the comment itself says 'realistic benchmarks are very hard'. In the same table parking_lot::Mutex and spin::Mutex were faster than the new std Mutex under light and no contention (parking_lot 0.695 ms and 0.940 ms, spin 0.605 ms and 0.765 ms), and under extreme contention parking_lot (313 ms) was about 11x slower than the new lock. name: ScyllaDB Rust driver (async Tokio CQL driver vs C++ driver)
baseline: DataStax Cassandra C++ driver ('cpp-multi', v2.16.0 .deb per the current Dockerfile, run with I/O threads = hardware_concurrency), plus the Scylla C++ driver fork ('cpp'), which the harness ran with a single I/O thread until commit 'Bump Scylla cpp driver to 2.16.2, remove single thread limitation for it' (2022-08-01)
workload: 'Basic' benchmark, inserts workload: 10,000,000 prepared INSERTs (pk, 2*pk, 3*pk) into one local ScyllaDB node started by scylla.sh, with 512, 1024, 2048, 4096 and 8192 requests in flight; total wall time per driver, one run per cell. The harness default (and config.py title) is 1,000,000 tasks at concurrency 1024.
claimed_speedup: Published chart images/bench10to7-inserts.svg (10,000,000 inserts, time in seconds; values read from the SVG bar geometry, derived from page data): concurrency 512/1024/2048/4096/8192: scylla-rust-driver 12.8/9.3/7.4/6.6/6.5 s; cpp-multi (DataStax C++ driver, multi-threaded) 13.4/9.9/7.7/6.7/6.3 s, so Rust is about 1.05x/1.07x/1.05x/1.02x faster and 0.97x (slower) at 8192, i.e. parity; cpp (Scylla C++ driver on one I/O thread) 54.9/53.0/56.5/53.8/64.1 s, about 4.3x-9.9x slower than Rust, but that baseline was single-threaded. The cited generate_chart/config.py (1,000,000 inserts, concurrency 1024: scylla-rust-driver 3734 ms vs cpp-driver 5510 ms, about 1.48x, derived from page data) is the chart generator's input file, matches the harness defaults, and does not correspond to any published chart. A ScyllaDB blog post (2021-07-13) reportedly says the Rust driver was 'generally either just as fast or even slightly faster' than cpp-multi (snippet only).
compiler_and_flags: Benchmark harnesses: C++ main.cpp built with Ubuntu 18.04 g++ (7.x) as 'g++ main.cpp -std=c++17 -lcassandra -O3 -flto' against prebuilt driver .deb packages (DataStax 2.16.0; Scylla cpp-driver 2.16.2 at HEAD, earlier version at chart time; library build flags not stated); Rust built with 'cargo build --release', [profile.release] lto = true, latest rustup toolchain at image build time, scylla crate from the git main branch, tokio 1.x multi-threaded runtime (#[tokio::main]).
stars_or_usage: 689 stars (scylla-rust-driver); benchmark repo cvybhu/rust-driver-benchmarks has 84 commits, last 2022-08-05
tradeoffs: Rust crate; C++ programs get it through the scylla-cpp-rust-driver bindings (ScyllaDB's C++ API over the Rust core), which the benchmark repo lists as a separate driver. Async Tokio runtime inside the driver.
caveats: Vendor benchmark (ScyllaDB). Against the fair multi-threaded C++ baseline (DataStax cpp-driver, 'cpp-multi') the published 2021-06-20 chart shows parity: Rust 2-7% faster at concurrency 512-4096 and about 3% slower at 8192. The large lead (4.3x-9.9x) is only over the Scylla C++ driver fork run on a single I/O thread, a limitation the harness removed on 2022-08-01 with no re-published chart, so that comparison is a crippled baseline. The cited config.py numbers (3734 vs 5510 ms) are the generator's input with the harness's default title and cannot be tied to a published run. The README itself says the chart 'is pretty old' and driver names changed. No hardware, no run count, no variance; values were read from SVG bar geometry, so they are approximate. The C++ driver libraries are prebuilt .deb packages whose build flags are not stated. A ScyllaDB 2021 blog post (scylladb.com, not reachable here) reportedly ran a 3-node Scylla 4.4 cluster on i3.4xlarge and found the Rust driver 'just as fast or even slightly faster' than cpp-multi; a later ScyllaDB write-up reportedly found it used about twice the CPU of the cassandra-cpp backend in a loopback test (snippets only). The scylla-rust-driver README makes no speed claim. The driver is Apache-2.0 OR MIT; the benchmark repo has no LICENSE file. A database driver rather than a general concurrency runtime, so the category fit is loose. [retier] Shard asymmetry: scylla.sh runs --smp 4, the Rust driver is shard-aware and the DataStax cpp-multi driver is not, yet the result is only parity. The benchmark is not rebuildable: Cargo.toml pins git main with no Cargo.lock, and main.rs uses removed APIs (scylla::prepared_statement, IntoTypedRows, execute). Chart provenance is unclear (local node versus the blog's 3-node i3.4xlarge cluster).
found_via: WebSearch: 'scylla-rust-driver faster than C++ driver benchmark throughput Rust driver vs cpp-driver'; opened github.com/cvybhu/rust-driver-benchmarks (README, generate_chart/config.py, commits), github.com/scylladb/scylla-rust-driver and its commits page.

verification.tier_reason: Vendor (ScyllaDB) benchmark repo cvybhu/rust-driver-benchmarks: the cited config.py does hold 3734 vs 5510 ms, but it is the chart generator's input with the harness's default title and no provenance; the published chart (images/bench10to7-inserts.svg, matplotlib, 2021-06-20) shows the Rust driver at parity with the multi-threaded DataStax C++ driver, and its large lead only over the Scylla C++ driver that the harness then limited to one I/O thread. Harness code and flags are public (g++ -O3 -flto; cargo --release with lto) but the drivers are prebuilt .deb packages and no hardware is stated, so not A; first-party vendor numbers, so C.
verification.notes: Downgrade of the claim, tier stays C: the fair C++ baseline in the published chart is at parity (flag as not faster), and the 1.48x figure is unprovenanced generator input while the big lead is over a single-threaded C++ driver (crippled baseline, since fixed in the harness). Usability corrected to copyable (driver is Apache-2.0 OR MIT).
