name: Stylo (Rust parallel CSS style engine in Firefox Quantum) vs Gecko's previous C++ style system
baseline: Gecko's previous sequential C++ style system (CSS selector matching and cascade) in Firefox before Quantum
workload: Firefox page load of Amazon's homepage, where style computation runs as a parallel work-stealing top-down cascade (rayon) instead of the old single-threaded C++ cascade.
claimed_speedup: 30% page load speedup for Amazon's homepage ('Parallelism leads to a lot of performance improvements, including a 30% page load speedup for Amazon's homepage'). Stylo replaces about 160,000 lines of C++ with 85,000 lines of Rust.
stars_or_usage: 340 stars (servo/stylo); ships in Firefox since Quantum (version 57) and in Servo
tradeoffs: Not a standalone library: it is wired into Gecko or Servo through Rust-to-C++ FFI and a DOM abstraction, and it needs those hosts to call back into C++ for some data. The blog says occasional calls into C++ code off the main thread surfaced thread-safety bugs in the C++ side (caches, global mutable state). Parallelism helps large pages and many cores; tiny documents gain little.
caveats: First-party blog (Rust blog post by a Servo/Mozilla engineer, 2017-11-14) with a single headline number: no workload details beyond 'Amazon's homepage', no hardware, core count, Firefox build flags, run count or comparison builds, and no benchmark code. The comparison is Firefox with Stylo against Firefox with the old C++ style system, so it mixes the rewrite's other optimizations with the parallelism; a Mozilla Hacks post (hacks.mozilla.org was blocked here, so seen only as a WebSearch snippet) says the engine borrows optimizations from other browsers and would be fast without parallelism, and gives a best-case 'up to 2, 4 or even 18 times faster' style-computation range that scales with core count (snippet only, not verified). Baseline is a production C++ build, probably with PGO and LTO, but this is not stated. The repo servo/stylo is Servo's downstream copy of the code that lives in mozilla-central (the Firefox repo, already on the known list); it carries no benchmark. The blog's 'two earlier C++ attempts to parallelize the style system failed' is a claim about engineering difficulty, not a measurement. [retier] global_style_data.rs caps the pool at 6 threads (STYLO_MAX_THREADS, bug 1431285), so the Hacks 'up to 18x' cannot come from threads alone. The old C++ style system shipped only up to Firefox 56, so the comparison cannot be rerun.
found_via: WebSearch 'Stylo Quantum CSS Rust parallel style system faster than Gecko C++ style system speedup cores hacks.mozilla.org' surfaced the Rust blog and Hacks posts; the Rust blog source was opened on raw.githubusercontent.com (rust-lang/blog.rust-lang.org) and servo/stylo on github.com.
why_faster: Rust's ownership and Send/Sync checking made it practical to run the top-down style cascade in parallel with a rayon work-stealing traversal (child styles are independent once the parent is computed), where two earlier C++ attempts failed on thread-safety bugs. Stylo also shares computed style structs through Arc. The Hacks post additionally credits optimizations borrowed from other browsers (snippet only).

verification.tier_reason: The Rust blog post (Manish Goregaokar, a Servo/Stylo developer, 2017-11-14) states 'a 30% page load speedup for Amazon's homepage' and '160,000 lines of C++ with 85,000 lines of Rust' verbatim, with no hardware, build, run count or benchmark code: first-party numbers without methodology, tier C.

name: Tokio (1M concurrent tasks, peak memory)
baseline: Asio C++20 coroutines (awaitable tasks) and concurrencpp
workload: Spawn N concurrent async tasks that wait on a timer and measure peak memory (port of the Rust '1 million concurrent tasks' memory benchmark to C++ coroutine libraries).
claimed_speedup: Peak memory at 1M tasks: tokio 214,136 KB, concurrencpp 605,972 KB, Asio 853,144 KB (about 2.8x and 4.0x less, derived from page data); at 100k tasks: 23,824 vs 61,460 vs 86,652 KB; at 10k: 6,908 vs 7,840 vs 10,244 KB. At 1 task tokio is the largest (3,092 KB vs Asio 1,668 KB). Libunifex hangs at 100k and 1M.
compiler_and_flags: C++20, CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE Release set in CMakeLists.txt (-O3 -DNDEBUG with GCC or Clang), compiler not named; Asio and concurrencpp fetched by FetchContent with no GIT_TAG (default-branch HEAD at build time, June 2023), libunifex GIT_TAG main; tokio_bench built by 'cargo build --release' from CMakeLists.txt (opt-level 3), tokio 1.28.2 per Cargo.lock, #[tokio::main] multi-thread runtime.
hardware: Intel i7-8550U (8 threads, about 1.99 GHz), 8 GB RAM, WSL Ubuntu 20.04.6 on Windows 10
tradeoffs: Tokio tasks are stackless futures sized by the compiler, so memory is small per task but not free of heap allocation per spawn; the C++ libraries allocate a coroutine frame per task. The result is about memory only, not throughput or latency.
caveats: Independent hobby replication (4 stars, 6 commits all on 2023-06-24) of the pkolaczk 'How Much Memory Do You Need to Run 1 Million Concurrent Tasks?' benchmark, not the tokio authors' work; the README notes the original methodology was criticised. Memory only (peak RSS from /usr/bin/time), no timing; run count not stated; WSL Ubuntu 20.04 on a laptop i7-8550U with 8 GB. C++ compiler unnamed and Asio/concurrencpp versions unpinned. Workloads match logically (N tasks each awaiting a 10 s timer, all alive at once), but the C++ programs differ in structure: Asio builds a vector of N lazily-started awaitables and then co_spawns each on one io_context thread; concurrencpp copies two shared_ptrs into every coroutine frame and uses one worker_thread_executor plus its timer_queue; tokio spawns each task on the default multi-thread runtime and keeps the JoinHandles. Tokio is the largest at 1 task (3,092 KB vs Asio 1,668 KB) and only pulls ahead from 10k tasks. Libunifex hangs at 100k and 1M. The tokio repo itself makes no comparison to C++ runtimes.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Rust async/await versus C++20 coroutines performance evaluation paper benchmark throughput' surfaced Xavorim/cpp_tasks_bench.

verification.tier_reason: Xavorim/cpp_tasks_bench README lists the exact peak-RSS figures (/usr/bin/time) for tokio, concurrencpp, Asio and libunifex at 1, 10k, 100k and 1M tasks on an i7-8550U under WSL; code is public (asio_bench/main.cpp, concurrencpp_bench/main.cpp, tokio_bench/src/main.rs) and CMakeLists.txt fixes Release and cargo --release, but the C++ compiler is not named and the C++ libraries are unpinned, so not A; a 4-star one-person repo is not a well-known independent suite, so C.

Shortcomings to record: one-person 2023 hobby benchmark, compiler unnamed, unpinned C++ library versions, memory-only single-run figures on WSL, tokio larger at 1 task, library-level not language-level claim.

name: Tokio TCP echo server (Boost.Redis echo benchmark, vs libuv)
baseline: libuv TCP echo server (C, epoll event loop, libuv docs tcp-echo-server example); the table also holds a Boost.Asio C++20 coroutine echo server that is slightly faster than Tokio
workload: TCP echo server serving 1000 concurrent client connections on localhost (the Boost.Redis echo_server_client driver, benchmarks.tex comment 'time ./echo_server_client 1000 5000'); metric is the total wall-clock seconds the client run took against each server, one server per language/library, each written from that library's own docs example.
claimed_speedup: Tokio 30.7 s vs libuv 43.6 s wall time for 1000 connections x 5000 echoes (about 1.42x less wall time, derived from page data); Boost.Asio (C++) 29.5 s is about 4% faster than Tokio (derived from page data). Each value is a single run; the Tokio value was recorded on 2022-07-16 after switching to a newer Tokio and the current_thread runtime (it was 42.2-43.2 s before), the libuv value by 2022-07-15. Go 35.6 s and Node.js 74.2 s are in the same table.
compiler_and_flags: Tokio server: #[tokio::main(flavor = "current_thread")], tokio = { version = "1.0", features = ["full"] } (benchmarks/rust/echo_server_direct/Cargo.toml has no [profile] section); cargo build profile and rustc version not stated. libuv server: 'gcc echo_server_direct.c -luv -O2 -o echo_server_direct' (benchmarks/c/libuv/README.md), linked against an unstated system libuv build. Asio server/client: CMake target with C++20 (benchmarks/CMakeLists.txt), compiler and optimisation level not stated.
stars_or_usage: 33.4k stars (tokio); suite repo boostorg/redis has 282 stars
tradeoffs: Rust async needs the Tokio runtime and a Rust toolchain; the benchmark deliberately uses the single-threaded Tokio runtime to match the single-threaded libuv loop. Calling it from C++ needs FFI or a separate process.
caveats: Numbers are the pgfplots source (benchmarks.tex) of the chart on the Boost.Redis doc page 'Echo server benchmark' (doc/modules/ROOT/pages/benchmarks.adoc); the rendered PNG on boostorg.github.io was not viewed. The chart is a composite of single `time` runs recorded on different dates by the Boost.Redis (C++) author on 'my machine' (localhost latency 0.07 ms; no CPU model, OS, Go/Rust/compiler versions, no repetitions or variance): libuv 43.568 s was recorded by 2022-07-15 (commit 3fb018c) and never re-run; Tokio moved from 42.2 s/43.2 s to 30.7 s on 2022-07-16 after switching to a newer Tokio and the current_thread runtime; Go moved from 81.0 s to 35.6 s on 2022-08-25 (commit f11622e) after its server was rewritten from bufio ReadBytes line echo to a raw 1024-byte read loop with GOMAXPROCS(1); Asio was re-measured at 29.5 s on 2022-10-07. Unequal work: the libuv server is the unmodified libuv docs tcp-echo-server example, which mallocs a 64 KiB read buffer (libuv passes 64*1024 as suggested_size, src/unix/stream.c) on every read callback and a write_req_t per echo and frees both after each write, while the Go, Tokio and Asio servers reuse one 1 KiB buffer per connection; the Go server was revised between runs, the libuv one never was. The libuv server is built per benchmarks/c/libuv/README.md with 'gcc echo_server_direct.c -luv -O2' (not -O3; system libuv build flags unknown). The load generator is the single-threaded Boost.Asio echo_server_client (1000 sessions x 5000 13-byte ping-pong messages) on the same host, which may set a floor near the Asio/Tokio results. All servers are single-threaded (Asio io_context with BOOST_ASIO_CONCURRENCY_HINT_UNSAFE_IO, Tokio current_thread, Go GOMAXPROCS(1), one libuv loop). The C++ Boost.Asio coroutine server in the same table is the fastest entry (29.5 s), so this is not a win over the best C++ result. The author gives no explanation for the gap beyond 'I expected Libuv to have similar performance to Asio and Tokio'. Measured in 2022 on a Tokio 1.x release of that time; the Tokio server binds 127.0.0.1 while the others bind 0.0.0.0 (no timing effect expected).
found_via: WebSearch: 'tokio vs boost asio benchmark echo server rust faster than C++ github' surfaced the Boost.Redis benchmark page; opened github.com/boostorg/redis benchmarks directory, benchmarks.tex, doc/modules/ROOT/pages/benchmarks.adoc and the rust/libuv/go/asio sources via raw.githubusercontent.com.

verification.tier_reason: Numbers are real (benchmarks.tex: Tokio 30.7 s, Libuv 43.6 s, Asio 29.5 s) and server code is public (benchmarks/rust/echo_server_direct/src/main.rs, benchmarks/c/libuv/echo_server_direct.c, benchmarks/cpp/asio/echo_server_client.cpp), but there is no CPU model, rustc version or cargo profile, each bar is one run from a different date (Tokio 2022-07-16 after a runtime switch, libuv by 2022-07-15), and the libuv side mallocs a 64 KiB read buffer and a write request per message at -O2 while Tokio reuses one 1 KiB buffer: crippled-baseline and cross-run precedents put the Tokio-over-libuv claim at D.

Shortcomings for decisions.json: composite single-run chart across July-October 2022, no hardware, versions or cargo profile, unequal buffer management, -O2 C build, single-threaded client may cap results.

name: Embassy (async Rust executor) vs FreeRTOS
baseline: FreeRTOS (C RTOS, used through the CMSIS-RTOS v2 wrapper in an STM32CubeIDE project) on an STM32F446ZE
workload: Same toy firmware on a NUCLEO-F446ZE at 180 MHz in Embassy, RTIC and FreeRTOS (CMSIS-RTOS v2 over ST HAL): one task blinks an LED every 100 ms, a button task waits on the EXTI13 user-button interrupt and toggles GPIO PG1 (interrupt-to-task latency read on an oscilloscope), formats a 32-byte message and queues it to a UART writer task. Per search-result summaries (blog unreachable), the post compares interrupt latency, program size, static RAM and ease of programming.
claimed_speedup: README quote: 'It obsoletes the need for a traditional RTOS with kernel context switching, and is faster and smaller than one!' No figures appear on any page that was opened; the blog post that carries them (tweedegolf.nl, async-rust-vs-rtos-showdown) could not be reached from this environment.
compiler_and_flags: Rust (rust/Cargo.toml): nightly toolchain (feature type_alias_impl_trait), [profile.release] opt-level = 3, lto = true, codegen-units = 1, incremental = false, debug = true (debug info only), embassy and embassy-stm32 from git master of early 2022. C (c/.cproject, STM32CubeIDE 1.8.0, MCU ARM GCC arm-none-eabi-): Release configuration C optimization -O3 with -g0 and no LTO (C++ option -Os, unused by this C project); the Debug configuration leaves the optimization level at the IDE default. The repo does not say which C configuration was measured, and no compiler versions are stated for either side.
hardware: STM32F446ZE (Arm Cortex-M4F) on NUCLEO-F446ZE
stars_or_usage: embassy-rs/embassy: 9.9k stars, 1.7k forks; tweedegolf/async-rtos-showdown: 18 stars, 2 forks, 3 commits (2022-01-04 to 2022-02-17)
tradeoffs: Cooperative async tasks, not preemptive threads: a task that does not yield blocks the others, and priorities work through multiple executors/interrupts. Needs Rust nightly features in the 2022 snapshot; no C++ API.
caveats: Tier D because no number could be read from any opened page; the blog post with the figures (tweedegolf.nl/en/blog/65/async-rust-vs-rtos-showdown) was unreachable (DNS ENOTFOUND), as were the zeli.app and hn.svelte.dev mirrors. Secondary search summaries (snippet only) say Embassy used less RAM and flash but FreeRTOS had better interrupt latency, so 'faster' is not established; Reddit r/embedded and Hacker News commenters said worst-case latency was not measured, only the standard deviation, and flagged the C app's static RAM figure. The verifier read the C side and found it does not do the same work as the Rust side: (1) the UART writer uses blocking polled HAL_UART_Transmit, while Embassy writes over DMA asynchronously; (2) the C message formatting uses newlib snprintf (configUSE_NEWLIB_REENTRANT 1), while Rust uses core::fmt into an ArrayString; (3) the C button task's 'only react to falling edges' block sets the same RTSR/FTSR bits as the rising-edge block (EXTI->RTSR |= pin; EXTI->FTSR &= ~pin), so the C firmware waits on two rising edges and never on a falling edge; (4) the EXTI path goes through the ST HAL callback and the CMSIS-RTOS v2 wrapper (osThreadFlagsSet) instead of native FreeRTOS calls. FreeRTOSConfig.h is the untuned CubeMX default: a static 15360-byte heap (configTOTAL_HEAP_SIZE), three 512-byte task stacks, trace facility, software timers, recursive mutexes and generic task selection (configUSE_PORT_OPTIMISED_TASK_SELECTION 0) all on, which inflates the C side's static RAM and flash. Build settings are not equivalent: the Rust side uses LTO and codegen-units = 1 at opt-level 3, the C Release build -O3 without LTO (larger code than -Os), and the repo does not say whether the Debug or Release C build was measured. The showdown repo is a Feb 2022 snapshot built on Embassy master of that date, so the result predates four years of Embassy and FreeRTOS changes. A cooperative executor versus a preemptive RTOS is not a like-for-like scheduling comparison. The only claim in the embassy repo itself is a README sentence linking the blog. [retier] Harness flaw in the only benchmark: the Rust firmware forgets the PG0 ISR-marker pin 'to use inside embassy', but rust/Cargo.lock pins unmodified upstream embassy 59f909e whose EXTI on_irq() never touches PG0 (the C and RTIC firmware do toggle it), so Embassy's latency instrumentation came from an unpublished local patch and that row cannot be reproduced. The C side waits on two rising edges, uses polled UART against DMA and has no LTO.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Embassy async rust vs FreeRTOS benchmark latency context switch'; opened github.com/embassy-rs/embassy README, github.com/tweedegolf/async-rtos-showdown (README, rust/Cargo.toml, c/.cproject, commits).
why_faster: README: async tasks compile into cooperatively scheduled state machines that share one stack, need no per-task stack sizing and no dynamic allocation, so no kernel context switch is paid.

verification.tier_reason: The benchmark repo (tweedegolf/async-rtos-showdown) holds the Embassy (rust/), RTIC (rtic/) and FreeRTOS (c/) firmware, but neither it nor the Embassy README carries a single number; the figures exist only in the tweedegolf.nl blog post, which is unreachable here (DNS ENOTFOUND), and two WebSearch passes returned no figures even in snippets, so the entry stays at D.
verification.notes: Confirm at D: Embassy is notable (9.9k stars) and the comparison code is public, but no numbers were reachable and secondary summaries say FreeRTOS won interrupt latency. Shortcomings to record: no numbers reachable (blog blocked); C baseline is untuned CubeMX FreeRTOS behind the CMSIS-RTOS v2 wrapper and ST HAL with a 15 KB static heap, blocking polled UART vs Embassy DMA, newlib snprintf vs core::fmt, a falling-edge EXTI configuration bug, and no LTO on the C side against LTO plus codegen-units = 1 on the Rust side; worst-case latency not measured; 2022 snapshot. If the blog is ever reached, the tier could rise only to C or B, not A, because the C and Rust firmware do different work and the measured C configuration and compiler versions are unstated.

name: CBQN (BQN array language) - CRLF-to-LF conversion versus plain C
language: BQN (implementation in C, SIMD kernels generated with Singeli)
baseline: Plain scalar C loop for the same line-ending conversion (crlf_to_lf), compiled with clang 15.0.7 -O3 -march=native
workload: Replace every CRLF with LF in a byte buffer of 100 to 1,000,000 bytes with a CRLF about every 100 characters; BQN one-liner (cr!=) with (0 shifted lf!=) filtered by Replicate versus a scalar C loop; the page also reports selection and compiler benchmarks.
claimed_speedup: Page text: BQN breaks even with C at a little under 200 bytes and hits 5x C's speed on inputs of a few thousand bytes or more with AVX-512 disabled, over 10x with AVX-512 until cache becomes a bottleneck. Page timings on a Tiger Lake i5-1135G7 (a CRLF every ~100 bytes): C (clang 15.0.7 -O3 -march=native) 0.555 ns/elt from 10k to 1M bytes (0.613 at 100 bytes); CBQN avx2/bmi2/pclmul build 0.893 (100 bytes, slower than C), 0.127 (3k), 0.106 (10k), 0.094 (30k), 0.107 (1M) ns/elt, about 4.4x at 3k and 5.2-5.9x from 10k up (derived from page data); CBQN native build (AVX-512) 0.0526 (10k), 0.0506 (30k), 0.0537 (100k), 0.0787 (1M) ns/elt, about 10.3-11.0x from 10k to 300k and 7.1x at 1M (derived from page data). The page's selection figures (0.04 ns per selection from a table of 32 or fewer 1-byte values via shuffles versus 0.2 ns via gather) are two CBQN code paths, not a C measurement. The compiler benchmark (implementation/bootbench.md) is a separate claim: boot3.bqn in CBQN compiles boot2.bqn in 270.6 us versus 415.5 us for dzaima's comp.c built with clang 15.0 (system values and error handling removed), average of 10,000 runs on a Skylake i5-6200U, i.e. 35% less time (about 1.54x, derived from page data); the two compilers use different algorithms and the C build flags are not stated.
compiler_and_flags: C baseline: clang 15.0.7, 'clang -O3 -march=native lineending.c' (gcc 12.2.1 also discussed: branching code, slightly faster at low density, much slower at high). CBQN built at commit 0d2631a2 with FFI, singeli x86-64 avx2 bmi2 pclmul (and a native build)
hardware: Intel Tiger Lake Core i5-1135G7
why_faster: Array primitives are implemented with hand-written SIMD, lookup tables and blocked multi-pass techniques (Replicate compresses with AVX2/AVX-512 mask operations, adapts to sparse inputs), which compilers do not generate from a scalar branching loop (no SIMD scan, movmask or compress idioms from portable C). The page itself says this is a best case: 'Your BQN programs are unlikely to outperform equivalent C programs' and specialized C is always faster.
tradeoffs: Whole-array style only: per-primitive call overhead, benefits grow with array length (hundreds to thousands of elements) and small element types; poor for sequential, data-dependent loops, cryptography with wrapping integer ops, and C++-style object dispatch. Interpreter, so C interop is through an FFI with copying. Licensing is a per-file mix with timsort (MIT) and Ryu (Apache-2.0/Boost) exceptions.
caveats: First-party measurement by the BQN author on one machine; both programs, the C compile line and the CBQN commit and build options are on the page, so it is reproducible (CBQN builds at -O3 with the system cc by default; the compiler used for CBQN is not named). The C baseline is the plain portable scalar loop the author took from his 2017 Dyalog talk; clang 15 makes it branchless and unrolls it 4x, so it is not crippled, but no SIMD-intrinsic or memchr/memcpy-chunk C version was tested and the page says specialized C is always faster. The win is CBQN's hand-written Singeli SIMD Replicate primitive (an adaptive sparse/dense compress) against compiler output for a scalar loop: a best case for BQN primitives, as the page itself says ('combinations of primitives never do so well'); density 1/100 is described as not particularly favourable. Not the same algorithm in the strict sense (data-parallel mask plus Replicate versus a sequential scan), but output is identical. The selection figures (0.04 versus 0.2 ns) compare two CBQN paths, not C. The compiler benchmark side claim (35% faster) ran on different hardware (i5-6200U), compares different compiler designs and states no C flags. The page dates from 2023 (clang 15.0.7, gcc 12.2.1; 'the C compilers of today (2023)') and CBQN has changed since. Licence: most files LGPL-3.0-only OR GPL-3.0-only OR MPL-2.0 at the user's choice; timsort files MIT and Ryu Apache-2.0 or BSL-1.0. [retier] The README says CBQN does not use AVX-512, yet slash.singeli has AVX-512 VBMI2 compress paths enabled only in native builds (make o3n); the >10x row depends on them, and default or has= builds (which accept only up to avx2) are likely below 5x (not measured). The BQN one-liner drops a trailing lone CR, but no tested prefix ends in CR, so outputs match.

name: DiffEqGPU.jl (GPU ensemble ODE solvers in Julia, GPUTsit5) vs MPGOS
baseline: MPGOS (Massively Parallel GPU ODE Solvers), a CUDA C++ ensemble ODE solver library: RK4 (fixed step) and RKCK45 (adaptive), built with nvcc -O3
workload: Lorenz system (3 states, float32), ensemble of 8 to 8,388,608 parameter sets (R from 0 to 21) integrated over t in [0,1] with dt 0.001 on one GPU; fixed-step and adaptive (Julia reltol=abstol=1e-8) variants; wall time per whole ensemble solve in ms.
claimed_speedup: No speedup numbers in the READMEs. The DiffEqGPU README says: 'See GPUODEBenchmarks for comparison of our GPU solvers against CPUs and GPUs implementation in C++, JAX and PyTorch'. Ratios below are MPGOS ms / Julia ms (derived from page data). Tesla_V100, fixed step: 8.5x to 10.0x for n=8 to 8192 (2.118/0.2317 = 9.1x at n=8), 2.8x at n=32768, then 0.88x at n=131072 and 0.65x at n=8,388,608 (94.157 vs 145.317 ms). Tesla_V100, adaptive: 6.9x at n=8, 1.4x at n=131072, 0.77x at n=524288, 0.70x at n=8,388,608 (48.808 vs 69.451 ms). RTX_5000, fixed step: 2.2x to 2.5x for n<=2048, 5.4x at n=2,097,152 and 4.8x at n=8,388,608 (886.082 vs 183.920 ms). RTX_5000, adaptive: 0.52x to 0.66x for n<=8192 (0.144 vs 0.253 ms at n=8), 1.08x at n=32768, 2.3x at n=8,388,608 (191.764 vs 83.490 ms).
compiler_and_flags: MPGOS: nvcc -o Lorenz.exe -O3 -std=c++11 --ptxas-options=-v --gpu-architecture=sm_70 -lineinfo -maxrregcount=128 (GPU_ODE_MPGOS/makefile), BlockSize 1024, PRECISION float. runner_scripts/gpu/run_ode_cpp.sh rewrites Lorenz.cu to SOLVER RK4 for the fixed-step run and SOLVER RKCK45 for the adaptive run, and rebuilds for each n. Julia: DiffEqGPU.vectorized_solve (fixed dt 0.001f0) and vectorized_asolve (dt 0.001f0, reltol = abstol = 1f-8), both with GPUTsit5(), timed as the BenchmarkTools minimum of CUDA.@sync (GPU_ODE_Julia/bench_lorenz_gpu.jl). GPU_ODE_Julia/Manifest.toml pins Julia 1.8.5 and DiffEqGPU 2.1.0. The CUDA toolkit and CUDA.jl versions are not stated; the README recommends CUDA >= 11.
hardware: NVIDIA Tesla V100 and an RTX 5000 (data folder names Tesla_V100 and RTX_5000; probably the Turing Quadro RTX 5000, but the files read do not say). Host CPU model, driver and CUDA toolkit version not stated.
stars_or_usage: 329 stars (DiffEqGPU.jl); 27 stars (GPUODEBenchmarks); part of the DifferentialEquations.jl ecosystem
tradeoffs: Specialised to many small independent ODEs (one trajectory per GPU thread); not a solver for one large ODE. Needs CUDA.jl (the only backend that the JAX, PyTorch and MPGOS comparison supports). Julia startup and compile time are excluded from the timings.
caveats: Mixed result, not a uniform win, and the harness favours Julia in three ways. (1) Asymmetric timing: MPGOS runs once per process (one Solve() kernel launch timed with clock(), which measures process CPU time, plus cudaEventSynchronize), with no warm-up and no repetition. Julia reports the BenchmarkTools minimum over many warm runs. The MPGOS floor of about 2 ms for every n<=8192 on the V100 (0.42 ms on the RTX 5000) looks like fixed first-launch or idle-clock overhead, and Julia's 6x to 10x V100 lead at small n probably comes from it (inference). (2) Unequal arithmetic in the C++ problem definition: GPU_ODE_MPGOS/Lorenz_SystemDefinition.cuh lines 11 and 13 use the double literals 10.0 and 2.666 with float state, so part of every right-hand-side evaluation runs in FP64 with float/double conversions. The Julia RHS uses 10.0f0 and 2.666f0. The RTX 5000 is probably the Quadro RTX 5000 (Turing), which runs FP64 at a small fraction of its FP32 rate, while the V100 runs it at half rate. This plausibly explains why MPGOS beats Julia 1.5x at n=8.4M on the V100 but loses 4.8x on the RTX 5000 (inference, not measured). (3) MPGOS is built for sm_70 only, so on the RTX 5000 (sm_75) it ran JIT-compiled PTX, also built with -maxrregcount=128. The methods also differ. Julia runs Tsit5 in both modes, while MPGOS runs RK4 (fixed step) and RKCK45 (adaptive). At fixed dt=0.001, Tsit5 makes about 6 RHS evaluations per step against RK4's 4. The tolerances do match: MPGOS defaults RelativeTolerance and AbsoluteTolerance to 1e-8 (SourceCodes/SingleSystem_PerThread_Interface.cuh, line 482), as Julia sets them. On the V100, Julia is slower than MPGOS for the largest ensembles (0.65x to 0.88x from n=131072 fixed step, 0.62x to 0.77x from n=524288 adaptive). On the RTX 5000 adaptive runs it is slower for n<=8192. The host CPU and the exact RTX 5000 model are not stated. Only float32 was tested. The benchmark repo was last committed 2024-01-04 and pins DiffEqGPU 2.1.0, so the data predate current DiffEqGPU.jl. The CMAME 2024 paper (Utkarsh et al., 'Automated translation and accelerated solving of differential equations on multiple GPU platforms') was not opened (journal and arXiv blocked). GPUODEBenchmarks only holds the scripts and data; the solver lives in DiffEqGPU.jl. [retier] MPGOS's Lorenz_SystemDefinition.cuh promotes to FP64 (10.0 and 2.666 double literals): from V100 to RTX 5000 at n=8.4M MPGOS slows 9.4x (fixed) and 3.9x (adaptive) while Julia slows 1.27x and 1.20x, so the RTX 5000 wins of 4.8x and 2.3x come from the crippled baseline; the V100 fixed-step gap of 1.54x matches Tsit5's 6 against RK4's 4 right-hand-side evaluations (equal per-evaluation cost). The small-n win comes from cold clock() timing of one MPGOS launch against a warm BenchmarkTools minimum. Benchmarked DiffEqGPU 2.1.0 (current 3.21.4).

name: Mojo (explicit SIMD) in mojo-analyze: Mandelbrot
baseline: Scalar C Mandelbrot in the same repo (c/mandelbrot.c, clang -O3 -ffp-contract=off, standard library only)
workload: Escape-time Mandelbrot over 800x600 pixels, max 500 iterations, Float64, checksum of per-pixel iteration counts verified equal across all variants; timing of the core computation only, 2 warmups and 7 measured trials, mean reported.
claimed_speedup: ANALYSIS.md Mandelbrot table: Mojo (SIMD) 0.0554 s, C (-O3, scalar) 0.0904 s (1.6x slower), Rust (scalar, release) 0.1114 s (2.0x slower). README: 'Mojo wins the SIMD-heavy Mandelbrot case ... 1.6x faster than C'. The same repo reports C ahead of Mojo on the other four categories (sieve 1.05x, word-frequency 1.6x, CSV aggregation 2.3x, JSON parsing 2.3x).
compiler_and_flags: Mojo 1.0.0 (pixi.toml allows mojo >=1.0.0,<2; ANALYSIS.md states 1.0.0): mojo build --fp-mode contract=off benchmarks/mandelbrot/mandelbrot.mojo, at the default optimisation level 3 (mojolang.org mojo build docs, WebSearch snippet only). C: Apple clang 21, clang -O3 -ffp-contract=off -o dist/mandelbrot-c c/mandelbrot.c (pixi.toml build-c). No -march/-mcpu, LTO or PGO on either side.
hardware: Apple M4 Pro, 14 cores, 24 GB RAM, macOS 26.5.2, arm64 (Linux x86_64 and arm64 CI runners are a secondary reference, no C row there yet)
tradeoffs: The Mojo kernel is hand-vectorised (SIMD[DType.float64, 4] with a per-lane active mask and a scalar remainder loop), so it costs more code than the C loop. Mojo needs --fp-mode contract=off here: the default fused-multiply-add contraction changed the checksum by 10 out of about 42.4 million; clang -O3 on this platform shows the same drift unless -ffp-contract=off.
caveats: Not a same-technique comparison, and the repo says so. The Mojo version restructures the pixel loop into SIMD[DType.float64, 4] batches with a per-lane active mask (two 128-bit NEON registers per vector on arm64). It keeps iterating each batch until its slowest lane escapes, then runs a scalar remainder loop. The C and Rust versions iterate one pixel at a time in a while loop with a data-dependent exit, which clang does not autovectorise, so C runs fully scalar. The 1.6x therefore measures hand vectorisation against scalar code, not Mojo code generation. A C version using clang vector extensions or NEON intrinsics would be the fair baseline, and none is provided. Both sides are optimised builds with FMA contraction turned off, and the checksums match (42411634). Single machine (Apple M4 Pro, macOS 26.5.2), 2 warm-ups and 7 timed runs, means reported (C stdev 0.0019 s). The Linux CI runs have no C row yet. Single-author repo with 0 stars and 0 forks. C is ahead of Mojo on the other four categories in the same repo (sieve 1.05x, word frequency 1.6x, CSV aggregation 2.3x, JSON 2.3x).
found_via: WebSearch (github.com): 'Mojo implementation README faster than C++ OR Rust OR numpy benchmark pure Mojo' led to iinoshirozheng/mojo-analyze; README, ANALYSIS.md and pixi.toml read
why_faster: Explicit 4-lane Float64 SIMD with per-lane escape masks in Mojo versus plain scalar loops in C and Rust that depend on autovectorisation (the source's own explanation).

name: turbovec (Rust TurboQuant vector index with Python bindings)
baseline: FAISS IndexPQFastScan (C++) at a matched bit rate (m = d sub-quantizers, 4-bit codes in the published 4-bit script); FAISS IndexPQ (LUT256, nbits=8) for the recall comparison
workload: Search speed: nearest-neighbour search over 100K normalised OpenAI text-embedding-3 vectors (d=1536 and d=3072), k=64, 1K-query batch, median of 5 runs, 2-bit and 4-bit, single- and multi-threaded, on one ARM and one x86 cloud VM (8 cells per bit width). GloVe d=200 appears only in the recall tables, not in the speed runs.
claimed_speedup: README: 'searches them 4.4x faster than FAISS, at matching recall'; '4.4x FAISS FastScan at 4-bit and 2.2x at 2-bit, on ARM and x86'. README table: search 4-bit '3.8-5.1x faster across the eight cells (ARM 4.0x, x86 4.9x)', search 2-bit '1.8-2.5x faster (ARM 2.05x, x86 2.35x)'. Spot check: benchmarks/results/speed_d1536_4bit_x86_mt.json gives 0.127 vs 0.588 ms/query, 4.6x (derived from page data). Project-recorded losses: whole-file save 1.0-1.4x slower and load to first search 1.0-1.5x slower than FAISS.
compiler_and_flags: Rust release build. x86_64 builds target x86-64-v2 via .cargo/config.toml, with #[target_feature]-gated AVX-512 and AVX2 kernels chosen at runtime (README). The FAISS version, build (pip wheel variant) and flags are not stated; the benchmarks/suite scripts import the Python faiss module and use the default OpenMP threads, or faiss.omp_set_num_threads(1) in the st scripts.
hardware: GCP c4a-standard-8 (Google Axion, ARM, 8 vCPUs) and GCP c3-standard-8 (Intel Xeon Platinum 8481C, Sapphire Rapids, 8 vCPUs), from docs/benchmarks.md.
tradeoffs: Brute-force scan of every vector with no graph index, so query cost grows linearly with corpus size (README advises another index for hundreds of millions of vectors); lossy 2- and 4-bit quantization; Python-facing API; atomic save and load are slower than FAISS write_index/read_index.
caveats: Not the same algorithm. turbovec runs a staged search: one bit plane scanned with a table kernel, a shortlist ranked on the lower planes, the best rescored exactly, so the first stage reads about a quarter of the 4-bit code bytes. The speed comparator, faiss.IndexPQFastScan(d, m=d, 4) with the default L2 metric and no refinement, scans every code. 'At matching recall' is not supported for the speed comparator. FastScan's recall is never measured, the recall tables compare against a different index (IndexPQ m=d/2, nbits=8), the speed runs use an uncalibrated index, and the README recall row reports the calibrated TQ+. Per docs/benchmarks.md, the calibrated index trails FAISS by 0.7 points at R@1 for d=1536 4-bit, and GloVe d=200 is the harder regime. The author ran it on cloud VMs; the FAISS version and build are not stated; timings include Python call overhead on both sides. The x86 kernel adapts FAISS FastScan's pack layout, nibble-LUT scoring and u16 accumulators. Vector search sits at the edge of the numerics-and-arrays category; the orchestrator may re-file it. [retier] The headline speed JSONs were last regenerated 2026-10-04 (1.1.0), before the 1.1.2 recall fix (#562: the staged search lost recall on bunched corpora), which costs up to 3% at 4-bit and 7-12% at 2-bit; the CHANGELOG admits the README figures predate it. The FAISS comparator is IndexPQFastScan(d, m=d, 4) with 1-D sub-quantizers, recall never measured and version unpinned. The staged path needs AVX-512 VBMI plus VNNI on x86 (AVX2 hosts unbenchmarked). Open issues #309/#310 (recall losses), #336 (writer contention), #282 (AVX-512 kernels not run in CI).

name: Clarabel.rs (Rust interior-point conic and QP solver) vs ECOS in qpbenchmark Maros-Meszaros
baseline: ECOS 2.0.14 (C interior-point conic solver, also homogeneous self-dual embedding based)
workload: Solve time (shifted geometric mean, shift 10, failed solves scored at the 1000 s limit) over the 62-problem dense subset of the Maros-Meszaros QP test set, four tolerance settings, solvers called from Python through qpsolvers 4.3.3.

Success rate at default 51.6% vs 12.9% (high accuracy 43.5% vs 0.0%). These gaps measure failures charged at the 1000 s limit, not solve speed: in results/qpbenchmark_results.csv every ECOS dense run ends within 0.03 s and every Clarabel dense run within 0.07 s, and on the 9 dense problems both solvers solve at default settings ECOS is faster on geometric mean (ECOS/Clarabel time 0.84, about 1.19x in ECOS's favour; derived from page data). Clarabel wins DUAL1-DUAL4, DUALC1 and DUALC5 by 1.05-1.55x and loses HS118, HS21 and HS53 by 1.6-4.8x; the same commonly-solved comparison gives ECOS/Clarabel ratios of 0.84 (high), 0.88 (mid) and 0.94 (low accuracy). On the full 138-problem set at default Clarabel (163.8) trails PIQP (1.0), QPALM (3.6), OSQP (12.7), SCS (15.1), HiGHS (30.7), ProxQP (53.3) and CVXOPT (94.1); ECOS is not run there.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated by the benchmark. Solvers are PyPI builds (clarabel 0.9.0, ecos 2.0.14) called from Python 3.12.4 through qpsolvers 4.3.3; ecos-python's setup.py passes no extra_compile_args (setuptools defaults of the Python build), and Clarabel.rs's Cargo.toml does not override the release profile.
hardware: Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-6500U CPU @ 2.50GHz (4 logical CPUs), benchmark version 2.3.0 run 2024-09-07 by the qpbenchmark author (@stephane-caron); thermal throttling listed as known limitation #88
stars_or_usage: 617 stars; default QP/conic solver in CVXPY per the paper snippet
tradeoffs: Rust crate with Python (pip install clarabel) and a separate Julia port (oxfordcontrol/Clarabel.jl); handles quadratic objectives natively; interior-point solves are dense in iterations but high accuracy, whereas ADMM solvers (OSQP, SCS) are cheaper per problem at low accuracy.
caveats: Not faster than ECOS on solve time in this suite: the 6x shifted-geometric-mean gap is produced by failures charged at the 1000 s limit, and ECOS fails 53 of 62 dense problems within milliseconds because qpsolvers converts each QP to an SOCP through a NumPy Cholesky factorisation that needs a positive definite P (qpbenchmark issue #60, open, labelled fairness: 'failing to solve the problem is no fault of the solver itself'). On the problems both solve, ECOS is faster on geometric mean (derived from results/qpbenchmark_results.csv). Clarabel's own failures also end in milliseconds (no timeouts), so its 51.6% success rate is low for an interior-point solver; the cause was not investigated. The report also lists CPU thermal throttling (#88) as a known limitation. Python wrapper and qpsolvers conversion overhead are included for every solver. Clarabel trails OSQP (C), SCS (C), HiGHS (C++), PIQP (C++) and others on the full and sparse sets. The broader 'faster than commercial and open-source solvers on QPs' claim is from the Goulart and Chen paper (arXiv 2405.12762, Mathematical Programming Computation per a search snippet; neither arxiv.org nor the Oxford repository copy could be opened), so its numbers are unverified. ClarabelBenchmarks (oxfordcontrol) holds the authors' benchmark code but commits no result tables.

name: D (gdc, ldc2) matmul with std.numeric.dotProduct in kostya/benchmarks
baseline: C/gcc 16.1.0 and C/clang 22.1.8 (-O3 -march=native -flto=auto, -std=c23) transposed dot-product matmul of 1500x1500 doubles
workload: Allocate, generate and multiply two 1500x1500 double matrices; the D version transposes b and calls std.numeric.dotProduct per output cell, the C version transposes b and runs one scalar accumulation loop.
claimed_speedup: kostya/benchmarks matmul table (median, Xeon E-2324G, README updated 2026-07-19): D/gdc 1.505 s, D/ldc2 1.722 s, D/dmd 1.880 s versus C/gcc 3.034 s and C/clang 3.067 s, i.e. gdc about 2.0x, ldc2 about 1.76x and dmd about 1.61x faster than gcc C (derived from page data). Rust 3.067 s, Zig 3.071 s and Nim/gcc 3.091 s tie with C. Not like for like: the D program calls std.numeric.dotProduct (two partial sums) while every tied language runs the single-accumulator loop; in the like-for-like plb2 matmul (same i-k-j loop in D and C, Apple M1) D ldc2 1.35.0 takes 0.57 s versus C clang 15.0.0 0.54 s, so D is about 5% slower there (derived from page data). BLAS-backed rows (D lubeck 0.042 s, C++ Eigen 0.081 s, NumPy, Arraymancer) are library comparisons and excluded.
compiler_and_flags: From common/commands.mk: C gcc 16.1.0 / clang 22.1.8 '-Wall -Wextra -pedantic -Wcast-align -O3 -march=native -flto=auto -Wa,-mbranches-within-32B-boundaries -std=c23'; D ldc2 1.41.0 '-O5 -release -boundscheck=off', gdc 14.2.0 '-O3 -frelease -finline -fbounds-check=off', dmd v2.111.0 '-O -release -inline -boundscheck=off'. The D builds carry no -march=native and no LTO, so the flag difference favours C.
hardware: Intel(R) Xeon(R) E-2324G, Debian forky/sid Docker image, README updated 2026-07-19
why_faster: Derived by the searcher from the source, not stated by the suite: Phobos std.numeric.dotProduct (std/numeric.d) unrolls 16-wide with two partial sums (sum0, sum1), a different floating-point reduction order; the C loop keeps one strict-FP accumulator and is built without -ffast-math, so the compiler cannot reassociate or vectorize it.
tradeoffs: Gain comes from one standard-library kernel, so a C programmer can match it by writing two or more accumulators or using -ffast-math; D's runtime and GC are not involved in the timed loop.
caveats: Not a language or compiler advantage: the high-level algorithm (transpose plus dot products) is the same, but the timed D path is Phobos' hand-unrolled two-accumulator dotProduct against a naive single-accumulator C loop, so summation order and results differ in the last bits (the harness only checks within 0.1 at n=101). Like for like (plb2, same loop in both languages) D ldc2 is slower than C. The C row is deliberately plain ('written as the average developer would'); C gets -march=native and -flto=auto that the D builds lack. gcc 16.1 and clang 22 are newer than the GCC 14 and LLVM bases of gdc and ldc2. Time includes allocation (D uses GC-allocated jagged arrays, C malloc/calloc rows) and matrix generation.

name: Fortran (gfortran) matmul in plb2
baseline: C (clang 15.0.0, make flags -O3 -fwrapv -flto) 1500x1500 double matmul with the same i-k-j loop order using double** rows

Elapsed wall time includes matrix generation and process startup.
claimed_speedup: matmul elapsed seconds on Apple M1: Fortran gfortran 13.2.0 0.51 s versus C clang 15.0.0 0.54 s, about 6% faster (derived from page data). Other compiled languages on the same row: Rust 0.56, Zig 0.56, Nim 0.56, Swift 0.56, D ldc2 0.57, V 0.57, Julia 0.76, Mojo 1.12. Fortran is the only language in the table that beats C on matmul.

why_faster: Not stated by the source. Searcher inference only: Fortran dummy arguments may not alias and arrays are contiguous, so gfortran can vectorize the inner loop without alias checks, whereas the C version indexes through double** rows.
tradeoffs: CC0 dedication (no patent grant). Fortran version needs gfortran; plb2 measures a naive triple loop, not tuned BLAS-level matmul.
caveats: Margin is about 6% (0.51 s versus 0.54 s) on one machine, single figures without variance in the table, and the rows were timed on different days (Fortran timing added 2024-01-04 as plb2 grew through January 2024), so this is a near-tie that may sit within run-to-run noise. name: Halide
baseline: Expert hand-tuned C++ (OpenMP + Intel IPP), ARM NEON intrinsics/assembly and CUDA implementations of the same image-processing pipelines used as baselines in the PLDI 2013 paper (local Laplacian filters, bilateral grid, camera pipe, etc.)
workload: Image-processing pipelines written once as an algorithm plus a separate schedule (tiling, fusion, vectorization, parallelism): local Laplacian filters (99 stages) and bilateral grid on quad-core x86, plus camera raw pipe and others on ARM/CUDA, versus the hand-tuned expert code for the same pipelines.
claimed_speedup: PLDI 2013 table as reproduced in the team's CVPR 2015 tutorial slides (halide/halide.github.com, assets/lectures/Halide_CVPR_intro.pdf), Halide over hand-tuned expert implementations: x86 blur 1.2x, bilateral grid 4.4x, camera pipeline 3.4x, healing brush 1.7x, local Laplacian 1.7x; ARM camera pipeline 1.1x; GPU bilateral grid 2.3x, and GPU healing brush 5.9x and local Laplacian 9x against CPU expert code (asterisked, GPU-vs-CPU). Abstract: up to 5x faster than hand-tuned C, intrinsics and CUDA.
hardware: Quad-core x86 desktop, ARM and CUDA GPU platforms (exact CPU models not confirmed; paper PDF could not be opened)
why_faster: Decouples the algorithm from its schedule: the programmer or autoscheduler explores loop tiling, producer-consumer fusion, recomputation vs storage, vectorization and parallelism without rewriting the algorithm, which finds locality/parallelism trade-offs that were too laborious to hand-code in C++.
tradeoffs: Embedded DSL: requires writing a Halide pipeline and a schedule (C++17 API or Python bindings), ahead-of-time or JIT compiled through LLVM; schedule quality depends on the expert or autoscheduler; image/array pipelines only, not general code. LICENSE.txt is MIT with apps/bgu under Apache-2.0.
caveats: Numbers come only from WebSearch snippets of the PLDI 2013 paper (Ragan-Kelley et al.; the PDF hosts are blocked here, so the table was never opened); the snippet tool said the table text was garbled, so the row attributions (2.1x local Laplacian, 5.9x bilateral grid) are inferred, and the 5.9x row exceeds the abstract's 'up to 5x' without explanation. The baselines are the authors' 2012-13 expert implementations on 2012 hardware with CPU models, compilers and flags unconfirmed. The local Laplacian baseline calls Intel IPP library routines, so part of that comparison is Halide against a vendor library rather than against hand-written C++. The algorithm is the same mathematical pipeline on both sides, but the win comes from a different loop organization (fusion, tiling, recomputation, vectorization and parallelism chosen by the schedule and an autotuner), not from better code generation for the same loop nest. The repo does not carry the paper's baselines or harness; apps/blur/test.cpp does time naive C++, hand-written SSE intrinsics (blur_fast) and Halide side by side but publishes no numbers (enrichment lead). Halide is a C++-embedded DSL compiled through LLVM, so pipelines are callable directly from C++. License is MIT for the core; apps/bgu is Apache-2.0 (both OSI). [retier] The record's earlier 5.9x was mis-attributed to bilateral grid (it is GPU healing brush, against CPU expert code) and its 2.1x is unmatched (the slides say 1.7x in the table and '2x vs Adobe' in the narrative). The asterisked GPU rows compare Halide's GPU schedule with CPU expert code (GPU-vs-CPU asymmetry). Repo harness flaw: apps/blur/test.cpp's naive baseline is single-threaded and the Makefile adds -fopenmp only for non-clang, so on clang the SSE baseline is single-threaded against Halide's .parallel(y); the paper baselines are absent from the repo.

name: Bessels.jl
baseline: SpecialFunctions.jl wrappers: openlibm (C, FreeBSD msun) j0/y0/j1/y1/jn/yn for integer-order and order-0 and 1 calls, AMOS zbes* routines (Fortran, via openspecfun) for non-integer order, so only the order-0 and order-1 rows have a C baseline
workload: Float64 evaluation of Bessel J, Y, I, K functions and gamma for random x and order nu between 0 and 100.
claimed_speedup: README Benchmarks (relative speed increase over SpecialFunctions.jl): besselj0 2.5x, bessely0 2.3x (the two rows whose baseline is openlibm C), besselj(nu,x) 6x, bessely(nu,x) 5x, besseli0 10x, besseli(nu,x) 7x, besselk0 10x, besselk(nu,x) 4x, Bessels.gamma 5x. README prose: 'in general 5-10x faster'.
compiler_and_flags: Julia 1.7.2 (no C/Fortran flags: baselines are prebuilt binary libraries)
hardware: Apple M1 run under Rosetta (x86 emulation)
why_faster: Different algorithms: piecewise polynomial/rational approximations per domain written in pure Julia that inline and vectorize, versus AMOS general-order series/recurrences and libm's older rational approximations.
tradeoffs: README admits accuracy is sometimes 'within a digit or two' of the baselines rather than better (its own error table vs ArbNumerics gives mean/max relative errors such as besselj0 3e-16/6e-14 and besselj(5.0,x) 3e-14/2e-11); positive real arguments mainly, limited complex support; Float64 focus.

The comparison harness is not in the repo: benchmark/benchmark.jl times only Bessels functions (no SpecialFunctions.jl calls), and its 'bessely' group actually times besselj0/besselj1. Most of the baseline is Fortran AMOS reached through SpecialFunctions' complex-argument path (besseli, besselk and non-integer besselj/bessely all call zbes* via openspecfun), and a Fortran-vs-Julia comparison is outside this catalogue's scope; only besselj0/bessely0 (2.5x, 2.3x) are measured against C code (openlibm j0/y0, which openlibm's Make.inc builds at -O3 by default), and that baseline goes through non-inlinable Julia ccall wrappers. name: fastGPT
baseline: HuggingFace transformers pipeline('text-generation', model='gpt2') on PyTorch, driven from Python by pt.py (transformers 4.26.1 per environment.yml; PyTorch version not pinned), with PyTorch's C++ ATen kernels and the same BLAS (Apple Accelerate or OpenBLAS); also picoGPT (NumPy)
workload: GPT-2 124M inference, 20 generated tokens from a 19-token prompt, greedy decoding with KV cache, on Apple M1 Max at 1 to 8 cores.
claimed_speedup: README Benchmarks (Apple M1 Max, 20 tokens): with KV cache, fastGPT (Accelerate) 0.299 s vs PyTorch (Accelerate) 0.346 s (1.16x, derived from page data); fastGPT (Accelerate, fast_tanh) 0.288 s; OpenBLAS 1/2/4/8 cores fastGPT 0.837/0.514/0.341/0.339 s vs PyTorch 0.873/0.539/0.386/0.392 s. Without cache: Accelerate fastGPT 0.717 s vs PyTorch 0.787 s and picoGPT 0.765 s; OpenBLAS fastGPT 2.343/1.603/1.209/1.018 s vs PyTorch 2.356/1.520/1.104/0.997 s, so PyTorch is faster at 2, 4 and 8 cores. Total run including model load and Python imports: fastGPT (Accelerate, fast_tanh) 0.401 s vs picoGPT (8 cores) 3.445 s and PyTorch (OpenBLAS, 4 cores) 4.867 s.
compiler_and_flags: gfortran, version unstated (a gfortran=14.2.0 pin is commented out in environment.yml and postdates the 2023 numbers); current cmake/UserOverride.cmake Release flags: -O3 -march=native -ffast-math -funroll-loops. PyTorch side: prebuilt binaries, version and build flags unstated.
hardware: Apple M1 Max
tradeoffs: GPT-2 only, greedy sampling only, no batching or training, GGUF model conversion script needed; builds with gfortran via fpm or CMake.
caveats: First-party numbers on one machine with one short prompt. The matmuls run through the same vendor BLAS in both programs, so the 3-16% gap is framework overhead (Python and HF transformers dispatch around each op, generate() bookkeeping) and kernel fusion, not Fortran code generation. The baseline is not a C/C++ program built at -O3: it is HF transformers on PyTorch driven from Python, timed by pt.py around the whole pipeline call (which also tokenizes and decodes), while fastGPT's 'Running model' time excludes its separately timed tokenizer. pt.py hard-codes OMP_NUM_THREADS=1, so the 2-8 core PyTorch rows needed an unrecorded edit. Flags are not equivalent: fastGPT uses -ffast-math (and an optional fast_tanh approximation) against prebuilt PyTorch. Without the KV cache, PyTorch beats fastGPT at 2, 4 and 8 OpenBLAS cores. The 0.401 s vs 4.867 s total-run comparison is dominated by Python imports and model loading. The README says speed comes 'by using Fortran' without a mechanism. [retier] The timed regions differ: fastGPT's 'Running model' timer leaves out its own tokenizer while pt.py times HF tokenization, and the README's own example (0.074 s encode plus 0.304 s run = 0.378 s) is slower than PyTorch's 0.346 s. The fast_tanh rows (0.288 s, 0.401 s total) cannot be rebuilt from the shipped code (gelu() calls the intrinsic tanh) and issue #25 shows fast_tanh changes 9 of 100 tokens on 1558M. The PyTorch Accelerate row ran only after symlinking libcblas.3.dylib over libopenblas.0.dylib (issue #26), PyTorch version unrecorded. Non-Apple default builds link omp_dummy, whose omp_get_wtime returns 0 (printed time 0.000).
found_via: Direct read of certik/fastGPT README Benchmarks section; the author's blog post 'fastGPT: faster than PyTorch in 300 lines of Fortran' is linked there (not opened)

name: FFTA.jl (pure Julia FFT) vs FFTW.jl on small static vectors
baseline: FFTW (C library) through FFTW.jl fft(x)
workload: One @btime of fft on a 64-element StaticArrays SVector of Float64, FFTA.fft vs FFTW.fft, as shown in the FFTA.jl README.
claimed_speedup: N=64 SVector: FFTA.fft 698.611 ns (8 allocations, 2.11 KiB) vs FFTW.fft 5.433 us (34 allocations, 4.70 KiB), about 7.8x (derived from page data); the README itself calls the example cherry-picked.
tradeoffs: Pure Julia and generic over element types (BigFloat, symbolic, StaticArrays), only 1D and 2D; the README itself says to use FFTW.jl for more performance.
caveats: Single cherry-picked README snippet (the author says so), no CPU, Julia version, FFTW_jll build or flags. Both calls go through AbstractFFTs' one-shot path, fft(x, region) = (y = to1(x); plan_fft(y, region) * y), so a plan is built on every call; for FFTW that means the FFTW planner runs per call on a copy of the SVector (complexfloat copies it into a ComplexF64 Array), so the 7.8x mostly measures planning and conversion overhead, not transform speed. FFTW with a reused plan is not compared, and the README itself sends users wanting performance to FFTW.jl. The repo's benchmark/ suite (separate Julia environments, fft($x) with a fresh plan per call, sizes up to 32768 and primes to 20000) commits no results; reports are CI artifacts kept 30 days and a docs page on github.io. Not a general speedup claim and not a Julia-versus-C codegen result. [retier] The 698.611 ns vs 5.433 us snippet dates from v0.2.2 (2021); since v0.2.3 FFTA.fft is AbstractFFTs.fft and with FFTW loaded FFTW's plan_fft wins dispatch (#66 open), so the snippet now times FFTW against itself. Issue #119's rerun: 4.922 vs 4.945 us with planned FFTW at 422 ns, and the maintainer concedes the snippet is obsolete. Issue #130 planned runs: FFTA 2.2-11.8x slower than FFTW (geomean; Neoverse-N1, Julia 1.12.6, FFTW 3.3.11). #118: Float32 twiddle error about O(n); Bluestein setup on every call.
found_via: Blogs / talks: README read while screening Julia numerics packages from github.com/topics/linear-algebra?l=julia and the JuliaMath organisation
why_faster: README: carrying Julia's type specialisation (generic code that works on small StaticArrays without heap workspace) into the FFT; no further mechanism given.

verification.tier_reason: The only numbers are one first-party @btime pair in the README (698.611 ns vs 5.433 us for N=64 SVector), with no CPU, Julia version or FFTW build stated; the repo's benchmark/ suite has no committed results (its report lives in 30-day CI artifacts and the github.io docs, not reachable here), so C.
verification.notes: Keep at C with shortcoming 'single cherry-picked one-shot timing at N=64 where FFTW's per-call planning dominates; no reused-plan comparison, no methodology'. Numbers match the README exactly; metadata checked (76 stars, MIT, last commit 2026-09-01, JuliaMath org, not a fork). Close to the crippled-baseline line (FFTW used without plan reuse), but both sides use the same one-shot API, so C rather than D.

retier.reason: Enricher: the README snippet dates from v0.2.2 and now times FFTW against itself (FFTA.fft dispatches to FFTW's plan_fft when FFTW is loaded, #66), the maintainer concedes it is obsolete, and planned runs in issue #130 put FFTA 2.2-11.8x slower than FFTW; claim invalid and not faster: C to D.

corrected_fields.caveats: Single README snippet, no CPU, Julia version or flags. FFTW.fft(x) on an SVector converts to an Array and builds a plan on every call (our reading of how FFTW.jl's fft works, not stated by the source), so the timing largely measures planning and allocation, not transform speed. The repo's benchmark/ suite (separate Julia environments for FFTA and FFTW, fft($x) with a fresh plan each call) has no committed results and the README steers users to FFTW.jl for speed. Not a general speedup claim; probably slower than FFTW with a reused plan.

name: Fortran (gfortran) in fortran-lang/benchmarks: poisson2d (optimized)
baseline: C (gcc -Ofast) optimized.c: the same Jacobi-iteration Poisson solver on an MxM double grid, written as a line-by-line transliteration of optimized.f90
workload: Jacobi iteration for a 2D Poisson equation (tolerance 1e-6, grid spacing 0.01, two charged squares) on an MxM double-precision grid for M=100, 200 and 300; whole-run time in seconds.
claimed_speedup: README timings (seconds, one run per cell, measured June 2021): optimized Fortran 0.18 / 6.25 / 31.4 against optimized C 0.37 / 6.80 / 32.8 for M=100 / 200 / 300. That is about 1.09x faster at M=200 and 1.04x at M=300 (derived from page data). The README says the M=100 C runs did nearly double the iterations, so that column is not comparable. The naive versions go the other way: naive Fortran 0.34 / 13.2 / 69.7 against naive C 0.42 / 7.25 / 33.7, so naive C is about 1.8-2.1x faster at M=200 and 300 (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: gfortran sourcefile.f95 -Ofast and gcc sourcefile.c -Ofast (from the README); compiler versions not stated; no -march, LTO or PGO on either side.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 5 3600 @ 3.6 GHz, WSL2 on Windows 10 (README)
tradeoffs: Toy 300x300 static-array Jacobi solver, not a library. Fortran needs gfortran; the repo also carries pure Python and Cython versions (Cython 229 s at M=300 versus 31-34 s for Fortran and C).
caveats: The margin is 4-9% on one machine, with a single run per cell under WSL2, and holds only for the hand-optimized pair (rho precomputed into an array, one copy per iteration). In the naive pair, naive C is about twice as fast as naive Fortran, so there is no consistent language-level win. (1) The timings predate PR #30 (Euler-37, merged 2022-03-05, titled 'change the precision problems in fortran files'). That PR changed a=0.01 to a=0.01_dp and y<0.8 to y<0.8_dp in both naive.f90 and optimized.f90. The timed Fortran therefore used a single-precision grid spacing (about 0.0099999998) and charge bound, and solved a slightly different problem from the C code; nobody re-timed after the fix. (2) The two programs do not solve the same instance even after the fix. C fills rhoa[i][j]=rho(i*a,j*a) with 0-based i, while Fortran fills rhoarr(i,j)=rho(i*a,j*a) with 1-based i, so the charge squares sit one cell apart relative to the grounded boundary and the iteration counts differ. The README gives no iteration counts, only 'approximately the same' for M=200/300 and 'nearly double' for C at M=100. A Discourse reply seen only as a search snippet reported about 320k Fortran against 304k C iterations on a 250x250 grid in an earlier version. A 4-9% margin is within that spread. (3) The C side keeps phi, phip and rhoa in malloc'd pointer-to-array buffers and passes them to out-of-line mmax/swap helpers without restrict. The Fortran side uses static arrays with whole-array assignment and maxval(abs()). A Discourse reply (snippet only) says the C code ran a few seconds slower with heap-allocated arrays. The gap is therefore at least partly a storage choice that C could also make, not a language property. (4) The Fortran loops run i outer and j inner over phiprime(i,j), which is stride-M access in column-major order. Any Fortran win therefore depends on gfortran interchanging the loops (-floop-interchange is part of -O3/-Ofast in GCC 8+), which was not verified. (5) The gcc and gfortran versions are not stated, the last commit is March 2022, and -Ofast enables -ffast-math on both sides. Timing uses clock() in C and cpu_time in Fortran, over the whole run in both. The linked Discourse thread (fortran-lang.discourse.group/t/performance-c-vs-fortran/1461) does not resolve here (ENOTFOUND); what it says was read from search snippets only.
found_via: Hacker News: WebSearch restricted to news.ycombinator.com ('Show HN Fortran OR Julia OR Chapel OR Futhark outperforms C++ numerical kernel github benchmark -O3') returned only discussion threads with no repo; I then opened github.com/fortran-lang/benchmarks directly (guessed from the org name) and read its README and four sources. news.ycombinator.com itself is DNS-blocked in this environment, so no thread was opened.

The suite is the Fortran community's own one-person benchmark with one run per cell, so it is not B.
verification.notes: Numbers verified on the README and all four sources read. Tier C stands (no compiler versions; the timed Fortran was later fixed for single-precision literals by PR #30), and the record is metadata-accurate (MIT, 26 stars, 10 forks, last commit 2022-03-05, abandoned). Shortcomings to record: 4-9% margin from a single run, inside the iteration-count spread; C and Fortran charge grids are offset by one cell; C baseline uses malloc'd buffers without restrict; Fortran loop order is cache-strided unless interchanged; naive C beats naive Fortran by about 2x; timings predate the PR #30 precision fix. Not a duplicate of the plb2 Fortran matmul entry (a different benchmark and suite).

baseline: C version of userfunc_mandelbrot in the same suite (c/perf.c, double complex, gcc 7.3.1 -std=c99, best timing over -O0 through -O3)
workload: JuliaLang Microbenchmarks userfunc_mandelbrot: escape-time iteration (maxiter 80, z = z*z + c) over a 21 x 26 grid of complex points, identical algorithm in every language, serial single core, best-of timing in ms, result checked against a sum of 14791.

name: Fortran (gfortran) in JuliaLang/Microbenchmarks: userfunc_mandelbrot
claimed_speedup: benchmarks.csv at a963d28 (2018, gcc/gfortran 7.3.1): userfunc_mandelbrot C 0.076702 ms, Fortran 0.053836 ms, so Fortran is 1.42x faster than C (derived from page data). The suite's current results (gh-pages dev/benchmarks.csv, generated 2026-04-21, gcc 13.3.0, both at -O2, separate GitHub Actions runners) reverse this: C 0.045061 ms, Fortran 0.05296 ms, so Fortran is 1.18x slower than C. In 2018 Fortran was slower than C on most other benchmarks (derived): matrix_multiply 1.16, matrix_statistics 1.54, recursion_quicksort 1.19, parse_integers 6.88, print_to_file 5.97; iteration_pi_sum 1.00 and recursion_fibonacci 0.99.
compiler_and_flags: 2018 run: C with gcc 7.3.1 '$(CC) -std=c99 -O$* perf.c ... -lopenblas $(LIBM) $(CFLAGS)' and Fortran with gfortran 7.3.1 '$(FC) -fexternal-blas -static-libgfortran -O$* perf.f90 ... -lopenblas' (Makefile at a963d28). Each language reports the best timing over -O0..-O3, per the julialang.org benchmarks page. Which level won is not published, and CFLAGS inherited from Julia's Make.inc are not visible. Current CI: gcc 13.3.0, both at -O2 (benchmarks/c2.csv and fortran2.csv), in separate ubuntu-latest jobs.
tradeoffs: gfortran source uses complex(dp) with z**2 and a hand-written abs2; Fortran I/O and string parsing rows are far slower than C in the same suite.
caveats: The 2018 result does not survive the suite's current run. With gcc 13.3.0, both at -O2, the same double-complex C code is faster than Fortran (Fortran 1.18x slower), though C and Fortran now run in separate GitHub Actions jobs on different runner VMs (bench-c, bench-fortran in .github/workflows/benchmarks.yml). In 2018, C was the outlier on this benchmark: Julia 0.052706, Rust 0.057636 and Go 0.059685 ms were also faster than C's 0.076702 ms. The harnesses differ slightly. C runs 5 trials of 100 calls, and each call mallocs, fills and frees a 546-int result array; it sums only the first call. Fortran runs 5 trials of 1000 calls and adds each result to a volatile integer. Both report the minimum per call. The inner escape-time loop is the same (maxiter 80, 21x26 grid, sum 14791). C uses C99 double complex for z*z+c, while Fortran uses complex(dp) with z**2. The source gives no mechanism. The earlier inference (C99 Annex G complex-multiply checks) is not supported by the 2026 run, where the same C code wins. The data are from the Julia v1.0.0 / gcc 7.3.1 era (2018), and julialang.org itself calls them 'a bit dated'. The win is on one benchmark of eight.

name: Fortran (gfortran) in niklas-heer/speed-comparison: Leibniz pi series
baseline: C (gcc 15.2.0, -O3 -flto -march=native with -fno-signed-zeros -fno-trapping-math -fassociative-math) and the clang / C++ builds of the same Leibniz loop in the same suite
workload: Single-threaded Leibniz series for pi, 1,000,000,000 terms per run (rounds.txt), timed with hyperfine; this historical run used two warm-up executions, three measured samples (TimesPerRun in the raw JSON) and a separate output execution; median wall time reported. Sources at revision c71e4cd81464b238172605982806c5bf827a70a1 (src/leibniz.f90, src/leibniz.c, src/leibniz.cpp).
claimed_speedup: Published snapshot 2026-09-05T193245, combined_results.csv medians in ms: Fortran 90 (gfortran 14.3.0) 141.67 vs C (gcc 15.2.0) 157.9, about 1.11x (derived from page data); vs C++ (g++) 158.78, about 1.12x (derived); vs C (clang 21.1.2) 146.07, about 1.03x (derived); vs C++ (clang++) 143.32, about 1.01x (derived). Min-max ranges: Fortran 141.04-144.35 ms, C++ clang++ 142.74-144.96 ms, C (clang) 143.63-150.61 ms, C (gcc) 155.46-160.78 ms, so the lead over the clang builds is inside the sample range.
compiler_and_flags: Fortran: gfortran 14.3.0 `gfortran leibniz.f90 -o leibniz -Ofast -flto -ffast-math -march=native -mtune=native`. C: gcc 15.2.0 `gcc -O3 -s -flto -march=native -mtune=native -fomit-frame-pointer -fno-signed-zeros -fno-trapping-math -fassociative-math -o leibniz leibniz.c -lm`. C++ clang++ 21.1.2 and C clang 21.1.2 use the same flag set (from docs/history/2026-09-05T193245/raw/*.json).
hardware: AMD EPYC-Genoa Processor, 4 threads, shared x86-64 VM (runner homelab-argo), kernel 6.18.38-talos
tradeoffs: The suite compares single implementations of one arithmetic loop, not Fortran as a whole. The Fortran loop is written differently from the C loop: it is unrolled by hand to four terms per iteration (src/leibniz.f90), while C/C++ use a one-term loop with an `i & 1` sign trick written to allow vectorisation (src/leibniz.c).
caveats: Evidence would qualify as A (code, compiler versions, flags and CPU model are all public for both sides) but no mechanism is established, so the tier is capped at C. The margin over the best C/C++ build (clang++ 143.32 ms) is about 1% and inside the three-sample ranges; the suite's README warns that three samples cannot establish a winner for small differences. Flags are not matched: gfortran is built with -Ofast -ffast-math (adds -freciprocal-math, -ffinite-math-only, -fno-math-errno) while C sets only -fno-signed-zeros -fno-trapping-math -fassociative-math, and the backends differ (gfortran 14.3.0 vs gcc 15.2.0). The sources are not line-for-line equivalent: the Fortran loop is hand-unrolled by four with compile-time signs (do i=1,rounds,4: pi = pi + x/(2i+1) - x/(2i+3) + x/(2i+5) - x/(2i+7), signed 32-bit counter), while the C and C++ loops compute each term's sign from the index parity (x = -1.0 + 2.0*(i & 1)) in unsigned arithmetic; both sum the same 1e9 terms with one division each. The CalculatedPi values differ by about 1.5e-10 (Fortran 3.141592654730, C 3.1415926545850823), so the lower accuracy column (9.440 vs 9.499 digits) reflects both the 12-digit printout and a different summation order. Nim (142.43 ms), Rust SIMD (141.31 ms) and Objective-C (142.95 ms) are also faster than gcc C in the same snapshot; Nim compiles through gcc, so that gap comes from source form, not language. Explicit-SIMD C++ (AVX2) is slower (290.67 ms). In the earlier snapshot docs/history/2025-12-14T070941 (gfortran 14.2.0) Fortran took 238.94 ms: about 1.06x faster than C (gcc) 253.23 ms (derived from page data) but slower than C++ (clang++) 223.89 ms and C++ (g++) 226.37 ms and level with C (clang) 237.46 ms, so only the lead over gcc-built C is repeatable, and in that snapshot g++-built C++ beat gcc-built C by 1.12x on the same loop, which shows how much of the gap is run-to-run and build variation. name: Fortran (Intel ifort) in floatingspeed lap3dkernel: direct 1/r kernel sum
baseline: Plain OpenMP C++ version of the same 1/r kernel direct summation in the same repo (c++SIMD/lap3dkernel.cpp without VCL), built with g++ 9 and icpc 2019
workload: Dense direct N-body sum of the 3D 1/r kernel from 10,000 sources to 10,000 targets in double precision, 12 OpenMP threads, throughput in Gpair/s.
claimed_speedup: No claim by the source. lap3dkernel/README results on an Intel Xeon Gold 6128 (12 OMP threads): C++ (GCC 9) + omp 4.1 Gpair/s, C++ (icpc 2019) + omp 4.1, Fortran (GCC 9) + omp 4.0, Fortran (ifort 2019) + omp 7.7 Gpair/s, i.e. ifort Fortran is 1.88x the plain C++ (derived from page data). Hand-SIMD C++ with the VCL library gets 6.1 (g++) and 4.0 (icpc), and with a custom double rsqrt 18.3 (g++) and 12.8 (icpc), which beat the Fortran. On the i7-7700HQ laptop gfortran 7 is 1.3 vs C++ 1.1 Gpair/s.
compiler_and_flags: Intel rows: icpc 2019 -fPIC -O3 -march=native -funroll-loops -mkl -qopenmp -std=c++17 and ifort 2019 -qopenmp -fPIC -O3 -march=native -funroll-loops -mkl (commented lines in lap3dkernel/run_all_tests.sh, added in commit b1c14d2 in the same change as the Xeon Gold 6128 results). GNU rows: g++ (9) -fPIC -O3 -march=native -funroll-loops -fopenmp -std=c++17 and gfortran (9) -O3 -fopenmp -funroll-loops -march=native from the same script. No -ffast-math on the GNU side; the Intel compilers use their default -fp-model fast=1. Exact Intel compiler update numbers are not given ('2019').
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6128 (2019 workstation, 3.4 GHz, AVX-512, 12 cores, 12 OMP threads)
stars_or_usage: 8 stars; main author Alex Barnett; copyright Simons Foundation, Inc.
tradeoffs: The ifort row needs the proprietary Intel Fortran compiler (2019 version); gfortran matches plain C++.
caveats: The source makes no Fortran-beats-C++ claim. The 1.88x ratio (7.7 vs 4.1 Gpair/s) is derived from the README table. The README notes say 'Clearly C++ w/ VCL beats others by 2x, and nearly 4x w/ custom rsqrt' (laptop section). The gap appears only with ifort: gfortran (4.0) ties g++ (4.1). Hand-vectorised C++ with VCL beats the Fortran: 6.1 (g++) and 18.3 Gpair/s (g++ with custom double rsqrt). Compared with icpc at identical flags, ifort is still 1.88x faster (derived from page data). Intel compiler versions are given only as '2019', and Intel has since discontinued ifort, so reproducing the result needs a legacy toolchain. One machine, 12 OMP threads, one reported figure per row (20 repetitions inside each run). The C++ README row does not say which plain kernel it reports (target-outer or source-outer loop). The kernels differ slightly in work: the Fortran stores coordinates as an array of structs x(3,n) and multiplies by an extra 1/(4 pi) prefactor, while the C++ uses separate X/Y/Z arrays. Neither plain version is tuned. The plain C++ kernel accumulates into pot[t] through plain pointers with no __restrict, which a C++ programmer can add. The SoA/SIMD Fortran variants added in 2026 reach 8.1 Gpair/s on a Ryzen 5700U, the same as C++ with VCL (8.1). The README results section is unfinished ('... (to finish)').

name: Gaius.jl (Julia multi-threaded divide-and-conquer BLAS-like matmul)
baseline: OpenBLAS gemm (C and assembly) with 6 threads (BLAS.set_num_threads(6)); for integer matrices Julia's generic matmul, since OpenBLAS has no integer matmul
workload: Square matrix multiplication for Float64, Float32 and Complex{Float64} (struct-of-arrays) across a range of sizes, shown as log-log plots.
claimed_speedup: README: 104x104 Float64 mul!: LinearAlgebra/OpenBLAS 68.529 us vs Gaius 31.220 us (about 2.2x faster, derived from page data); A*B 68.949 us vs Gaius.mul 32.950 us (about 2.1x, derived); 150x150 Complex{Float64}: Gaius on StructArrays 515.587 us vs OpenBLAS 546.481 us (about 1.06x, derived). Plots: 'Gaius outperforms OpenBLAS over a large range of matrix sizes, but does begin to appreciably fall behind around 800 x 800 matrices for Float64 and 650 x 650 matrices for Float32'; the plots also show OpenBLAS ahead at the smallest size (about 2x2). Integer plots compare with Julia's generic matmul, not C.
compiler_and_flags: Julia 1.4.0-rc2.0 (LLVM 8.0.1, znver1), JULIA_NUM_THREADS=6; OpenBLAS version not stated; built on LoopVectorization.jl.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 5 2600 six-core (Linux)
tradeoffs: Matmul only (README: other BLAS routines not implemented); README says it is 'not stable or well tested' and 'not actively maintained' and points to Octavian.jl (already catalogued) and Tullio.jl as successors; Julia-only.
caveats: Author-run on Julia 1.4.0-rc2.0 (2020, LLVM 8.0.1, Ryzen 5 2600 Zen+, no AVX-512); the repo has no benchmark script, the OpenBLAS version is unstated, and the BLAS thread count for the REPL timings is not shown (the plots used BLAS.set_num_threads(6)). The lead is a small-to-medium size win (plots: OpenBLAS ahead at about 2x2 and beyond about 800 for Float64, 650 for Float32; Float32 is roughly level near 60-100), plausibly helped by OpenBLAS's threading overhead at small sizes (not measured). Different algorithm (recursive divide-and-conquer vs OpenBLAS's packed GEMM). Integer results compare with Julia's single-threaded generic matmul, not with C. The README calls Gaius unstable and unmaintained and points to Octavian.jl (already listed in wave 8) as the more performant pure-Julia BLAS; built on LoopVectorization.jl (also listed in wave 8). [retier] The numbers are 2020 blocked_mul! code on Julia 1.4.0-rc2 (commit 2892760); a later README edit made both REPL lines unqualified mul!, which Gaius does not export, so as written both call LinearAlgebra. The code has since been reworked (#57, #63, #83, #88); the covector _mul! takes k = 1, so v'*A is never blocked or threaded (#79 open); the complex adjoint path negates the input A in place. Issue #11: at n=9737 Gaius 5.516 s vs OpenBLAS 0.891 s.

No -O3, -march=native or -ffast-math. The checked-in disassembly shows scalar x86_64 code calling powf, expf and sqrtf from libm per element, with ljg_cpu2 calling dist3 through the PLT (not inlined); the aarch64 build unrolls 4 lanes but still calls powf and expf per lane. stars_or_usage: 2 stars (benchmark repo); the library JuliaGPU/AcceleratedKernels.jl has 203 stars
tradeoffs: Benchmark repo accompanies the AcceleratedKernels.jl paper; the Julia kernel code is not a reusable library.
caveats: Not like for like: the C code is built at -O2 without fast-math (wave 14 asks for -O3) and calls libm powf for the ^12 and ^6 terms and libm expf per element (confirmed in the checked-in .s files), while the Julia loop is compiled under @fastmath, where literal integer powers become multiplications and LLVM may vectorize exp; the repo's own 'C (hand-written powf)' row (ljg_cpu2, integer powers by multiplication) narrows the gap to 1.9x on M3 Max and 1.1x on Intel, and the remainder is plausibly fast-math vectorization (inference). Julia loses on the RBF kernel (318.35 vs 210.57 ms on M3 Max, 734.22 vs 641.26 ms on Intel). AcceleratedKernels.jl on CPU vs C OpenMP is parity. The repo has no README and makes no Julia-beats-C claim; the paper abstract (arXiv 2507.16710, snippet only, arXiv blocked here) says arithmetic kernels perform on par with C and OpenMP and that Julia is sometimes more consistent than conventional C compilers. Results also in ArithmeticBenchmarkTable.png and Benchmark.xlsx; the dataset is mirrored on IEEE DataPort (DOI 10.21227/94q9-p565, snippet only).

name: Julia Base sort! in LilithHafner/InterLanguageSortingComparisons
baseline: C++ std::sort on std::vector<double> (src/script.cpp, Apple clang 13 under the g++ name) and C qsort with a comparator callback (src/script.c), same suite
workload: Sorting-dominated workload: fill a vector of 3^i uniform random Float64 values, sort it, compute a dot product; the sorting time is inferred by subtracting a no-sort control run; ns per element for 3 to 3^15 elements.
claimed_speedup: data.txt at 3^14 = 4,782,969 elements, ns per element of sorting: Julia 1.9.0-beta3 35.1, Julia 1.8.5 92.5, C++ 207.6, C gcc 307.2, so Julia 1.9 is 5.9x and Julia 1.8 2.2x faster than C++ (derived from page data). README: 'Julia and Rust outperform other languages'.
compiler_and_flags: Commands recorded in data.txt: C 'gcc script.c' and C++ 'g++ -std=c++11 script.cpp', both Apple LLVM 13.0.0 (clang-1300.0.27.3) with no -O flag (-O0); Julia 1.9.0-beta3 and 1.8.5 with default settings; Rust 1.67.0 'cargo run --release'.
hardware: 2019 MacBook Air, 1.6 GHz dual-core Intel Core i5, 8 GB
tradeoffs: Algorithm difference: the AcceleratedKernels.jl README calls Julia's Base CPU sort a radix sort, unlike std::sort's introsort and the C qsort comparator version; Julia JIT warm-up is not in the per-element numbers.
caveats: Crippled baseline: the C and C++ programs were compiled without any optimization flag (-O0) while Rust used --release, so std::sort's templated comparisons run unoptimized and the 5.9x (Julia 1.9 vs C++) and 8.8x (Julia 1.9 vs C) figures are mostly a build artifact. The C++ figure is not a sort time: script.cpp prints total runtime (vector allocation, generation, sort and dot product) times a fixed 0.85 (comment says 0.8, label says 80%) instead of subtracting the no-sort control, and it stops at 3^14 (N = 14) while the other languages run to 3^15. script.cpp also constructs a fresh default-seeded std::default_random_engine for every vector, so all repetitions of one size sort identical data. The C row is qsort with a function-pointer comparator, a different algorithm from std::sort and from Julia's sort!. Each data point is a single trial (README says so). No LICENSE file (raw LICENSE and LICENSE.md requests returned 404; the repo page shows no license), so reference only. The repo owner works on Julia's Base sorting (general knowledge, not verified in this run), so the Julia side is close to first-party. A sorting-heavy workload rather than numerics proper.

why_faster: Not stated for C++; the README only says the benchmark isolates sorting speed. Julia's Base sort uses a different (radix-based) algorithm for Float64 at these sizes, inferred from the AcceleratedKernels README calling it a radix sort.

baseline: C version of userfunc_mandelbrot in the same suite (perf.c at the repo root at commit a963d28, now c/perf.c; C99 double complex). Built with gcc 7.3.1 -std=c99 -O$N for N = 0..3; bin/collect.jl keeps the minimum over all four builds and 5 runs each.
workload: JuliaLang Microbenchmarks userfunc_mandelbrot: escape-time iteration (maxiter 80, z = z*z + c) over a 21 x 26 grid of complex points, identical algorithm in every language, serial single core, best-of timing in ms, result checked against a sum of 14791.
hardware: Intel Core i7-3960X 3.30 GHz, 64 GB DDR3-1600, openSUSE LEAP 15.0, single core (from the julialang.org benchmarks page, seen only as a search snippet because the host did not resolve here)
