name: Julia in JuliaLang/Microbenchmarks: userfunc_mandelbrot
claimed_speedup: benchmarks.csv (Julia v1.0.0 era data): userfunc_mandelbrot C 0.076702 ms, Julia 0.052706 ms (1.46x faster than C, ratio 0.69 of C time, derived from page data). On the other benchmarks Julia takes 0.98x to 2.19x of C time: pi_sum 1.01, matrix_multiply 0.98 (both languages call OpenBLAS), quicksort 1.00, print_to_file 1.09, fibonacci 1.33, matrix_statistics 1.63, parse_integers 2.19 (derived).
compiler_and_flags: C: gcc 7.3.1 -std=c99 -O$N for N = 0..3 plus Julia's Make.inc CFLAGS, linked with OpenBLAS and openlibm; bin/collect.jl takes the best time over all levels and runs. No -march=native, no -ffast-math or -fcx-limited-range. Julia v1.0.0 default optimisation (-O2, JIT for the host CPU), compile time excluded. Compiler and Julia versions are from julialang.org/benchmarks (search snippet only).
tradeoffs: Julia is JIT compiled; the timings exclude compile time and Julia start-up. Only a micro benchmark of 546 grid points.
caveats: The only clear Julia win of the eight benchmarks: Julia is also nominally ahead on matrix_multiply (0.975 of C time, both call OpenBLAS) and recursion_quicksort (0.997), but those are ties (derived from page data). The data is from the Julia 1.0.0 era (gcc 7.3.1, 2012 CPU) and was added to the repo as 'add original benchmarks.csv data (#65)' in 2022. Current CI results sit on julialang.github.io (blocked here). The source gives no mechanism. Reading the code, the C version multiplies C99 double complex values (z*z+c) without -ffast-math or -fcx-limited-range. GCC then adds a NaN check after each complex multiply, with a __muldc3 recovery call on the slow path, as C99 Annex G requires. Julia's z^2 and Fortran's complex multiply use the plain formula without that check (GCC applies Fortran rules to gfortran). gfortran, which uses the same gcc 7.3.1 backend and the same algorithm, runs in 0.053836 ms, matching Julia's 0.052706 ms (derived from page data). That points to C's complex-arithmetic semantics rather than better Julia codegen. The C build has no -march=native, while Julia JITs for the host CPU; this probably does not matter here because the i7-3960X has no FMA. Both sides allocate the 21x26 result array on each call (C malloc/free, Julia comprehension). The Rust (0.75 of C time) and Go (0.78) rows of the same benchmark also beat C and are not recorded here.

name: llama2.mojo
baseline: llama2.c (karpathy/llama2.c, OpenMP build); also llama.cpp CPU
workload: CPU inference of llama2 models (TinyStories 15M/42M/110M and TinyLlama-1.1B) in tokens per second, multi-threaded.
claimed_speedup: README (last run 2026-09-12, Mojo 1.0.0, PR #102 build). Same-session 4 vCPU Intel Xeon Skylake AVX-512 VM: llama2.c OpenMP 4 threads 292/117/53/5.2 tok/s vs llama2.mojo -j 4 327/150/66/6.8 for stories15M/42M/110M/TinyLlama-1.1B (1.12x/1.28x/1.25x/1.31x, derived from page data); single-threaded llama2.c 105/40/16/1.7 vs llama2.mojo -j 1 154/54/22 (1.35-1.47x, derived from page data). upgradelog.md reports another run of the same build at -j 4 400/159/58 and -j 1 143/51/21 against the same llama2.c figures, and the author states +-10% run-to-run noise with both sides at the VM's ~20 GB/s memory-bandwidth ceiling. The Mac M1 Max table (llama2.mojo 1283/506/218 tok/s with 8 workers vs llama2.c 730/270/102 and llama.cpp 890/420/187) pairs a 2026 Mojo run with llama2.c and llama.cpp figures carried over unchanged from the Nov 2023 README (then labelled 6 threads, Mojo 1025/490/195), so its 1.8-2.1x ratio is cross-run. i7-8700 (2023 run): parity, 440 vs 435, 63 vs 64 and 7.25 vs 7.25 tok/s. The headline 'outperforms llama2.c by 30% ... llama.cpp by 20%' dates from the 2023 M1 Max figures.
compiler_and_flags: Mojo 1.0.0 (Modular 26.5) for the 2026-09 runs (the README now targets Mojo 1.1.0, whose threading change was not re-benchmarked); llama2.c compiler, flags and commit not stated for any table (upstream 'make runomp' is gcc -Ofast -fopenmp -march=native); llama.cpp version, build and model format not stated.
hardware: Apple M1 Max (Mojo column 2026 with 8 workers; llama2.c and llama.cpp columns from a Nov 2023 run with 6 threads); 4 vCPU Intel Xeon Skylake AVX-512 VM, Ubuntu 26.04 (same-session 2026 table); Intel Core i7-8700 3.2 GHz, Ubuntu 20.04 (2023 table).
tradeoffs: Needs the Mojo toolchain and MAX (parallelize), and tracks Mojo releases closely (updated for Mojo 1.1); single-file inference tool, not a general tensor library.
caveats: First-party numbers. The M1 Max headline table is a cross-run comparison: the llama2.c and llama.cpp columns are the Nov 2023 figures (6 threads) left unchanged when only the Mojo column was re-measured on 2026-09-12 with 8 workers, so its 1.8-2.1x ratio and the llama.cpp comparison are not valid evidence; the 2023 i7-8700 table shows parity. The valid same-session evidence is the Xeon Skylake 4 vCPU VM table: 1.12-1.31x at 4 threads (the author notes both sides sit at the VM's ~20 GB/s memory-bandwidth ceiling with +-10% noise, and another run in upgradelog.md shows 400 vs 292 tok/s on stories15M) and 1.35-1.47x single-threaded, with the llama2.c compiler, flags and commit unstated. Greedy output is byte-identical to llama2.c, so the work is the same. The multi-thread win comes from a persistent spin-barrier worker pool (31 barriers per token, per-worker redundant RMSNorm) against llama2.c's per-call OpenMP parallel for, and the single-thread win from tuned SIMD tiling (nelts), both reproducible in C; the optimisation was done by coding agents (agents-optimization.md). The Mojo 1.1 update (2026-09-19) replaced the TaskGroup pool with one max.algorithm.parallelize dispatch per forward pass and was not re-benchmarked. The linked engiware.com M1 Max comparison does not resolve (DNS failure) and arXiv 2502.01651 is blocked here, so no independent numbers were read.

The pairs are cross-session: in the last same-run measurement (2023-08-09, commit 19988eb) llama2.zig was 606 vs 548 (about 1.11x, derived from page data); the 660 came eight days later after page-aligning the weights, and the 463 was re-measured on 2023-08-17 while the 579 dates from 2023-08-15 or earlier.

why_faster: README: SIMD matrix multiplication with Zig @Vector (about 115 to 430 tok/s from that change alone), comptime-generated fused matmul, vector-aligned allocation and SIMD versions of other core functions.
tradeoffs: Single-threaded only, small models; Zig toolchain version moved from 0.11 dev to 0.16 (CI pinned in 2026) so the table predates current Zig.
caveats: First-party 2023 numbers on one CPU, single runs, gcc version unstated and neither the llama2.c nor the llama2.zig commit pinned (the figures predate the 2024 Zig 0.12/0.14 ports). The Aug 2, 2026 commits were not only CI: they changed the hot path (independent matmul accumulators, attention sums in registers, vectorised RMSNorm, Zig 0.16 port) without re-running the README benchmark, and the current matmul uses 8 or 4 independent vector accumulators, a different accumulator structure from llama2.c's loop; the measured 2023 code (9b225a2) used one vector accumulator per output row. Both sides of the -Ofast row are fast-math builds for the native ISA; the 5x gap to the -O3 row is not a fair comparison because without -ffast-math gcc cannot vectorise the dot-product reduction. The 20-25% win comes from explicit @Vector SIMD, comptime-fused q/k/v and w1/w3 matmuls sharing loads of x, and SIMD-aligned allocation, all doable in C with intrinsics. The README Todo says llama2.c is faster on ~100K-parameter models (expf cost; GCC much better than clang there), and llama2.c's OpenMP build is 2.4x faster than single-threaded llama2.zig. [retier] First-party 2023 numbers on one CPU, single runs, gcc version unstated and neither the llama2.c nor the llama2.zig commit pinned. The table is a cross-session composite: the llama2.c runfast row (548) was last re-run on 2023-08-09 (commit 19988eb), when llama2.zig measured 606 (about 1.11x); afterwards only the llama2.zig row was updated (612 on Aug 15, 656 on Aug 16, 660 on Aug 17), and the top-p row pairs a llama2.zig 579 from Aug 15 or earlier with a llama2.c 463 re-measured on Aug 17. The 2026-08-02 commits changed the hot path (independent matmul accumulators, attention sums in registers, vectorised RMSNorm, Zig 0.16 port) without re-running the benchmark, and the figures predate the 2024 Zig 0.12/0.14 ports. Multi-threaded llama2.c (make runomp) is not compared.

One machine, no run count, and a 1.17x edge that earlier read 1.07x at a different OpenMP thread count. It ports llm.c train_gpt2.c at 2d43e5b (May 2024); the README notes that upstream llm.c has since added register tiling to its CPU matmul, so the baseline is stale. The C compiler, flags and revision built are not stated (the commit message calls it the 'naive train_gpt2.c'). The numbers were measured on Mojo 1.0.0b2, not the 1.0.0 the repo now pins. A use-after-free in read_to_dtype_pointer (checkpoint loading, outside the timed loop) was fixed on 2026-08-13, after the benchmark. Mojo exposes only B=4-way parallelism in matmul_forward while C's OpenMP spreads B*T=256 rows over 10 threads, so the comparison mixes scheduling and codegen differences. The project's stated aim is matching C, and the gap is within what thread settings changed between runs. [retier] Harness asymmetry: llm.c train_gpt2.c at 2d43e5b runs AdamW, GELU, layernorm, residual, encoder, attention backward and cross-entropy single-threaded while the Mojo port parallelises all of them (its matmul_forward splits over only B=4), so the 1.17x step-time edge likely comes from parallel coverage. name: Yao.jl (Julia quantum circuit simulator) in Roger-luo/quantum-benchmarks
baseline: Qulacs 0.1.9 (C++ library driven from Python through pybind11, one Python call per gate or circuit) and QuEST via pyquest-cffi 0.1.1 (C library driven from Python through cffi, one Python call per gate), single-thread full-amplitude state-vector simulation
workload: Minimum time per gate application for X, H, CNOT and T gates on 4 to 25 qubits, and minimum time for a parameterized QCBM circuit (layers of per-qubit Rx/Rz rotations with ring CNOT entanglers) on 4 to 25 qubits, single thread (OMP/MKL/JULIA threads set to 1), Yao v0.6.1 per RESULTS.md (yao/Manifest.toml at the May 2020 refactor pins Yao 0.6.2 and YaoBlocks 0.10.3) against qulacs, QuEST (pyquest-cffi), qiskit-aer, ProjectQ, Cirq and PennyLane.
claimed_speedup: Read off the repo's 'relative to Yao' chart images images/gates_relative.png and images/pcircuit_relative.png (log scale, no tables; ratios approximate; bin/plot uses the minimum time for every package). Parameterized circuit (QCBM) at 25 qubits: qulacs about 1.9x and pyquest-cffi (QuEST) about 8x Yao's time; below about 11 qubits qulacs is faster than Yao (about 0.34x of Yao's time at 4 qubits). This circuit does unequal work: Yao makes 19n state-vector passes (each qubit's rotation chain fused into one 2x2 matrix, 8 mid layers, 9 entanglers) while qulacs and QuEST apply 41n separate gates (9 mid layers, 10 entanglers), a 2.16x pass ratio (derived from the benchmark scripts) that covers the whole qulacs gap. Single gates at 25 qubits (same work, one pass each): pyquest-cffi about 2.4x (X), 1.8x (H) and 2.5x (CNOT) Yao's time but about 0.75x on T (QuEST faster); qulacs about 1.0x on X, CNOT and T and about 0.6x on H (qulacs faster), and qulacs is faster than or equal to Yao on all four gates at most sizes between about 11 and 20 qubits (down to about 0.3x on H).
compiler_and_flags: Julia 1.3.0 (LLVM 6.0.1 ORCJIT, skylake target, run without -O flags so Julia's default -O2), BLAS Intel MKL, Python 3.7.3 (from RESULTS.md). Not stated on the results page, derived from package sources: qulacs 0.1.9 exists on PyPI only as an sdist, built by pip through its CMake Release config (CMake default -O3 -DNDEBUG plus -march=native -mtune=native -mfpmath=both, AVX2 SIMD kernels enabled by default, OpenMP limited to 1 thread by OMP_NUM_THREADS=1); pyquest-cffi 0.1.1 is an sdist that builds QuEST through QuEST's own CMake, which sets -O2 (QuEST v3.2.0 CMakeLists; the exact QuEST version bundled by pyquest-cffi 0.1.1 was not checked). GCC version not stated.
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6230 @ 2.10GHz (single thread); Tesla V100 for the CUDA rows
stars_or_usage: 1.0k stars and 131 forks (Yao.jl); the benchmark repo, now yardstiq/quantum-benchmarks (old Roger-luo URL redirects), has 129 stars
tradeoffs: Julia JIT start-up and compilation time is not part of the per-gate timings. Qulacs is faster on small circuits and the advantage of Yao appears only at 20 or more qubits.
caveats: First-party: the suite is written by Yao's author (reviewed by maintainers of several competitors per its acknowledgements). Results are marked 'only up to date till 2020'; the chart images were last regenerated on 2020-05-29 and the benchmark repo's last commit is 2022-05-17, with old package versions (qulacs 0.1.9, Julia 1.3.0). RESULTS.md and the README give only chart images, so every ratio is read off a log-scale chart. Unequal work in the parameterized circuit: YaoBlocks 0.10.3 PutBlock apply! calls instruct!(r, mat_matchreg(r, content), locs), so Yao's put(i=>chain(Rz, Rx, Rz)) is one dense 2x2 pass per qubit per layer, and Yao's build_circuit(k, 9, ...) has 8 mid layers and 9 entanglers where qulacs/QuEST build_circuit(n, 9, ...) has 9 and 10, giving 19n Yao passes against 41n qulacs/QuEST gate passes (2.16x); the reported 1.9x over qulacs is therefore not a per-gate or language win (qulacs' QuantumCircuitOptimizer gate fusion was not used). Single gates use different target qubits (Yao qubit 2 one-based, qulacs and QuEST qubit 3 zero-based) and Yao starts from rand_state while qulacs/QuEST start from |0>. qulacs and QuEST are timed through Python (pybind11 and cffi), so below about 10 qubits their numbers are dominated by Python call overhead; pyquest-cffi's QCBM function also calls np.random.rand inside the timed region. QuEST is built at -O2 (QuEST's CMake default) rather than -O3; qulacs is built at -O3 -march=native with AVX2 kernels and matches or beats Yao on single gates at large sizes. RESULTS.md's text calls panel d 'Toffolli' but the chart and bin/plot show the T gate; the relative charts label their y axis 'ns' though they plot ratios. The current quest/ directory holds a newer C++ google-benchmark harness (QFT only) that did not produce these charts. The baseline is not a C or C++ program at a stated -O3. [retier] The Yao QCBM uses zero angles Rx(0)/Rz(0) where other packages use random angles; YaoArrayRegister 0.6.2's dense 2x2 path has no identity check, so values differ but speed does not. JIT latency (issue #422).

C/C++ rows: GCC 16.0.1 20260322 (trunk r16-8246, Ubuntu build) and Clang 22.1.8. 'prod' (c/Makefile CFLAGS_PROD, cpp/Makefile CXXFLAGS_PROD): -O2 -DNDEBUG -fstack-protector-strong -fno-omit-frame-pointer, linked with -Wl,-z,relro,-z,now -Wl,--gc-sections. name: Futhark
baseline: Hand-written OpenCL reference implementations from Rodinia 3.1 (CUDA for Myocyte on NVIDIA), Parboil 2.5 (MRI-Q) and FinPar (LocVolCalib, OptionPricing); the four Accelerate benchmarks (Crystal, Fluid, Mandelbrot, N-body) were compared against Accelerate 0.15.1 (a Haskell DSL with a CUDA backend), not C/C++.
workload: 16 GPU benchmarks manually translated to Futhark (Rodinia Backprop, CFD, HotSpot, K-means, LavaMD, Myocyte, NN, Pathfinder, SRAD; FinPar LocVolCalib, OptionPricing; Parboil MRI-Q; Accelerate Crystal, Fluid, Mandelbrot, N-body), datasets in the paper's Table 2; runtime averaged over 10 runs, excluding input upload, result readback and OpenCL context creation and kernel build on both sides (Rodinia timing patched to match).
claimed_speedup: PLDI 2017 paper: from about 0.6x (slower, FinPar LocVolCalib on AMD W8100) to 16x (Rodinia NN on GTX 780 Ti) against hand-written OpenCL/CUDA reference implementations; geometric mean 1.81x over the 12 benchmarks that have a low-level CUDA/OpenCL implementation; Futhark slower on 4 of those 12 (geometric mean 0.79x on them). Table 1 runtimes on GTX 780 Ti, reference vs Futhark in ms: NN 178.9 vs 11.0, Backprop 46.9 vs 20.7, K-means 1597.7 vs 572.2, Myocyte 2733.6 vs 555.4 (CUDA reference), Pathfinder 18.4 vs 7.4, SRAD 19.9 vs 16.1, MRI-Q 20.2 vs 15.5, OptionPricing 136.0 vs 106.8; slower: CFD 1878.2 vs 2235.9, HotSpot 35.9 vs 45.3, LavaMD 5.1 vs 6.7, LocVolCalib 1211.1 vs 1293.2. Artifact W8100 speedup files: srad 5.60, nn 5.14, hotspot 3.58, backprop 3.21, pathfinder 2.77, lavaMD 1.25, mri-q 1.24, OptionPricing 1.19, cfd 0.86, kmeans 0.79, LocVolCalib 0.62.
compiler_and_flags: Futhark compiler git 78c956ba58057ca6773cefb466efef2fa65c1386 with the OpenCL backend and no benchmark-specific flags; references built by their own suite Makefiles with gcc/g++ (-lOpenCL) and nvcc (CUDA 8.0 on NVIDIA). The paper and artifact state no host compiler versions or optimisation flags; Rodinia OpenCL Makefiles in the yuhc/gpu-rodinia mirror use g++ -g -O2 (backprop) and -g -O3 (nn). GPU kernels on both sides are compiled by the vendor OpenCL driver.
hardware: NVIDIA GeForce GTX 780 Ti with CUDA 8.0 and AMD FirePro W8100 (OpenCL benchmarks only); host CPU not stated.
stars_or_usage: 2.8k stars, 210 forks; futhark-benchmarks 48 stars; futhark-pldi17 artifact 8 stars
tradeoffs: Purely functional ML-family language; programs are rewritten in Futhark and called from C, Python or other hosts through generated code; sequential/irregular code does not fit.
caveats: The wins are mostly not a language-level effect: the paper attributes them to the hand-written references leaving work unoptimised, namely Rodinia NN leaving 100 reduce operations sequential on the CPU, Backprop leaving a reduction sequential, K-means not parallelising the cluster-centre update, and Myocyte/MRI-Q lacking coalescing or locality optimisation; the authors say the 0.79x geometric mean on the 4 slower benchmarks is 'a better estimation of where Futhark stands in relation to hand-optimised GPU code'. HotSpot and Pathfinder references use time tiling that Futhark lacks. Same benchmarks but different parallelisation strategies, so same_algorithm is false for the large speedups (NN 16x, Backprop, K-means, Myocyte). Accelerate rows compare against a Haskell DSL, not C. Timings exclude transfer and kernel build on both sides. Numbers are from 2017 Futhark on 2013-2014 GPUs; the C and multicore CPU backends are not compared against C here, and futhark-benchmarks itself publishes no results. futhark-website performance.md compares against Thrust and Rodinia HotSpot only as graphs, without numbers or hardware in the text. A 2026 arXiv snippet (seen only by the search agent) reports big-integer multiplication about 1.35x slower than hand-coded CUDA. Paper PDF: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/diku-dk/futhark-website/HEAD/publications/pldi17.pdf. [retier] Harness flaws in futhark-pldi17 (code reading): the K-means Rodinia timer wraps cluster(), whose allocate() in the yuhc/gpu-rodinia copy creates a new OpenCL context, builds kmeans.cl and uploads the features on every run although the paper says those were excluded (W8100 reference runs: first 1876.9 ms, rest 1128.7-1154.6 ms; the GTX 2.79x has no per-run data); the NN patch raises Rodinia's -r 5 to -r 100, growing the sequential CPU top-k work 20x, so the 16x headline rests on that parameter. lavaMD sleeps 3 s between timed reference runs; Myocyte is a CUDA reference against Futhark OpenCL.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/futhark; github.com/orgs/diku-dk/repositories

Main shortcoming for the orchestrator: the large speedups come from under-optimised Rodinia references (sequential CPU reductions in NN and Backprop, an unparallelised K-means update), and the authors themselves estimate 0.79x against hand-optimised GPU code, so same_algorithm is false and this is not a language win; consider whether the NN and Backprop rows fall under the crippled-baseline precedent. name: .NET 11 preview JIT (C#): benchLANG binary trees vs C and C++ at -O3
baseline: C (GCC 16.2.0: gcc -O3 -march=native -flto -funroll-loops -ffp-contract=off) and C++ (g++ -std=c++20 with the same flags) binary-trees programs that allocate every node with malloc/free (C) or new/delete (C++)
workload: CLBG-style binary trees, depths 4 to 18: allocate, traverse and (in native code) free complete binary trees of individually allocated nodes; the README says the workload measures allocator plus GC plus pointer chasing, with native frees inside the timer and GC runtimes collecting when they like.
claimed_speedup: C# (.NET SDK 11.0.100-preview.7) 0.931 s vs C 1.010 s and C++ 1.147 s: about 1.08x faster than C and 1.23x faster than C++ (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: C: gcc 16.2.0 -O3 -march=native -flto -funroll-loops -ffp-contract=off -s; C++: g++ 16.2.0 -std=c++20 with the same flags (nixpkgs-unstable pins, run_benchmarks.sh). C#: .NET SDK 11.0.100-preview.7, built as a file-based app with dotnet build -c Release -o out Program.cs (no .csproj in the repo) and run as dotnet out/Program.dll (default tiered JIT and default GC, no Native AOT).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X locked at 3.5 GHz (cpupower performance governor, min and max 3500 MHz), 48 GB DDR4-3600 CL16, Arch Linux
why_faster: Source (README workload note): native code frees every node inside the timed region while GC runtimes collect when they like. Likely mechanism (inference): bump-pointer allocation in the runtime and deferred or concurrent reclamation against glibc malloc and free per node.
tradeoffs: Whole-process peak RSS 122.1 MiB for C# vs 33.3 MiB for C; Fibonacci(45) takes 3.793 s vs 1.694 s for C.
caveats: One run per language (no variance) from a single machine on 2026-09-03. The C and C++ programs are naive per-node malloc/free (new/delete in C++) and walk every tree a second time to free it inside the timer, while the .NET GC never traces dead trees; an arena or pool allocator in C would beat the runtimes here. The native malloc-based rows for the same algorithm already spread from 0.986 s (Fortran) through 1.010 s (C), 1.033 s (Rust), 1.109 s (Ada) and 1.119 s (Zig) to 1.147 s (C++), so the 8% C# margin over C lies inside the run-to-run and implementation spread of one algorithm; the 1.23x figure is against the slowest of those rows. Several runtimes beat C on this workload in the same table (Java 0.347 s, Nim 0.809 s, Bun 0.816 s, OCaml and Dart 0.865 s), which points at glibc per-node malloc/free rather than a .NET-specific code-generation win. The benchmark is 1 of 5 workloads, and C wins overall (total 9.762 s vs Java 13.536 s, C# 11.914 s, OCaml 16.233 s; C is faster than C# on Fibonacci 1.694 s vs 3.793 s, strings 2.132 s vs 2.235 s and Mandelbrot 2.201 s vs 2.229 s). Managed runtimes keep default settings with JIT warm-up inside the timed region and may use extra GC and JIT threads, so wall time is not CPU time; .NET 11 was a preview SDK.

name: Bun (JavaScriptCore JIT 1.3.13): benchLANG binary trees
baseline: C (GCC 16.2.0, malloc and free per node, 1.010 s) and C++ (GCC 16.2.0, new and delete per node, 1.147 s)
workload: CLBG-style binary trees in one process after four other workloads: a stretch tree of depth 19, a long-lived tree of depth 18, then 2^(22-d) short-lived trees for each even depth d from 4 to 18, each built and checked; C and C++ free every tree with a recursive free pass (malloc/free or new/delete per node) inside the timer, the JS version just drops the references (no free pass).
claimed_speedup: JS (Bun) 0.816 s vs C 1.010 s and C++ 1.147 s: about 1.24x faster than C and 1.41x faster than C++ (derived from page data). JS (Node v26.8.1) is slower at 1.444 s. Peak RSS 336.1 MiB for Bun vs 33.3 MiB for C.
compiler_and_flags: C: gcc -O3 -march=native -flto -funroll-loops -ffp-contract=off -s (GCC 16.2.0); C++: g++ -std=c++20 with the same flags. JS (Bun) 1.3.13: bun run directly, JIT default (no flags).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X locked at 3.5 GHz (performance governor), 48 GB DDR4-3600 CL16, Arch Linux with i3-wm; results dated 3 September 2026, one run per language
why_faster: Stated by the suite's methodology: 'Binary trees: ... Allocator + GC + pointer chase, native code frees inside the timer, GC runtimes collect when they like'. Agent inference: per-node malloc/free (C, C++) against bump-pointer allocation and deferred or concurrent collection in a managed runtime; the C/C++ programs do not use an arena.
tradeoffs: 10x the peak memory of C; other columns are much slower than C (fib 7.735 s vs 1.694 s).
caveats: One run per language ('1 run/lang'), no variance. In-program wall times from a monotonic clock: JIT warm-up is inside the managed runtimes' timed region, but their garbage collection can run partly after the timer stops ('GC runtimes collect when they like'), while C/C++ pay an extra recursive free traversal inside the timer. The column is an allocator benchmark, not a codegen one: Java 0.347 s, Nim 0.809 s, Dart AOT 0.865 s, OCaml 0.865 s, C# 0.931 s and Fortran 0.986 s also beat C's 1.010 s, so per-node glibc malloc/free is the bottleneck and an arena or pool allocator in C/C++ would likely beat every managed runtime (compare the Arena variant in LangArena, where C wins by about 6x). Only the binary-trees column is a Bun win: on primes, fib, strings and mandelbrot Bun loses to C (total 16.732 s vs 9.762 s). Bun's peak RSS is 336.1 MiB vs 33.3 MiB for C. Bun's win is modest (about 1.24x) and rests on one run; Node v26.8.1 is slower than C (1.444 s). The earlier caveat about an 'Updated May 2026' header no longer applies: the current README says results are from September 2026.

name: C# (Staged) on .NET: Brainfuck bench.b in kostya/benchmarks
baseline: C++/g++ brainfuck (brainfuck/bf.cpp): an AST-walking interpreter with std::vector ops, g++ -O3 -march=native -flto
workload: Run the bench.b Brainfuck program; the staged C# version builds a closed generic type per Brainfuck program (static abstract interface members, ref structs) and lets RyuJIT compile it, inside the timed region.
claimed_speedup: bench.b: C# (Staged)/.NET Core 0.373 s (36.62 + 0.25 MiB, 14.33 J) vs C++/g++ 1.097 s (3.38 MiB, 46.21 J), C/gcc 1.112 s, C/clang 1.136 s, C++/clang++ 1.167 s (about 2.9x vs g++, derived from page data). The non-staged C#/.NET Core interpreter takes 1.280 s, slower than C++/g++.
compiler_and_flags: C++ baseline: g++ 16.1.0 -O3 -march=native -flto=auto -Wa,-mbranches-within-32B-boundaries -std=c++23 (common/commands.mk GCC_CPP_BUILD); clang++ 22.1.8 row uses the same flags plus -stdlib=libc++; C rows -std=c23. C# (Staged): .NET 10.0.100, dotnet build -c Release, root Directory.Build.props sets TieredCompilation=false (every method JIT-compiled once at full optimisation, no tier-0 or dynamic PGO), ServerGarbageCollection=true, ConcurrentGarbageCollection=true; RyuJIT targets the host CPU at run time.
hardware: Intel Xeon E-2324G (README Environment section); Debian forky/sid Docker image
tradeoffs: Run-time compile inside the process: needs the .NET JIT and about 36 MiB resident versus about 3.4 MiB for the C++ interpreter; wins only for programs long enough to amortize compilation.
caveats: Different algorithm: the C++ baseline (brainfuck/bf.cpp) interprets a vector<Op> AST instruction by instruction, as brainfuck/README.md requires of every implementation ('interprets all bf instructions, one by one, without any squash or other hacks'), while the staged C# variant compiles the Brainfuck program to native code at run time (type construction and JIT inside the timed region), so it is listed as a separate '(Staged)' row. No C++ counterpart that also specializes on the program (template staging, LLVM ORC or asmjit, a BF-to-C compiler) was benchmarked, so the result shows runtime specialization beating an interpreter, not the .NET runtime beating C++ at the same work. The plain C# interpreter in the same suite is slower than C++/g++. The staged tape is a byte array with != 0 loop tests, the C++ tape a vector<int> with > 0 tests (outputs agree by checksum). The staged variant was contributed by hez2010 in PR #511 (merged 2025-11-17). It uses about 11x the memory of the C++ row (36.9 vs 3.38 MiB). Results are medians from one suite run on one machine (Xeon E-2324G), timed between libnotify start and stop messages, so process start-up is excluded for every language.

name: ClangJIT (Clang with JIT extensions for C++ templates)
baseline: The same Eigen expression (m = Ones + 0.00005*(m + m*m)) compiled ahead of time with runtime-sized Matrix<T,Dynamic,Dynamic> and float/double/long double dispatch, by the same Clang at -march=native -ffast-math -O3; the wiki also reports an AoT build specialized for one fixed size, which matches the JIT.
workload: Eigen bench/benchmark.cpp adapted: 40,000,000 repeats of small dense matrix operations; AoT runtime-sized matrices versus JIT-instantiated fixed-size matrices for sizes 3, 7 and 16, JIT compile time excluded from the runtime rows.
claimed_speedup: Runtime, double, 40,000,000 repeats, times reported by the code (JIT compile time excluded): size 3 JIT 1.0 s vs AoT dynamic-size 8.05 s vs AoT single fixed-size specialization 1.01 s; size 7 JIT 8.34 s vs AoT 20 s vs single specialization 8.45 s; size 16 JIT 35.3 s vs AoT 36.2 s vs single specialization 35.1 s (about 8x, 2.4x and 1.03x over dynamic-size AoT and parity with size-specialized AoT, derived from page data). Compile time (user): JIT only 3.5 s vs AoT double only 5.3 s and AoT float/double/long double with dispatch 9.7 s; one fixed-size specialization 2.95-4.95 s; includes and main only 2.58 s.
compiler_and_flags: ClangJIT (Clang fork, -fjit, [[clang::jit]] attribute) with -march=native -ffast-math -O3 on both sides per the wiki; the Clang used was built with GCC 8.2.0 in CMake RelWithDebInfo mode. Eigen version, ClangJIT commit and the benchmark's main() are not given.
hardware: Xeon E5-2699 (exact variant not stated)
tradeoffs: Needs a custom Clang/LLVM fork (not upstream); the program links the compiler infrastructure and compiles templates at run time (JIT start-up cost, memory, requires source or serialized AST available at run time); restrictions on decltype(auto), explicit specializations and pointer arguments listed on the wiki; the WG21 proposal P1609 for [[jit]] has not been adopted.
caveats: The run-time win is over Eigen's dynamic-size code path; the wiki's 'single specialization' AoT rows (1.01 s, 8.45 s, 35.1 s) equal the JIT rows, so JIT code is no faster than AoT C++ -O3 code that knows the size; the real advantage is lower compile time than instantiating many sizes or types ahead of time. JIT compile time is excluded from the runtime rows. First-party wiki, single runs without variance, CPU generation of the Xeon E5-2699 not stated, Eigen version not stated, main() omitted from the listings. The SC19 P3HPC paper (arXiv 1904.08555) was not reachable (arxiv.org, open-std.org P1609R0 and deepai blocked), so only the wiki was checked. Clang fork, last commit 2019-12-30. It is C++ with a JIT extension rather than another language, so it could also sit beside Easy::jit in wave 12 jits. [retier] JIT compile time is excluded and never reported; issue #31 measured about 93 ns of dispatch per call of a cached JIT function (global mutex plus argument hashing), hidden by calling once with the loop inside; the result is never consumed; single run; the AoT size-specialised build ties the JIT at every size. Open crash issues #17, #25, #28; LLVM 9.0 base.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Clang-JIT C++ template instantiation at runtime speedup over ahead-of-time compiled code paper github' surfaced arXiv 1904.08555 and P1609; repo wiki then opened on github.com.
why_faster: Runtime values (matrix dimensions) become template arguments instantiated at run time, so the optimizer sees fixed sizes and can unroll and vectorize; only the sizes actually used are compiled (wiki: 'performance benefits of many AoT specializations, sometimes better, at a low compile-time cost').

name: dotnet JIT (C# on .NET 11): LangArena Distance::NGram
baseline: C++ using std::unordered_map<uint32_t,int> for 4-gram counts (g++ 16, clang++ 22); best C/C++ configuration is C++/Clang++/PGO at 0.822 s
workload: Count 4-gram frequencies of many generated string pairs in two hash maps and compute the n-gram overlap score.
claimed_speedup: C#/JIT 0.516 s vs C++/G++ 0.863 s and C++/Clang++ 0.877 s (prod, -O2). The best of the 16 gcc/clang C and C++ configurations is C++/Clang++/PGO at 0.822 s (C++/G++/Fast at -O3 0.85 s), so C# is about 1.67x faster than C++/G++ prod and 1.59x faster than the best row (derived from page data). Other .NET rows also win, including NativeAOT builds with no JIT: C#/SC-JIT 0.475 s, C#/R2R 0.526 s, C#/AOT 0.609 s. F#/JIT 0.534 s and Julia/Default 0.58 s also win. Java/OpenJDK at 2.072 s is slower, and the C version (uthash, one malloc per distinct gram) is slower still: best C/Clang/Fast 1.789 s, C/Clang prod 1.811 s. The timed loop is 100 iterations over 10 string pairs (lengths 4 to 20,003 over a 10-letter alphabet), after 20 untimed warm-up iterations.
compiler_and_flags: C/C++ (cpp/Makefile, c/Makefile; versions from the results file): Clang 22.1.8 and GCC 16.0.1 20260322 (trunk, Ubuntu package build), libstdc++ (no -stdlib flag). 'prod' (headline rows): -O2 -DNDEBUG -fstack-protector-strong -fno-omit-frame-pointer, -std=c++20 for C++. 'Fast': -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -DNDEBUG -pipe -fstack-protector -ftree-vectorize -funroll-loops. 'Unsafe': -O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG -pipe -fno-stack-protector -fomit-frame-pointer -ffast-math -fvisibility=hidden -fno-common -fstrict-overflow -fno-trapping-math. 'PGO': -O2 plus -fprofile-instr-use (Clang) or -fprofile-use (GCC). -flto=thin (Fast) and -flto=full (Unsafe) are passed only on the link line (LDFLAGS) while objects are compiled without -flto, so no link-time optimisation actually takes place. Managed side: dotnet 11.0.100-rc.1.26425.128, 'dotnet build -c Release' (Optimize=true) run as 'dotnet Benchmark.dll' with default tiered JIT; the C#/AOT rows are NativeAOT with IlcInstructionSet=native and IlcOptimizationPreference=Speed; Julia 1.13.1 run as 'julia --project=. --threads=16 benchmark.jl' (Julia/Max adds -O3 --check-bounds=no --math-mode=fast); Temurin OpenJDK 27+35 run as 'java -Xmx2g -jar'. Every language, C and C++ included, runs untimed warm-up iterations (20 percent of the timed count) before the timed loop.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X 8-Core Processor, 78GB RAM, x86_64 Linux (results file 2026-10-05, host kostya-ms7c37)
why_faster: Inferred from the sources, not stated by the suite: .NET Dictionary<uint,int> keeps entries in flat arrays, while libstdc++ std::unordered_map allocates a node per distinct key, and each string pair builds two maps. This is a container-implementation effect rather than JIT code quality.
tradeoffs: C# peak RSS about 41 MB. .NET 11 is a release candidate (11.0.100-rc.1) in this run.
caveats: This is a container comparison more than a JIT one. .NET NativeAOT builds with no JIT (C#/AOT 0.609 s, C#/SC-AOT 0.61 s) also beat every C/C++ row, so the runtime-jit-beats-aot category fits poorly. The C++ side uses node-based std::unordered_map<uint32_t,int>, reserved to the string length, with the default identity hash and prime-modulo buckets. An open-addressing map would likely close the gap. The C version (uthash with one malloc per distinct gram) is about 2x slower than the C++ one. The C# side does slightly more work: Encoding.ASCII.GetBytes copies both strings on every call. Every language, C and C++ included, runs untimed warm-up iterations (20 percent of the timed count, cpp/src/benchmark.cpp and csharp/BenchmarkBase.cs) before the timed loop, so steady state is compared on both sides; the record's statement that only JIT languages get a warm-up was wrong. -flto appears only on the link line in cpp/Makefile, so the 'Fast' and 'Unsafe' rows get no actual LTO (the hot code sits in one translation unit, so this is probably immaterial). Java does not share the win, so this is not a general JIT property. One measurement per test and configuration (no variance). LangArena's README calls it 'a subjective benchmark' and says AI tools helped translate the tests between languages. Rows were selected as tests where a managed-runtime row beats every C/C++ row; most tests go the other way (for example Sort::Quick, Sort::Merge and Binarytrees::Arena). Ratios are derived from the results file, not stated by the suite.
found_via: GitHub: kostya/benchmarks README links to LangArena; parsed results/2026-10-05-kostya-ms7c37.js for tests where a Java, C# or Julia row is faster than every Clang/GCC C and C++ row

name: DSL-JSON (Java, HotSpot) vs nlohmann/json, json-c and Boost.PropertyTree in kostya/benchmarks JSON
baseline: nlohmann/json (C++), json-c (C library called from a C++ driver) and Boost.PropertyTree (C++) as built by kostya/benchmarks; DSL-JSON does NOT beat RapidJSON (all variants incl. SAX Precise), Boost.JSON, simdjson, yyjson, yajl, gason or DAW JSON Link in the same table
workload: Parse a generated 524,288-object JSON file (generate_json.rb: x, y, z doubles plus name and opts fields, pretty-printed) and compute the mean of x, y and z; the README reports median time of the benchmark execution (data loading and code self-testing are not measured).
claimed_speedup: Time in seconds (lower is better), from the kostya/benchmarks README Json table (median of runs, UPDATE: 2026-07-19): Java (DSL-JSON) 0.571; C++/clang++ (Nlohmann) 1.182; C++/g++ (Nlohmann) 1.266; C++/clang++ (json-c) 1.185; C++/g++ (json-c) 1.187; C++/clang++ (Boost.PropertyTree) 2.589; C++/g++ (Boost.PropertyTree) 2.907. That is about 2.1-2.2x faster than Nlohmann and json-c, 4.5-5.1x faster than Boost.PropertyTree (derived from page data). In the same table it is slower than C++/g++ (simdjson On-Demand) 0.060, C++/clang++ (DAW JSON Link NoCheck) 0.070, C++/clang++ (simdjson DOM) 0.103, C++/g++ (gason) 0.127, C/gcc (yyjson) 0.131, C++/g++ (RapidJSON) 0.154, C/gcc (yajl) 0.362, C++/g++ (Boost.JSON) 0.374 and C++/clang++ (RapidJSON SAX Precise) 0.500.
compiler_and_flags: C++ built with g++ 16.1.0 (-std=c++23) and clang++ 22.1.8 (-std=c++23 -stdlib=libc++), both with -Wall -Wextra -pedantic -Wcast-align -O3 -march=native -flto=auto -Wa,-mbranches-within-32B-boundaries (common/commands.mk); nlohmann/json is a depth-1 git clone of HEAD (version not pinned) used as the single header; json-c is the Debian libjson-c-dev package linked with -ljson-c, so the json-c library itself is a distribution build, not compiled with the suite's -O3 -march=native flags. Java side: DSL-JSON 2.0.2 (json/json-java/Maven.list, fetched with coursier) compiled by json/json-java/Makefile with plain 'javac -proc:full' (annotation processor generates the converter; the --release 26 flag of common/commands.mk JAVAC_BUILD is not used by this test), run as 'java -cp <fat jar> bench.TestJava' with no JVM flags (HotSpot defaults). The README Environment table lists Java 24.0.2, while the current docker/Dockerfile pins JDK 26.0.1, so the exact JDK of the 2026-07-19 run is ambiguous.
hardware: Intel(R) Xeon(R) E-2324G (README Environment section; Docker on Debian forky/sid); README results marked UPDATE: 2026-07-19
tradeoffs: Fast path needs compile-time databinding (annotation processor generates converters for @CompiledJson classes); the reflection variant is described as only comparable to Jackson. JVM warm-up and heap are part of the cost: the table shows 277.81 MiB base + 163.69 MiB peak increase for Java versus 113.33 + 447.88 MiB for g++ nlohmann and 113.21 + 123.44 MiB for g++ RapidJSON.
caveats: Beats only the slow C/C++ JSON libraries; the fast ones (simdjson, DAW JSON Link, gason, yyjson, RapidJSON, yajl, Boost.JSON, RapidJSON SAX Precise) are about 1.1-9.5x faster than it in the same table (derived from page data), so this is not Java beating the C/C++ incumbent for fast JSON. Work is not identical: the Java test deserialises straight into generated Root/Coordinate classes that declare only coordinates and x, y, z (name, opts and info are skipped, not materialised) with JsonReader.DoublePrecision.LOW (reduced number-parsing accuracy), while the nlohmann test builds a full DOM (std::map objects, std::string keys and values) and calls get<double>. The C++ timed window also includes destruction of the nlohmann DOM when calc returns, whereas Java leaves its objects to the GC; the json-c driver never frees its tree. JIT warm-up is not separated: the self-test calls calc twice on tiny inputs, so the timed run is a single cold-ish parse (this hurts Java, not the baselines). Results are printed but not cross-checked between languages. json-c is a Debian prebuilt library. The README says implementations are written 'as the average software developer would write them'. The DSL-JSON README cites this benchmark only as 'fastest performing Java JSON library' and makes no C++ comparison; its FAQ explanation of speed is the library author's own. JDK version ambiguous (README table Java 24.0.2, Dockerfile JDK 26.0.1). [retier] From the 2.0.2 source (commit d1f7a8d): DoublePrecision.LOW only raises the fast-path limit to 19 characters, so the x and y fields (about 21-22 characters, exponent form) still go through exact Double.parseDouble and only z takes the approximate path; the kostya README flags reduced-precision C++ variants but not this one, and nothing cross-checks output. Released 2.0.2 throws AIOOBE in approximateDouble on 2E15 (#283), fixed only on unreleased master; XXE report #296. RapidJSON SAX Precise is still faster (0.433-0.500 s vs 0.571).
found_via: Blogs / talks slice. WebSearch (github.com, 'benchmark repo C# .NET OR Java OR Julia OR LuaJIT OR SBCL outperforms C++ clang -O3 ...') did not name it; found by parsing every JIT-language row of the kostya/benchmarks README Json, Base64, Matmul and Primes tables against the best C/C++ rows. Only the Json table has managed-runtime rows ahead of any C/C++ library.
why_faster: From the DSL-JSON README FAQ: almost zero allocations, works on byte level, better algorithms for byte[] to type conversion, minimized unexpected branching, and compile-time databinding (generated converters) instead of reflection.

name: HotSpot Java Math.sin/% loop vs C libm sin/fmod at gcc -O3: xemantic/java-2-times-faster-than-c
baseline: C loop calling libm sin() and fmod() (src/main/c/almost_pseudo_random.c) built with gcc -O3 -lm; the README's 'Clang' row again comes from a gcc build
workload: Sum fmod(sin(i * 100000.0) + 1.0, 1.0) for 1,000,000,000 iterations (a trigonometry-based pseudo-random function from The Book of Shaders).
claimed_speedup: Java 51.235 s vs GCC C 1 m 4.433 s and 'Clang' C 1 m 4.878 s (real time, one run each): about 1.26x faster than gcc C (derived from page data). Contributed Go finished in 28.191 s (faster than both), Rust in 1 m 7.944 s.
compiler_and_flags: C: gcc -O3 -lm with no -ffast-math (build-gcc.sh); compiler and glibc versions not stated. Java: Gradle build with source level 15, default JVM flags.
hardware: Intel Core i7-8550U @ 1.80GHz (4 cores, 8 threads), about 16 GB RAM (README /proc/cpuinfo dump)
why_faster: Author cannot fully explain it and lists hypotheses: HotSpot inlines aggressively after profiling, C math functions come from a library and cannot be inlined, and Java's % operator on doubles may map to better machine code.
tradeoffs: Measures the speed of the runtime's sin and floating-point remainder implementation against glibc's, not general code generation; JVM start-up and memory not compared.
caveats: One run per implementation (shell 'time') on a laptop CPU without frequency locking; gcc, glibc and JDK versions not stated (Gradle targets Java 15, and the README mentions 'the newest JVM of Java 15'). The 'Clang' row was built by build-clang.sh, which calls gcc. The loop spends nearly all its time in sin(): arguments reach 1e14, far outside the fast range of both libraries, so the gap measures two sin implementations rather than language code generation. Issue #13 (2025-06-12) profiles the repo's C ring program with gprof and finds glibc's large-argument reduction __branred at 47.88% and __sin_fma at 17.32% of run time. Java's Math.sin is a HotSpot intrinsic generated from Intel LIBM assembly (current openjdk master stubGenerator_x86_64_sin.cpp, main path only for |x| < 90112); the 2021 JDK build was not checked. Rust, which also calls glibc sin, took 1m7.944s (about C's time), and Go, with its own sin and slightly different results (checksum 4.999999924931206e+08), took 28.191 s. The Java checksum prints as 4.9999999712235045E8 against 499999997.122350 for C (same value to the printed digits). gcc ran without -ffast-math or -fno-math-errno, so sin and fmod stay library calls, which matches Java's strict semantics.

name: HotSpot Java ring-of-nodes mutation vs C at gcc -O3: xemantic/java-2-times-faster-than-c
baseline: C ring-of-nodes program (src/main/c/java_2_times_faster_than_c.c, malloc and free per node and per payload) built with gcc -O3; the README's 'Clang' row comes from build-clang.sh, which actually invokes gcc
workload: Build a ring of 10,000 nodes with a pseudo-random payload of 0-49 bytes, then run 1,000,000 mutations that each delete and insert up to 200 nodes; node count and checksum are identical in every implementation.
claimed_speedup: Java (HotSpot) 8.569 s vs GCC C 12.800 s and 'Clang' (actually gcc) C 12.726 s (real time, one run each): about 1.49x faster than C (derived from page data). The project title claims 2x and the README dialogue says 'almost 2 times faster'; the measured ratio is about 1.5x.
compiler_and_flags: C: gcc -O3 -lm (build-gcc.sh); build-clang.sh also calls gcc -O3, not clang; compiler and glibc versions not stated. Java: Gradle build with source and target level 15, run as java -cp build/classes/java/main with default JVM flags (JDK build not stated).
hardware: Intel Core i7-8550U @ 1.80GHz (4 cores, 8 threads), about 16 GB RAM (README /proc/cpuinfo dump)
why_faster: Author's hypothesis: certain algorithms gain performance just from being expressed with automatic memory management, because the C version pays a malloc and a free per node and per payload while the JVM allocates and reclaims in bulk. The README adds that better memory management in C (issue #1) can beat the Java version.
tradeoffs: JVM needs a runtime and has higher memory use (not measured in the README). The C version could be sped up with a pool or arena allocator, which the author deliberately did not add.
caveats: One run per implementation measured with the shell 'time' on a laptop CPU without frequency locking (no variance). gcc, glibc and JDK versions are not stated (Gradle targets Java 15), the C build has no -march=native while the JIT targets the host CPU, and the 'Clang' row was built with gcc by build-clang.sh. A large share of the C time is libm, not memory management: issue #13 (2025-06-12) profiles this C program with gprof and finds glibc's large-argument sin reduction __branred at 47.88% and __sin_fma at 17.32% of run time, against about 13% for malloc, _int_malloc, _int_free and free together; every new node and every mutation count calls sin() on arguments up to about 1e13, and the second benchmark in the repo shows HotSpot's sin faster than glibc's (Java 51.2 s vs C 64.4 s for 1e9 calls). The C version pays two malloc and two free calls per node (node and payload, including malloc(0) for empty payloads) where the JVM bump-allocates and never traces dead nodes; the author calls the title provocative, says it applies only to this algorithm, and notes that better memory management in C (issue #1, where one commenter's one-slot reuse cut a run from 1m7s to 14s, no Java figure) can beat the Java version. Contributed Rust (13.824 s, glibc sin) was slower than C; Go (14.542 s) ran different work (node count 13553, checksum 486105193130, because its sin differs); C# took 34.037 s.

name: Julia 1.13: LangArena Sort::Self (built-in sort vs std::sort)
baseline: std::sort on std::vector<int32_t> (g++ 16, clang++ 22); best C/C++ configuration is C++/G++ prod at 0.982 s
workload: Copy a large array of random 32-bit integers and sort it with each language's built-in sort (std::sort, Arrays.sort, Julia sort!).
claimed_speedup: Julia/Default 0.116 s vs C++/G++ 0.982 s (prod -O2, also the best of the 16 gcc/clang C and C++ configurations), C++/G++/Fast at -O3 0.998 s and C++/Clang++ 1.022 s: about 8.5x (derived from page data). Java/OpenJDK at 0.187 s is about 5.3x faster than std::sort (derived). C# Array.Sort at 1.057 s is slightly slower. The C rows use qsort with a comparison callback (best C/mycc/LLVM/Default 1.957 s, C/Gcc/Fast 1.964 s). The timed loop is 50 sorts of a copied 400,000-element array after 10 untimed warm-up sorts. The suite's same-algorithm sorts show no managed-runtime win: Sort::Quick Julia/Default 1.307 s vs C/Gcc 1.15 s, and Sort::Merge Julia/Default 1.602 s vs C/Clang 1.09 s.
compiler_and_flags: C/C++ (cpp/Makefile, c/Makefile; versions from the results file): Clang 22.1.8 and GCC 16.0.1 20260322 (trunk, Ubuntu package build), libstdc++ (no -stdlib flag). 'prod' (headline rows): -O2 -DNDEBUG -fstack-protector-strong -fno-omit-frame-pointer, -std=c++20 for C++. 'Fast': -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -DNDEBUG -pipe -fstack-protector -ftree-vectorize -funroll-loops. 'Unsafe': -O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG -pipe -fno-stack-protector -fomit-frame-pointer -ffast-math -fvisibility=hidden -fno-common -fstrict-overflow -fno-trapping-math. 'PGO': -O2 plus -fprofile-instr-use (Clang) or -fprofile-use (GCC). -flto=thin (Fast) and -flto=full (Unsafe) are passed only on the link line (LDFLAGS) while objects are compiled without -flto, so no link-time optimisation actually takes place. Managed side: dotnet 11.0.100-rc.1.26425.128, 'dotnet build -c Release' (Optimize=true) run as 'dotnet Benchmark.dll' with default tiered JIT; the C#/AOT rows are NativeAOT with IlcInstructionSet=native and IlcOptimizationPreference=Speed; Julia 1.13.1 run as 'julia --project=. --threads=16 benchmark.jl' (Julia/Max adds -O3 --check-bounds=no --math-mode=fast); Temurin OpenJDK 27+35 run as 'java -Xmx2g -jar'. Every language, C and C++ included, runs untimed warm-up iterations (20 percent of the timed count) before the timed loop.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X 8-Core Processor, 78GB RAM, x86_64 Linux (results file 2026-10-05, host kostya-ms7c37)
why_faster: The suite's own docs/ai_analysis.js says Julia specializes sort! on Int32 at run time and picks a radix or counting sort (O(n)), and docs/ai_critic.js says this is the standard library choosing a better algorithm for the data type, not the language being faster ('You're comparing algorithms, not languages').
tradeoffs: Julia peak RSS about 405 MB; JIT latency excluded by the warm-up phase.
caveats: Not the same algorithm. std::sort is a comparison introsort. Julia's default sort! for Int32 runs ComputeExtrema and skips counting sort because the range (about 1,000,000) exceeds half the length. It then picks its stable LSD RadixSort, because 20 bits + 70 < 22 ln(399,999), which is about 284 (base/sort.jl ConsiderRadixSort). The suite's own docs/ai_critic.js says 'You're comparing algorithms, not languages'. A radix sort in C++ would be expected to match or beat it. The Java row is probably not a JIT win either. OpenJDK ships an AVX2 sort intrinsic (libsimdsort, avx2-32bit-qsort.hpp, C++ based on Intel x86-simd-sort) that Arrays.sort(int[]) can use on AVX2 CPUs such as this Ryzen; whether it ran here was not checked. Every language, C and C++ included, runs untimed warm-up iterations (20 percent of the timed count, cpp/src/benchmark.cpp and csharp/BenchmarkBase.cs) before the timed loop, so steady state is compared on both sides; the record's statement that only JIT languages get a warm-up was wrong. -flto appears only on the link line in cpp/Makefile, so the 'Fast' and 'Unsafe' rows get no actual LTO (the hot code sits in one translation unit, so this is probably immaterial). One measurement per test and configuration (no variance). LangArena's README calls it 'a subjective benchmark' and says AI tools helped translate the tests between languages. Rows were selected as tests where a managed-runtime row beats every C/C++ row; most tests go the other way (for example Sort::Quick, Sort::Merge and Binarytrees::Arena). Ratios are derived from the results file, not stated by the suite.
found_via: GitHub: kostya/benchmarks README links to LangArena; parsed results/2026-10-05-kostya-ms7c37.js for tests where a Java, C# or Julia row is faster than every Clang/GCC C and C++ row

verification.tier_reason: The harness meets A methodology (cpp/src/sort.cpp std::sort vs julia/src/benchmarks/Sort.jl sort!, flags in cpp/Makefile, versions and CPU in the results file) and the rows match. However, the two sides run different algorithms. For this Vector{Int32} (400,000 values in 0..999,999), Julia's default sort! dispatches to its LSD RadixSort per base/sort.jl, while std::sort runs introsort, so the language-level claim is capped at C (same_algorithm false precedent: OrdinaryDiffEq.jl, Julia matmul-no-blas).
verification.notes: Downgrade A to C: the numbers match the results file, but the win is Julia's standard-library radix sort against comparison-based std::sort (same_algorithm false). It is an algorithm win, not a language win, and the same-algorithm Sort::Quick and Sort::Merge tests show C ahead. Shortcomings to record: different algorithm; the Java row is likely the JDK's x86-simd-sort intrinsic; a single run; a subjective suite. Consider a category override out of runtime-jit-beats-aot (for example numerics-and-arrays).

name: NonuniformFFTs.jl (Julia NUFFT, CPU and GPU) vs FINUFFT and cuFINUFFT
baseline: FINUFFT v2.4.1 (C++, CPU) and cuFINUFFT (CUDA C++, GPU), both compiled locally and called through FINUFFT.jl v3.4.0
workload: Type-1 and type-2 3D non-uniform FFTs on a uniform 256^3 grid, random points in [0, 2*pi)^3 with point density N/M^3 from 1e-4 to 10, tolerance 1e-6, Float64 complex data; each time includes set_points plus the transform.
claimed_speedup: Docs and README text match the record (CPU 'comparable'; GPU default method 'slightly faster than CuFINUFFT at low point densities, but slightly slower at large ones'; shared-memory method gives 'important gains'). Numbers come from the raw medians in benchmark/CPU+CUDA/results.H100_jean-zay/*.dat (ComplexF64, 256^3, tol 1e-6, set_points plus exec; all ratios derived from page data). GPU type 1: at density 1e-4 (1,678 points) NonuniformFFTs global-memory 0.00322 s vs CuFINUFFT 0.00536 s (1.66x faster); at density 1 (16.8M points) NonuniformFFTs shared-memory 0.0415 s vs CuFINUFFT's best 0.1774 s (4.27x faster) while the default global-memory method is 0.2809 s vs 0.1809 s (1.55x slower); at density 10 (167.8M points) shared-memory 0.300 s vs CuFINUFFT's best (its own SM method) 0.822 s (2.74x faster; 6.97x against CuFINUFFT GM 2.089 s) while the default method is 3.187 s (1.53x slower than CuFINUFFT GM). GPU type 2: 1.92x faster at density 1e-4 (0.00280 s vs 0.00538 s) but slower at high density with either method (best 0.0295 s vs 0.0223 s at density 1, 1.32x slower; 0.2166 s vs 0.1087 s at density 10, 1.99x slower). CPU (24 threads): type 1 ranges from 1.93x faster (atomics variant, 0.105 s vs 0.202 s at density 1e-4) to 1.78x slower (atomics, 1.273 s vs 0.717 s at density 1), and 1.03-1.17x faster at density 10; type 2 is 1.84x faster at density 1e-4 (0.0867 s vs 0.1598 s) and 1.56x at 1e-3 (FFT-dominated cases), 0.89-0.96x at densities 0.1 and 1, and 1.05x at density 10.
compiler_and_flags: FINUFFT v2.4.1 built with Nvidia nvc++ (version not stated) via CMake 'Release' with default flags (actual flags not printed); cuFINUFFT built with nvcc from CUDA 12.8, CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=90; both called through FINUFFT.jl v3.4.0 with locally compiled binaries. FINUFFT options: tol 1e-6, modeord=1, spread_sort=1, spread_kerevalmeth=1, FFTW.ESTIMATE, nthreads = Julia thread count (24); cuFINUFFT gpu_sort=1, gpu_kerevalmeth=1, gpu_method 1 and 2; upsampfac left at the library default (only the 1e-14 reference plans set 2.0). NonuniformFFTs.jl v0.8.3 (2025-07-11), sigma=1.5, HalfSupport(4), FFTW.ESTIMATE, KernelAbstractions/CUDA.jl; Julia version not stated (benchmark Project.toml has no Manifest or compat). BenchmarkTools @benchmark medians. Script: benchmark/CPU+CUDA/run_benchmarks.jl.
hardware: Jean Zay (IDRIS): 2x Intel Xeon Platinum 8468 (24 cores used) and one NVIDIA H100 SXM5 80 GB (1/4 of a node). A second run on one AMD Instinct MI300A (Adastra) compares only the CPU against FINUFFT.
why_faster: Docs, GPU only and hedged: the shared-memory variant 'completely avoids atomic operations on shared memory', which 'seems to speed up things quite a bit and might explain the important gains' over cuFINUFFT. The implementation is described as 'heavily inspired' by the cuFINUFFT paper, so the algorithm family is the same but not identical.
tradeoffs: Julia package; one KernelAbstractions.jl code base targets CUDA, AMD and other GPUs. Also offers real-valued non-uniform data transforms (extra gains, not available in FINUFFT).
caveats: Author's own benchmark; the docs show only SVG plots, numbers exist only in the raw .dat files. The CPU result is parity (wins and losses by up to about 2x either way depending on density), not a win. The GPU win is limited to type 1 with the non-default shared-memory method at densities of about 1 and above, or to very sparse problems; the default global-memory method is about 1.5x slower than CuFINUFFT at high density, and type 2 at high density is slower than CuFINUFFT with either method. The docs say CuFINUFFT's gpu_method=2 'seems to be considerably slower in nearly all cases', but the raw data show it beating CuFINUFFT's method 1 for type 1 at densities of 1 and above (0.822 s vs 2.089 s at density 10), so fair comparisons must use CuFINUFFT's SM curve. The two libraries do not do the same work: NonuniformFFTs uses sigma=1.5 with a width-8 Kaiser-Bessel-type kernel while (Cu)FINUFFT uses its own kernel with its default upsampling factor (not set by the script); measured errors are of the same order (type 1 about 1.7e-6 vs 1.4e-6 on GPU, 1.3e-6 vs 3.7e-6 on CPU). The docs say points are uniform in [0, 2*pi)^3, but run_benchmarks.jl draws standard-normal coordinates (randn, Xoshiro(42)) for both libraries, so the point cloud is clustered. FINUFFT was built with nvc++ rather than GCC or Clang, and the CPU sides probably use different FFTW builds (locally built FINUFFT vs FFTW.jl), which would dominate the sparse-point CPU rows (not verified). The 'real data' gains solve a different (real-valued) problem. On AMD GPUs the default method scales badly. Only one GPU model (H100), one grid size and one tolerance (1e-6); Julia version not stated. Not a JIT-versus-AOT effect: the GPU gains come from a different shared-memory spreading design. [retier] Parameters differ between libraries: cuFINUFFT auto-selects upsampfac 2.0, ns 7 and a 512^3 grid while NonuniformFFTs ran sigma 1.5, width 8 and a 384^3 grid (2.37x smaller FFT, 1.49x more kernel work per point); the GPU low-density wins (1.66x/1.92x) and default-method losses (1.53-1.55x) track those ratios, and only the shared-memory type 1 wins on its own merit. CPU FINUFFT 2.4.1's heuristic picks upsampfac 1.25, ns 10, and its error 3.73e-6 misses tol 1e-6 (NonuniformFFTs 1.28e-6). The package default sigma is 2.0, not the benchmarked 1.5. Open #95 (GPU Float32 points just below 0 index out of bounds) and #69 (up to 11.5x slower than cuFINUFFT in 2D on GPU).

name: OCaml 5.4.1: benchLANG binary trees vs C and C++ at -O3
baseline: C (GCC 16.2.0: gcc -O3 -march=native -flto -funroll-loops -ffp-contract=off) and C++ (g++ -std=c++20 with the same flags) binary-trees programs that allocate every node with malloc/free (C) or new/delete (C++)
workload: CLBG-style binary trees, depths 4 to 18: allocate, traverse and (in native code) free complete binary trees of individually allocated nodes; the README says the workload measures allocator plus GC plus pointer chasing, with native frees inside the timer and GC runtimes collecting when they like.
claimed_speedup: OCaml 5.4.1 0.865 s vs C 1.010 s and C++ 1.147 s: about 1.17x faster than C and 1.33x faster than C++ (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: C: gcc 16.2.0 -O3 -march=native -flto -funroll-loops -ffp-contract=off -s; C++: g++ 16.2.0 -std=c++20 with the same flags (nixpkgs-unstable pins, run_benchmarks.sh). OCaml 5.4.1: ocamlopt -O3 -unsafe -inline 200 -nodynlink monotonic.c bench.ml -o bench -ccopt -s. flake.nix installs the plain nixpkgs `ocaml` package, and nixpkgs' pkgs/development/compilers/ocaml/generic.nix defaults flambdaSupport to false, so -O3 has no effect and the OCaml side is a non-flambda (closure-mode) build.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X locked at 3.5 GHz (cpupower performance governor, min and max 3500 MHz), 48 GB DDR4-3600 CL16, Arch Linux
why_faster: Source (README workload note): native code frees every node inside the timed region while GC runtimes collect when they like. Likely mechanism (inference): bump-pointer allocation in the runtime and deferred or concurrent reclamation against glibc malloc and free per node.
tradeoffs: Whole-process peak RSS 89.7 MiB for OCaml vs 33.3 MiB for C; OCaml is slower than C on primes (3.200 s vs 2.725 s), Fibonacci (4.897 s vs 1.694 s) and strings (5.000 s vs 2.132 s).
caveats: One run per language (no variance) from a single machine on 2026-09-03. The C and C++ programs allocate every node with malloc/new and walk every tree a second time to free it inside the timer (languages/C/bench.c make_tree/free_tree), while OCaml just drops the references and its minor GC never traces dead young trees; an arena or pool allocator in C would likely beat the runtimes here. The column is an allocator benchmark, not a codegen one: the malloc-based native rows spread from 0.986 s (Fortran) through 1.010 s (C), 1.033 s (Rust), 1.109 s (Ada) and 1.119 s (Zig) to 1.147 s (C++), and Java 0.347 s, Nim 0.809 s, Bun 0.816 s, Dart AOT 0.865 s and C# 0.931 s also beat C. ocamlopt is an ahead-of-time compiler, so the win comes from the OCaml GC runtime, not from a JIT. Binary trees is 1 of 5 workloads and C wins overall (total 9.762 s vs OCaml 16.233 s); OCaml loses primes (3.200 s vs 2.725 s), Fibonacci (4.897 s vs 1.694 s), strings (5.000 s vs 2.132 s) and Mandelbrot (2.271 s vs 2.201 s). OCaml peak RSS 89.7 MiB vs 33.3 MiB for C. OCaml uses 63-bit tagged ints where C uses long long; the analyzer checks that checksums agree. The -O3 flag is ignored because the nixpkgs OCaml is built without flambda.

name: OpenJDK HotSpot (Java 25): benchLANG binary trees
baseline: C (GCC 16.2.0, malloc and free per node, 1.010 s) and C++ (GCC 16.2.0, new and delete per node, 1.147 s)
workload: CLBG-style binary trees with depths 4 to 18: a stretch tree, a long-lived tree, then many short-lived trees built, checked and (in C/C++) freed, one allocation per node.
claimed_speedup: Java 0.347 s vs C 1.010 s and C++ 1.147 s: about 2.9x faster than C and 3.3x faster than C++ (derived from page data). Peak RSS 987.8 MiB for Java vs 33.3 MiB for C and 35.4 MiB for C++.
compiler_and_flags: C: gcc -O3 -march=native -flto -funroll-loops -ffp-contract=off -s (GCC 16.2.0); C++: g++ -std=c++20 with the same flags. Java: OpenJDK 25.0.4, javac bench.java then java bench with default heap and default GC.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X locked at 3.5 GHz (performance governor), 48 GB DDR4-3600 CL16, Arch Linux with i3-wm; results dated 3 September 2026, one run per language
why_faster: Stated by the suite's methodology: 'Binary trees: ... Allocator + GC + pointer chase, native code frees inside the timer, GC runtimes collect when they like'. Agent inference: per-node malloc/free (C, C++) against bump-pointer allocation and deferred or concurrent collection in a managed runtime; the C/C++ programs do not use an arena.
tradeoffs: About 30x the peak memory of C; whole-process CPU time exceeds wall time because of GC and JIT threads; needs a JVM.
caveats: One run per language ('1 run/lang'), no variance. In-program wall times from a monotonic clock: JIT warm-up is inside the timed region, young-generation collections run inside it too, but garbage still live in the heap when the timer stops is never collected ('GC runtimes collect when they like'), while C/C++ walk every tree a second time to free it inside the timer. The Java run uses JVM ergonomics (default G1 with parallel GC worker threads on a 12-core CPU); the README defines CPUx = (user+sys)/wall but the published table does not show it, so extra GC-thread CPU time is not visible. Peak RSS 987.8 MiB for Java vs 33.3 MiB for C: the win trades about 30x memory for time. The column is an allocator benchmark: Nim 0.809 s, Bun 0.816 s, OCaml and Dart AOT 0.865 s, C# 0.931 s and Fortran 0.986 s also beat C's 1.010 s, so per-node glibc malloc/free is the bottleneck and an arena or pool allocator in C/C++ would likely beat every managed runtime (compare the Arena variant in LangArena). Only the binary-trees column is a Java win: Java loses Fibonacci (4.109 s vs 1.694 s), strings (4.075 s vs 2.132 s) and Mandelbrot (2.275 s vs 2.201 s) and ties primes (2.730 s vs 2.725 s); total 13.536 s vs C 9.762 s.

name: OpenJDK HotSpot (Java 27) and GraalVM JIT: LangArena Etc::Words
baseline: C++ splitting with std::istringstream and counting in std::unordered_map<std::string,int> (g++ 16, clang++ 22); best C/C++ configuration is C++/G++/PGO at 1.587 s
workload: Split a large generated text into words and count word frequencies, then report the most frequent word.
claimed_speedup: Java/OpenJDK 1.272 s vs C++/G++ 1.638 s (prod, -O2), C++/G++ -O3 'Fast' 1.651 s, best of all 16 C/C++ configurations 1.587 s: about 1.25x faster than the best row and 1.29x faster than the prod row (derived from page data). Java on GraalVM JIT 1.15 s (1.4x faster than the best row); C#/JIT 1.422 s also wins; Julia 1.857 s does not.
compiler_and_flags: C/C++: Clang 22.1.8 (official LLVM release tarball; the clang_cpp container aliases g++ to clang++ and links the system libstdc++, no -stdlib=libc++) and GCC 16.0.1 20260322 (trunk, Ubuntu build), -std=c++20, glibc malloc. Headline 'prod' build (cpp/Makefile CXXFLAGS_PROD): -O2 -DNDEBUG -fstack-protector-strong -fno-omit-frame-pointer, linked with -Wl,-z,relro,-z,now -Wl,--gc-sections (not -O3). The same suite also builds 'Fast' (-O3 -march=native -mtune=native -pipe -fstack-protector -ftree-vectorize -funroll-loops), 'Unsafe' (-O3 -march=native -ffast-math -fno-stack-protector -fomit-frame-pointer -fvisibility=hidden -fno-trapping-math) and 'PGO' (-O2 plus -fprofile-instr-use or -fprofile-use) variants of every C and C++ benchmark; the Makefile passes -flto=thin (Fast) and -flto=full (Unsafe) only at the link step while the objects are compiled without -flto, so those builds probably get no LTO (inference from cpp/Makefile). All 16 Clang/GCC x C/C++ x prod/Fast/Unsafe/PGO configurations were compared here (instrumented PGO/Gen rows excluded). Managed side: Temurin OpenJDK 27+35 run as 'java -Xmx2g -jar' (default G1 GC, C2 JIT), GraalVM CE 25.4.4.1.1 (JDK 25.0.4.1.1) with -Xmx2g, dotnet 11.0.100-rc.1 (Release), Julia 1.13.1 with --threads=16 (versions and run commands from the results file).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X 8-Core Processor, 78GB RAM, x86_64 Linux (results file 2026-10-05, host kostya-ms7c37)
why_faster: Not stated by the suite. The C++ version tokenizes with istringstream operator>> and allocates std::string keys; the Java version uses String.split and HashMap (agent inference: library-level differences).
tradeoffs: Java peak RSS about 309 MB (GraalVM about 445 MB).
caveats: The win comes from the C++ tokenizer and per-node hash-map allocation, not from JIT compilation: C#/AOT and the AOT languages Rust, Crystal and Zig also beat every C++ row, so the 'runtime-jit-beats-aot' framing does not fit; a std::string_view split loop in C++ would likely change the result (inference, not measured). Both versions do the same work (whitespace split, hash count, max scan) over 50,000 words of 3-8 letters (all within libstdc++'s small-string buffer), 360 timed iterations. The C version (strdup of the whole text every iteration, strtok_r, uthash with strdup'd keys) is slower still at 1.963-2.084 s. Memory trade: Java/OpenJDK RSS 309 MB vs C++ 7.5-7.9 MB. Margin is modest (1.25x over the best C++ row, C++/G++/PGO 1.587 s) and rests on one run per configuration, although all 16 C/C++ configurations land between 1.587 and 2.042 s. LangArena's own README calls it 'a subjective benchmark', and the author says AI tools helped translate the tests between languages. benchmarks.rb runs each test once per configuration in its own process and records that single in-process timing (no repeats, no variance). Every language, C and C++ included, runs a warm-up of 20% of the iterations before the timer starts, so JIT compilation and startup are excluded. The headline C/C++ 'prod' rows are -O2 with hardening flags, but the -O3, PGO and fast-math variants were also measured and still lose on this test; the Makefile's LTO flags are link-only, so no configuration had real LTO. Rows were selected by the search agent as tests where a managed-runtime row beats every C/C++ row; most other tests in the suite go the other way (for example Sort::Quick, Sort::Merge and the Binarytrees::Arena variant). The per-benchmark ratios are derived from the results file, not stated by the suite.

name: Racket (Staged): Brainfuck bench.b in kostya/benchmarks
baseline: C++/g++ brainfuck (brainfuck/bf.cpp): an AST-walking interpreter with std::vector ops, g++ -O3 -march=native -flto
workload: Run the bench.b Brainfuck program; the staged Racket version generates a lambda from the program with syntax objects and calls eval (compiled by Racket CS / Chez Scheme) inside the timed region, with unsafe fixnum and vector operations.
claimed_speedup: bench.b: Racket (Staged) 0.885s (MAD 0.000) vs C++/g++ 1.097s, C/gcc 1.112s, C++/clang++ 1.167s (about 1.24x vs g++, derived from page data); memory 101.37 + 0.06 MiB vs 3.38 + 0.00 MiB. On mandel.b the staged Racket version is slower than C++/g++ (15.722s vs 10.143s). The same-algorithm (non-staged) Racket interpreter is slower than C++/g++ on both (1.761s and 35.373s).
compiler_and_flags: C++ baseline: g++ 16.1.0 -Wall -Wextra -pedantic -Wcast-align -O3 -march=native -flto=auto -Wa,-mbranches-within-32B-boundaries -std=c++23 (common/commands.mk GCC_CPP_BUILD, libstdc++); clang++ 22.1.8 row uses the same flags with -stdlib=libc++. Racket 9.2 (Racket CS) run as PLT_CS_COMPILE_LIMIT=100000 racket bf-staged.rkt (common/commands.mk RACKET_RUN), so the large eval'd form is compiled to machine code rather than interpreted.
hardware: Intel Xeon E-2324G (README Environment section); Debian forky/sid Docker image
tradeoffs: About 100 MiB resident versus 3.4 MiB; uses unsafe ops (#%declare #:unsafe) so no bounds checking, the same as the C++ baseline's unchecked indexing.
caveats: Not the same algorithm: the C++/g++ baseline (brainfuck/bf.cpp) is a tree-walking interpreter that dispatches every Brainfuck instruction at run time, while the staged variant compiles the Brainfuck program to native code at run time; the suite's own brainfuck/README.md says implementations interpret every instruction one by one, so the staged rows deviate from the suite rule. The repository has no C or C++ staged/JIT counterpart, so the result shows runtime compilation beating an interpreter, not the language beating C++ at equal work. The timed region (between the notify calls) includes parsing and the run-time compile on both sides, but verify() runs one staged compile of a hello-world program before timing, warming the compiler machinery. Measurements run with QUIET=1 (analyze.rb, 10 attempts, median with MAD), so output flushing does not matter. Single machine (Xeon E-2324G), single suite. Wins only on bench.b (1.24x) and loses on mandel.b (15.722s vs 10.143s, 1.55x slower), so the bench.b win does not generalise; the bench.b margin is well outside the reported MADs on this machine. On bench.b C++/g++ is not the fastest AOT interpreter either (V/gcc 0.985s, Rust 1.008s, D/ldc2 1.078s). The generated code uses unsafe fixnum and vector operations (#%declare #:unsafe); bf.cpp also indexes std::vector without bounds checks, so safety checks are comparable.
found_via: Suite-repo check after WebSearch for Julia/Java/.NET beating C++ returned only blog and forum threads; opened github.com/kostya/benchmarks README, brainfuck/ Makefile and staged sources via raw.githubusercontent.com.
why_faster: Runtime code generation specialized to the input program (eval of a generated lambda), derived from reading brainfuck/bf-staged.rkt; the README gives no explanation.

name: Bun (JavaScriptCore JIT 1.4.2): alya-lang/benchmarks binary trees
baseline: C (gcc 13.3.0 -O2, malloc and free per node, binary_trees.c)
workload: Binary trees at depth 14: stretch tree, long-lived tree, then repeated pairs of short-lived trees built, checked and (in C) freed.
claimed_speedup: Bun 98.3 ms vs C 126.3 ms (median of 10 timed runs after 1 warm-up): about 1.28x faster (derived from page data). Of the 14 benchmarks in the same table, Bun beats C only on this one.
compiler_and_flags: gcc (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0 invoked by cross_lang/runner.ts as 'gcc -O2 binary_trees.c -o binary_trees_c' (no -march, no LTO); Bun 1.4.2 run as 'bun run binary_trees.js' (installed by oven-sh/setup-bun@v2 at CI time); Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS x64 on a GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest runner (.github/workflows/benchmark.yml).
tradeoffs: Bun process start (about 24 ms cold start per the README) is inside the measured time; Bun peak RSS about 36 MB vs about 3 MB for C.
caveats: This suite exists to compare the new Alya language; the Bun-versus-C row is incidental, first-party to Alya, and the repo gives no mechanism for Bun. C is built at -O2, not -O3. Runs happen on a shared GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest VM (CPU model not stated, noisy neighbours) and the README is rewritten by CI on each dispatch, so the numbers drift between commits. Timing is whole-process wall clock via spawnSync (1 warm-up, median of 10), so Bun's runtime start-up and JIT warm-up are inside its 98.3 ms and C's process start is inside 126.3 ms; the workload is only about 100 ms. The work differs in memory management: the C version calls glibc malloc per node and walks every tree again with a recursive free_tree inside the timed region, while the JS version never frees and leaves dead trees to the GC (possibly never collected before exit). Bun beats C on only this 1 of 14 rows; C wins the other 13 by 1.9x to 9x. The README's start-up, binary-size and RSS table rows for Bun and C are hard-coded strings in runner.ts, not measurements.

caveats: The README does not claim to beat XGBoost; the wins are read off its own tables and are regime-specific (CPU only at 10M rows x 10 features, 1.06-1.17x; GPU only at depth 11 with 100 features, 1.13-1.35x training). name: HotSpot Java IntMap put latency vs C++ clang++ -O3: coralblocks/CoralBench
baseline: C++ IntMap as it stood in December 2024 (src/main/c/int_map.hpp at commit 46103a6: std::vector<std::vector<Entry>> buckets, 64-bit size_t keys, no bucket reserve, so the first three puts into each bucket malloc and reallocate the vector inside the timed region), built with clang++ 18.1.0 -Ofast -march=native -flto -std=c++17 and driven by src/main/c/int_map_benchmark.cpp. The current header (pre-sized buckets since commit 9281b82, 32-bit keys since 259d856, both 2026-08-28) has never been benchmarked in the README.
workload: Integer-keyed hash map put, get and remove: 3,000,000 measured operations per method, map capacity 1,000,000, warm-up 0, per-operation latency in nanoseconds from the repo's Bench class.
claimed_speedup: No valid speedup. The hidden README section shows PUT 31.34 ns avg for HotSpot with Graal JVMCI (Oracle GraalVM 25.0.4.1, re-run 2026-08-28) and 32.40 ns for HotSpot C2 against C++ 47.75 ns (about 1.5x, derived from page data); GET 26.92 ns and 29.13 ns vs C++ 25.98 ns (parity); DEL 36.29 ns and 37.73 ns vs C++ 25.93 ns (C++ about 1.4x faster). The C++, C2, -Xcomp and native-image outputs are unchanged from the December 2024 README (Java 23.0.1 era), and the C++ PUT figure was measured on code whose PUT grew bucket vectors inside the timer.
compiler_and_flags: C++ numbers: Ubuntu clang 18.1.0, clang++ -Ofast -march=native -flto -std=c++17 (December 2024 README); commit f11598d later changed the README commands to -O3 without re-running, so the -O3 commands shown next to the C++ output did not produce it. Java JVMCI run: Oracle GraalVM 25.0.4.1 HotSpot, java -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch -Xms4g -Xmx4g -XX:NewSize=512m -XX:MaxNewSize=1024m. HotSpot C2 (-XX:-UseJVMCICompiler), -Xcomp and native-image outputs date from the earlier Java 23.0.1 run. The C++ standard library is not stated (Ubuntu clang defaults to libstdc++ unless -stdlib is given).
hardware: Intel Xeon E-2288G @ 3.70GHz, Ubuntu 18.04.6 LTS, kernel 4.15.0-20-generic
tradeoffs: Java run needs a 4 GB pre-touched heap and a JVM. Worst-case PUT latency is higher in Java (maximum 211.7 us vs 18.4 us for C++), although the 99.9th-percentile maximum is lower (277 ns vs 1,040 ns).
caveats: The Java-vs-C++ section sits inside an HTML comment (<!-- ... -->) that the author added in commit d3f73f5 ('Revise benchmark data and Java version in README', 2026-08-28), so it does not render on github.com and reads as withdrawn or unfinished. Unequal work: the C++ map that produced the 47.75 ns PUT figure started with empty bucket vectors (no reserve), so PUT paid malloc plus vector reallocation and copy for the first three entries of every bucket inside the timer, while the Java IntMap pre-sized every bucket ArrayList to initialBucketSize = 3 and only bump-allocated an Entry; the author added the matching reserve to C++ on 2026-08-28 (commit 9281b82 'Pre-size C++ IntMap buckets') but did not re-run C++. The 2024 C++ map also used 64-bit size_t keys and 64-bit modulo against Java's 32-bit int keys. Cross-run comparison: the JVMCI figures were re-measured with Java 25.0.4.1 in 2026 (PUT 28.04 ns became 31.34 ns), while C++ and the other Java modes are 2024 outputs; the environment block lists only the 2026 versions. Not the same data structure: C++ stores entries inline in each bucket vector, Java stores references to pooled Entry objects. Mixed result even as published: Java ties GET and loses DEL. One run per configuration with warm-up 0, so JIT compilation is inside the measured region; the C++ and Java Bench classes use different histogram maps (std::unordered_map vs CoralDS LongMap) outside the timed span.
