name: Java HotSpot vs g++ -O3 virtual-call microbenchmark (gist)
baseline: C++ virtual dispatch compiled with g++ 4.0.1 -O3 -fomit-frame-pointer -march=pentium4
workload: Call a virtual perform() 400 million times through a base pointer that alternates every iteration between two derived classes (A adds 1, B adds 4).
claimed_speedup: C++ runs 1796.2, 1682.14, 1673.19, 1678.66, 1685.71, 1671.59, 1702.79, 1714.34, 1652.46, 1651.8 ms; Java 1.6.0_07 -server runs 967, 1036, 769, 740, 716, 718, 717, 716, 716, 717 ms; Scala 2.7.3 runs 1016, 951, 716, 717 ms. Units are not printed on the results gist but are milliseconds per the sources (C++ clock()-based CPU time, Java System.currentTimeMillis wall time). About 2.3x faster at steady state (1651.8 / 716) and 1.7x even on Java's first run (1651.8 / 967) (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: g++ -O3 -fomit-frame-pointer -march=pentium4 Bench.cpp (gcc version 4.0.1, Apple Inc. build 5493, Target: i686-apple-darwin9, so a 32-bit build since no -m64 is passed); javac Bench.java and java -server Bench on Java HotSpot(TM) 64-Bit Server VM (build 1.6.0_07-b06-57, mixed mode)
hardware: PowerMac 2x2.8 GHz Xeon (8 cores), 4GB RAM
tradeoffs: Java needs warm-up (first runs 967 and 1036 vs 716 steady state) and a JVM; a toy loop.
caveats: From 2009 with Apple g++ 4.0.1 targeting 32-bit i686 with -march=pentium4 on a Xeon, against a 64-bit HotSpot VM, so the targets differ. No profile-guided optimization or modern speculative devirtualization for C++, which could remove the alternating indirect call; a current GCC or Clang was not measured. One call site microbenchmark (400 million alternating virtual calls incrementing a global), not a general claim. The C++ main() calls bench() 5 times, so the 10 C++ numbers come from two program runs; Java runs 10 iterations in one JVM, so later runs are fully JIT-compiled. C++ times process CPU time (clock()), Java wall time. Benchmark sources are in two other gists (87516 C++, 87518 Java); no license; CPU model not stated beyond '2.8 GHz Xeon'. Mechanism not stated by the author. Tier capped at C. [retier] From 2009 with Apple g++ 4.0.1 targeting 32-bit i686 (-march=pentium4) on a Xeon against a 64-bit HotSpot VM, so the targets differ; no PGO or modern speculative devirtualisation for C++. name: Julia (no BLAS) matmul with @fastmath @simd ivdep in kostya/benchmarks
baseline: C/gcc matmul (matmul/matmul.c, Attractive Chaos): B is transposed, then a scalar dot-product triple loop (t += p[k] * r[k]) on double** rows; gcc 16.1.0 -O3 -march=native -flto=auto -std=c23, no -ffast-math and no restrict
workload: 1500x1500 double matrix multiply (MSIZE 1500) written as plain loops (no BLAS) in each language.
claimed_speedup: Matmul (MSIZE 1500): Julia (no BLAS) 1.113s (MAD 0.017) vs C/gcc 3.034s (MAD 0.001) and C/clang 3.067s (about 2.7x vs C/gcc, derived from page data); energy 49.41 J vs 113.24 J. The other plain-loop rows (Rust 3.067s, Zig 3.071s, Go 3.153s, Java 3.057s) cluster with C. Library-backed rows (C++/g++ Eigen 0.081s, Julia with OpenBLAS threads: 1 0.170s) are a different algorithm class and are not the claim.
compiler_and_flags: C baseline: gcc 16.1.0 -Wall -Wextra -pedantic -Wcast-align -O3 -march=native -flto=auto -Wa,-mbranches-within-32B-boundaries -std=c23 (common/commands.mk GCC_BUILD); the C/clang row uses clang 22.1.8 with the same flags (CLANG_BUILD). Julia run as julia --optimize=3 --check-bounds=no matmul.jl 1500 (common/commands.mk JULIA_RUN, matmul/Makefile run[matmul.jl]) with no -t flag; README Environment lists Julia v"1.11.6" while docker/Dockerfile at HEAD pins julia-1.12.6.
hardware: Intel Xeon E-2324G (README Environment section); Debian forky/sid Docker image
tradeoffs: Julia's @fastmath/@simd ivdep license reassociation and assumed no loop-carried dependence; JIT warm-up inside the timed run; Julia uses about 256 MiB base + 51 MiB peak increase versus 2 MiB + 68 MiB for the C program.
caveats: Not an equal-work, equal-optimisation comparison. The C inner loop is a scalar floating-point reduction (t += p[k] * r[k]) that gcc and clang at -O3 may not reorder or vectorise without -ffast-math, so it runs as one serial dependency chain; the Julia inner loop uses the other loop order (c[m,n] += a[m,k] * b[k,n] down a column-major column), whose iterations are independent and vectorise without reassociation, plus @simd ivdep (no alias checks), @fastmath (FMA contraction and reassociation allowed) and @inbounds. The C file is built with -std=c23, an ISO mode in which GCC's documented default is -ffp-contract=off, so the gcc build does not even fuse multiply-adds. A C version with the same loop order or with -ffast-math would likely close most of the gap. The Julia file wraps the outer loop in Threads.@threads, but neither JULIA_RUN nor docker/Dockerfile sets -t or JULIA_NUM_THREADS, so Julia's default of one thread applies (inferred from the build files, not stated on the README). The timed region includes matrix generation and allocation on both sides; Julia is warmed by calc(101) before timing, so JIT compilation of mul is outside the timed region. The README's Julia version (1.11.6) disagrees with the Dockerfile at HEAD (1.12.6), so the version behind the published row is uncertain. Capped at C for the mismatched optimisation level and loop structure.
found_via: Suite-repo check after WebSearch for Julia/Java/.NET beating C++ returned only blog and forum threads; opened github.com/kostya/benchmarks README, brainfuck/ Makefile and staged sources via raw.githubusercontent.com.
why_faster: Per-statement fast-math and ivdep annotations allow the LLVM vectorizer to reassociate and vectorize the inner loop that strict-FP gcc -O3 does not (derived from reading matmul/matmul.jl and matmul.c; not stated in the README).

verification.tier_reason: The measurement meets A methodology (matmul/matmul.jl vs matmul/matmul.c, flags in common/commands.mk and matmul/Makefile, gcc 16.1.0, Intel Xeon E-2324G) and the 1.113s vs 3.034s rows are on the README, but the two sides do not do the same work at the same optimisation level: the Julia loop is an axpy loop order with @fastmath, @simd ivdep and @inbounds, while the C loop is a strict-FP scalar dot-product reduction with no -ffast-math, so the language-level claim is capped at C (unequal-work precedent, as for the batch-06 staged brainfuck rows).

Corrected compiler_and_flags (the baseline is C built with gcc -std=c23, not g++ -std=c++23) and baseline_stdlib (C with glibc only, no libstdc++). compiler_and_flags: c++ -std=c++11 -O3 (Debian 4.9.1-15 gcc 4.9.1; -march=native was slower); Julia 0.3.4-pre and 0.4
why_faster: Stated by the README: the time is almost all random number generation, and Julia's rand(Bool) is much faster than the GNU C++11 <random> bernoulli_distribution path; the author says this does not support 'Julia is faster than C++'.
tradeoffs: Toy benchmark; Julia versions 0.3 and 0.4 are obsolete (the 2024 commit only updated the scripts).
caveats: Not the same work: libstdc++ std::bernoulli_distribution(0.5) goes through generate_canonical<double>, which consumes two 32-bit std::mt19937 outputs plus floating-point arithmetic per coin flip, while Julia 0.3/0.4 rand(Bool) drew from its dSFMT-backed global MersenneTwister (a different SIMD generator), so this compares RNG front ends and generators, not compilers (verifier inference from rwtest_simple.cc, rwtest_simple.jl and libstdc++ <random>; the README itself says the result does not support 'Julia is faster than C++' and that a faster C++ program is possible). The C++ timer is std::clock (CPU time) while Julia uses @elapsed (wall time). The Julia scripts were updated in Sep 2024 ('Update Julia scripts from 2014 to 2024') but the numbers are from Julia 0.3/0.4 and gcc 4.9.1 in 2014-2015; current Julia defaults to Xoshiro256++, so a rerun today would compare a different generator. No licence file (LICENSE and LICENSE.md return 404), so the code is reference only. CPU model not stated, single timing per language. [retier] Harness flaw: Julia 0.3's randbool() is ((dsfmt_randui32() & 1) == 1) with dsfmt_gv_genrand_uint32 a ccall into libdSFMT, so the 1.27 s 'Julia' time is a loop calling the C dSFMT library 3e8 times, not JIT code; the C++ side pays two mt19937 calls plus a division per flip (gcc 4.9 libstdc++ generate_canonical<double,53>). C++ bugs affecting only the output: new int[] never zeroed, freed with delete instead of delete[]. The scripts at HEAD (2024) are not the code that was timed.

name: LuaJIT 2.0 FFI: dyu/ffi-overhead plusone() call loop
baseline: C and C++ (gcc 5.4.1 -O2) calling plusone() in the shared library libnewplus.so through the dynamic linker
workload: Call the C function plusone(int) in a loop 500,000,000 times (while (x < count) x = plusone(x)) and report elapsed milliseconds.
claimed_speedup: LuaJIT 891 ms and 905 ms vs C 1182 and 1182 ms (C++ 1182 and 1183 ms) for 500M calls of plusone() in libnewplus.so: about 1.3x faster, 1.78 vs 2.36 ns per call (derived from page data). Julia 0.6.3 ccall (894 and 889 ms) wins by the same margin.
compiler_and_flags: C and C++: gcc/g++ 5.4.1 with -O2 -fPIC -Wall -Wextra (Tuprules.tup CFLAGS; C++ adds -std=c++14 -fno-rtti). The executables are linked at -O2 with -Lnewplus -lnewplus -Wl,-rpath,$ORIGIN/newplus (Tupfile), so each call to plusone goes through the PLT; gcc 5.4 has no -fno-plt. libnewplus.so is built from newplus/plus.c with the same -O2 -fPIC. LuaJIT 2.0.4 runs hello.lua with default JIT settings, loads the same .so with ffi.load and calls newplus.plusone. Julia 0.6.3 uses ccall. Ubuntu 14.04; 2 samples per language (run-all.sh); timing by gettimeofday in milliseconds (newplus/plus.c current_timestamp).
hardware: Intel i7-3630QM laptop (4 cores, HT), 16 GB RAM
tradeoffs: Gain only applies to call-boundary overhead for very small functions.
caveats: Measures foreign-call overhead for a trivial function, not code quality. The C and C++ rows call through the PLT of a shared library; the LuaJIT FFI and Julia ccall paths call the resolved address directly. The independent skeeto/dynamic-function-benchmark (Unlicense; benchmark.c and Makefile with -O3 -fpie) shows plain C reaching the same direct-call speed (1.01 ns vs 1.76 ns through the PLT). The accompanying nullprogram.com article 'When FFI Function Calls Beat Native C' (2018-05-27) explains this exact ffi-overhead result by the PLT, but the blog was unreachable (search snippet only). Repo issue #15, open since 2019-12-16, asks for a direct-addressed (non-PLT) C/C++ row; it was never added. C is compiled at -O2, not -O3 (irrelevant to the call itself, since plusone sits in a separate shared object). The toolchains are from 2018 (luajit 2.0.4, julia 0.6.3, gcc 5.4.1 on Ubuntu 14.04). Only 2 samples per language are shown, timed with a millisecond gettimeofday clock. The loop is 'while (x < count) x = plusone(x)'; issue #13 notes that loop overhead is part of every row. Many other languages in the table are slower than C (Go 37,975 ms, Node 9,163 ms, Java 4,469 ms).

name: LuaJIT 2.1: print_to_file in JuliaLang/Microbenchmarks
baseline: C fprintf loop (c/perf.c printfd: fprintf(f, "%ld %ld\n", i, i+1) to /dev/null) built with gcc 13.3.0 -std=c99 -O2
workload: Write 100,000 formatted lines to /dev/null; each language runs the benchmark 5 times internally, the Makefile invokes each script 3 times, and the overall minimum is reported.
claimed_speedup: LuaJIT 6.26 ms vs C 8.02 ms (0.78x of the C time, about 1.28x faster, derived from page data). Rust 4.17 ms (0.52x) is also faster than C; Julia 10.17 ms (1.27x) and Java 58.74 ms are slower.
compiler_and_flags: C: gcc 13.3.0 -std=c99 -O2 (the Makefile copies benchmarks/c2.csv, built from bin/perf2, into benchmarks/c.csv; the workflow passes no extra CFLAGS), linked with OpenBLAS. LuaJIT 2.1.1703358377 from Ubuntu's apt luajit package, run as 'luajit lua/perf.lua'.
hardware: GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest runners (x86_64). Each language runs in its own workflow job (bench-c, bench-lua, ...) and so on its own runner VM, and the results are only collected afterwards. No CPU model is stated, and the C and LuaJIT runs may have used different CPUs. Single-thread environment variables are set.
tradeoffs: The win covers formatted integer output only; LuaJIT needs its runtime and the result excludes start-up.
caveats: Cross-machine comparison: C and LuaJIT run in separate GitHub Actions jobs (bench-c, bench-lua) on separate shared runner VMs with no CPU model recorded. The C side is built at -O2, not -O3. The work is dominated by formatting libraries, not compiled user code. C calls glibc fprintf(f, "%ld %ld\n", ...), which parses the format string in vfprintf on every line. LuaJIT's trace recorder (recff_format in src/lj_ffrecord.c) specialises string.format to the constant '%d %d\n' and turns each plain %d into an integer-to-string conversion (lj_strfmt_wint in src/lj_strfmt.c), and f:write then calls fwrite. So the gap is LuaJIT's runtime formatter against glibc printf, not a code-generation win (inference from the sources; the suite states no mechanism). Rust is faster still at 4.17 ms (0.52x). This is the only one of 8 benchmarks that goes LuaJIT's way. It is slower than C on the other seven: recursion_fibonacci 5.20x, userfunc_mandelbrot 2.54x, matrix_statistics 2.29x, recursion_quicksort 2.24x, parse_integers 1.21x, matrix_multiply 1.14x, iteration_pi_sum 1.07x. Times are best-of-15 minimums in milliseconds. The suite is maintained by the Julia project and is first-party for Julia but third-party for LuaJIT.

name: LuaJIT vs C and C++ hash-table word count (spion gist)
baseline: C (hand-written chained hash table, gcc -O3) and C++ (std::unordered_map<string,int> with a custom hash, g++ -O3 -std=gnu++0x)
workload: Count occurrences of the 19 words of a hard-coded, pre-split sentence over 1,000,000 passes in a string-keyed hash table, one lookup per word per pass. C: hand-written table of 256 buckets indexed by the key's first character, strcmp along each chain, malloc per new counter. C++: std::unordered_map<string,int> over a vector<string> with a custom hash returning s[0], cnt[*it] += 1. Lua: a plain table, `if map[text[i]] then map[text[i]] = map[text[i]] + 1`.
claimed_speedup: Original 2012 'benchmark' transcript (one `time` run each, real time): C 0.234 s, C++ 0.321 s, Node 0.317 s, LuaJIT 0.161 s, so LuaJIT 1.45x faster than C and 1.99x faster than C++ (derived from page data). Author's 2020-05-26 rerun comment (no versions or hardware): C 0.173 s, C++ 0.36 s, Node 0.5 s, LuaJIT 0.08 s (2.2x vs C, 4.5x vs C++, derived from page data); at 10x iterations LuaJIT 0.76 s, C 1.44 s, C++ 3.35 s (1.9x vs C, 4.4x vs C++, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: gcc -O3 test.c; g++ -O3 -std=gnu++0x test.cpp; luajit test.lua with default options; no gcc, g++ or LuaJIT versions are given for the 2012 transcript or the 2020 rerun. The gcc 8.3.0, Node v15.12.0 and LuaJIT 2.0.5 named in mbossX's 2021 comment belong to that commenter's own separate 100M-iteration array-based programs (C 0.001 s, LuaJIT 1.774 s), not to the author's numbers.
stars_or_usage: 72 gist stars, 6 forks (2026-10-11); widely cited in LuaJIT vs C discussions
tradeoffs: Toy workload with a tiny hard-coded dictionary and pre-split words.
caveats: The author's a-warning.md (added 2015-08-18) says the benchmark 'has been misleading for a while': hard-coded text, small dictionary, pre-split words, no allocation cost. The author's own 2013 comment in test.lua says 'luajit probably optimizes away all dictionary lookups', which he did not verify. The C and C++ baselines use a first-character hash, so words sharing an initial letter collide and pay full string compares, while Lua strings are interned with a cached hash and compared by pointer; the author notes the default std::hash made C++ 2x slower. Timings are single `time` runs including process startup, with no CPU model and no compiler or LuaJIT versions. Comments show the C++ side can be beaten back: jh3141's fork (2014-12-06, g++ and clang++ -O3) reached 90 ms vs LuaJIT 95 ms and 71 ms with clang++, but it replaced the hash table with a vector of pairs plus a cached next-item pointer and interned pointers, a benchmark-specific structure that does not settle the hash-table comparison either; later array-based C versions (Zack24 2017, mbossX 2021) do no hashing. Source files last changed 2012-07-14 (test.c) and 2013-10-16 (test.lua comment only). No license. [retier] The author's a-warning.md (2015-08-18) calls the benchmark misleading: hard-coded text, small dictionary, pre-split words, no allocation cost. The gap comes from LuaJIT's interned, pre-hashed string keys against the C version's first-character hash with strcmp chains and libstdc++ std::unordered_map overhead, not from JIT versus AOT; the 10x rerun (0.76 vs 1.44 s) rules out start-up cost, and the 'optimizes away all dictionary lookups' remark was never checked with -jdump (about 4-8.5 ns per word fits one real interned-key lookup). In the thread, ayosec's Rust 0.104 s ran 100,000 passes against C's 1,000,000 (10x less work) and marcomagdy's pointer-keyed unordered_map still took 0.495 s against LuaJIT's 0.186 s. test.c uses implicit int, so it fails to build on GCC 14+ and Clang 16+ by default. No licence; single `time` runs.

name: NativeMinuit.jl (pure-Julia port of C++ Minuit2)
baseline: C++ Minuit2 (ROOT's standalone Minuit2 built through CMake, default Release, C++17) running MIGRAD on the same objectives
workload: Wall time of one full MIGRAD minimization with Strategy(0) and no parameter limits, including construction of the cost function and its random data, on five objectives: quad_4d (4 parameters from 1.0, step 0.1), rosenbrock_2d (start -1.2, 1.0), rosenbrock_10d, gauss_ll_10_1000 (10 independent Gaussian means, 100 points each) and gauss_ll_2_100 (mu and sigma of a Gaussian NLL over 100 points). Medians of 50 samples per side.
claimed_speedup: Julia/C++ time ratios 0.147x (quad_4d: 0.81 us vs 5.50 us), 0.253x (rosenbrock_2d: 9.50 vs 37.62 us), 0.371x (rosenbrock_10d: 58.11 vs 156.62 us), 0.718x (gauss_ll_10_1000: 32.26 vs 44.96 us), 0.888x (gauss_ll_2_100: 20.16 vs 22.71 us): about 1.1x to 6.8x faster (derived from page data). README: 'Faster than C++ Minuit2 on every benchmark in the test corpus'.
compiler_and_flags: Julia 1.12 (default -O2) with OpenBLAS 0.3.29 and BLAS threads set to 1 (benchmark/perf-config.toml); Julia times are BenchmarkTools medians of 50 samples (evals policy auto). C++: benchmark/cpp/CMakeLists.txt sets C++17 and CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE Release by default (CMake's Release flags for Clang and GCC are -O3 -DNDEBUG). It builds C++ Minuit2 from reference/Minuit2_cpp, a gitignored checkout that docs/UPSTREAM.md pins to GooFit/Minuit2 commit 57dc936a2b74d0b4dda1254c3dd63e7c61a97c84 (tag 6.24.0). C++ times are medians of 50 single-shot std::chrono samples. The C++ compiler is not named. Minuit2's CMakeLists has no BLAS dependency (it has its own small linear algebra), so 'single-threaded BLAS on both sides' only affects the Julia side.
hardware: Apple M3
why_faster: Stated by the README: a parametric CostFunction{F} devirtualizes the FCN call site at compile time, whereas C++ Minuit2 pays for shared_ptr ref-counting and ABObj expression-template dispatch.
stars_or_usage: 14 stars; registered in the Julia General registry
tradeoffs: Needs the Julia runtime and JIT warm-up (the README table does not say whether compile time is excluded); a derivative work of Minuit2, so LGPL applies; not a drop-in for C++ callers.
caveats: First-party numbers from the port's author, on microsecond toy objectives of 2 to 10 parameters where per-call overhead dominates. The table appears to date from the 0.1.0-alpha Phase 0 gate: the CHANGELOG entry of 2026-05-25 reports 'max ratio 0.887x, mean 0.47x', which matches the README rows, and the repo shows no rerun for the current 0.7.x code. The C++ side is Minuit2 6.24.0 (2021), pinned in docs/UPSTREAM.md, built from a gitignored checkout; newer ROOT Minuit2 releases were not compared. The C++ compiler is not named, though CMake's Release default is -O3 -DNDEBUG. The timed regions differ in setup: C++ builds MnUserParameters with std::string names per run, and Julia builds a CostFunction. The gauss_ll rows use different random datasets (Julia's global-RNG randn, which advances with every sample, vs a C++ mt19937_64 reseeded per run). The CHANGELOG says Rosenbrock results agree only 'within Strategy(0) cross-impl variance', and the README does not show the nfcn per fit, so equal work per fit is not demonstrated. CHANGELOG 0.7.1 records a 4x build-to-build swing in warm fit time across Julia 1.12 precompile images (13 vs 51 us on the migrad! path, since fixed), so microsecond Julia timings are fragile. The README says AI coding agents helped write the port and its documentation. [retier] The gauss_ll timed regions include random data generation with different generators on each side; a g++ 13.3 -O3 microbenchmark on a Xeon puts the C++ GaussNLLNDim(10,1000) constructor alone at 13.2 us and GaussNLL(100) at 1.9 us against README gaps of 12.7 and 2.55 us, so those rows may mostly time the RNG. The table times the low-level migrad kernel; CHANGELOG 0.7.1 puts the warm user-facing migrad! on the 4-parameter quadratic at about 11 us against C++ 5.50 us (different runs). The Julia runner is a time_ns loop, not BenchmarkTools, and the perf-config [blas] num_threads=1 is never read by run_perf.jl.

name: Node.js (V8 Irregexp JIT) regex-dna in kostya/jit-benchmarks
baseline: C regex-dna (regexdna/test.c, Mike Pall's 2009-era Benchmarks Game program) using libpcre (PCRE1) with pcre_study(re, 0, ...), so PCRE's JIT is not enabled and every match runs in PCRE's interpreter; gcc 12.2.0 -O3 -march=native -fomit-frame-pointer -funroll-loops, linked with -lpcre
workload: Benchmarks Game regex-dna on a fasta file generated by regexdna/helper.c with n=3,500,000 (ONE 7M, TWO 10.5M and THREE 17.5M bases): nine case-insensitive variant-count regexes and eleven IUB-code substitutions after stripping headers and newlines; single thread, one process run, timed externally from the 'started' message (after input reading and line stripping) to process exit.
claimed_speedup: regexdna: Node 1.06s vs C 5.6s (about 5.3x, derived from page data), one measured run per row (Runs 1); memory 622.4 MB vs 86.7 MB. PHP (PCRE2 via preg_*) takes 1.39s (JIT) and 1.40s on the same nine caseless counts and eleven substitutions.
compiler_and_flags: C: gcc -O3 -march=native -fomit-frame-pointer -funroll-loops -Wno-unused-result -Wno-implicit-function-declaration ... -lpcre (tools/languages.rb c build_cmd plus tools/benchmarks.rb build_flags for regexdna); gcc 12.2.0 per README Versions; libpcre version not stated. Node.js 19.7.0 run as node test.js with default flags.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X, 80 GB DDR4-3200, Docker on Ubuntu 22.10
tradeoffs: Node uses 622 MB vs 86.7 MB for the C program.
caveats: Crippled baseline: the C program calls pcre_study with flags 0, so libpcre runs its interpreter, while V8's Irregexp compiles each regex to native code; the comparison measures regex-engine mode (interpreted PCRE1 vs compiled Irregexp), not JavaScript against C. The PHP rows, which drive PCRE2 through preg_* with the same nine caseless counts and eleven substitutions (PHP's pcre.jit setting defaults to on), take 1.39s and 1.40s, 4x faster than the C row, so a C build with PCRE or PCRE2 JIT would likely land near Node. The Crystal row (0.34s) is not the same work: its test.cr does all eleven substitutions in one gsub pass with an alternation and a hash, uses case-sensitive variant regexes and maps S to (c|t), so it is no evidence for what JIT-enabled C would reach. The C program dates from before PCRE gained a JIT (PCRE 8.20, 2011). Single measured run per row (Runs 1). Numbers are from round 1 (2023-02-28) with node 19.7.0 and were not rerun; the only 2026 commit adds a README link. The README states no mechanism. The win belongs to V8's Irregexp engine (C++), not the JavaScript language.

name: OrdinaryDiffEq.jl (DifferentialEquations.jl) ODE solvers vs Sundials, ODEPACK and Hairer codes
baseline: Sundials CVODE_Adams and ARKODE (C) and liblsoda (C port of ODEPACK lsoda), plus Hairer dopri5/dop853/odex (Fortran), called through Julia wrappers with a Julia right-hand side.
workload: Work-precision diagrams (wall time versus error at tolerances 1e-6 to 1e-13) for non-stiff ODEs: Lotka-Volterra, Pleiades and Three-Body.
claimed_speedup: SciMLBenchmarks README summary (no numbers): non-stiff 'OrdinaryDiffEq.jl's methods are the most efficient by a good amount', the Vern methods do best, ARKODE and Hairer dopri5/dop853 are 'far less efficient than the Vern methods', CVODE_Adams and lsoda 'tend to not do very well'; stiff: ARKODE is inconsistent and KenCarp4 is 'much more efficient in most cases'. Rigid Body work-precision plot (RigidBody_wpd_5_1, 3 equations, AMD EPYC 7502): Vern7/Vern8 take about 2e-5 to 1e-4 s while CVODE_Adams and ARKODE (explicit, order 6) take about 1e-4 to 1e-3 s over the same error range, roughly 5-10x at matched error (read off the plot, derived from page data). On the stiff Pollution page (20 equations) FBDF is only modestly ahead of CVODE_BDF in the high-tolerance plot, and the page's own conclusion reads 'Sundials CVODE_BDF the best here'.
compiler_and_flags: Julia 1.11.9 (LLVM 16.0.6, znver2) for OrdinaryDiffEq; Sundials C library via Sundials.jl v6.7.1 and Sundials_jll v7.5.0+0 (BinaryBuilder build, compiler and flags not stated); ODEInterface_jll v0.0.2 and LSODA_jll v0.1.2 for the secondary baselines
hardware: AMD EPYC 7502 32-Core (128 threads), Linux; Julia 1.11.9, LLVM 16.0.6 (znver2), per the RigidBody and Pollution page appendices
tradeoffs: Julia JIT start-up and package precompilation; wins depend on the Verner high-order Runge-Kutta methods and algorithm-specific interpolation that the C and Fortran codes do not provide.
caveats: First-party suite run by the SciML project on its own solvers. Algorithm versus algorithm: Vern7/8/9 and Tsit5 against Dormand-Prince, Adams and ARKODE methods, so the win is not the language's (same_algorithm false). In this harness the Sundials C solvers are driven through Sundials.jl wrappers with a Julia right-hand side called back across the C boundary on every function evaluation, and each timed solve includes wrapper setup; on 3-equation problems solved in 20 microseconds to 1 ms this fixed overhead weighs heavily, and the Julia methods also get a StaticArrays out-of-place variant (prob_choice 2) that the C library cannot use. Numbers exist only as plots; the RigidBody page notes that some of the gap depends on each library's error norm. The win is not universal: on the stiff Pollution problem the page's conclusion names Sundials CVODE_BDF the best, and FBDF is only modestly ahead in its high-tolerance plot. Fortran baselines (dopri5, dop853, radau, ODEInterface) are out of scope for a C/C++ baseline. [retier] DiffEqDevTools times solve(prob, alg, sol.u, sol.t, sol.k), which OrdinaryDiffEqCore reuses, while Sundials.jl ignores those arrays, rebuilds the SUNContext, CVodeCreate and NVector on every timed run and drives CVODE in CV_ONE_STEP mode, so the 5-10x figures overstate the C solvers' loss. v7 defaults to AutoSpecialize while the benchmark forces FullSpecialize; the Pollution prose says CVODE_BDF is best while its plot 16_1 shows Rodas5P about 2-3x faster; issue #2586 reports fixed-step implicit methods 70-100x slow.
found_via: Checked SciML/SciMLBenchmarksOutput markdown (NonStiffODE) after the Julia-vs-C++ WebSearch returned only forum threads.
why_faster: Pages credit the Verner methods and algorithm-specific interpolants; Julia specialization of the user's ODE function (FullSpecialize, StaticArrays) is implied by the setup but not argued as the cause.

The C solvers are BinaryBuilder Sundials_jll builds with no compiler or flags stated and the suite is run by the SciML project on its own solvers, so first-party C, not A or B.
verification.notes: Keep at C as an algorithm win, not a language win (same_algorithm false, language_level_claim false); benchmark_url moved to the RigidBody output page, which has the plots and the hardware appendix. Shortcomings: first-party, numbers only in plots, C solvers driven through Julia callbacks with wrapper setup inside the timing, Sundials_jll build flags unstated, and the Pollution page names CVODE_BDF the best.

name: pflua (pflang packet-filter compiler on LuaJIT) vs libpcap BPF interpreter and Linux kernel BPF JITs
baseline: libpcap's user-space BPF interpreter (pcap_offline_filter in the Debian system libpcap, version and build flags not stated) running bytecode from pcap_compile with libpcap's optimizer on; also the 2011 Linux kernel BPF JIT and the 2014 Linux eBPF JIT (C, built with gcc -O3 as user-space shared objects in pflua-bench), whose filters run as JIT-emitted machine code
workload: Run pflang (tcpdump filter language) expressions 'accept all', 'ip', 'tcp', 'tcp port 5555' and 'icmp' over a 60-64 MB capture of 961,180 ICMP ping packets ('tcp' and 'tcp port 5555' match none of them), in millions of packets per second (MPPS). One discarded warm-up set, then 20 sets per engine in one process (bench.mk ITERATIONS?=20; the README says 50); each measurement loops over all packets for at least 0.1 s and checks the expected match count. Results committed 2015-02-03.
claimed_speedup: pflua-bench README conclusion: 'In many circumstances, pflua is the fastest pflang implementation out there, by a long shot.' (the pflua README says 'by a wide margin'). Medians of the 20 runs in results/ping-flood (derived from page data), MPPS pflua vs libpcap vs linux-bpf vs linux-ebpf: 'tcp' 89.9 vs 37.9 vs 62.2 vs 56.1; 'tcp port 5555' 89.9 vs 37.9 vs 61.8 vs 57.6; 'icmp' 89.9 vs 54.8 vs 83.5 vs 77.7; 'ip' 91.6 vs 68.0 vs 85.3 vs 78.7; 'accept all' 127.9 vs 92.1 vs 109.8 vs 95.4. About 2.4x libpcap and 1.45x the 2011 Linux BPF JIT on 'tcp'. The bpf-lua engine (libpcap's BPF translated to Lua) gets 88.4 MPPS on 'tcp', within 2% of pflua.
compiler_and_flags: pflua and bpf-lua: LuaJIT from the pflua submodule built with its default make. linux-bpf-jit and linux-ebpf-jit: gcc -g -Wall -fPIC -O3 (their Makefiles; gcc version not stated). libpcap: Debian system library loaded with ffi.load("pcap"), version and build flags not stated.
hardware: Intel Core i7-3770 (x86-64), Debian GNU/Linux (3.14-2), otherwise unloaded machine (pflua-bench README)
why_faster: Source (pflua README, Performance section): LuaJIT trace compilation emits machine code specialised to the traffic actually seen; pflua can hoist and eliminate bounds checks while BPF must check every packet access; it works in network byte order while BPF converts to host order; it uses LuaJIT's register allocator and optimizer whereas the Linux kernel JIT has a limited optimizer.
stars_or_usage: 312 stars (pflua); 26 stars (pflua-bench); written for the Snabb user-space networking toolkit
tradeoffs: Needs LuaJIT; filters are compiled at run time and the speed depends on LuaJIT trace behaviour; pflua is a filter engine only, not a full libpcap replacement, and the project says there may be bugs or differences against libpcap.
caveats: First-party benchmark by the pflua authors; libpcap version and flags and the gcc version are not stated, so tier C. The comparison is LuaJIT-compiled code against a C interpreter (libpcap) and two other runtime JITs (Linux BPF/eBPF), not against AOT-compiled C doing the same work, so it is a weak fit for runtime-jit-beats-aot. Harness asymmetry: pflua and bpf-lua predicates are Lua functions inlined into the LuaJIT trace of the timing loop, while libpcap (pcap_offline_filter, plus a pcap_pkthdr written per packet) and the Linux JITs (run_filter in a .so) are called through the FFI per packet; the 'accept all' row, which does no filtering, already differs (127.9 vs 92.1 vs 109.8 vs 95.4 MPPS). Subtracting the 'accept all' time per packet (derived from page data), the 'tcp' filter costs about 3.3 ns in pflua vs 15.5 ns in libpcap and 7.0 ns in linux-bpf, but the 'icmp' filter costs 3.3 ns in pflua vs 2.9 ns (linux-bpf) and 2.4 ns (linux-ebpf), so pflua's 'icmp' lead over the Linux JITs is call overhead. libpcap runs with its optimizer on (pf/libpcap.lua passes optimize=true), so it is not an unoptimised interpreter. The workload is homogeneous and 'tcp' filters match no packet, which suits a tracing JIT; on the real-world wingolog.org-2 capture pflua is sometimes slower than libpcap and the Linux JITs (README blames LuaJIT trace state-transfer costs). The README prose (about 180 MPPS, 'all results are faster than the accept all loop') does not match the committed CSVs, where 'accept all' is the fastest row for every engine. Results date from 2015-02-03; last commits 2017-01-30 (pflua) and 2016-12-05 (pflua-bench). [retier] The project's own native C driver (test-native/pf_test_native.c, gcc -O3) measured libpcap 'icmp' at 73.9 MPPS and accept-all at 110.6 against 54.8 and 92.1 in the bench.lua CSV, so pflua's icmp lead shrinks from 1.64x to 1.22x (cross-run). Filters plateau at 89.9-91.6 MPPS whatever the filter and bpf-lua ties; pflua loses to the Linux BPF JIT in 5 of 18 rows and beats libpcap 1.30-7.1x in all 18. Snabb's lib/pflua holds later fixes (native codegen xor/or bug, 2020).
found_via: WebSearch: 'github LuaJIT OR Java OR JVM outperforms C DPDK OR C implementation packet processing OR database OR codec benchmark JIT faster' led to Igalia/pflua; opened the pflua README, the pflua-bench README and results/ping-flood CSVs (libpcap.csv, linux-bpf.csv, linux-ebpf.csv, pflua.csv)

Main shortcomings: first-party, libpcap build unstated, per-packet FFI call overhead favours pflua (its icmp lead over the Linux JITs disappears after subtracting the accept-all loop), win is LuaJIT trace compilation not pflua's optimizer (bpf-lua ties it), weak category fit (JIT vs interpreter and other JITs), 2015 data.

name: Proteus (programmable runtime specialization and JIT layer on LLVM for C++, CUDA and HIP)
baseline: Ahead-of-time compiled CUDA/HIP/C++ kernels (typical AoT compilation of the same application)
workload: End-to-end GPU application speedup from specializing kernels at run time on argument values and launch parameters (CGO 2025 paper), including JIT compile overhead.
claimed_speedup: CGO 2025 chart as reproduced on CGO 2026 tutorial slide 10 (olympus-hpc.github.io): end-to-end speedup over AoT with a warm persistent cache (JIT compile excluded) up to 2.80x on an AMD MI250X and 1.78x on an NVIDIA V100 (WSM5); cold-cache maxima 2.52x and 1.35x, with V100 cold SW4CK 0.93x and LULESH 0.99x. The '1.23x over Jitify' from news snippets is not reproducible from the slide bars.
compiler_and_flags: Public harness (Olympus-HPC/proteus-benchmarks): AOT and Proteus variants of each HeCBench program are built from the same main.cu by the same Makefile with Clang (PROTEUS_CC), -std=c++14 -O3 -ffast-math, CUDA default --cuda-gpu-arch=sm_70; the Proteus build only adds -fpass-plugin=libProteusPass.so and -DENABLE_PROTEUS. The paper's exact compiler versions and flags were not read (paper blocked).
hardware: NVIDIA V100 and AMD MI250X (CGO 2026 tutorial slide 10).
stars_or_usage: 54 stars, 397 commits; integrated experimentally in RAJA (per search snippet)
tradeoffs: Links an LLVM-based JIT runtime into the application; compile overhead is paid on first use (mitigated by in-memory and persistent caches); the annotation interface needs Clang to build the application with the Proteus pass.
caveats: Numbers are snippet only: the CGO 2025 paper (Georgakoudis, Parasyris, Beckingsale, pp. 507-522, peer-reviewed, would be tier B if read), its CGO program page, the LLNL newsroom and HPCwire were all unresolvable from this environment, and the Proteus README and docs carry no numbers or paper link. 'Up to' maxima are best cases on selected applications; the public harness (Olympus-HPC/proteus-benchmarks: HeCBench adam, feynman-kac, LULESH and others, plus RAJAPerf and LBANN configs) builds AOT and JIT variants with identical -O3 -ffast-math flags but publishes no results, and GPU models are not stated (the CUDA Makefile default sm_70 suggests a V100-class part, unconfirmed). End-to-end times include JIT compile overhead per the paper abstract snippet. The repo has moved: github.com/Olympus-HPC/proteus now resolves to llnl/proteus. [retier] The headline 2.80x and 1.78x are warm persistent-cache bars: driver.py fills the cache in an untimed warm-up run, so JIT compile time is excluded (the record's earlier 'including JIT overhead' was wrong). The harness never checks outputs (the ADAM reference check is commented out, -ffast-math).
found_via: WebSearch: 'Proteus portable runtime optimization GPU kernel execution LLVM JIT speedup over ahead-of-time paper LLNL Olympus-HPC'; repo README opened on github.com and raw.githubusercontent.com.
why_faster: Runtime values (kernel arguments, array contents, launch bounds) become constants so LLVM can fold, unroll and prune kernel code beyond what static compilation can; the README says it uses runtime context to specialize 'and enable optimizations beyond static compilation'.

verification.tier_reason: The numbers (up to 2.8x AMD, 1.78x NVIDIA end-to-end vs AOT; 1.23x average over Jitify) come from the CGO 2025 paper and were seen only in WebSearch snippets of the CGO program page, LLNL newsroom and HPCwire (all unresolvable here), so the wave-14 rule keeps it at C; the public harness Olympus-HPC/proteus-benchmarks (driver.py, hecbench.toml, per-benchmark Makefiles with aot/proteus/jitify builds) has no results, GPU models or CPU stated.
verification.notes: Metadata checked: 54 stars, 10 forks, 397 commits, Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception, last commit 2026-10-09 (active). The repo URL now redirects to github.com/llnl/proteus (README clones LLNL/proteus; the Olympus-HPC org no longer lists it), so consider a repo_url override to https://github.com/llnl/proteus while keeping the merged id. Retier to B if the CGO 2025 paper becomes readable; harness code at github.com/Olympus-HPC/proteus-benchmarks shows AOT and JIT builds use identical flags.

name: Ripserer.jl (Julia persistent homology) vs Ripser and Cubical Ripser (C++)
baseline: Ripser (C++, master commit 286d369) and Cubical Ripser (C++, commits 6edb9c5 for 2D and a063dac for 3D)
workload: Persistent homology of Vietoris-Rips filtrations (datasets from the Ripser paper and PH-roadmap, parsed as Float32, parse time included) and of cubical image filtrations; minimum of five runs.
claimed_speedup: Docs: 'very close to Ripser, usually within around 30%' and 'on very sparse inputs ... can sometimes outperform Ripser'. Ripserer/Ripser time ratios from the page: Alpha-Rips 0.807 (636 ms vs 789 ms), 0.741 (872 ms vs 1.179 s), 0.744 (56 ms vs 76 ms), 0.942 (5.844 s vs 6.203 s) and 1.058 (49.431 s vs 46.707 s, slower); sparse=true mode 0.993 and 0.998 on o3_1024 and o3_4096, 0.932 on random16, but 1.267 on dragon2000 and 1.304 on fract-r; dense mode is slower on 5 of 6 sets (ratio 1.04 to 1.99, o3_4096 151.5 s vs 76.2 s) with random16 at 0.803. Versus Cubical Ripser: 0.96 on bonsai64 (2.875 s vs 2.996 s), slower elsewhere (up to 2.631).
compiler_and_flags: Ripserer v0.15 (Julia version not stated; the RipsererBenchmarks.jl Manifest.toml does not record it). Ripser (commit 286d369) built by the harness (RipsererBenchmarks.jl src/ripser.jl get_ripsers runs `make all`) from its Makefile line `c++ -std=c++11 -Wall ripser.cpp -o ripser -Ofast -D NDEBUG`; Cubical Ripser 2D (6edb9c5) and 3D (a063dac) Makefiles compile every file with `c++ -std=c++11 -Ofast`. The compiler behind `c++` and its version are not stated. Timing: BenchmarkTools, samples=5, minimum reported.
hardware: Laptop with Intel Core i5-4200U @ 1.60GHz and 8 GB RAM
tradeoffs: Uses more memory than Ripser on small inputs (heap includes the Julia runtime, for example 138 MiB vs 33 MiB on alpha_3_sphere_3000) but supports higher-dimensional cubical complexes, critical simplices and representative cycles.
caveats: Mostly parity or slower: dense mode is 1.04-1.99x slower on 5 of 6 Rips sets (o3_4096 151.5 s vs 76.2 s), so the docs' 'usually within around 30%' holds only with sparse=true; sparse mode is 0.993-1.304; wins of about 1.06-1.35x appear only on very sparse Alpha-Rips inputs and tiny random16. Ripser is timed as an external process (launch plus stdout text output) against in-process Ripserer, which favours Ripserer on short runs. Ripserer's heap is 3-5x Ripser's on Alpha-Rips (includes the Julia runtime). Against Cubical Ripser, which the docs say uses a more specialized algorithm, Ripserer wins only bonsai64 (0.96) and is up to 2.6x slower elsewhere. Single 2020-era run (Ripserer v0.15, 2020 Ripser commits) on an old dual-core laptop; compiler and Julia versions not stated. [retier] The docs' 'dense' table pits Ripserer's dense mode against Ripser, which picks sparse mode itself below max distance (ripser.cpp 286d369); sparse=true is the like-for-like mode. Ripser is timed as a subprocess (launch, stdout capture) against in-process Ripserer after BenchmarkTools warm-up. RipsererBenchmarks.jl's load_sparse adds 1.0 to every Alpha-Rips edge length, so Ripserer gets different filtration values than Ripser (probably timing-neutral; outputs never cross-checked). Mod{M} reruns a trial-division is_prime on every operation for M != 2; the docs claim Julia 1.0+ while Project.toml needs 1.6.

name: SymbolicUtils.jl / Symbolics.jl (Julia symbolic engine) vs SymEngine (C++): SciMLBenchmarks SymEngineComparison
baseline: SymEngine v0.12.0 (C++ symbolic library, via SymEngine.jl v0.13.2 and SymEngine_jll)
workload: Ten symbolic workloads adapted from SymEngine's own C++ benchmark suite plus SymbolicUtils-native ones: diff of expand((x^y+y^z+z^x)^50), 15-term Taylor series, trig-product substitution, 10^5-draw random-expression substitution (dense and sparse rule), variable search on shared and unshared expression sets, numeric evaluation of a 10000-deep expression, code-generation init, and the call of the generated function with common-subexpression elimination.
claimed_speedup: Summary table (SymEngine s vs SymbolicUtils s; the SymbolicUtils column is the faster of two variants): SymbolicUtils faster in 4 of 10 rows: compiled call with CSE 6.93256e-7 vs 3.13135e-7 (2.2x), variable search on dissimilar expressions 4.67036e-4 vs 2.13078e-4 (2.2x), variable search on common subtrees 1.02663e-3 vs 4.89876e-4 (2.1x), sparse-rule substitution 1.10077e-3 vs 5.92595e-4 (1.9x). The per-variant tables show the plain variants: search_variables! without IRStructure is slower than SymEngine (1.37841e-3 vs 1.02663e-3 common, 5.97345e-4 vs 4.67036e-4 dissimilar), and the plain Substituter wins the sparse rule by only 1.28x (8.61063e-4 vs 1.10077e-3) on a 2810-node tree against SymEngine's 3271-node tree. The compiled call without CSE is 1.0665e-5 vs 2.559e-6 (4.2x). SymEngine faster in the other 6 rows: diff of expand 6.95691e-3 vs 0.332787 (48x), eval_double of a 10000-deep expression 0.0116745 vs 0.331982 (28x), codegen init without CSE 1.15092e-3 vs 1.34645e-2 (12x; with CSE 1.66448e-4 vs 3.34998e-3, 20x), series 1.99123e-3 vs 1.98982e-2 (10x), trig-product substitution 1.478e-5 vs 6.0009e-5 (4.1x), dense-rule substitution 1.13195e-3 vs 3.95472e-3 (3.5x). All ratios derived from page data.
compiler_and_flags: Julia 1.13.0 (LLVM 20.1.8, JIT target znver2), SymbolicUtils v4.46.6, Symbolics v7.39.2, SymEngine.jl v0.13.2 over the prebuilt SymEngine_jll v0.12.0+0. Per the public Yggdrasil recipe (S/SymEngine/build_tarballs.jl, symengine commit 088aa01) SymEngine_jll is built with CMake and no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE, which SymEngine's CMakeLists defaults to Release (CMake's -O3 -DNDEBUG), for a generic x86_64 target, with WITH_SYMENGINE_THREAD_SAFE=yes, GMP integers and no LLVM (derived from public build recipe; compiler version not stated). Timings are minimum over samples (Chairmarks).
hardware: 128 x AMD EPYC 7502 32-Core Processor (128 virtual cores), Linux x86_64 CI runner
why_faster: Per the benchmark text: the substitution and search wins use SymbolicUtils' IRStructure acceleration structure, which visits shared subexpressions once; the compiled-call win is a native Julia function produced by Code.toexpr plus eval (JIT compiled), against SymEngine's LambdaRealDoubleVisitor, which the file describes as 'an interpreter over the expression tree'.
tradeoffs: The JIT path pays a large setup cost: codegen init is 12x slower than SymEngine's. Core operations (expand, differentiate, series, deep evaluation) are 10-48x slower than SymEngine in this run.
caveats: First-party benchmark by the Symbolics/SciML maintainers, single CI run without variance; the file says the first workload set 'plays to SymEngine's strengths', and SymEngine wins 6 of 10 rows by 3.5-48x. Two of the four SymbolicUtils wins (variable search) need an IRStructure populated outside the timed region; the plain search_variables! is 1.28-1.34x slower than SymEngine, and the IR-backed substitution likewise reuses an IR built in warm-up, so the IR rows exclude the DAG construction SymEngine's subs and free_symbols pay for. The plain Substituter's 1.28x sparse-rule win is on a tree 14% smaller than SymEngine's (2810 vs 3271 nodes). SymEngine 'variable search' is free_symbols converted to a Julia Vector and unioned into a Julia Set through ccall-based hashing, not an identical operation. The compiled-call row is JIT-compiled native code against SymEngine's tree interpreter (the jll has no LLVM backend), and the SymbolicUtils codegen-init row times only toexpr plus eval, so LLVM compilation of the generated function, which happens on the first call, is in neither row. SymEngine_jll is SymEngine 0.12.0 (three releases behind 0.15.0) built thread-safe (atomic reference counts) for generic x86_64 without TCMalloc, not SymEngine's tuned configuration, and its compiler version is not stated. [retier] The compiled-call rows (the 2.2x and 4.2x JIT wins) evaluate at x=0.0, where log(0) = -Inf makes every call return +Inf and every x function sees argument 0, so they mostly time dispatch overhead and favour the JIT. The 10-row summary omits the expand table, where SymEngine is 41-361x faster. The IRSubstituter warm-up fills the IR and clear_cache! empties only the index cache, so no timed sample pays the IR build; Chairmarks minima drop GC pauses; a global hash-consing ReentrantLock serialises expression construction across threads.
found_via: Julia ecosystem candidate; opened SciML/SciMLBenchmarks.jl benchmarks/Symbolics (github.com tree) and the rendered SciMLBenchmarksOutput markdown on raw.githubusercontent.com (docs.sciml.ai is blocked).

verification.tier_reason: First-party SciML benchmark (SciMLBenchmarks.jl benchmarks/Symbolics/SymEngineComparison.jmd) with Julia 1.13.0 and EPYC 7502 stated; the SymEngine side is the prebuilt SymEngine_jll 0.12.0 whose compiler is not stated (flags only derivable from the Yggdrasil recipe), so not A; C. Downgraded as a claim: two of the four 'wins' exist only with an IRStructure built outside the timed region.
verification.notes: Summary numbers on the page match the record, but the headline '4 of 10 rows faster' overstates the language win: the two search wins and most of the sparse-substitution win come from an IRStructure precomputed outside the timed region (plain variants lose search and win sparse substitution by only 1.28x on a smaller tree), and the compiled-call win is JIT code against SymEngine's interpreter in an LLVM-less, thread-safe SymEngine_jll build. SymEngine is already listed in COPYABLE.md with this same page as its benchmark, so this is the reverse claim on the same benchmark; keep as tier C with these shortcomings. Metadata checked: MIT LICENSE.md, 560 stars, last commit 2026-10-11, not a fork.

retier.reason: Enricher: the compiled-call rows behind the JIT wins evaluate at x=0.0, where every call returns +Inf and the rows time dispatch overhead (degenerate-workload precedent, ThreadPool), and the summary omits the expand table where SymEngine is 41-361x faster; no valid like-for-like win remains: C to D.

name: Visual Basic .NET (CLR JIT) vs C: Fourmilab fbench
baseline: The C version of fbench built with GCC 3.2.3 -O3 on Linux (the table's reference row, relative time 1)

name: lua-resty-core (LuaJIT FFI API for ngx_lua) vs the ngx_lua built-in Lua C API
baseline: the Lua C API implementation of the ngx.* and ngx.shared.* functions in lua-nginx-module (ngx_lua, C)
workload: Calls of the ngx_lua API functions from Lua code running under LuaJIT through the FFI-based reimplementation versus the C API implementation; no workload is specified.
claimed_speedup: No numbers. README: 'its FFI implementation is both faster, safer, and more complete than the Lua C API of the ngx_lua module.' Caveat in the same README: 'You will only observe speedup when you get a good part of your user Lua code JIT compiled.'
stars_or_usage: 855 stars, 288 forks; part of the OpenResty project
tradeoffs: Requires LuaJIT with FFI and a matching nginx build; replaces parts of the C API, so API coverage differs ('more complete' per README).
caveats: Qualitative claim only: no benchmark in the README and none found elsewhere (one web search turned up package mirrors and an api7.ai explainer without timings, snippet only). 855 stars, under the 1k notability guideline, kept for project notability (loaded by default since OpenResty 1.15.8.1). Not Lua beating C: the FFI path still calls C functions exported by lua-nginx-module (e.g. ngx_http_lua_ffi_shdict_get declared via ffi.cdef in lib/resty/core/shdict.lua); the gain is that LuaJIT traces are not aborted by Lua C API calls, so it is a JIT-versus-interpreter effect rather than JIT code beating AOT C. The README's own caveat: 'If the user Lua code is not JIT compiled, then use of this library may lead to performance drop in interpreted mode.' License text in the README is the two-clause BSD text (SPDX id inferred). No hardware, versions or flags. [retier] The baseline is gone: lua_load_resty_core has been a no-op since ngx_lua v0.10.16, and current ngx_lua exposes shdict, md5, base64 and escape_uri only as ngx_http_lua_ffi_* functions, so a head-to-head needs ngx_lua 0.10.15 or older. The only numbers found show a slowdown (issue #15: latency 20 ms to 250 ms on OpenResty 1.7.7.2). base.lua requires ngx_lua exactly 0.10.32 while the README says 0.10.25 and dist.ini 0.10.30. JIT versus interpreter, not JIT versus AOT C (off-category).
found_via: Blogs / talks slice. Fetched github.com/topics/luajit (no performance claims in the 20 repository descriptions shown), then read the README of openresty/lua-resty-core, which states the FFI-versus-C-API speed claim.
why_faster: README: the Lua C API 'will never be JIT compiled and the user Lua code is always interpreted (slowly)', while the FFI-based API calls can be JIT compiled by LuaJIT.

verification.tier_reason: README states the FFI implementation is 'both faster, safer, and more complete than the Lua C API of the ngx_lua module' with no numbers, benchmark code or links; one web search found only qualitative restatements (api7.ai learning-center article, a vendor of an OpenResty-based gateway, snippet only, no timings).
verification.notes: Tier D confirmed; metadata matches (855 stars, 288 forks, last commit 2026-08-24, BSD two-clause text in README). Kept rather than rejected per wave policy despite tier D under 1k stars. Main shortcomings: no numbers; the FFI API still calls C functions, so the win is trace-compilation of the calling Lua code, not Lua beating C; slower in interpreted mode per its own README; arguably off-category for runtime-jit-beats-aot.

name: Crystal: LangArena Etc::Words
baseline: C++ splitting with std::istringstream and counting in std::unordered_map<std::string,int>, and C using strtok_r with uthash (strdup per new word); both built by g++/gcc 16.0.1 and clang 22.1.8; best C/C++ configuration is C++/G++/PGO at 1.587 s
workload: Split a generated text of 50,000 space-separated words (3 to 8 lowercase letters) into words, count frequencies in a hash map, then report the most frequent word, the vocabulary size and a checksum; 360 timed iterations after 72 untimed warm-up iterations (run.js). Each harness checks the final checksum against run.js (1998586832), so Crystal does the same work as C and C++.
claimed_speedup: Crystal 0.88 s (peak RSS 8.8 MB) vs C++/G++/PGO 1.587 s (best of the 16 Clang/GCC C and C++ configurations), C++/G++ 1.638 s and C++/Clang++ 1.707 s (prod, -O2), C++/G++/Fast 1.651 s (-O3 -march=native) and C/Clang 1.988 s: about 1.80x faster than the best C/C++ row, 1.86x faster than C++/G++ prod and 2.26x faster than C/Clang (derived from page data). Zig 0.91 s, Rust 1.021 s and Go 1.129 s also beat every C/C++ row. The lead is stable across five monthly runs: 1.79x on 2026-07-14 (Crystal 1.20.3, 0.901 s vs C++/G++ 1.611 s), 1.81x on 2026-08-14, 1.80x on 2026-09-03, 1.82x on 2026-09-18 and 1.80x on 2026-10-05 (derived from the results files). The suite's 'Crystal/O3' row (crystal build -O3 without --release) is much slower at 3.105 s, slower than every C row.
compiler_and_flags: C/C++ (cpp/Makefile, c/Makefile; versions and build commands from the results file): Clang 22.1.8 and GCC 16.0.1 20260322 (trunk r16-8246, Ubuntu snapshot package), libstdc++ (no -stdlib flag), -std=c++20 for C++. Headline 'prod' rows (make -j prod): -O2 -DNDEBUG -fstack-protector-strong -fno-omit-frame-pointer, linked with -Wl,-z,relro,-z,now -Wl,--gc-sections. 'Fast': -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -DNDEBUG -pipe -fstack-protector -ftree-vectorize -funroll-loops. 'Unsafe': -O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG -pipe -fno-stack-protector -fomit-frame-pointer -ffast-math -fvisibility=hidden -fno-common -fstrict-overflow -fno-trapping-math. 'PGO': -O2 plus -fprofile-instr-use (Clang) or -fprofile-use -fprofile-correction (GCC). -flto=thin (Fast) and -flto=full (Unsafe) appear only in the link flags while objects are compiled without -flto, so those builds probably get no LTO (inference from cpp/Makefile). All 16 Clang/GCC x C/C++ x prod/Fast/Unsafe/PGO configurations were compared (instrumented PGO/Gen rows and the author's mycc/cproc compilers excluded). Crystal 1.21.1 [73ea5c2b1] (2026-09-26): headline row 'crystal build main.cr --release' (Crystal 1.21.1's src/compiler/crystal/command.cr defines --release as '-O3 --single-module'; LLVM backend, Boehm GC); the 'Crystal/O3' hack row is 'crystal build main.cr -O3', i.e. without --single-module, which plausibly explains its 3.5x slower time (inference, not stated by the suite).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X 8-Core Processor, 78GB RAM, x86_64 Linux (results file 2026-10-05, host kostya-ms7c37)
why_faster: Not stated by the suite. Code reading (crystal/main.cr, cpp/src/words.cpp, c/src/words.c): the C++ baseline tokenizes with istringstream operator>> and copies each word into a std::string key of a node-based unordered_map; the C baseline strdup's every distinct word into uthash; Crystal splits on ' ' with a block and updates its built-in Hash. Agent inference: a tokenizer and container difference, not code generation.
tradeoffs: Crystal peak RSS 8.8 MB vs 5.3 MB for C and 7.8 MB for C++ in the same run.
caveats: Mostly a standard-library and idiom comparison (tokenizer, hash container and allocator), so it says little about Crystal's code generation; a C++ version with string_view tokenizing and a flat hash map would likely close the gap (inference, not measured). Crystal allocates a new String per word as well, so the gap is not zero-copy splitting. The Crystal harness runs GC.collect after the timer stops, so the last collection is untimed, while C++ frees its map nodes inside every timed iteration. Only the --release build wins; the suite's Crystal/O3 build (no --single-module) runs 3.105 s, slower than every C and C++ row. LangArena calls itself 'a subjective benchmark' and says AI tools helped translate the tasks between languages; it publishes one measurement per test and configuration (no variance), though the lead is stable across five monthly runs. The headline C/C++ rows are -O2 with hardening flags, but the -O3 -march=native Fast, Unsafe and PGO rows also lose; the Makefiles' LTO flags are link-only. The row was selected because a non-C/C++ language beats every C and C++ configuration; most other tasks in the suite go the other way. Ratios are derived from the results files, not stated by the suite.

name: csv-zero (Zig SIMD CSV field iterator)
baseline: zsv (C library, built from src/c/zsv with 'cc -O3 main.c -lzsv'; labelled 'zsc (c)' in the result CSV) and lazycsv (C++ header library, g++ -O3 -march=native); Rust simd-csv and csv also measured
workload: Iterate a whole CSV file and count its fields with a 64 KB input buffer (csv-race harness): four real-world files (nfl.csv, worldcitiespop.csv, GTFS mbta stop-times, game.csv) and generated files from about 1 KB to about 9.9 GB, with and without quoting.
claimed_speedup: csv-race result-all.csv wall times, csv-zero vs zsv (C) vs lazycsv (C++): ~32 MB no-quotes 52 col 6.62 ms vs 14.1 ms vs 18.7 ms; ~696 MB 574 ms vs 1.50 s vs 1.25 s; ~3.2 GB no-quotes 603 ms vs 1.32 s vs 1.65 s (Rust simd-csv 870 ms); ~9.9 GB quoted 7.73 s vs 12.7 s vs 12.1 s. csv-zero is the fastest of the 5 parsers on all 10 files. Ratios are 1.36x to 2.61x against zsv and 1.08x to 2.85x against lazycsv (derived from page data). On the four real-world files csv-zero takes 0.78 to 2.86 ms (775 us on nfl.csv vs zsv 1.78 ms). These files are only 0.72 to 2.6 MB, so the rows include process start-up (the ~1 KB file takes 427 us). Independent corroboration: LangArena results/2026-10-05-kostya-ms7c37.js (AMD Ryzen 7 3800X), CSV::Parse runtime: Zig 0.974 s, best C row C/Clang 2.223 s, C++/Clang++ 2.348 s. The Zig implementation imports csv-zero (zig/build.zig.zon). Rust (0.881 s) and Zig/Unchecked (0.585 s) are faster still.
compiler_and_flags: csv-race at the Dec 2025 results commit: Zig 0.15.2 'zig build --release=fast' (build.zig uses standardTargetOptions, so the default target is the native CPU); zsv harness 'cc -O3 main.c -lzsv' against a manually built, system-installed libzsv whose flags are not stated; lazycsv 'g++ -std=c++17 -O3 -march=native'; Rust 'cargo build --release'. The cc and g++ versions are not stated. Timed with poop -d 10000 (perf counters). The harness moved to Zig 0.16 (May 2026) after the results were taken.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 5 PRO 5650U, 30 GB RAM, Linux 6.17.8-arch1-1 (csv-race README)
why_faster: README of csv-zero: SIMD-accelerated scanning, a zero-allocation field iterator that returns slices into one internal buffer, and strict RFC 4180 validation that simplifies fast paths. The author's blog post with details (peymanmo.com) was not opened (host blocked).
stars_or_usage: 38 stars (csv-zero); companion harness csv-race has 2 stars
tradeoffs: Low-level API: yields fields (with a last-column flag), not records, and allocates nothing; strict RFC 4180 (an unquoted field containing a double quote is an error); no type conversion; Zig 0.15 to 0.17 toolchain churn; a C API exists per the README.
caveats: The harness is written by the csv-zero author, and the task only counts fields, so it isolates scanning and says nothing about downstream parsing. No harness step checks that the parsers report the same field count. The result chart set shows the top five parsers only; result-all.csv holds the five measured here (csv-parser, rapidcsv, csv-core and a Go parser are built by the Makefile but not in the CSV). 'zsc (c)' is the zsv library linked with -lzsv from a manual build whose flags are not stated, and its harness is built without -march=native. lazycsv and csv-zero (native Zig target) both target the host CPU. lazycsv memory-maps the input (10.6 GB peak RSS on the 9.9 GB file) instead of using a 64 KB buffer. The four real-world files are 0.72-2.6 MB samples (nfl 1.36 MB, worldcitiespop 0.96 MB, mbta 0.72 MB, game 2.6 MB), so those rows partly measure process start-up. The results date from 2025-12-22/23. Later harness changes: a Zig 0.16 pin, and a fix by the simd-csv author (2026-07-30) that removed double buffering in the Rust csv and simd-csv harnesses, so those two Rust rows are understated. csv-zero's CRLF chunk-boundary fix (2026-01-06) does not affect these LF-only files. Single machine (laptop-class Ryzen 5 PRO 5650U), one table. The csv-zero README claims it outperforms every library in csv-race but gives no numbers; the numbers come from result-all.csv. In LangArena the C/C++ CSV implementations were not inspected, and Rust beats the Zig row there. zsv (C) is already catalogued as a separate entry; this record is about the Zig library.

name: evtx (Rust Windows Event Log parser and evtx_dump)
baseline: libevtx evtxexport (C, libyal), built from source by the repo's benchmark script
workload: Convert a 30 MB Windows Security event log (samples/security_big_sample.evtx) to XML text written to /dev/null; wall-clock time measured with hyperfine (warmup 2, 5 runs by default in the script).
claimed_speedup: README (June 2026, evtx 0.12.2 PGO build, bench commit 99a6def), 30 MB security_big_sample.evtx to XML: evtx 71.6 ms on 1 thread, 20.7 ms on 8 threads vs libevtx (C) 2.439 s as printed (about 34x and 118x), but the libevtx figure was carried over from January 2026 while the evtx columns were re-measured in June (cross-run); the same-run comparison is about 8.8x (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: evtx: Cargo release profile opt-level 3, codegen-units 1, lto thin; README numbers come from build_pgo.sh (RUSTFLAGS -Cprofile-generate then -Cprofile-use, features fast-alloc (tikv-jemallocator) and wevt_templates); rustc version not stated. The committed bench script itself builds a plain 'cargo build --release --bin evtx_dump' without fast-alloc or PGO (README says PGO is worth 2-5%). libevtx: scripts/bench_all_parsers.sh clones libyal/libevtx at HEAD (unpinned), runs synclibs.sh/autogen.sh, './configure --enable-static --disable-shared --enable-static-executables' and make with no CFLAGS (autoconf default, normally -g -O2); C compiler and version not stated.
hardware: 12-core AMD Ryzen 3900X, Arch Linux; evtx columns measured June 2026 on Linux 7.0.11-arch1-1 (bench commit 99a6def), libevtx figure from the January 2026 run on Linux 6.17.9-arch1-1 (bench commit e01782a); hyperfine, 2 warmups and 5 runs by script default.
why_faster: README credits a compiled-template rewrite (docs/compiled-templates.html, not opened), PGO and, for the 8-thread column, parallel chunk parsing. The one-thread gap over libevtx has no stated mechanism.
stars_or_usage: 966 stars, 86 forks; evtx crate 310,212 downloads on crates.io (latest 0.12.3, 2026-09-22); PyPI wheel via pyevtx-rs
tradeoffs: Read-only parser; CDATA nodes and EVTHandle nodes are unimplemented. Safe Rust with optional multithreading. Outputs XML or JSON.
caveats: Category fit is weak: the input is a binary log format (binary XML templates) and the output is XML text. The headline 34x/118x ratios in the current README are cross-run: the evtx columns were re-measured in June 2026 after the compiled-template rewrite while the libevtx 2.439 s figure was carried over from January 2026 (different kernel); the only same-run comparison is January 2026 (8.8x single-threaded, 31x at 24 threads). Optimisation levels are not matched: evtx uses opt-level 3, thin LTO, codegen-units 1, PGO and jemalloc, libevtx is a stock autoconf build (likely -g -O2, no LTO or PGO) at an unpinned HEAD. The committed bench script does not reproduce the PGO/jemalloc binary the README measured. No check that evtxexport -f xml and evtx_dump emit equivalent XML. The multi-thread columns compare a parallel program against single-threaded evtxexport. First-party, one machine, one input file, compiler versions absent. The speed-up is a design win (per-template compiled output, SIMD UTF-16 escaping, arena allocation), not a language-level one. [retier] The committed bench script does not rebuild the README binary (PGO plus jemalloc vs plain release; libevtx unpinned HEAD), and build_pgo.sh trains on samples/, which include the benchmark input. libevtx always computes 2 CRC-32s per chunk while evtx skips them unless --validate-checksums. The '100% safe Rust' claim is overstated (utf16-simd has 42 unsafe blocks); open #289: non-0/1 bool values silently become true.

name: mail-parser (Rust e-mail parser)
baseline: GMime 3.2.15, VMime (commit 5b01911), libEtPan! 1.10.1 and Dovecot 2.4.5 lib-mail (all C or C++, built with -O3 and called through C/C++ shims); the Rust mailparse 0.17.0 crate is also measured
workload: Parse RFC 5322/MIME e-mail messages (one message per call) in three workloads: full (parse and read every decoded leaf body with charset conversion to UTF-8), headers (decoded Subject, first From address, Date, Message-ID) and structure (content type of every MIME part), over eleven corpora (3,292 messages, 17.8 MiB: test suite, Enron sample, large attachments, newsletters, long header blocks, forwarded messages, 1 MB plain text).
claimed_speedup: README, geometric mean over the corpora shown in the README tables (7 corpora for full, 6 for headers and structure), with range: full workload 31x GMime (13 to 177), 20x VMime (7.8 to 80), 15x libEtPan! (5.7 to 69), 9.3x Dovecot (4.4 to 24), 3.0x mailparse; headers 14x GMime, 33x VMime, 19x libEtPan!, 5.2x Dovecot; structure 14x GMime, 31x VMime, 17x libEtPan!, 3.9x Dovecot. Example, full workload, Enron 3,000 messages: mail-parser 2,420 MiB/s vs GMime 65, VMime 70, libEtPan! 96, Dovecot 366 MiB/s (results/summary.md: 37.10x, 34.77x, 25.23x, 6.60x).
compiler_and_flags: Rust side: mail-parser 1.0.0 from the repository (the unreleased rewrite; crates.io latest is 0.11.9, which the harness also measures but the published tables leave out), feature full_encoding, rustc 1.98.1, release profile (opt-level 3, debug line-tables only; no LTO or PGO set), criterion 0.8.2. C/C++ side (benches/compare/README.md, vendor/build.sh OPT=-O3): Apple clang 21.0.0 (clang-2100.3.34.2); GMime 3.2.15 configure CFLAGS=-O3 --disable-crypto; VMime master 5b01911 CMake Release CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_RELEASE='-O3 -DNDEBUG'; libEtPan! 1.10.1, 22 parser sources compiled at -O3; Dovecot 2.4.5 lib-mail/lib-charset/lib configure CFLAGS=-O3; shims compiled by build.rs at opt_level 3 (-std=gnu11, -std=c++17). GLib (Homebrew 2.90.0) and the macOS system iconv used for charset conversion are prebuilt system libraries, not built by the harness.
hardware: Apple M4 Mac mini (4 performance and 6 efficiency cores, 16 GB), macOS 26.6.2, measured 2026-09-28; median over three runs of criterion's median (30 samples, 3 s measurement, 0.5 s warm-up), runs gated on a machine-wide idle lock.
why_faster: README feature list: SIMD kernels find boundaries and header fields (NEON on aarch64, AVX2 and SSE2 on x86-64), SIMD base64 and quoted-printable decoders (encodify), simdutf8 for UTF-8 validation, perfect hashing (hashify) for header names, charset labels and HTML entities, lazy decoding (bodies are not transfer-decoded or charset-converted until read) and zero-copy strings that borrow from the input.
stars_or_usage: 462 stars, 64 forks; mail-parser crate 4,234,073 downloads on crates.io (latest release 0.11.9); parser inside Stalwart Mail Server
tradeoffs: Rust API; C++ callers need FFI. Bodies are decoded lazily, so the headers and structure workloads skip body work. Legacy CJK multi-byte charsets need the optional encoding_rs dependency. Does not build messages (separate mail-builder crate).
caveats: The measured mail-parser is 1.0.0 from the repository, an unreleased rewrite; the latest crates.io release (0.11.9) decodes every body during parse and is not in the published tables. First-party harness, but results/check.md shows equal message, part and leaf counts on Enron and the generated corpora and decoded bytes within 2% on the test suites (Dovecot -6%); mailparse and Dovecot dashes-crlf cells do work that is not comparable (excluded from README tables); GMime finds no From mailbox in 327 Enron messages. Wins include lazy decoding: headers and structure never decode bodies, so large-attachment corpora reach 80,868 MiB/s. C/C++ libraries are driven through project-written shims, built without crypto, SSL and other optional features; charset conversion goes through macOS's system iconv and the C shims validate UTF-8 with GLib's g_utf8_validate_len, while mail-parser uses its own decoders and simdutf8, so part of the full-workload gap is library choice outside the parser. GMime, VMime and libEtPan! copy the input or bodies as their users would. One machine (Apple M4, NEON path); the AVX2/SSE2 x86-64 path is not measured. The nearest competitor is the Rust mailparse crate, 2.8x to 3.2x behind. Wins come from SIMD kernels, perfect hashing, lazy and zero-copy design, not from the language alone.

baseline: PCRE2 (interpreter and JIT) and RE2 (C/C++ regex engines); Hyperscan also measured
workload: rebar curated barometer: about 38 regex search benchmarks (literals, alternations, dates, Unicode classes, bounded repeats, dictionaries, ReDoS-style patterns, noseyparker rules) across many engines; corroborated by the LangArena Etc::LogParser task (13 log-grep patterns over generated web-server log lines).
claimed_speedup: rebar README summary of search-time benchmarks (geometric mean of per-benchmark speed ratios to the best engine, lower is better): hyperscan 2.37 (28 benchmarks), rust/regex 1.12.2 3.08 (38), pcre2/jit 10.47 6.00 (34), re2 10.39 (31), pcre2 interpreter 114.75 (33). The compile-time summary goes the other way: pcre2 1.41, pcre2/jit 6.20, rust/regex 11.85, re2 12.28. Intersection derived from the repo's recorded CSVs record/curated/2025-12-19/*.csv (median search times; derived from page data, re-computed by the verifier): vs PCRE2 JIT rust/regex is faster in 21 of 34 benchmarks, geometric-mean time ratio 2.13x; vs RE2 faster in 27 of 31, 4.3x; vs the PCRE2 interpreter faster in 32 of 33, 44x; vs Hyperscan faster in only 12 of 28 (Hyperscan about 1.45x faster overall). LangArena results 2026-10-05, Etc::LogParser (13 patterns, count all matches): Rust 0.302 s vs C with PCRE2 JIT 0.485 s (clang -O2), 0.488 s (gcc -O2) and 0.486 s (gcc -O3 -march=native 'Fast' build), about 1.6x; vs the C++ version, which uses RE2, 0.993-0.998 s (about 3.3x). In the same file, Template::Regex ({{(.*?)}} replacement): Rust 3.699 s vs C with PCRE2 JIT 1.155-1.173 s, so PCRE2 JIT is about 3.2x faster there; vs C++ RE2 4.84-4.90 s, Rust is about 1.3x faster.
compiler_and_flags: rebar: engine versions only (rust/regex 1.12.2, pcre2 10.47, re2 2025-11-05). PCRE2 (with SUPPORT_JIT) and RE2 are compiled from vendored source by the cc crate inside each engine's Cargo release profile (lto = fat, codegen-units = 1, default opt-level 3, so -O3 by the cc crate's default). This is derived from engines/pcre2/build.rs, engines/re2/build.rs and their Cargo.toml files; no compiler version is stated. LangArena: rustc 1.99.0, 'cargo build --release' with regex 1.12. C: clang 22.1.8 and gcc 16.0.1, prod flags -O2 -DNDEBUG -fstack-protector-strong -fno-omit-frame-pointer, Fast flags -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -funroll-loops with -flto=thin, linked against the system libpcre2-8. C++ is linked against the system libre2. The system PCRE2 and RE2 versions and build flags are not recorded in the results file.
hardware: rebar does not state the machine. LangArena results file: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X 8-Core Processor, 78 GB, x86_64 Linux.
why_faster: rebar analysis: finite-automata engines (lazy DFA, one-pass DFA) with SIMD literal prefilters (memchr, Teddy) avoid backtracking and give DFA-speed matching on most patterns; PCRE2 JIT stays faster where JIT-compiled backtracking is cheap (small anchored patterns, capture-heavy cases).
stars_or_usage: 4.0k stars; the regex engine behind ripgrep and much of the Rust ecosystem
tradeoffs: No backreferences or look-around (linear-time guarantee in exchange). Pattern compilation is slower than PCRE2 and RE2. Unicode tables add binary size. Rust API; C++ needs the rure C binding or FFI.
caveats: rebar's summary geometric means cover different benchmark subsets per engine (28 to 38), so only the intersection numbers compare like for like; the verifier re-computed them from the repo's recorded CSVs and they match. rebar is written by the regex crate's author, and its README says the analysis is biased towards that crate (BIAS.md). rebar states no CPU or compiler version. Hyperscan beats regex overall, and PCRE2 JIT wins 13 of the 34 shared benchmarks. LangArena is independent, with public code, compilers, flags and CPU. Its C LogParser time is the same at -O2 and at -O3 -march=native (0.486 s), so the opt level does not explain the gap. The PCRE2 and RE2 it measures are system libraries whose versions and build flags are not recorded. The C++ LangArena rows use RE2, not PCRE2. LangArena's Template::Regex task shows a 3.2x loss to PCRE2 JIT. The win is a library and engine-design effect (lazy DFA plus SIMD literal prefilters), not a language effect. [retier] The rebar numbers (regex 1.12.2, 2025-12-19) predate the 1.13.1 correctness fix (#1354, PR #1364, 2026-07-15: wrong match spans from the reverse-suffix and inner optimisations); the PR's rebar diff shows curated cloud-flare-redos 1.80x/1.97x slower, and recomputing with those rows moves the PCRE2 JIT comparison from 2.13x to about 2.05x and RE2 from 27 of 31 at 4.3x to 26 of 31 at about 4.1x. LangArena's LogParser harness has no flaw inflating Rust (fixed checksum; all 17 C builds 0.485-0.501 s). PCRE2 JIT is 3.2x faster on Template::Regex captures; compile is slower; Hyperscan is faster overall.
found_via: WebSearch 'Rust crate "faster than glibc" string search OR strstr OR strtod OR memmem benchmark SIMD' surfaced memchr and rebar; then opened rebar README (raw.githubusercontent.com) and its record/curated/2025-12-19 CSVs, and kostya/LangArena results/2026-10-05-kostya-ms7c37.js (https://github.com/kostya/LangArena/blob/master/results/2026-10-05-kostya-ms7c37.js).

Its results file results/2026-10-05-kostya-ms7c37.js states the CPU (AMD Ryzen 7 3800X), clang 22.1.8, gcc 16.0.1 and rustc 1.99.0, and the C flags are in c/Makefile. rebar alone would be tier C: it is written by the regex crate's author, it lists engine versions but no CPU or compiler version, and its flags are only derivable from Cargo profiles.
verification.notes: Every number checked: the rebar README summary tables, the intersection ratios re-computed from the 2025-12-19 CSVs (21/34 at 2.13x vs PCRE2 JIT, 27/31 at 4.3x vs RE2, 32/33 at 44x vs the PCRE2 interpreter, 12/28 at 0.69x vs Hyperscan) and the LangArena runtimes all match. name: Rust: LangArena Distance::NGram
baseline: C++ using std::unordered_map<uint32_t,int> for 4-gram counts (g++ 16, clang++ 22); best C/C++ row is C++/Clang++/PGO at 0.822 s, C/Clang is 1.811 s
workload: For 10 generated string pairs (lengths 4 to 20,003 over a 10-letter alphabet, so at most 10,000 distinct 4-grams), count 4-gram frequencies of each string in two hash maps (reserved to the string length) and compute the n-gram overlap score; 100 timed iterations after 20 untimed warm-up iterations (run.js).
claimed_speedup: Rust 0.533 s vs C++/G++ 0.863 s and C++/Clang++ 0.877 s (prod, -O2), C++/G++/Fast 0.85 s (-O3 -march=native), best of the 16 Clang/GCC C and C++ configurations C++/Clang++/PGO 0.822 s, C/Clang 1.811 s: about 1.54x faster than the best C/C++ row and 1.62x faster than C++/G++ prod (derived from page data). Rust/WMO (codegen-units 1) 0.388 s. Peak RSS 4.3 MB vs 6.6-7.1 MB for the C++ rows.
compiler_and_flags: C/C++ (cpp/Makefile, c/Makefile; versions and build commands from the results file): Clang 22.1.8 and GCC 16.0.1 20260322 (trunk r16-8246, Ubuntu snapshot package), libstdc++ (no -stdlib flag). Headline 'prod' rows (make -j prod): -O2 -DNDEBUG -fstack-protector-strong -fno-omit-frame-pointer, linked with -Wl,-z,relro,-z,now -Wl,--gc-sections; C++ adds -std=c++20. 'Fast': -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -DNDEBUG -pipe -fstack-protector -ftree-vectorize -funroll-loops. 'Unsafe': -O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG -pipe -fno-stack-protector -fomit-frame-pointer -ffast-math -fvisibility=hidden -fno-common -fstrict-overflow -fno-trapping-math. 'PGO': -O2 plus -fprofile-instr-use (Clang) or -fprofile-use -fprofile-correction (GCC). The Makefiles pass -flto=thin (Fast) and -flto=full (Unsafe) only on the link line while the objects are compiled without -flto, so no link-time optimisation actually takes place (inference from the Makefiles). All 16 Clang/GCC x C/C++ x prod/Fast/Unsafe/PGO configurations were compared (instrumented PGO/Gen rows excluded). Rust: rustc 1.99.0 'cargo build --release' (default release profile from rust/Cargo.toml: opt-level 3, 16 codegen units, no LTO, no target-cpu). Both harnesses run 20 percent untimed warm-up iterations.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X 8-Core Processor, 78GB RAM, x86_64 Linux (results file 2026-10-05, host kostya-ms7c37)
why_faster: Not stated by the suite. Rust's std HashMap (hashbrown SwissTable) is flat open addressing, while C++ std::unordered_map<uint32_t,int> allocates a node per distinct 4-gram, and the test builds two maps per string pair (this agent's inference from the containers used).
tradeoffs: Flat hash tables use less memory per entry than node-based std::unordered_map.
caveats: Container comparison: a C++ open-addressing map (absl::flat_hash_map, boost::unordered_flat_map) would likely close the gap (inference, not measured), and the suite only uses std::unordered_map. Other languages also beat every C/C++ row: Zig 0.52 s, C#/JIT 0.516 s (a separate verified record of the same test), Go 0.603 s, Julia 0.58 s. The C version (uthash, one malloc per distinct gram) is slower still at 1.789-1.844 s for the non-instrumented Clang/GCC rows. LangArena calls itself 'a subjective benchmark' and says AI tools helped translate the tests between languages. The suite publishes one measurement per test and configuration (no variance). The headline C/C++ 'prod' rows are -O2 with hardening flags, but the -O3 Fast, Unsafe and PGO variants were also compared and Rust still wins; the Makefiles' -flto flags are link-only, so the 'LTO' builds probably get no LTO. The per-benchmark ratios are derived from the results file, not stated by the suite. Rows were picked by the search agent as text tests where a Rust, Zig or Go production row beats every C and C++ row; most other text tests in the suite go the other way (for example Base64::Encode and Base64::Decode, where C is about 3x faster than Rust, and Distance::Jaro, which is a tie).
