name: Rust: LangArena Etc::Words
baseline: C++ splitting with std::istringstream operator>> and counting in std::unordered_map<std::string,int> (cpp/src/words.cpp; g++ 16 and clang++ 22, libstdc++); best C/C++ row is C++/G++/PGO at 1.587 s. The C rows (c/src/words.c) strdup the whole text per iteration, tokenize with strtok_r and count in uthash with a malloc plus strdup per distinct word, at about 1.96-2.0 s.
workload: Split a generated 50,000-word text (words of 3 to 8 random lowercase letters separated by single spaces) into words, count frequencies in a hash map, then fold the top word, its count and the vocabulary size into a checksum; 360 timed iterations, text generation untimed.
claimed_speedup: Rust 1.021 s vs C++/G++/PGO 1.587 s (best of the 16 C/C++ configurations), C++/G++/Unsafe 1.631 s, C++/G++ 1.638 s (prod, -O2), C++/G++/Fast 1.651 s (-O3 -march=native) and C/Clang 1.988 s: about 1.55x faster than the best C/C++ row and 1.60x faster than C++/G++ prod (derived from page data). Peak RSS 5.4 MB (C++ 7.8 MB). Other rows also beat every C/C++ row: Crystal 0.88 s, Zig 0.91 s, Go 1.129 s, Rust/PGO 0.898 s. Earlier monthly runs show a smaller Rust lead over the best C/C++ row: 1.18x on 2026-08-14 (1.37 vs 1.623 s), 1.21x on 2026-09-03 (1.329 vs 1.613 s), 1.53x on 2026-09-18 (1.054 vs 1.612 s); the jump followed the 2026-09-06 commit 'rust: count Words with borrowed &str keys' (derived from the results files).
compiler_and_flags: C/C++ (c/Makefile, cpp/Makefile; versions from the results file): Clang 22.1.8 and GCC 16.0.1 20260322 (trunk r16-8246, Ubuntu package build), libstdc++ (no -stdlib flag), -std=c++20 for C++. Headline 'prod' rows (make -j prod): -O2 -DNDEBUG -fstack-protector-strong -fno-omit-frame-pointer, linked with -Wl,-z,relro,-z,now -Wl,--gc-sections (not -O3, no -march). 'Fast': -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -DNDEBUG -pipe -fstack-protector -ftree-vectorize -funroll-loops. 'Unsafe': -O3 -march=native -ffast-math -fno-stack-protector -fomit-frame-pointer -fvisibility=hidden -fno-trapping-math. 'PGO': -O2 plus -fprofile-instr-use (Clang) or -fprofile-use (GCC). -flto=thin (Fast) and -flto=full (Unsafe) appear only in LDFLAGS while objects are compiled without -flto, so those builds probably get no LTO (inference from cpp/Makefile). All 16 Clang/GCC x C/C++ x prod/Fast/Unsafe/PGO rows were compared (instrumented PGO/Gen rows excluded). Rust: rustc 1.99.0, 'cargo build --release' with the default release profile (opt-level 3, no LTO, no target-cpu flag; rust/Cargo.toml).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X 8-Core Processor, 78 GB RAM, x86_64 Linux (results file 2026-10-05, host kostya-ms7c37; the run's change note says the host moved from Ubuntu to Arch Linux)
why_faster: Not stated by the suite. Rust iterates split_whitespace() and keys a HashMap with &str slices into the original text (no per-word allocation) against C++ istringstream plus std::string keys in std::unordered_map (this agent's reading of the sources).
tradeoffs: Zero-copy word keys; the Go and Rust versions keep a reference to the whole text while the map is alive.
caveats: Standard-library and idiom comparison (istringstream tokenizer plus node-based unordered_map against a borrowed-slice tokenizer and an open-addressing map), not code generation; a C++ version with std::string_view keys and a flat hash map would likely close the gap. Half the current margin comes from the 2026-09-06 Rust change to borrowed &str keys (1.2x before, 1.55x after). The C version does extra work (strdup of the whole text each iteration, malloc plus strdup per distinct word). The same test appears under Java in the wave jitaot file. LangArena calls itself 'a subjective benchmark' and says AI tools helped translate the tests between languages. One measurement per test and configuration (no variance reported), although the harness checks each run's checksum against run.js. The headline C/C++ 'prod' rows are -O2 with hardening flags, but the -O3 -march=native Fast and Unsafe rows and the PGO rows also lose. Ratios are derived from the results file, not stated by the suite. Rows were picked as text tests where a non-C row beats every C and C++ row; most other text tests go the other way (Base64::Encode and Base64::Decode, where C is about 3x faster than Rust; Distance::Jaro is a tie).

name: z-fasta (Zig FASTA index, extract and stats tool)
baseline: samtools faidx 1.24 with HTSlib 1.24 (C); also measured: fastahack, SeqKit (Go), noodles and rust-bio (Rust), pyfaidx (Python).
workload: Build a samtools-compatible .fai index (`z-fasta index --emit-fai`) of uncompressed FASTA (human genome ~2.9 GiB, transcriptome ~459 MiB, proteome ~13 MiB), and fetch one 1 kbp region through an existing index; warm cache.
claimed_speedup: README (v0.3.5, measured 2026-10-10) and bench/index/REPORT.md Table 5, .fai index build, z-fasta `index --emit-fai` vs samtools faidx: human genome 0.3824 s vs 8.1614 s (21.3x), transcriptome 0.1546 s vs 1.7112 s (11.1x), proteome 0.0113 s vs 0.0650 s (5.8x); fastahack (C++) 20.8901 s on the genome (54.6x, REPORT.md only). One 1 kbp positional GET through an existing index: human genome 2.3 ms vs 8.2 ms, transcriptome 8.2 ms (.zfi) or 28.3 ms (.fai) vs 301.8 ms, proteome 2.7 ms (.zfi) vs 17.9 ms. Stats is compared with noodles and SeqKit only, not samtools.
compiler_and_flags: z-fasta 0.3.5 built with Zig 0.16.0, `zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast -Dstrip=true`; build.zig uses standardTargetOptions and no -Dtarget/-Dcpu is passed, so the binary targets the host (native) CPU. samtools 1.24 and HTSlib 1.24 built from source by tools/install.sh with plain `./configure` and `make`, i.e. package-default flags (htslib Makefile `-g -Wall -O2 -fvisibility=hidden`, samtools Makefile `-g -Wall -O2`) for generic x86-64; C compiler not named.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 3950X (README Performance section); Linux x86_64 (glibc 2.43 target in the report provenance); zebrac 0.6.2, 5 measured samples after 3 warmups, 5000 ms budget per command, warm cache.
stars_or_usage: 9 stars, 0 forks (GitHub repo page, 2026-10-11); new project (v0.3.5, 244 commits).
tradeoffs: Uncompressed FASTA only; own .zfi index plus samtools-compatible .fai for representable FASTA; one static executable (about 800 KiB) with no runtime dependencies; scope limited to index, get, validate and stats.
caveats: First-party benchmark with the author's own runner and reports. name: Sassy (SIMD approximate string matching)
baseline: Edlib (C++ Myers bit-vector aligner); parasail (C) and SWOffinder also compared in the paper
workload: Searching short DNA/ASCII patterns (up to about 1000 characters) in long texts allowing k edit errors, synthetic data and a human genome search.
claimed_speedup: Paper abstract (Bioinformatics, May 2026; repo copy in doc/abstract.md): Sassy1 is 4-15x faster than Edlib for patterns up to 1000 bp and reaches a text throughput up to 2 Gbp/s; for CRISPR off-target detection of 61 guides in a human genome it is 100x faster than SWOffinder and only slightly slower than the index-based CHOPOFF. 'Over 100x faster than parasail' appears in the published abstract only as quoted by a WebSearch snippet (snippet only; not in the repo copy). Sassy2 (bioRxiv, March 2026) is an additional 10-50x faster than Sassy1 for short (<200 bp) texts and 2.5-4.5x for long (>8 kbp) texts; README: Sassy2 2x faster with AVX-512 and pre-encoded patterns 10-20x faster for short texts (internal comparisons).
compiler_and_flags: Sassy: Rust >= 1.91, release profile opt-level 3 (debug info on; dist profile adds LTO and one codegen unit) with .cargo/config.toml target-cpu=native; the Edlib eval is built with 'cargo build --release -p evals'. Edlib (C++) is called through edlib-rs, whose build.rs uses the cmake crate; the cmake crate derives CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE from the Cargo profile, and with sassy's release profile (debug = true) that is RelWithDebInfo (CMake default -O2 -g), with no -march=native; edlib-rs's .cflag("-D CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release") only adds a C preprocessor define and Edlib's CMakeLists sets no build type. Parasail built from its CMake (flags unstated, striped SSE4.1/AVX2 kernels tried); Ish built with ISH_SIMD_TARGET=sse.
why_faster: Bit-packing with SIMD (AVX2/NEON) where the bit-vectors run along the text direction ('tiling in the text direction'), with the text split into 4 parts searched in parallel; complexity O(k ceil(n/W)) with W=256.
stars_or_usage: 169 stars, 18 forks; crates.io 6101 downloads (2287 recent, v0.2.6); also on bioconda and PyPI (sassy-rs); third-party DuckDB/R bindings (ducksassy)
tradeoffs: Needs AVX2 or NEON; supports ASCII, DNA and IUPAC alphabets; best for patterns up to about 1000; C bindings, Python bindings and a CLI exist.
caveats: Edlib numbers come from the peer-reviewed paper's abstract (repo copy doc/abstract.md); the full paper, its hardware and the eval CSVs were not opened (bioRxiv, doi.org and the KIT library PDF host were unreachable). The win is algorithmic, not a language effect: Sassy tiles bit-vectors along the text with 256-bit AVX2 lanes over 4 text chunks, while Edlib runs scalar 64-bit Myers/Hyyro bit-vectors. In the public evals harness Edlib is probably compiled at RelWithDebInfo (-O2 -g, generic x86-64) while Sassy gets opt-level 3 plus target-cpu=native, so optimisation levels are not matched (not a crippled -O0 build). The parasail >100x figure is snippet only. Requires AVX2 or NEON at compile time (scalar feature is slower).

name: awkrs (Rust AWK)
baseline: mawk 1.3.4 and GNU gawk 5.4.0 (C); BSD awk on macOS also timed
workload: hyperfine on 1,000,000-line inputs: '{ print $1 }', sum of first column, multi-field print, regex filter, associative-array count, conditional field print, field arithmetic, string concatenation, no-match gsub, plus a CPU-bound BEGIN loop.
claimed_speedup: README tables (hyperfine mean ms on 1M-line inputs, Apple M5 Max). Rows are awkrs (JIT) / awkrs (bytecode) vs mawk 1.3.4 vs gawk 5.4.0. { print $1 }: 15.7 / 16.1 vs 66.2 vs 100.8 (mawk relative 4.22x). Sum first column: 13.0 / 12.9 vs 37.5 vs 62.9 (2.90x). Multi-field print: 56.4 / 55.8 vs 156.6 vs 266.1 (2.81x). Regex filter: 11.1 / 11.1 vs 19.3 vs 351.4 (mawk 1.74x, gawk 31.72x). Associative array: 340.0 / 343.7 vs 610.0 vs 342.4 (parity with gawk). NR%2 field print: 30.2 / 30.7 vs 71.1 vs 116.1 (2.36x). Field computation: 19.0 / 18.8 vs 57.7 vs 100.5 (3.08x). String concat print: 51.0 / 50.5 vs 121.0 vs 182.2 (2.39x). No-match gsub: 13.8 / 13.9 vs 74.3 vs 436.3 (mawk 5.39x). CPU-bound BEGIN loop: 9.2 / 9.6 vs 9.7 vs 20.7 (mawk 1.06x, within noise). Generated 2026-04-10 with awkrs 0.1.18. The README says the bytecode row represents today's default path for these programs.
compiler_and_flags: awkrs: cargo build --release with the default release profile (no [profile.release] in Cargo.toml, so opt-level 3, no LTO); rustc version not stated. Baselines: Homebrew bottles /opt/homebrew/bin/gawk (GNU Awk 5.4.0) and /opt/homebrew/bin/mawk (1.3.4 20260302), build flags not stated. BSD awk is /usr/bin/awk. Locale is not pinned (the script does not set LC_ALL).
hardware: Apple M5 Max, macOS arm64
why_faster: README: on regular files a raw byte path parses the Nth whitespace field straight from an mmap'd buffer, a 'slurp inline' path does a byte memmem scan for gsub, and a fused-superinstruction bytecode VM runs the rest; optional rayon parallelism (-j, default 1) and a fusevm/Cranelift numeric offload that does not engage on these string/field programs.
tradeoffs: Not a full gawk (documented parity gaps: interactive debugger, extension loading, multibyte field splitting not audited); parallel mode only for parallel-safe programs.
caveats: First-party, single machine (Apple M5 Max, macOS 25.4). Numbers are from awkrs 0.1.18 (2026-04-10) while the crate is now 0.5.7, so they have not been re-run on current code. The README's 2026-06-01 caveat says the JIT rows came from a Cranelift module that has since been removed; the bytecode rows are within 0.5 ms. The wins come from special-cased fast paths, not from Rust codegen: single-rule programs such as { print $1 }, { s += $1 } and no-match literal gsub are recognised and run as raw byte scans over an mmap'd file, skipping the VM. The baselines run their general record loops through read(). Baseline flags are unknown (Homebrew bottles, probably distro-default -O2, not a verified -O3). The locale is not set, and gawk's 351 ms regex and 436 ms gsub rows may reflect UTF-8 multibyte matching, while awkrs works on bytes. Each hyperfine time includes process startup on 10-25 ms runs. Parity only on the associative-array case (gawk) and the BEGIN loop (mawk). The repo has 1 star and no third-party reproduction. [retier] All nine file benchmarks hit single-rule inline fast paths; only the BEGIN loop uses the VM, where it ties mawk. The benchmarked raw paths use parse_number_bytes (a whole-field parse with no awk numeric prefix, so '12ms' counts as 0, bare nan/inf poison sums, -n is ignored, from_utf8_unchecked is UB) and five inline loops strip CR while the VM path keeps it; the bench inputs (sequential integers, LF) hide both. baseline: GNU coreutils 8.32 `sort -u | wc -l` and `sort | uniq -c`, and GNU awk 5.3.2 (`a[$0]++`), all C programs.

Report: `sort huge.txt | uniq -c` 28m46.811s and gawk 5.3.2 `a[$0]++` 25m03.082s vs unsorted `cuniq --memmap -c` 3m07.817s (9.2x and 8.0x, derived from page data); like-for-like sorted report `cuniq --memmap -cs` 3m26.898s vs `sort | uniq -c` (8.3x, derived from page data). README: 'For counting cuniq reliably outperforms GNU sort in all cases', with one stated exception for sorted reports on inputs with almost no duplicates.

PERFORMANCE.md gives `RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=native" cargo +nightly bench -Z build-std=std ... --target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` for the criterion benches and a `release-optimized-debug` profile build for profiling; README mentions profile-guided optimization and recommends `-C target-cpu=native` installs. why_faster: PERFORMANCE.md optimization list: hash table instead of sorting (O(n)), memory-mapped input, memchr newline search, no UTF-8 validation, ahash, leaking large structures instead of freeing, multithreaded hashing and HyperLogLog for the estimate mode.

tradeoffs: Exact mode keeps every distinct line in memory; near-exact mode ignores 64-bit hash collisions; estimate mode is approximate; -c output is unsorted unless -s; hashing loses to sorting when nearly every line is unique.

name: cw (Rust wc replacement)
baseline: wc from FreeBSD base (C) and GNU coreutils 8.30 wc (gwc, C)
workload: Counting bytes, lines, words, characters and max line length of a 341,152,640-byte XML file (Dickens_Charles_Pickwick_Papers.xml) and of test-utf-8.html, single file and many files via xargs; timed with hyperfine-style 'times faster' output.

The -lL (1.73x / 15.07x) and -mlL (9.05x / 3.88x; 9.42x / 18.95x) rows time a LinesLongest fast path with a line-length bug and count characters where GNU wc -L counts display width, so they are struck.
compiler_and_flags: cw built with 'cargo build --release --features runtime-dispatch-simd' (recommended in README); baseline build flags and Rust version not stated; gwc is GNU coreutils 8.30.
hardware: FreeBSD 12 on a 2.1 GHz Westmere Xeon (README; exact CPU model not stated)
why_faster: README: line counts use the bytecount crate (SIMD, runtime dispatch), line-length mode uses the memchr crate, -m has a UTF-8 character-counting fast path, and --threads counts several files in parallel. The author notes gwc is pessimised in places by FreeBSD's weak memchr.
tradeoffs: Byte-oriented unless -m; ignores locale (no locale support yet per README Future list); UTF-8 only; no test suite listed at time of README; word counting uses a slow path.
caveats: First-party numbers from one FreeBSD 12 machine, measured in January 2019 with cw 0.4-0.5 (the README's benchmark sections were last edited on 2019-01-18; the record's '2020-2021' was wrong), against GNU coreutils 8.30. The README itself says gwc is pessimised on FreeBSD by the system's weak memchr, so Linux/glibc ratios will be smaller; GNU coreutils 9.0 (2021) added an AVX2 newline-counting path to wc -l (WebSearch snippet only), so the -l ratios are outdated. The 70x to 124x -m ratios compare a UTF-8-only byte-counting fast path against locale-aware multibyte decoding in both wc implementations; without -m cw counts bytes and ignores the locale. The win comes from algorithms and crates (SIMD bytecount, memchr, threading), not from Rust code generation (same_algorithm false). Input files other than the Dickens XML are not included, the hyperfine commands are shown only as output, and build flags for both wc binaries and the rustc version are not stated. Several rows depend on multi-threading or the optional runtime-dispatch-simd feature. Unmaintained since March 2021. [retier] Correctness bug in the -lL fast path (src/count.rs LinesLongest, same code in benchmarked v0.5.0 and HEAD): the line-length carry is overwritten when a 32 KiB read holds no newline (47,231 for an 80,000-byte line), the first line of each file is counted one byte short, a leading empty line underflows (release prints 18446744073709551615), all -L paths skip an unterminated last line. gwc -L counts display width (tabs, wcwidth), so the -L rows measure different work; -m rows count continuation bytes with no validation against an mbrtowc loop; locale not stated. CHANGELOG 0.8.0 was never tagged or published (crates.io latest 0.7.0, 2019).

name: fastgrep (Rust grep)
baseline: GNU grep 3.12 (C)
workload: Recursive searches over a generated corpus of 200 files x 5,000 lines of Rust-like source (sparse and dense matches, case-insensitive, regex, single 100k-line file) and a scaling test of 50 to 500 files.
claimed_speedup: README benchmark table (warm trigram index, LC_ALL=C): -rn 'fn main' 8.82 ms vs GNU grep 32.99 ms (3.74x); -rc 'use ' 8.55 ms vs 84.75 ms (9.91x); -rni error 37.49 ms vs 82.57 ms (2.20x); -rn 'impl\s+Drop' 45.24 vs 73.43 (1.62x); very sparse SubscriptionManager 5.41 vs 39.35 (7.28x); single file 3.70 vs 5.21 (1.41x); but -rl 'fn main' 7.50 ms vs GNU grep 7.12 ms (0.95x, GNU grep faster). Scaling: 1.48x at 50 files, 2.43x at 200, 3.08x at 500.
compiler_and_flags: fastgrep 0.1.9 at commit 5094623, Rust 1.99.0, repository release profile: opt-level = "s", LTO, codegen-units 1, panic = abort, stripped; Criterion 0.8.2, one subprocess per iteration with output captured in memory, warm filesystem cache, LC_ALL=C, default thread counts. GNU grep 3.12 is Homebrew's ggrep (build flags not stated).
hardware: Apple M2 Max (12 logical CPUs), 32 GB, macOS 27.0.1
why_faster: README: parallel by default across all CPU threads, lazy trigram index that skips non-matching files on repeat searches, SIMD-accelerated literal search.
stars_or_usage: 2 stars; crates.io 431 downloads (113 recent), current version 0.1.10
tradeoffs: Output order is non-deterministic (multi-threaded); deliberate deviations from GNU grep (binary files, long lines). Index cache stored under the OS cache directory and invalidated by mtime and size. Not every GNU grep flag implemented.
caveats: Very new (crate first published 2026-03-04), first-party numbers on a small synthetic corpus (about 1M lines; runs of 4-85 ms that include process start-up). The win is mostly 12-thread parallelism against single-threaded GNU grep: the --no-index mode is faster than the default warm-index mode in 4 of the 5 indexed rows (e.g. 7.31 vs 8.82 ms on 'fn main', 7.64 vs 8.55 ms on 'use '), and the index helps only on the very sparse query (5.41 vs 6.30 ms); every file contains 'fn main', 'use ' and 'impl Drop', so the index cannot skip files for them. No per-thread or single-threaded comparison is published, so no faster per-byte scan is shown (literal and regex search come from the memchr and regex crates). GNU grep wins -rl (7.12 vs 7.50 ms). fastgrep is built at opt-level s (size), not a speed-tuned build, while GNU grep is a Homebrew bottle with unstated flags. Deliberate behaviour differences (100 MiB file-size limit, 15000-byte line truncation, unordered parallel output) change semantics versus GNU grep. [retier] Very new (crate first published 2026-03-04), first-party numbers on a small synthetic corpus (about 1M lines; runs of 4-85 ms including process start-up). The win is mostly 12-thread parallelism against single-threaded GNU grep: --no-index is faster than the default warm-index mode in 4 of the 5 indexed rows and the index helps only on the very sparse query; GNU grep wins -rl 'fn main' (7.12 vs 7.50 ms). Correctness bug in src/pattern.rs extract_literal_prefix: it keeps the character before a ?, * or { quantifier, so colou?r gets the required prefix 'colou' and https?:// gets 'https'; that prefix drives the warm-index file filter, the -c count path and the over-4-MiB parallel chunk path, which only look at lines containing it, so lines with only 'color' or 'http://' are missed. The benchmarked patterns do not use those quantifiers.

Remaining asymmetries: ferrocat reads the template and existing catalog from in-memory strings inside the timed loop while msgmerge reads two files and writes to a pipe from a fresh process; MiB/s counts output bytes, and ferrocat's merge output is about 7% larger per operation than msgmerge's (2,115,311 vs 1,971,324 bytes), so the merge MiB/s ratio (61x) overstates the time ratio (56x); the README full-update cell (150 MiB/s) comes from a different report than the msgmerge cell. Numbers were measured on ferrocat 2.2.0; the current release is 3.4.2. Zero stars, so the project is unproven in the field. The speed-up is design (byte-oriented scanning, move-not-clone merge paths) against a general GNU tool, not a language-level effect.

why_faster: Not stated by the suite. The loop is nearly identical in Go and C++; the Go key is a zero-copy substring plus strings.TrimSpace, while the C++ test copies the key with substr and trim (this agent's reading of the sources, small effect).

Go's harness calls runtime.GC() after warm-up so the timed loop starts with a clean heap, but collections during the loop (a new output buffer of about 1.5x the template per iteration) are timed; Go uses 75 MB peak RSS against 41 MB for C. The C/C++ prod rows are -O2 with hardening flags, but the -O3 -march=native Fast and Unsafe rows and the PGO rows were also compared and lose, and the Makefiles pass the LTO flags only at link time. name: hist-rs (hist, Rust unique-line counter)
baseline: Plain 'sort | uniq -c | sort -n' as found on PATH (the README calls it coreutils; on macOS the default sort and uniq are the BSD-derived system tools unless GNU coreutils shadows them; implementation and versions not stated), in the default locale and with LC_ALL=C; also uutils coreutils sort/uniq with --parallel 1 and an awk pipeline (awk implementation not stated; README links the gawk manual).
workload: justfile: nucgen -n 1000000 -l 20 writes 1M FASTQ records, i.e. 4M lines: 1M unique '@seq.N' headers, 1M random 20-nt sequences (effectively all unique), 1M identical '+' lines and 1M identical 20-character '?' quality lines (nucgen src/main.rs and src/write.rs), so about 2M distinct lines out of 4M. Each tool reads the file on stdin and writes to a file; hyperfine --warmup=10 --shell=bash. Second benchmark (bench-stream) prints first occurrences only (hist -u).
claimed_speedup: README table (MacBook M3 Pro, hyperfine): hist 231.5 ms vs naive 'sort | uniq -c | sort -n' 5637.6 ms (24.35x), with LC_ALL=C 1219.5 ms (5.27x), awk count pipeline 1265.4 ms (5.47x), uutils sort 3.84x. Independent run in issue #3 (pixelb, Linux GNU sort, LC_ALL=C, 10M records): hist 12.864 s vs 36.238 s, about 2.8x (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: hist: Cargo.toml [profile.release] lto = true, codegen-units = 1, debug = false (default opt-level 3); .cargo/config.toml rustflags -C target-cpu=native; edition 2024; rustc version not stated. Baselines are prebuilt system or installed binaries with unknown versions and build flags.
hardware: MacBook M3 Pro (README)
why_faster: Not stated in the README. Inference from Cargo.toml (hashbrown, bumpalo): hash-table counting over an arena instead of an O(n log n) sort of all lines.
tradeoffs: Holds every distinct line in memory (a hash table), so memory grows with the number of unique lines; output order is by abundance rather than the stable sort order of uniq.
caveats: Most of the headline 24x comes from locale-aware collation in the default-locale sort: with LC_ALL=C the gap is 5.27x and against uutils sort (single-threaded) 3.84x. The input is not 'almost all unique': half of its 4M lines are two values repeated 1M times each, the other half are unique, so the hash table holds about 2M keys. The speedup is algorithmic (hash counting with hashbrown over a bumpalo arena, then sorting only the distinct entries) against a three-process pipe that sorts every line; it is not a language-level effect. Outputs are not byte-identical: hist writes 'count<TAB>line' through a csv writer (lines containing tabs or quotes get quoted, non-UTF-8 lines error), ties come out in unstable order, and the awk row sorts descending. First-party, one machine, no baseline versions. No LICENSE file in the repo: MIT is declared only in Cargo.toml and on crates.io (0.1.8), and the README badge links a LICENSE.md that returns 404. name: huniq (Rust sort | uniq replacement)

claimed_speedup: readme.md tables (seconds / peak KB), input = /usr/share/dict/* repeated N times. Uniq mode (the 'shell' lane is `sort -u` per benchmark.sh, not `sort | uniq`): 1 repetition huniq2-rust 0.26 s vs huniq1-c++ 1.67 s, awk 1.63 s, datamash 1.78 s, sort -u 7.30 s; 100 repetitions 43.65 s vs 154.99 s (C++), 239.66 s (awk), 285.94 s (datamash), 1062.07 s (sort -u). Count mode (shell = `sort | uniq -c`), 100 repetitions: 90.80 s vs 150.41 s (C++), 163.13 s (awk), 322.70 s (datamash), 933.67 s. README: 'beats the C++ implementation by a factor of between 6.5 ... and 3.5', 'Compared to sort -u: huniq is around 30 times faster' (28x at 1 repetition, 24x at 100, derived from page data), count mode 'between 25% and 50% faster than the C++ implementation and between 5x and 10x faster than sort | uniq -c'. caveats: Author-run with no machine, compiler or tool versions stated, and the huniq version measured is not named; benchmark.sh loops until aborted and times each tool with `time` while a shell loop cats /usr/share/dict/* into it, so the producer can bound the fastest lanes. name: hwc (Haskell wc)
baseline: GNU coreutils wc (C, single-threaded)
workload: wc-style counting of bytes, words, lines, UTF-8 characters and maximum line length; only the requested statistics are computed.
claimed_speedup: README: 'about 4-6 times faster than GNU coreutils' wc, depending on the exact subset of statistics being computed' (single-threaded Haskell vs single-threaded C). No per-run timings in the repository README.
compiler_and_flags: stack.yaml resolver lts-15.2 (GHC 8.8 series, bytestring 0.10.10.0) with package.yaml ghc-options -fllvm -O2 -Wall and executable RTS option -with-rtsopts=-A2m; LLVM version not stated. GNU wc version, build flags and the locale it ran in are not stated.
why_faster: README: statistics are computed in a composable, efficient manner so that only the ones the user requests are calculated; the implementation write-up (0xd34df00d.me blog post, derived from Chris Penner's wc post) was not opened (host blocked).
tradeoffs: Depends on the GHC LLVM backend and bytestring-mmap; abandoned since 2020; counts UTF-8 characters only.
caveats: Numbers are a single ratio sentence in the README with no hardware, file size, GNU wc version, locale or timing method; the author's Habr article ('Побеждая C двадцатью строками Haskell: пишем свой wc', Feb 2020) and blog post could not be opened (hosts do not resolve here). hwc does less work than GNU wc: src/Data/WordCount.hs splits words on ASCII whitespace only (bytes 9-13 and 32), counts characters as non-continuation bytes without UTF-8 validation, and counts every byte >= 32 as one column for max line length (no display-width handling, so -L is wrong for multibyte text), whereas GNU wc in a UTF-8 locale decodes multibyte characters. The line count is Data.ByteString.count, which in bytestring 0.10.10.0 calls the C helper c_count (fps_count), so the -l path is C code; input is mmapped via bytestring-mmap. Habr search snippets (snippet only) describe a third-party response that measured, on a 1.8 GB file, system wc 19.416 s, a simple Haskell version 2.811 s, a simple C version 3.067 s and an optimized hand-written single-threaded C version 0.637 s, so the gap is to GNU wc's general implementation, not to C; a Habr commenter also notes the simplified spec (Unicode ignored). Measured against a 2020 coreutils; later coreutils releases (which reworked wc's line counting) were not compared. Abandoned since March 2020. [retier] Numbers are a single ratio sentence in the README with no hardware, file size, GNU wc version, locale or timing method; the author's Habr article and blog post could not be opened. hwc does less work than GNU wc: ASCII-only whitespace for words, characters counted as non-continuation bytes without UTF-8 validation, output format not wc's. Correctness bug in -L: the backspace rule max 0 (curLen - 1) on Word64 underflows, so a backspace followed by a line end or EOF reports 18446744073709551615 and '\babc' gives 2 where GNU wc 8.32 gives 3 (simulated in Python; hwc not run here). -l alone runs bytestring's C fps_count loop and -c alone is O(1), as in GNU. The baseline is stale: coreutils 9.0 made -l up to 5x faster with AVX2, 9.5 calls wc much faster, and 9.11 sped up -m 2.6x on non-ASCII UTF-8. Pinned to GHC 8.8 with the LLVM backend; abandoned since 2020-03-15.

name: mojo-regex (Mojo regular expression library)
baseline: CPython 3.12 re module (C implementation) and the Rust regex crate
workload: 80 regex micro-benchmarks (literals, alternations, phone-number DFA patterns, is_match, findall) with pre-compiled patterns, 500 ms target runtime per case, median timing.
claimed_speedup: Page (mojo-regex 0.13.0, comparison.md): Mojo vs Python re geomean 24.54x over 76 shared benchmarks (Mojo wins 74, Python 1); Mojo vs Rust regex geomean 3.47x over 71 rows as printed, but 13 of those rows use a different input, pattern or operation on the Rust side, and the matched-input geomean over the remaining 58 rows is 2.77x (derived from page data). CHANGELOG v0.20.0: the Mojo 1.0 build is about 13% slower than the published v0.13.0.
compiler_and_flags: Mojo 0.26.2 stable, default optimisation (benchmarks run with mojo run); CPython 3.12 re (build flags of the interpreter not stated); Rust regex 1.10 with Cargo profile.release opt-level 3, lto = true, codegen-units = 1, RUSTFLAGS -C target-cpu=native (benchmarks/rust/Cargo.toml, run_comparison_with_rust.sh). rustc version not stated.
tradeoffs: Missing features: named groups, case-insensitive matching, non-greedy quantifiers, word boundaries, Unicode character classes, multiline and dot-all modes, lookaround and negated shorthand classes (\S, \D, \W). Invalid patterns can fail the build when used with the compile-time API.
caveats: First-party, hardware not stated, so tier C. Several extreme rows compare different work: (1) the five is_match_* rows time Mojo's bool-only is_match, which can stop after the first matching character, against Python's bool(pattern.match(text)), which runs the full greedy match over a 10,000-character input (7,434x to 18,013x); (2) wildcard_match_any hits a pattern-string special case in src/regex/matcher.mojo (_is_wildcard_match_any: pattern == ".*" returns Match(0, start, len(text)) without scanning), so no regex runs; that shortcut also ignores newlines, which '.' should not match, and is only correct here because the test text has none (stb-zip/Pipa-style row, 5,454x vs Python and 45,718x vs Rust); (3) no_literal_baseline and alternation_common_prefix time Mojo match_first (one anchored match) against Rust find_iter().collect() over the whole 6,000-character text (844.7x and 177.9x). The Mojo harness has no black_box equivalent, so sub-2 ns rows are at loop-overhead level and may be partly hoisted (not confirmable without running). The Python column includes CPython interpreter call overhead (roughly 100+ ns per call), which dominates nanosecond rows, so it is not a clean measurement of the C sre engine; Rust regex is not a C/C++ baseline. The compile-time (comptime) API is not used in the comparison table. comparison.md was produced with Mojo 0.26.2 while the code now targets Mojo 1.0.0. Missing features (case-insensitive, non-greedy, word boundaries, lookaround, named groups) mean the engine supports a smaller regex language than re or Rust regex. Rows missing from one side are blank. [retier] The Rust harness (bench_engine.rs, lib.rs) uses a different input, pattern or operation from Mojo on 13 of 71 rows: literal_match_short/long bury 'hello' 10x deeper for Rust (Rust about 2.5x/1.4x faster per byte); range_lowercase, range_digits and predefined_digits match 3 bytes at offset 0-3 on Rust's text, so Rust's 3 wins are artefacts; group_alternation uses (a|b)* vs (a|b); match_all_simple 'a' vs 'hello'; texts 10-50x shorter on 4 more rows. The '.*' shortcut returns the whole text across newlines (correctness bug).
found_via: GitHub: direct check of the msaelices/mojo-regex README ('Beats Python's C-based re module on 96% of benchmarks') after github.com/topics scans for regex engines in Zig and Go.
why_faster: Hybrid DFA, NFA, PikeVM and lazy-DFA engine chosen per pattern; an optional compile-time API builds the DFA in Mojo's comptime interpreter so matching needs no runtime compilation, pattern hashing or cache lookup (README).

name: runiq (Rust duplicate-line filter)
baseline: GNU sort -u and uniq (coreutils; versions not stated); also uq and huniq
workload: Filtering duplicate lines from 25,000,000 JSON documents (1.9 GB, 20.67% duplicates) and 100,000,000 documents (7.7 GB, 55.69% duplicates), sorted and unsorted input, output to /dev/null.
claimed_speedup: README tables, 25M lines (1.9 GB, 20.67% duplicates), unsorted: runiq -f quick 12.1 s and 298.7 MB vs sort -u 380.2 s and 8.33 GB (about 31x faster, derived from page data); sorted input: runiq -f sorted 10.3 s and 1.3 MB vs uniq 24.9 s and 1.6 MB (about 2.4x, derived). 100M lines (7.7 GB, 55.69% duplicates), unsorted: runiq -f quick 34.7 s vs sort -u 2529.9 s (about 73x, derived); sorted: runiq -f sorted 24.9 s vs uniq 105.8 s (about 4.2x, derived). huniq (Rust) is level with or slightly faster than runiq -f quick (11.9 s and 31.2 s).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the measurements; Cargo.toml release profile now sets lto = true (added 2025-12-13, after the README tables were last changed in January 2024). rustc version, coreutils version and build, and locale not stated.
why_faster: README: filters that use hash sets, a bloom filter ('compact') or a streaming sequential check ('sorted') instead of sorting the whole input; memory and speed optimised.
tradeoffs: Compact filter is probabilistic; simple filter uses 2.3 GB to 5 GB of memory; sorted filter only detects adjacent duplicates, like uniq.
caveats: The author says the numbers are a reference for his own tuning, 'not meant to be a competition'; no hardware, compiler, coreutils version, locale or timing tool is given, and the tables date from the January 2024 README updates. The unsorted comparisons are algorithmic (hash set against GNU sort's full external sort, which also produces sorted output rather than first-occurrence order), and GNU sort's speed depends heavily on the locale, which is not stated. The 'quick' filter keeps only xxh64 digests, so a hash collision could drop a unique line (negligible at these sizes but not exact). The sorted-input comparison with uniq is the like-for-like one (src/filters.rs SortedFilter compares each line with the previous one, as uniq does); its 2.4x to 4.2x margin is not explained. huniq, another Rust tool, matches runiq.

name: rust-sort (Rust GNU sort replacement)
baseline: macOS system /usr/bin/sort (Apple's BSD-derived sort shipped with macOS 15.5), labelled 'GNU sort (system)' in the README; benchmark.sh defaults REFERENCE_SORT to the system 'sort' and its own usage text labels /usr/bin/sort as BSD and /usr/local/bin/gsort as GNU. uutils (rust_coreutils) sort is a second column. Current GNU coreutils sort was not measured.
workload: benchmark.sh: 100K, 1M and 10M lines generated deterministically with seq/awk (not random): numbers (i*7919) mod 32749 (at most 32749 distinct small integers), strings 'str_'+((i*13) mod 9973)+'_text' (9973 distinct values), floats and i mod 100 duplicates; flags -n, text, -rn, -u, -nu, -f, -R, -s, -g, -nru; each command timed once with /usr/bin/time -l (10 ms resolution) in the user's default locale.
claimed_speedup: README table (one timed run each) against the macOS system /usr/bin/sort labelled 'GNU sort (system)': 1M lines -n 1.00 vs 0.03 s (33.3x); 1M text 0.57 vs 0.03 (19.0x); 1M -rn 0.95 vs 0.03; 10M -n 6.21 vs 0.45 (13.8x); 10M text 6.00 vs 0.43 (14.0x); 10M -f 8.09 vs 0.42 (19.3x); 10M -g 24.17 vs 2.24; 10M -u 2.50 vs 0.55; 10M -s 3.28 vs 0.55. The 10M -f row timed a plain byte sort (see caveats) and the -n and -rn rows run paths that misorder or reverse their output, so only the plain text rows against the BSD sort stand.
compiler_and_flags: rust-sort: Cargo.toml [profile.release] opt-level = 3, lto = true, codegen-units = 1, panic = abort; rustc version not stated (rust-version 1.70). Baseline: Apple's prebuilt system sort, build flags unknown.
hardware: Apple M2 Max MacBook Pro, 32 GB, macOS 15.5
why_faster: README: zero-copy operations, SIMD acceleration and intelligent algorithm selection; multi-threaded.
stars_or_usage: 1 star; crates.io 982 downloads (gnu-sort 1.0.5, metadata says MIT OR Apache-2.0)
tradeoffs: Not byte-identical GNU behaviour in every flag; unique and stable modes lose to uutils per its own table.
caveats: Baseline mislabelled: the 'GNU sort (system)' column is the macOS system sort, which is Apple's BSD-derived sort, not GNU coreutils (benchmark.sh defaults to the system 'sort' and its usage text itself names /usr/bin/sort BSD and gsort GNU); eBay tsv-utils TipsAndTricks reports current GNU sort is often more than twice as fast as the macOS sort, and uutils sort beats the same column by about 8x at 10M lines, so the speedup over current GNU sort is probably far smaller than 33x. rust-sort runs rayon parallel sorts (par_sort_unstable_by, parallel radix and hash sort) above 8192 lines on a 12-core M2 Max against a single-process system sort. Test data are low-cardinality arithmetic sequences (at most 32749 distinct small integers, 9973 distinct strings), which suit its radix and hash paths, although the README says 'randomly generated'. Each case is one /usr/bin/time run with 10 ms resolution, though performance_comparison_table.md claims 'average of multiple runs'; the two result tables disagree slightly and both are dated December 2024 while the repo's code is from 2025. macOS only; not validated against the GNU coreutils test suite. LICENSE file is MIT while Cargo metadata says MIT OR Apache-2.0. 1 star; marketing-style README. [retier] Baseline mislabelled: the 'GNU sort (system)' column is Apple's BSD-derived macOS sort (benchmark.sh defaults to the system sort and its own usage text names /usr/bin/sort BSD and gsort GNU); eBay tsv-utils reports current GNU sort often more than twice as fast as the macOS sort and uutils sort beats the same column by about 8x at 10M lines. Harness flaw by code reading: files over 100 MiB go through external_sort.rs, which passes only the numeric and unique flags, and the 10M-line strings file is 138.9 MB, so the 10M -f row (0.42 s vs 0.43 s for plain text) timed a plain byte sort and the '19x case-insensitive' headline is invalid. Correctness bugs: -r without -k is reversed twice outside the numeric path (ascending output); -n's radix path validates only the first 100 lines and then uses an unvalidated byte - b'0' (wraps in release), misordering later decimal or text lines; -nu and -fu dedupe by exact bytes; the external merge's double-reversed heap emits unsorted output; multi-file merge ignores -n, -r, -f and -u; stdin is silently truncated at 2 GB. Issue #1: 92 GB RSS and OOM on 1.5 TB input. One run per cell, macOS 15.5, no CPU model.

The sort -n fast path (src/commands/sort.rs sort_numeric_fast) parses each whole trimmed line with Rust's f64 parser (a line with a non-numeric suffix becomes 0, unlike GNU's leading-number parse), sorts with an unstable sort and has no last-resort whole-line comparison, so it does less work than GNU sort -n and can order ties differently. errata.md lists known shell parsing gaps. 1 star, crates.io 60 downloads. name: Spellbook (Rust Hunspell-format spellchecker, rewrite of Nuspell)
baseline: Hunspell and Nuspell (C++), single-word check()
workload: Criterion median time to check one word against the stock en_US dictionary for ten word shapes (in-dictionary, number, prefix and suffix stripping, title and upper case, hyphen breaks, compound), plus a Valgrind DHAT heap total for checking one word.
claimed_speedup: check(): 'earth' 42.82 ns vs Hunspell 197.25 ns and Nuspell 125.89 ns; '8675,309.0' 14.14 ns vs 220.89 and 112.92 ns; 'light-weight-like' 779.06 ns vs 4,329.10 and 1,248.90 ns; 'unearthed' 264.98 ns vs 405.81 and 521.53 ns. Not faster on every row: compound word '20000th' 676.08 ns vs Nuspell 656.35 ns (Hunspell 3,204.10 ns). DHAT total allocation for one check: Spellbook 2,580,386 bytes in 44,741 blocks vs Nuspell 4,437,599 bytes in 50,419 blocks and Hunspell 3,325,493 bytes in 90,736 blocks.
compiler_and_flags: Spellbook: cargo bench with Criterion 0.8 (benches/check.rs). Hunspell and Nuspell: vendored C++ sources compiled by the cc crate in the-mikedavis/ffi-dictionaries build.rs with no explicit opt_level or flags, nightly Rust toolchain (rust-toolchain.toml), timed with libtest #[bench]. Under cargo bench the bench profile inherits release opt-level 3, which the cc crate passes as -O3, so both sides are probably optimised at level 3 without -march (inferred from Cargo and cc defaults; not stated). No compiler versions or CPU stated.
tradeoffs: Only check() is benchmarked; the author says dictionary load and suggestion matter less and does not measure them. Hunspell-format dictionaries. Rust crate; the repo ships no benchmark of its own against Hunspell, the C++ numbers come from a separate FFI harness.
caveats: First-party numbers, CPU and compiler versions not stated, so tier C. The two sides use different harnesses (Criterion median vs nightly libtest #[bench]); the C++ side is called through an FFI shim (Nuspell_spell/Hunspell_spell taking a const char*) with c"word" literals, a small per-call cost. The word_with_suffix row is not apples to apples: the table labels it 'earthed' for all three, but ffi-dictionaries benches/nuspell-check.rs and hunspell-check.rs time 'earthly' (a literal stem that short-circuits on lookup), while Spellbook's benches/check.rs times 'earthed' with a comment on that difference. Not faster on every row: compound_word '20000th' 676.08 ns vs Nuspell 656.35 ns. Spellbook is mainly a rewrite of Nuspell, so the gain is from data-structure choices (hashbrown and foldhash vs Nuspell's own hash table with std::hash, compact stem and flagset representation), not Rust codegen; the author labels the string-search explanation a suspicion and did not profile. The ffi-dictionaries harness is GPL-3.0 and has 1 star. Only en_US is in the comparison table (check.rs also benches fr_FR, without a C++ comparison). [retier] The published C++ harness (the-mikedavis/ffi-dictionaries, last commit 2026-04-14, libtest #[bench] on 'earthly') does not match the published numbers (compare.md 2026-06-07 labels every column a Criterion median for 'earthed'; the C++ word_with_suffix row rose from 236.94/141.47 ns to 353.01/273.76 ns), so the C++ columns came from an unpublished local harness. The November 2024 table had the Nuspell and Spellbook EARTH and unearth rows swapped; DHAT totals are dictionary load plus one check; '20000th' ties Nuspell; pre-0.4.2 fr_FR suggest 1.47 s vs Hunspell 243 ms (issue #15).
found_via: GitHub: helix-editor/spellbook README (Rust rewrite of Nuspell) links docs/compare.md; WebSearch 'Rust rewrite of C++ library faster than Nuspell OR hunspell...' returned the crate.
why_faster: Per the author: Spellbook uses hashbrown (SIMD group probing) with foldhash for the stem table where Nuspell rolls its own hash table with std::hash; Rust's standard library string search and equality are well optimised; small-string and small-slice optimisations cut memory. The author labels the string-search point a suspicion and does not profile it.

name: stepreduce-rs (Rust port of stepreduce)
baseline: stepreduce C++ original (uses libstdc++ std::regex) by Seth Hillbrand
workload: Lossless size reduction of one 1 MiB STEP CAD text file (00010546_919044145dd24288a1945b5c_step_008.step), output to /dev/null, hyperfine with 3 warmups.
claimed_speedup: README hyperfine: cpp-baseline 505.4 ms, rs-baseline 145.2 ms (about 3.5x), rs-find-numbers 104.5 ms, rs-prealloc 97.2 ms, which hyperfine reports as 5.20 +/- 0.10 times faster than the C++ original. A README note dated 2026-02-25 says that after optimizations (C++ issue #3) the C++ project is now slightly faster again than the Rust code.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the README and the bench/ directory is not committed. The Rust author's GitLab issue #3 (2026-02-14) asks whether 'cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release . && make' is the proper optimized build, implying a Release build of the C++ side; the C++ CMakeLists.txt sets no default build type (C++20, OpenCASCADE linked), so a plain cmake build would carry no -O flag. Rust side: Cargo release defaults (no custom [profile.release]; dev/test dependency opt-level 2).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X
why_faster: README: 'probably attributable primarily to the use of the Rust regex crate' against the slow C++ std::regex, then about 1.5x more from finding numbers without a regex and preallocating. The attribution is the author's guess, not a profile.
tradeoffs: GPL-3.0-or-later like the original. Output is verified identical to the C++ program by about 80 generated test files.
caveats: Superseded by the README's own update: after the C++ project changed, it is 'now slightly faster again than this Rust codebase', so the 5.2x figure is obsolete. The measured C++ baseline was the 2026-02-05 rewrite (GitLab commit fb5e2f81), which used libstdc++ std::regex for NUM_PATTERN, NAME_PATTERN, REF_PATTERN and UNCERTAINTY_PATTERN; commit 06fdbc67 on 2026-02-15 (the day after issue #3) replaced those regexes with hand-written parsing and also fixed a C++ correctness bug ('Missed an identity element ... led to some breakage in repeated patterns'), so the numbers were taken against baseline code later fixed for correctness. Single 1 MiB input file in a niche format (STEP CAD), hyperfine with 3 warmups; the gap is a std::regex-versus-regex-crate illustration, not a language result. The Rust port was produced with LLM help and the author disclaims correctness beyond the test suite. The original C++ project is on GitLab (sethhillbrand/stepreduce, GPL-3.0-or-later; GitLab reports no detected license object); its issue page carries embedded text addressed to AI agents, which was ignored. [retier] parse.rs breaks on the first non-UTF-8 line, so a Latin-1 byte silently truncates DATA plus the footer with no error; the CLI can overwrite its input; remap_references panics on '#' plus digits beyond u32, including inside quoted strings. The benchmarked 2026-02-14 builds predate two geometry-loss fixes (CDSR root 2026-02-15, SHAPE_REPRESENTATION_RELATIONSHIP root 2026-03-01); C++ had the same bugs. LibrePCB #1693: C++ is now about 4% faster, and output now diverges from C++ master.

name: The Platinum Searcher (pt, Go code search)
baseline: The Silver Searcher (ag, written in C: ggreer/the_silver_searcher has src/main.c) and ack (Perl); versions of all three tools not stated.
workload: Recursive search for EXPORT_SYMBOL_GPL in the Linux kernel source tree, timed with the shell `time` builtin (one run per tool).
claimed_speedup: README benchmark (one run per tool, shell time, Linux kernel tree): ack 32.613 s total (30.18 s user, 2.32 s system, 99% cpu), ag 1.069 s total (1.57 s user, 1.76 s system, 311% cpu), pt 0.991 s total (2.29 s user, 1.26 s system, 358% cpu). README Features claim pt is 'about 3-5x faster than ack' and 'as fast as' ag. By wall time pt is about 1.08x (8%) faster than ag and about 33x faster than ack (derived from page data), but it uses more CPU time than ag (3.55 s vs 3.33 s, derived from page data).
tradeoffs: Honours .gitignore, skips dot-directories unless --hidden, reads UTF-8, EUC-JP and Shift_JIS; binaries for macOS, Windows and Linux (README).
caveats: Single run on an unspecified machine, with no tool versions, Go version, kernel tree revision or flags; the 8% wall-time gap over ag is within one-run noise, and pt spends more total CPU time than ag. The runs are listed in the order ack, ag, pt, so pt probably ran on the warmest page cache (inference; order of execution not stated). Both ag and pt are multithreaded, so the result is a tool-versus-tool comparison, not a language-level one; the README states no mechanism. Last commit 2018-09-05 (Travis CI and wercker badges). ripgrep, already in the catalog, is the common choice today. [retier] The README kernel numbers date from 2015-12-07 (commit a86ecd3, about v2.0.x) and predate the v2.2.0 grep rewrite; the January 2014 'faster than ag' commit 374b952 changed only the pt row and reused the ack and ag rows (cross-run). The independent ripgrep 0.8.0 README has pt -w -e '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND' at 14.208 s against ag's 0.589 s. bufio.Scanner's 64 KiB limit with scanner.Err() unchecked makes -e, -i, -S, -w and context paths silently drop the rest of a file (#168 open); log.Fatalf on any open error aborts the run (#106, #192). Abandoned since 2018.
found_via: Recalled as a Go grep alternative while reviewing GitHub grep topic pages; its README was opened directly (no search query surfaced it).

name: tuc (Rust cut replacement)
baseline: the system cut binary (C; GNU or BSD and version not stated), also awk, uutils cut, hck and choose in the same table
workload: Select fields 1, 8 and 19 (sequential and non-sequential order) from the first 1,000,000 lines of the UCI HEPMASS all_train.csv with a single-character delimiter, and from a multi-character-delimiter text file (data-multichar.txt), output to /dev/null (benchmark.sh, hyperfine --warmup 3 -m 5).
claimed_speedup: README table means: tuc -d , -f 1,8,19 1.080 s vs system cut 5.726 s (5.30x), uutils cut 1.764 s, hck 1.276 s, choose 4.347 s, awk 35.852 s (33.2x); non-sequential fields 1.093 s vs cut 5.723 s (non-sequential order); multi-character delimiter ('   '): tuc 1.464 s vs awk -F'   ' 14.471 s (9.88x) and 'tr -s | cut' 5.310 s (3.63x). With a regex delimiter (-e'\s+') tuc takes 9.870 s, no faster than hck (9.834 s).
compiler_and_flags: benchmark.sh runs 'cargo build --release'; Cargo.toml [profile.release] lto = true, codegen-units = 1, panic = 'abort', strip = 'debuginfo'; edition 2024, README says rustc >= 1.85.0 is required (exact rustc version not stated); default features regex and fast-lane. The system cut and awk implementations, versions and build flags are not stated.
why_faster: The README does not state a mechanism. Visible in the table and Cargo.toml: memory-mapped input (the --no-mmap rows are about 1.14x slower) and the memchr and bstr crates (agent observation, not a source statement).
stars_or_usage: 821 stars, 16 forks; crates.io tuc 19,805 downloads; packaged in several distributions (repology badge)
tradeoffs: GPL-3.0-or-later (copyleft); not a drop-in cut (own CLI with ranges, negative indices, regex delimiters, JSON output); mmap input has the usual caveats on files that change while read.
caveats: First-party tables added to the README on 2025-09-11 (v1.3.0); the hardware, rustc version and the cut and awk implementations and versions are not stated (benchmark.sh uses GNU sed -i syntax, wget and the uutils 'coreutils' multicall binary, which suggests Linux and probably GNU cut, but this is not stated). Only the first 1,000,000 lines of HEPMASS all_train.csv are used and output goes to /dev/null, so write costs are excluded. cut cannot split on a multi-character delimiter, so that table compares against 'tr -s | cut' and awk pipelines. uutils cut (Rust) is also 3.2x faster than the system cut, and hck in literal mode is only 1.18x slower than tuc, so the gap is to the system cut's implementation rather than to C. With a regex delimiter (-e'\s+') tuc (9.870 s) is no faster than hck (9.834 s). Means of at least 5 runs after 3 warmups. [retier] The tuc command omits -j, so its output (fields concatenated) differs from cut's; in the non-sequential table cut prints file order. The timings match hck's README full 7M-line run (Ryzen 9 3950X) within about 5% although benchmark.sh keeps only 1M lines. Two awk rows copied from hck are broken (-F'[:space:]+' lacks the outer brackets; '$8 $19' is missing a comma); the 33x-vs-awk is against an unnamed awk about 7x slower than mawk. GNU coreutils 9.11 added cut -w, so the 'tr -s | cut' baseline is dated.

name: Vaporetto (Rust pointwise Japanese tokenizer)
baseline: KyTea (C++ pointwise word segmenter, 2020-04-03 build); MeCab 2020-09-14 also timed with other models
workload: Tokenizing the Aozora Bunko text of 'I Am a Cat' (Soseki Natsume), elapsed time measured 100 times (mean and std reported), KyTea and Vaporetto both using the KyTea compact SVM model based on BCCWJ and UniDic; whether model loading is excluded is not stated. Measured on Vaporetto v0.4.0 (wiki last edited 2022-06-09), not the current 0.6.5.
claimed_speedup: README: 'Vaporetto is 8.7 times faster than KyTea.' Wiki Speed-Comparison (Vaporetto v0.4.0, mean of 100 runs, ms): KyTea 219.6 (std 2.9), Vaporetto 29.0 (0.6), Vaporetto charwise 25.3 (0.4), so 7.6x and 8.7x (derived from page data); MeCab IPAdic 102.9 and UniDic 255.1, Lindera 397.1, sudachi.rs 286.2 and rust-tinysegmenter 272.7 use other dictionaries or models. arXiv 2406.17185 abstract: 5.7 times faster than the current approach based on the same model without loss of accuracy; NLP2022 paper: 5.4x vs KyTea (both snippet only).
compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.60.0 and GCC 11.2.0 (wiki); optimisation flags not stated for either side. The workspace Cargo.toml has no profile override (cargo release default opt-level 3); how KyTea was configured is not stated.
hardware: Intel Core i7-8086K @ 4.00GHz, 64 GiB, CentOS 7.5
why_faster: Not spelled out on the pages opened; the README lists the double-array Aho-Corasick paper (daachorse) among its references, which suggests the feature lookup is built on it.
tradeoffs: Needs a Vaporetto model (converted from a KyTea model or trained); pointwise prediction, not full morphological analysis.
caveats: First-party wiki table from 2022 (Vaporetto v0.4.0) with a single corpus; no benchmark script is published (evaluate/ is an accuracy tool), build flags for both sides and whether model loading is excluded are not stated; the KyTea comparison is the only like-for-like row (same model); the 8.7x headline is the charwise variant (7.6x for the default mode), and the authors' own papers report smaller gains (5.7x in arXiv 2406.17185, 5.4x in NLP2022, snippet only). The speedup comes from a restructured inference algorithm, not from Rust versus C++. [retier] Public harness: legalforce-research/tokenizer-speed-bench (author's commits) loads the KyTea and Vaporetto models outside the timer, preloads lines and times segmentation only, with the KyTea library built -O3 through its own configure. name: Vibrato (Rust MeCab reimplementation)
baseline: MeCab (C++ Japanese morphological analyzer), 2020-09-14 build
workload: Tokenize all 2,346 lines (158.8 characters on average) of 'I Am a Cat' (Aozora Bunko). Each tool reads the lines into memory, then times only the tokenization loop with a steady clock, single-threaded. run_all.sh runs 101 iterations, each a fresh process, and iteration 0 is a warm-up. MeCab uses mecab-ipadic 2.7.0 or unidic-cwj 3.1.1, and Vibrato uses its v0.5.0 precompiled dictionaries built from the same sources. The MeCab driver calls tagger->parse() with -Owakati, which builds a space-separated output string. The Vibrato driver calls worker.tokenize() and only counts tokens.
claimed_speedup: Wiki Speed-Comparison table: Vibrato 0.5.0 ipadic 42 ms vs MeCab ipadic 87 ms (about 2.1x, derived from page data); Vibrato unidic-cwj 75 ms vs MeCab unidic-cwj 179 ms (about 2.4x, derived from page data); the Vibrato raw-connector variant takes 1364 ms (7.6x slower than MeCab) and dual-connector 170 ms (about equal).
compiler_and_flags: From tokenizer-speed-bench compile_all.sh (tag vibrato-0.5.0-benchmark): MeCab (taku910/mecab submodule) is built with its own ./configure, whose configure.in sets CFLAGS/CXXFLAGS to '-O3 -Wall' under GCC. The MeCab driver is built with 'g++ -std=c++11 -O3 ./main.cc -lmecab'. The Vibrato 0.5.0 crate is built with RUSTFLAGS='-C target-feature=+avx2' cargo build --release (release profile, opt-level 3). No gcc or rustc version is stated, and MeCab gets no -march, so only the Rust side is built for AVX2.
hardware: Intel Core i9-12900K, 64 GB DDR5, Ubuntu 22.04
why_faster: README: reimplementation of the MeCab algorithm simplified and optimised; for dictionaries with a large connection matrix (unidic-cwj, 459 MiB) cache-efficient id mappings make it faster.
tradeoffs: Rust library, C++ needs FFI or the CLI. Uses its own compiled dictionary format (zstd compressed system.dic.zst), converted from MeCab dictionaries; MeCab-compatible output options exist.
caveats: First-party benchmark run by the authors' organisation (LegalForce / daac-tools): one corpus (one novel) on one machine. Compiler versions are not stated. The two sides do not do equal work. (1) MeCab's parse() with -Owakati formats an output string, while Vibrato only builds the lattice and counts tokens. (2) Vibrato runs with default settings, not the MeCab-compatible -S -M 24 options, so its tokens can differ from MeCab's (README 'MeCab-compatible options'), and outputs were not compared. (3) Only Vibrato is compiled with AVX2 (+avx2); MeCab uses generic x86-64 -O3. (4) MeCab mmaps its dictionary and 459 MiB unidic matrix, so the timed loop likely pays page faults that Vibrato, which reads the whole dictionary into memory before timing, does not. This is an inference from the harness, not a measurement. The raw-connector compact model (1364 ms) is 7.6x slower than MeCab, and the dual-connector model (170 ms) is roughly level with it. The speedup is largest with the large-matrix unidic dictionary. The numbers are for Vibrato 0.5.0 (early 2023) and have not been re-run for later releases. [retier] Runs were not pinned to a core on the hybrid i9-12900K; the headline depends on dictionaries whose connection ids were remapped with BCCWJ CORE statistics (v0.5.0), so self-compiled dictionaries are slower until the map step runs. The benchmark corpus has only 47 ASCII spaces, so the non-compatible default mode barely matters. Dictionary load is untimed (issue #150: 14 s and about 1 GB for UniDic against MeCab's 28 ms). The benchmark calls read_unchecked, removed in 0.5.2; the paper result is from a search snippet only.

The win comes only from parallelism: multicore-wc runs one thread per core on disjoint file ranges and streaming-wc processes 1 MB chunks in parallel with Streamly's aheadly, against single-threaded wc; multicore user time is 4.22 s vs 2.07 s wall for wc, and single-core Haskell is slower than wc. Whatlang (Rust) and Lingua (Rust) are also compared.

'cargo bench --features benchmark' implies the bench profile (rustc opt-level 3); the gcc crate used by cld2-sys passes cargo's OPT_LEVEL to the C++ compiler, so CLD2 was presumably built at -O3 with -std=c++03 (inferred from cld2-sys/build.rs, not stated). rustc and C++ compiler versions are not given.
hardware: iMac 3.6 GHz 8-core Intel Core i9 with 40 GB RAM (stated for the Lingua README table)
why_faster: Whichlang README: a small multiclass logistic regression over hashed 2-4-gram letter and codepoint features projected into a 4,096-dimension space (the hashing trick), with no dependencies. Whatlang's comparison table lists CLD2 as quadgram based; the link between model size and speed is this agent's inference.
stars_or_usage: 461 stars; about 469,000 crates.io downloads (latest 0.1.1, 2025-01-21); used by Quickwit
tradeoffs: Supports only 16 languages (CLD2 supports about 83 per the Whatlang README table); the author reports 99.5% accuracy on a private validation set, and accuracy is lower for short inputs. No HTML handling.

The 0.28 s vs 1.70 s accuracy-reporter row times statistics collection and report writing too, and Lingua's CLD2 adapter maps each result by iterating all Lingua languages and allocating an ISO-code String per candidate, which penalises the CLD2 row. CLD2 build flags (-O3) are inferred from the gcc crate, not stated; the cld2 binding crate is deprecated and bundles CLD2 sources from about 2015. Whichlang supports only 16 languages; Lingua reports it is less accurate than Lingua on that common set. [retier] The cld2 1.0.2 crate's to_c_str_or_null returns a dangling CString pointer when hints are passed (the benchmark uses default hints, so the numbers are unaffected). name: Zig (benchLANG strings workload, 19x19 word equality)
baseline: C (GCC 16.2.0, `-O3 -march=native -flto -funroll-loops`, glibc memcmp per equal-length pair) and C++ (g++ same flags, std::string_view ==, libstdc++).
workload: benchLANG 'Strings': 5M iterations of comparing every pair of the 19 words of a constant sentence for equality (19x19 pairs per iteration).
claimed_speedup: README results table (3 September 2026, one run per language), String Operations column: Zig 1.504 s, C 2.132 s, C++ 2.190 s, C# 2.235 s, D 2.351 s, Go 2.532 s, Ada 2.603 s, Rust 2.621 s, Nim 2.804 s. Zig is 1.42x faster than C and 1.46x faster than C++ (derived from page data). Zig is not faster overall: Fibonacci Zig 3.181 s vs C 1.694 s, and C ranks first on total runtime (9.762 s vs Zig 10.737 s, Zig factor 1.10x).
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.16.0 `zig build-exe -OReleaseFast -mcpu=native -fstrip -lc`; C `gcc -O3 -march=native -flto -funroll-loops -ffp-contract=off -s` and C++ `g++ -std=c++20` with the same flags, GCC 16.2.0 from nixpkgs-unstable.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X locked at 3.5 GHz, 48 GB DDR4-3600, Arch Linux; one run per language, 3 September 2026
tradeoffs: ReleaseFast removes Zig's safety checks. The Nix flake pins every toolchain, and the analyzer marks the ranking invalid if checksums differ between languages (README).
caveats: One run per language (the runner supports --runs 3 but the published table is a single run); the CPU is locked at 3.5 GHz and the gap is 42%, so noise alone is unlikely to explain it. The win belongs to the Zig standard library's equality routine, not to Zig codegen: std.mem.eql inlines a branch-light short-slice compare (three byte XORs below 4 bytes, four overlapping 4-byte loads up to 16 bytes) and returns early when both slices share a pointer, which skips the byte compare on the 19 diagonal pairs of each iteration; the C and C++ versions call out-of-line glibc memcmp (variable length, so GCC presumably does not inline it; disassembly not checked) for each of the 103 equal-length pairs of the 361 per iteration. A C version with an inlined compare would likely close the gap (inference). The input is a compile-time constant 19-word sentence (README says constant folding counts as a result); C tokenises a strdup copy with strtok at run time while Zig tokenises the constant slice, so LLVM may specialise more (not checked). Zig 0.16.0's lib/std/mem.zig was not readable (the tag is not on the GitHub mirror); the eqlBytes code was read at 0.15.1 and master. Rust and Go are also slower than C on this task, and C ranks first overall in the same repository.

compiler_and_flags: zigmark: Zig 0.16.0, built by the flake's mkZigmark helper with -Doptimize=ReleaseFast, ReleaseSmall and ReleaseSafe. cmark, cmark-gfm, discount, lowdown and pandoc are the nixpkgs packages pulled in as runtimeInputs of the `bench` app in flake.nix; their versions and build flags are not stated. caveats: Harness asymmetry: in flake.nix the cmark and cmark-gfm commands are run through a generated /bin/sh wrapper (`exec cmark "$@" > /dev/null`) because cmark has no -o option, while zigmark, lowdown and discount are spawned directly by hyperfine -N; every baseline run therefore pays an extra shell start-up (about 1 ms per spawn with dash in the verifier's container; NixOS's /bin/sh is bash, which is heavier), on runs that take 2 to 5 ms in total, and hyperfine's --output=null would have avoided it. The same wrapper means the cmark and cmark-gfm peak-RSS figures are the maximum of the shell and cmark, since Linux carries the pre-exec high-water mark into ru_maxrss. Benchmark output is auto-written into the README by the repo's own bench app. The PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0 licence forbids commercial use, so the code is reference-only. baseline: jq (C); the README row is labelled 'jq/jaq' so it is not clear which of the two produced each number; ripgrep (Rust) is also compared
workload: Search, filter, extract, re-format and aggregate over a 1 GB JSONL file with 6.7 million lines; GB/s per workload, zog reading a file (background reader thread with 8 MB double buffering) or a pipe. Whether the file was in the page cache, the dataset's shape and the exact queries and baseline command lines are not given.
claimed_speedup: README: '20-50x faster than jq/jaq for typical queries', '4.1x faster than ripgrep for complex multi-condition logic', aggregations '40x faster than jq'. Table, GB/s zog(file) / zog(pipe) / ripgrep / jq-jaq: simple key match 4.03 / 2.38 / 2.30 / 0.07; substring match (HAS) 2.49 / 2.09 / 1.53 / 0.07; numeric comparison 3.39 / 2.41 / 2.97 / 0.10; field extraction (TSV) 2.83 / 2.21 / N/A / 0.10; JSON re-formatting 2.77 / 2.18 / N/A / 0.10; aggregations 2.41 / 1.91 / N/A / 0.05; complex logic (OR/AND) 2.24 / 1.93 / 0.54 / 0.06. Ratios against jq/jaq: about 28-58x in file mode and 22-38x in pipe mode (derived from page data).

The repo migrated from Zig 0.13.0 to 0.16.0 on 2026-07-02, so the README numbers may predate that.
hardware: Only 'a modern NVMe SSD' is named; no CPU model
why_faster: Repository description: zero-allocation JSONL search engine using SIMD (field matching without building a DOM); jq parses every line into a full value tree. Mechanism is from the repo description, not from a profile.
tradeoffs: Query language is limited to the supported match, extract and aggregate forms; it is a filter tool, not a general jq replacement.
caveats: First-party only: no CPU, no benchmark script or dataset in the repository, no baseline versions or flags, and jq and jaq are merged into one column. zog does different and weaker work than jq: it does not parse or validate JSON, ignores nesting (a key inside a sub-object matches as if it were a root key), matches numbers literally (90 does not equal 90.0) and assumes single-line UTF-8 JSONL, so its results can differ from jq's on the same query. zog(file) uses two threads (reader plus scanner) against single-threaded jq. ripgrep cannot express numeric comparisons natively, so its rows are some unstated regex approximation. A tool-versus-tool result, not a language comparison; arguably belongs in a JSON category as much as text. [retier] First-party only: no CPU, benchmark script, dataset, baseline versions or flags, and jq and jaq share one column. zog does different and weaker work than jq: it does not parse or validate JSON, ignores nesting, matches numbers literally and assumes single-line UTF-8 JSONL. Correctness bugs in the measured code (src/scanner.zig, present at benchmarked commit 7e83065): the WHERE matcher accepts any occurrence of the quoted key text with no colon check (`error exists` matches {"level":"error"}) and neq is true if any occurrence differs; --format json leaves strings unquoted when the first byte is a digit, '-', 't', 'f' or 'n' and truncates objects and arrays, so the JSON re-formatting row is not equivalent to jq; single-field SELECT and aggregates can return an empty value (sum undercounts); unchecked i64 overflow on 19+ digit integers; lines over 8 MiB end the scan. README numbers date from 2026-02-27, before the Zig 0.16 std.Io port (v1.0.0 unmeasured); the Linux release is built for baseline x86-64 (SSE2, not AVX2).

name: bitdp (compile-time derived bit-parallel alignment kernels)
baseline: edlib (C++), ksw2 extz2_sse (C) and parasail scan16/diag16 (C)
workload: Edit-distance and other linear-gap global alignment of independent DNA pairs (1 kbp and 150 bp sets, real Illumina reads, a 32-guide CRISPR scan of E. coli K-12), measured in GCUPS on one core with every tool's total cost cross-checked.
claimed_speedup: bench/RESULTS.md (medians of three runs, GCUPS, one core, Ryzen 7 8840U under WSL2): on 5,000 random 1 kbp pairs at 15% divergence, batched bitdp 35.20 (4 lanes AVX2) and 34.89 (8 lanes AVX-512) vs edlib 21.73, ksw2 extz2_sse 2.20, parasail scan16 5.19 and diag16 1.98 (1.62x edlib); unbatched bitdp is slower than edlib on every DNA set (18.07 vs 21.73 at 1 kbp, 5.69 vs 6.19 at 150 bp, 4.33 vs 4.42 on reads), so the win needs batching, and the AVX-512 batch is no faster than AVX2.
compiler_and_flags: bitdp: Zig 0.16.0 -Doptimize=ReleaseFast, built twice: -Dcpu=znver4 (AVX-512, 8 lanes of 64 bits) and -Dcpu=x86_64_v3 (AVX2, 4 lanes). Baseline harnesses built with gcc 15.2.0 -O3 -march=native: bench/baselines.c linked against the Ubuntu packages parasail 2.6.2 and edlib 1.2.7 (the libraries themselves are distro builds, their compile flags are not stated, and the Ubuntu parasail has no AVX-512 kernels), and bench/ksw2_baseline.c compiled together with ksw2 commit 289609b (ksw_extz2_sse, 128-bit SSE). BGSA from its repository at commit dffcf9e (2022-02-24), kernels from its own generator, built with make cc=gcc.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 8840U (Zen 4, AVX-512), Ubuntu under WSL2 (kernel 6.6.114.1), one core, no threading
tradeoffs: Research code, not yet stable; global and search modes with linear gap costs only; at most 32 distinct score differences and 24 substitution costs; compile-time derivation takes seconds to about 15 s (375 MB of compiler memory for BLOSUM62); batched mode needs many independent pairs to fill SIMD lanes.
caveats: Single author, single machine (Ryzen 7 8840U under WSL2). The comparison is batched SIMD lanes (one alignment per lane) against single-pair tools, a different regime from edlib's per-pair banded algorithm; on 150 bp pairs a single bitdp pair is slower than edlib. Against BGSA, the closest same-regime tool (C++, hand-derived kernels), bitdp reaches only 0.73-1.20 of its speed for edit distance and trails BGSA's packed BitPAl, so the win over C/C++ comes from batching and the derived kernel, not from Zig. edlib and parasail are Ubuntu package builds, not rebuilt at -O3 -march=native; parasail's NW kernels are affine-gap kernels run with open = extend for linear gaps. parasail's striped kernels were excluded because they returned wrong costs on some pairs (426 of 100,000 on the 150 bp edit set). The 13.3 s genome-scan figure is the repo's own scalar reference loop. Research code, API not stable. [retier] Unbatched bitdp is slower than edlib on every DNA set, not only at 150 bp; the AVX-512 batch is no faster than AVX2. edlib and parasail are Ubuntu builds; ksw2 and parasail run as affine engines; the genome scan is forward strand only against a scalar loop. All tools' cost sums agree.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/bioinformatics?l=zig topic page
why_faster: Bit-parallel kernel derived at compile time from the recurrence (14 word operations per column for unit edit costs versus 15 for Myers) with one alignment per SIMD lane for independent pairs.

name: ckmeans (Rust optimal 1-D k-means) vs Ckmeans.1d.dp C++
baseline: Ckmeans.1d.dp C++ implementation (kmeans_1d_dp, methods 'linear' (default) and 'loglinear'; the code behind the R package and the ckmeans-1d-dp Python package), vendored in bench_cpp
workload: Optimal 1-D k-means (dynamic programming) on seeded random inputs: Uniform(1,3) and Uniform(0,1000) at n = 110,000 and 1,000,000, k from 3 to 50, a bimodal normal input, and BIC selection of k in 1..9; Criterion point estimates, one run of the full suite.
claimed_speedup: bench_cpp/README.md (Criterion point estimates, ms, one run of the full suite, Apple M2 Pro): Uniform(1,3) n=110,000 k=5 rust_indices 13.2 / rust_optimal 14.5 vs cpp_linear 26.0 / cpp_loglinear 25.3; k=20 49.7 / 52.7 vs 105.3 / 90.7; n=1,000,000 k=5 126.7 / 142.9 vs 254.9 / 249.8; k=20 513.5 / 556.1 vs 995.4 / 940.5; Uniform(0,1000) n=110,000 k=3 7.6 / 9.1 vs 16.5 / 16.1, k=50 114.4 / 120.0 vs 256.0 / 193.0; bimodal k=7 16.0 / 17.6 vs 31.3 / 28.7; BIC selection of k in 1..9 rust_optimal 26.7 vs 54.5 / 50.9 (n=110,000) and 263.1 vs 510.2 / 515.9 (n=1,000,000). The slowest Rust call (rust_optimal, which does the BIC step) against the faster C++ method is 1.6x to 1.9x faster in every row; rust_indices against the faster C++ method is 1.7x to 2.1x; the widest gap, fastest Rust against slowest C++, is 2.3x (Uniform(0,1000) k=30 and k=50) (all derived from page data). PR #41 (merged 2026-10-01) said 'Rust is 23 to 48 % faster than the C++ code in all cases'; that statement predates the 2026-10-02 commits that vectorised the split-point search, sped up the BIC step and replaced the table (a37c045).
compiler_and_flags: Rust: rustc 1.99.0, cargo bench with the bench profile inheriting bench_cpp/Cargo.toml [profile.release] lto = true, codegen-units = 1 (opt-level 3), no -C target-cpu; split-point search dispatched at run time through fearless_simd (NEON on aarch64). C++: Apple clang 17.0.0 via the cc crate in bench_cpp/build.rs with opt_level(3) (-O3), -DNDEBUG, -std=c++11, warnings off, no LTO, no -march; the 11 Ckmeans.1d.dp sources that the ckmeans-1d-dp Python package compiles plus a C shim (cpp/shim.cpp).
hardware: Apple M2 Pro
stars_or_usage: 12 stars, 1 fork; crates.io 'ckmeans' 23,737 downloads (1,409 recent), version 2.2.0; also published to npm as @urschrei/ckmeans (WASM)
tradeoffs: The vendored C++ code is LGPL-3.0-or-later and the Rust crate is BlueOak-1.0.0. Rust ckmeans_indices returns sorted data plus index ranges rather than per-value labels; the C++ call also returns labels, centres and sizes, and the Rust wrapper needs a mutex because kmeans_1d_dp() sorts through a static pointer. Results are identical to the scalar search (README).
caveats: Library win, not a language-level claim: the Rust crate and the C++ code solve the same objective and the agreement tests check identical clusters, but the implementations differ (Rust: flat matrix, stack-based divide-and-conquer column fill computing SSQ once per candidate, split-point search with four independent minima vectorised through fearless_simd; C++: SMAWK for 'linear' and scalar divide-and-conquer for 'loglinear'), so the speedup mixes algorithm constant factors, accumulator structure and explicit SIMD. The C++ call does a BIC step with Kmin = Kmax = k (6 to 10 percent of its time) that rust_indices and rust_clusters skip, writes a per-value label array in input order, and is wrapped in a Rust mutex plus an O(n) finiteness check; rust_optimal does the same BIC step and is still 1.6x to 1.9x faster. LTO and codegen-units = 1 apply to the Rust side only (C++ built as a static library without LTO); neither side sets a target CPU. Single run of the suite on one Apple M2 Pro, benchmark written by the crate author; the bench_cpp crate (2026-10-01, 5456a98) and its results were added in October 2026 commits, and PR #41 links a claude.ai/code session. The vendored C++ in bench_cpp/vendor is LGPL-3.0-or-later (benchmark only); the crate itself is BlueOak-1.0.0, which is OSI-approved per the SPDX license list 3.29.0 and includes a patent licence. The repository's Cargo badge says 'passively-maintained'.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Rust crate README benchmark comparison with C++ library faster than abseil OR folly OR boost ...' surfaced urschrei/ckmeans PR #41; then opened bench_cpp/README.md, the crate README, Cargo.toml files and the commits page.
why_faster: Source (README, 'Implementation' table): flat contiguous matrix for cache locality, stack-based divide-and-conquer column fill with a single-pass inner loop that computes the sum of squares once per candidate (the two-pointer approach computes it twice), pre-allocated stack, and a vectorised split-point search with run-time SIMD selection.

baseline: GNU cp -r (coreutils, C); the same table also lists rsync, tar piping, fcp, xcp and wcp
workload: Copying directory trees generated by ftzz (10 to 1M files, 0 B or 1 GiB total, default depth, depth 0, 5 files per directory) with hyperfine --warmup 3 -N on an xfs /tmp.
compiler_and_flags: cargo b --workspace --release; Cargo.toml [profile.release] sets lto = true, codegen-units = 1, strip = true, panic = abort. rustc version not stated. GNU cp is the distro binary of an el9_1 (RHEL 9 family) system; its coreutils version and build flags are not stated.
hardware: Intel i7-7700, 15 GiB RAM, Linux 5.14.0-162.18.1.el9_1.x86_64, /tmp on xfs (/dev/sda6)
stars_or_usage: 535 stars; packaged in several distributions (Repology badge in README)
tradeoffs: Linux is the primary target (other platforms use the rayon-style implementation). Non-goal: compatibility with coreutils cp options. Much higher total CPU time than cp (System 23.7 s vs 15.3 s at 1M files, 0 B).
caveats: The win is parallel copying, not Rust code generation: the single-threaded Rust cp_stdlib in the same table (std::fs::copy per file) matches GNU cp (19.496 s vs 18.436 s at 1M files, 0 B). The tables were last regenerated in March 2023 (commits 4cb8736 and ebf11a7, 2023-03-23/24) and the code has changed since. cpz is not the fastest tool in every row: in a flat directory of 100,000 files the Rust xcp wins (0 B: xcp 1.133 s, cpz 1.365 s, cp -r 1.618 s; 1 GiB: xcp 1.209 s, cpz 2.080 s, cp -r 2.464 s), and cp_rayon and fcp edge it at 5 files per directory with 1 GiB. Total CPU time rises: at 1M files, 0 B, cpz uses 26.48 s user+system against 18.10 s for cp -r (derived from page data). The run script also builds and runs wcp (C++) but no wcp row appears in any results table. cpz copies with copy_file_range, which can clone extents on a reflink-enabled xfs, while an older GNU cp may do a byte copy; cp_stdlib uses the same syscall and still matches cp, so this is not the main factor. Source and destination on the same xfs SATA partition, one machine, warm page cache with no sync between runs; the variance on the cpz rows is large (+- 0.976 s at 1M files). The author's blog overview (alexsaveau.dev/blog/fuc) does not resolve from this environment.
