name: Fucina (Zig tensor runtime and LLM inference engine)
baseline: llama.cpp CPU backend (ggml kernels, llama-bench with -ngl 0), same GGUF file and thread count
workload: Prompt prefill (pp) and decode (tg) tokens per second for Qwen3 0.6B/1.7B, Qwen3.5, Qwen3-30B-A3B MoE and Gemma-4-26B-A4B GGUF models in several quantizations, CPU-only on both sides, paired same-machine runs over many prompt lengths.
claimed_speedup: docs/BENCHMARK.md (snapshot 2026-07-04, updates 2026-07-10), ratio = Fucina / llama.cpp tok/s. Apple M1 Max, 8 threads: of 236 sweep cells Fucina faster in 221, parity 13, llama.cpp faster 2; dense prefill per-format geomeans 1.18-1.81x (Qwen3 0.6B seven formats and 1.7B; Qwen3.5-0.8B 1.07x on 4 lengths); Qwen3-30B-A3B MoE prefill pp64-256 1.44-2.09x; dense decode Q4_K_M/Q4_K_S +15 %, Q8_0 +14 %. Intel i9-13950HX (AVX2 + AVX-VNNI, no BLAS either side): dense Qwen3-0.6B paired-gate median ratios 1.32-1.95 per quantized format (maxima up to 2.56); 2026-07-10 dispatch fix took x86 dense decode Q5_K_M to 1.016, Q5_K_S 1.055, Q6_K 1.057; 30B MoE mid-batch pp15-33 moved from 0.36-0.52x to Q5_K_M 1.15-1.22x and Q6_K 0.97-1.05x. llama.cpp wins or open gaps: Qwen3.5-0.8B Q8_0 pp32 0.86x, 30B Q6_K decode 0.88x on M1 (no page-cache prewarm), MoE decode 0.87-0.95x on M1 and 0.971-0.972x on x86, Q6_K 30B pp31-33 0.965-0.987x and pp64-256 0.93-0.97x on x86, Gemma-4-26B pp1-9 0.85-0.99x on x86, Gemma-4-26B mid-batch prefill on M1 0.72-0.91x cool (listed as an open gap, while the scoreboard reports 1.17-2.15x from a session in which llama.cpp ran below its own best values), and pp256 with Q4_K-transcoded experts about 15-17 % behind.
compiler_and_flags: Fucina: Zig 0.16.0, zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast with the default native target (no -Dtarget); off macOS the default is -Dblas=none, on macOS the default build uses Accelerate CBLAS for f32 GEMMs at m >= 16. llama.cpp: build 30af6e2 pinned in tools/fetch_refs.sh, whose --build step runs cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DGGML_METAL=OFF -DLLAMA_CURL=OFF (CPU-only, Accelerate BLAS left on under macOS). The x86 llama-bench build was verified as GGML_BLAS=OFF, GGML_NATIVE=ON (-march=native), GGML_LLAMAFILE=ON, GGML_CPU_REPACK=ON, GGML_OPENMP=ON, but its binary reported build_commit unknown; the x86 leg of another record says both engines were compiled on the box with gcc-12 / zig native. The C/C++ compiler for the M1 llama.cpp build is not stated.
hardware: Apple M1 Max (arm64, 8 threads, macOS) and Intel Core i9-13950HX (Raptor Lake 8P+16E, AVX2 + AVX-VNNI, no AVX-512, Linux)
tradeoffs: CPU-first runtime written in pure Zig (needs Zig 0.16); covers GGUF Qwen3, Qwen3.5 and Gemma-4 families plus training, speculative decoding and ASR/TTS runners; llama.cpp still wins several MoE decode and small-batch cells.
caveats: Author-run, first-party record with one dated snapshot (2026-07-04) against a pinned llama.cpp build, so results age as llama.cpp advances. On the M1 llama.cpp's Accelerate/AMX path switches on at batch >= 32 and the document says that transition costs it heavily at pp32-129 (up to 7.2x at f16 pp32), so part of the prefill win is a llama.cpp threshold effect; Fucina's own macOS default build also routes f32 GEMMs at m >= 16 to Accelerate, so the M1 rows are not BLAS-free on either side (the x86 rows are). Gemma-4 and Qwen3.5 M1 rows use best-of Fucina numbers (flagged by the author as favourable to Fucina), and the Gemma mid-batch session had llama.cpp below its strongest recorded values; the same document lists Gemma-4-26B mid-batch prefill on M1 as an open gap at 0.72-0.91x cool, contradicting the scoreboard's 1.17-2.15x. The x86 llama-bench binary reported build_commit unknown, so its commit rests on the recorded build flags. Laptop thermals and page cache move results by several percent; some cells are same-day reruns after a 2026-07-10 scheduler fix. Fucina's loops include logits/sampler work llama-bench skips (biases against Fucina). Different kernels and scheduling from ggml, so this is not a Zig-versus-C++ language comparison. tools/gen_optim_goldens.py is under CC-BY-NC-4.0 (rest MIT). [retier] MoE prefill rows are not like-for-like: bench_gate.py feeds Fucina a 4-token seed repeated (ids_repeated) while llama-bench feeds random IDs (std::rand() % n_vocab); the document's own counters show about 52 of 128 experts active at pp256 against about 124 under uniform input, so those ratios are likely flattered (dense rows unaffected). The 'biased against Fucina' note is overstated: the prefill timer stops before the sampler. The native Linux build auto-links MKL, OpenBLAS or BLIS; the thread ceiling is 8 at build time.

name: ipnsort and driftsort (Rust std slice::sort_unstable and slice::sort)
baseline: C++ standard library sorts: std::sort and std::stable_sort of libstdc++ and libc++ (benchmark variants cpp_std_gnu / cpp_std_libcxx in the repo)
workload: Sorting 10k u64 values with a hot cache across seven input patterns (ascending, descending, random, random_d20, random_p5, random_s95, random_z1) on Zen 3; unstable contestants include rust_ipnsort_unstable (research-repo commit 757478b) and the pre-2024 Rust std sorts vendored mid 2022; MSVC rows are listed but not in the Linux plots.
claimed_speedup: Plot values in writeup/sort_safety/assets/unstable-hot-u64-10k.png (10k u64, hot, Zen 3, time in us): rust_ipnsort_unstable vs libstdc++ std::sort / libc++ std::sort: ascending 2.07 vs 49.3 / 6.23 (23.8x / 3.0x), descending 3.16 vs 32.2 / 11.4 (10.2x / 3.6x), random 77.0 vs 297.6 / 265.1 (3.9x / 3.4x), random_d20 24.3 vs 136.5 / 97.6 (5.6x / 4.0x), random_p5 12.4 vs 57.2 / 16.7 (4.6x / 1.35x), random_s95 83.4 vs 182.2 / 84.2 (2.2x / 1.01x), random_z1 56.8 vs 222.9 / 200.2 (3.9x / 3.5x) (ratios derived from page data). The text's 'current Rust standard library unstable sort ... outperforms the C++ standard library counterparts' refers to the pre-2024 pdqsort-based rust_std_unstable (random 136.9 us). Stable plot: driftsort is not tested; the then-current rust_std_stable beats libstdc++ std::stable_sort on random (253.0 vs 318.6 us) but loses on random_d20 (250.5 vs 190.5) and random_p5 (156.8 vs 69.8) and loses to libc++ on random, random_d20 and random_z1.
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.75.0-nightly (2023-10-03) with --release and lto=thin; C/C++ built through build.rs with opt_level(3) and -std=c++20 (-march=native only for the AVX2/AVX-512 contestants); clang 16.0.6 and gcc 13.2.1. The libstdc++ and libc++ variants are separate cargo features (cpp_std_sys, cpp_std_libcxx).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X (Zen 3), Linux 6.5, CPU boost enabled
stars_or_usage: 545 stars; ipnsort and driftsort replaced the sorts in the Rust standard library (rust-lang/rust PR 124032)
tradeoffs: Generic over Ord with arbitrary user comparators; written with a lot of unsafe Rust for code-gen reasons but designed to avoid UB on non-strict-weak orderings and panics (the writeup's Ord and exception safety analysis). Needs Rust; stable sort needs auxiliary memory.
caveats: Bias disclaimer: the ipnsort author wrote the analysis. Only 10k u64 on one CPU with 2023 toolchains (rustc 1.75 nightly, gcc 13.2.1, clang 16.0.6); the bitsetsort-derived libc++ std::sort of LLVM 17 is 'so far untested'. Driftsort (today's slice::sort) does not appear in this benchmark or in any C++ comparison found (the driftsort and ipnsort introductions compare only against Rust sorts), so the stable half of the record has no evidence against C++; the Rust stable sort shown (rust_std_stable, vendored mid 2022) is slower than libstdc++ std::stable_sort on random_d20 and random_p5 and slower than libc++ on random, random_d20 and random_z1. The ipnsort tested is the research-repo version at 757478b, not necessarily the code merged into std by rust-lang/rust PR 124032 (merged 2024-06-20). The win is algorithmic, not a Rust language effect: C++ pdqsort (144.4 us random) matches the pdqsort-based rust_std_unstable (136.9 us) and C crumsort (95.6 us) is close to ipnsort (77.0 us). ipnsort roughly ties libc++ on random_s95 (83.4 vs 84.2 us). Neither side uses -march=native for these contestants.
found_via: GitHub: Voultapher/sort-research-rs README and writeup/sort_safety; not in KNOWN_LIST.
WebSearch 'driftsort ipnsort Rust sort faster than C++ std::sort benchmark sort-research-rs', then the repo's writeup/sort_safety/text.md Performance section and build.rs
why_faster: Newer algorithms than the introsort-style C++ std implementations: ipnsort (pattern-defeating quicksort lineage with a branchless cyclic Lomuto partition and small-sort networks) and driftsort (adaptive merge sort that falls back to quicksort for low-cardinality input); the author attributes the gap to old C++ implementations, not to the language.

name: Nim ref-object binary trees (LangArena Binarytrees::Obj) vs C++ make_unique tree
baseline: C++ version of the same test (std::make_unique per tree node, g++ and clang++) and the C version (malloc per node)
workload: LangArena Binarytrees::Obj: build a complete binary tree of depth 20 of individually allocated nodes, sum it, and free it; 30 iterations (run.js).
claimed_speedup: Nim/Clang (prod row, default ORC) 1.55 s and Nim/GCC/ARC 1.193 s vs C++/G++/Fast 2.098 s (the best of the C and C++ prod, Fast, Unsafe and PGO configurations; only the instrumented C++/Clang++/PGO/Gen build is lower, at 2.081 s), C++/G++ 2.101 s and C/Clang 2.482 s. That is about 1.35x faster at default and 1.76x with ARC than the best C/C++ configuration (derived from page data). The lead held in the three previous runs (2026-08-14 to 2026-09-18: Nim/Clang 1.51-1.55 s vs best C/C++ 2.02-2.15 s). Memory: Nim/Clang 102 MB and Nim/GCC/ARC 69 MB vs C++/G++ 70 MB.
compiler_and_flags: C/C++ 'prod' build: make -j prod with -O2 -DNDEBUG -fstack-protector-strong -fno-omit-frame-pointer, -std=c++20 (clang 22.1.8, g++ 16.0.1 20260322 trunk), glibc malloc. The suite also builds 'Fast' (-O3 -march=native -mtune=native -ftree-vectorize -funroll-loops, -flto=thin passed only at link), 'Unsafe' (-O3 -march=native -ffast-math, -flto=full at link) and PGO variants of every C and C++ test, all in the results file. Nim 2.2.12: Nim/Clang (the suite's 'prod' Nim row) is nim c --threads:on -d:release --cc:clang; Nim/GCC/ARC (a 'hack' row) is nim c --threads:on -d:release --cc:gcc --gc:arc. In Nim's config/nim.cfg, -d:release turns on opt:speed, so the generated C is compiled at clang -O3 or gcc -O3 -fno-ident -fno-math-errno, both with -fno-strict-aliasing. Nim/Clang uses the default ORC memory manager (Nim doc/mm.md). No build passes -d:useMalloc, so Nim's own allocator is used.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X 8-Core Processor, 78GB RAM, x86_64 Linux (host kostya-ms7c37, results dated 2026-10-05)
why_faster: Not stated by the suite. Unverified inference: Nim's ref objects are allocated by Nim's own allocator and released by reference counting (ARC or ORC) at scope end, so the per-node allocate and free path avoids glibc malloc and free that the C and C++ tests hit once per node. The suite's own index-based Arena variant of this test removes the per-node allocation.
tradeoffs: About 45 percent more memory than C++ in this test; reference counting adds a count word per object.
caveats: The win is allocation-strategy specific: an arena or pool allocator in C or C++ beats it, and the suite's Binarytrees::Arena rows go the other way (C/Gcc/Fast 0.255 s, C++/G++/Fast 0.53 s, Nim/Clang 1.049 s). The 1.76x figure is the non-default ARC 'hack' configuration; the default ORC 'prod' row gives 1.35x and uses 46% more memory than C++ (102 vs 70 MB). Nim's generated C is compiled at -O3, while the headline C/C++ prod rows are -O2; the -O3 Fast and Unsafe rows also lose. Nim's node carries a 64-bit int item, where C and C++ use a 32-bit int. ORC as the default and the -O3 mapping were checked in Nim's doc/mm.md and config/nim.cfg on the devel branch, not in the 2.2.12 tag. V (Clang) 0.806 s, Crystal 1.175 s and Java also beat C++ on this test; Rust (2.62 s), Zig (6.31 s) and C3 (3.4 s) are slower. LangArena calls itself a subjective benchmark, and its README says AI tools helped translate the tests. Each configuration is timed once per monthly run with no variance reported, though four monthly runs agree. Rows were selected by the search agent as tests where the language beats every C/C++ configuration; most other tests in the suite go the other way. Ratios are derived from the results file, not stated by the suite.

name: zipir (Zig streaming DEFLATE-family compression library and CLI)
baseline: zlib-ng 2.3.3 (zlib and raw DEFLATE), ISA-L igzip, and bgzip with libdeflate 1.26 or zlib-ng (htslib 1.24)
workload: Single-threaded whole-command compression at each tool's fast, balanced and dense level (zipir 1/5/9, zlib-ng 1/5/9, ISA-L igzip 0/1/2, bgzip 1/5/9) and decompression of gzip, zlib, raw DEFLATE and BGZF: FASTQ (57.2 MB and 20.2 MB), PRIDE XML (48.0 MB), mzIdentML (1.2 MB) and Canterbury tar (2.8 MB); BGZF compression uses a BAM (76.2 MB) and a VCF (11.5 MB) in place of the FASTQ files; decompression adds Silesia tar (211.9 MB). 3 warmups and 25 interleaved rounds per batch, medians; output size reported beside compression speed; process start-up and file I/O included.
claimed_speedup: Whole-command single-threaded times on one Ryzen 9 3950X, geometric means over files (peer time / zipir time). Decompression: on zlib and raw DEFLATE zipir is the fastest of the timed streaming tools, zlib-ng takes 1.24x its time (zlib 1.17-1.27x, raw 1.18-1.28x); only zlib-ng and the Zig std library were timed on those formats, libdeflate and ISA-L were not. gzip decompression is level with ISA-L igzip (1.01x, per file 0.81-1.25x) and zlib-ng takes 1.10-1.26x. BGZF decompression: bgzip + libdeflate is 1.07x faster than zipir, bgzip + zlib-ng takes 1.06-1.24x. Compression against zlib-ng at the same nominal level (zlib and raw DEFLATE): level 1 1.35x with 34% larger zlib-ng output, level 5 1.08x (0.93-1.23x) with 2% larger output, level 9 2.01x (1.20-3.87x) with 2% larger output. Losses: ISA-L igzip is faster on gzip compression in all three lanes (0.83x, 0.28x and 0.13x of zipir's time) with 15-22% larger output; bgzip + libdeflate is 1.04x and 1.02x faster at no larger output on BGZF compression levels 1 and 5. Presets table: zipir fast 332.8 MB/s at ratio 3.183 against zlib-ng level 2 at 148 MB/s and ratio 3.257 and ISA-L igzip level 2 at 371 MB/s and ratio 3.205, so ISA-L is about 1.1x faster than zipir fast at a matched ratio (derived from page data). Peak RSS: zipir 0.55-0.62 MiB, the C tools 1.6-5.0 MiB.
compiler_and_flags: zipir 0.1.2 (compression rows commit 5f25547 with uncommitted changes, decompression rows commit ff8e9e8) through Zig adapters built with Zig 0.16.0 -Doptimize=ReleaseFast -Dstrip=true -Dcpu=native, single-threaded. Peers built by tools/install.sh with GCC 16.2.1: zlib-ng 2.3.3 static via CMake CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release with WITH_NATIVE_INSTRUCTIONS=ON (minigzip CLI for gzip; a C adapter over the native API compiled cc -O3 -DNDEBUG -march=native for zlib and raw DEFLATE); ISA-L igzip 2.32.1 static, CMAKE_C_FLAGS_RELEASE -O3 -DNDEBUG -march=native with nasm; libdeflate 1.26 static at -O3 -DNDEBUG -march=native; htslib 1.24 bgzip -@1 with htslib's default compiler flags, linked statically to libdeflate or to zlib-ng in compat mode.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 3950X (Zen 2, AVX2, no AVX-512), Linux 7.2.7-200.fc44 (Fedora 44), schedutil governor, every batch pinned to CPU 4, machine in normal use (1-minute load average 1.1-6.6), one host, measured 2026-09-27.

caveats: First-party report, one host, machine in normal use (matched interleaved rounds pinned to one CPU keep ratios fair). Compression rows were timed in zipir-only runs at commit 5f25547 with uncommitted changes and spliced against peer rows from a different run (zipir ff8e9e8); a later control batch agreed within -2.1% to -0.7%. name: C3 compiler (c3c) compile throughput vs gcc and g++ in nordlow/compiler-benchmark
baseline: C (gcc 15.3.0 and 16.2.1, clang 23.1.1) and C++ (g++ 15.3.0 and 16.2.1, clang++ 23.1.1) compiling the same generated arithmetic translation unit
workload: nordlow/compiler-benchmark: compile (and run) one massive synthetic translation unit of arithmetic call chains, reported as microseconds per generated function ('Total=Build+Run [us/f]'), untemplated and templated variants.
claimed_speedup: README table (Ryzen AI 7 350), us per generated function. Total=Build+Run untemplated: C3 (c3c 0.8.5) 153 vs C gcc-15 392 (2.6x), C gcc 16.2.1 454 (3.0x), C++ g++-15 303 (2.0x), C++ g++ 16.2.1 486 (3.2x), C++ clang++ 23.1.1 236 (1.5x); C3 is 1.3x slower than C clang 23.1.1 (118). Templated: C3 255 vs g++-15 600 (2.4x) and g++ 16.2.1 566 (2.2x); 2.4x slower than clang++ templated (107). Link-free Compile column: C3 109.3 (256.6 templated) vs gcc-15 193.8 (1.8x), gcc 16.2.1 400.1 (3.7x), g++-15 269.6 / 665.0 (2.5x / 2.6x), g++ 16.2.1 372.3 / 524.8 (3.4x / 2.0x); clang 77.9 and clang++ 82.4 / 128.7 compile faster than c3c. Check column: C3 15.0 is slower than gcc -fsyntax-only (11.9 and 11.8) and clang (13.5). All ratios derived from page data.
compiler_and_flags: From the public harness script cbench (./benchmark is a symlink to it; the C/C++, C3 and Odin blocks are identical in the 'benchmark' script at the table commit d16d0a5, 2026-10-09): gcc, g++, clang and clang++ get -Wall -Wextra (C) or -Wno-c++11-extensions (C++) and no -O flag, so default -O0; check uses -fsyntax-only, compile uses -c, build links through the driver's default system linker. c3c: check 'compile-only -q -O0 -C', compile 'compile-only -q -O0', build 'compile -q -O0 -o main' (c3c links with its default linker, 'cc' per its help text; the standard library is included by default). Versions: c3c 0.8.5, gcc/g++ 15.3.0 and 16.2.1, clang/clang++ 23.1.1. Each cell is the minimum of --run-count=10 repetitions (capped at 3 or 2 for steps over 1 s or 3 s) divided by 40,000 generated functions (200 x 200), with tasks run concurrently in a multiprocessing pool and each worker pinned to one core via os.sched_setaffinity.
hardware: AMD Ryzen AI 7 350 (8+8) at 5.09 GHz, Arch Linux; README says 'as of 2026-09', tables last updated in commit d16d0a5 on 2026-10-09
license: MIT (compiler source under src is LGPL-3.0)
stars_or_usage: 5.9k stars, 408 forks (c3lang/c3c); benchmark repo nordlow/compiler-benchmark 167 stars, 17 forks, MIT
tradeoffs: Templated builds are 1.7x slower than untemplated (153 to 255 us/f); the compiler source is LGPL-3.0 while the rest of the repository is MIT.
caveats: Compile-time claim, not run-time: both sides build unoptimised code (gcc/g++/clang default -O0, c3c -O0), so the -O3 rule for run-time baselines and the crippled-baseline precedent do not apply; the win is the wave's off-baseline case and is recorded as a toolchain compile-speed entry. Not a language-level win: clang compiles the C version faster than c3c compiles the C3 version (Total 118 vs 153, Compile 77.9 vs 109.3) and clang++ templated beats C3 templated (107 vs 255), and C3's semantic check (15.0 us/f) is slower than gcc's -fsyntax-only (11.9), so the gap is GCC's -O0 code generation against c3c's LLVM -O0 path. C and C++ get -Wall -Wextra or -Wno-c++11-extensions; tcc (4), cuik (76) and cproc (86) compile C faster still. Synthetic arithmetic call chains in one translation unit with no headers, standard library or modules; the README says real builds are dominated by headers, module resolution and parallelism. Noisy cells: gcc-15 Total 392 is double its Compile 193.8, clang++ untemplated Total 236 is nearly 3x its Compile 82.4, clang++ templated Total 107 is below its Compile 128.7, and the README prose (clang 87, GCC ~418-455, c3c +77% templated) comes from a different run than the tables. The built binaries' results are never checked. Single machine, single sample run by an independent D-community developer.
found_via: GitHub: README of nordlow/compiler-benchmark (found by the sys shootouts search for D; this row and the other systems-language rows of the same table were not recorded there).
why_faster: README: no C3-specific mechanism is stated; the suite attributes the spread mostly to the cost of the GCC front end and optimizing backend.

name: ixy network driver in Rust (C2Rust-transpiled unsafe build versus C)
baseline: ixy C user-space network driver packet forwarder (gcc, and clang with the same LLVM version)
workload: CPU cycles and instructions per forwarded 64-byte packet by the ixy forwarder at batch sizes 32 and 8 on an Intel 82599-class NIC, measured with CPU performance counters (paper: The Case for Writing Network Drivers in High-Level Programming Languages, ANCS 2019).
claimed_speedup: Rust-vs-C-performance.md: the C2Rust-transpiled, fully unsafe Rust driver forwards a packet in 91 cycles with 121 instructions, 'faster than the original code', also when C is compiled with clang on the same LLVM version. The C rows in the same document are 94 cycles and 127 instructions at batch 32 (108 and 139 at batch 8), so about 3% fewer cycles than C at batch 32 (derived from page data; the document does not state the batch size of the C2Rust run). The idiomatic safe Rust driver is slower: 100 vs 94 cycles at batch 32 and 120 vs 108 at batch 8, executing 65% more instructions.
compiler_and_flags: C baseline: emmericp/ixy CMakeLists.txt compiles with -g -O2 -march=native -fomit-frame-pointer (current HEAD; the file was last changed in November 2019). ixy.rs Cargo.toml sets no profile overrides (cargo release default opt-level 3, no target-cpu). Compiler versions and the C2Rust build's flags are not stated.
hardware: Intel Xeon E3-1230 v3 per the Rust-vs-C document (the repo README names an E3-1230 v2 at 3.3 GHz for the throughput graphs)
tradeoffs: Faster variant is entirely unsafe transpiled Rust without bounds checks; the safe idiomatic driver pays about 65% more instructions that out-of-order execution mostly hides.
caveats: The C2Rust claim is a tongue-in-cheek addendum added to the repository on 2019-10-30, after the ANCS 2019 paper; whether the paper contains it could not be checked (arXiv and net.in.tum.de blocked here). The transpiled C2Rust driver is not published in the ixy-languages organisation as far as I could find. The difference is 3 cycles per packet from one run on one Intel Xeon E3-1230 v3, with no variance reported, and the batch size of the C2Rust run is not stated. The C baseline is built at -O2 -march=native, not -O3, while Rust release builds default to opt-level 3, so optimisation levels are not matched. The document gives no mechanism beyond 6 fewer instructions per packet. Hardware differs between this document (E3-1230 v3) and the README throughput graphs (E3-1230 v2). name: mosdepth (Nim BAM/CRAM depth calculator)
baseline: samtools depth (C, htslib); README table also lists bedtools genomecov (C++) and sambamba depth (D)
workload: Per-base depth on a 30X whole-genome BAM/CRAM with one thread, 500-base window mean depth with three threads, and an exome BAM against 1,195,764 exons.
claimed_speedup: Per-base depth about 2x as fast as samtools depth (BAM: mosdepth 25:23 vs samtools 50:12, relative 1.98; CRAM samtools 1.79x slower); sambamba 5.71x and bedtools 5.31x slower; window depth genome-wide in under 9 minutes of user time with 3 threads (8:44, relative 0.34); exome in 1 minute 38 seconds on one CPU.
compiler_and_flags: Nim with --mm:refc (nim.cfg) and -d:release; nim.cfg comment: nim c -a -d:static -d:release mosdepth.nim with htslib configured --with-libdeflate --disable-libcurl. Nim's release build passes -O3 -fno-ident -fno-math-errno to gcc (nim-lang/Nim config/nim.cfg gcc.options.speed). samtools' default Makefile uses CFLAGS -g -Wall -O2; the flags of the samtools, bedtools and sambamba builds actually timed are not stated.
tradeoffs: Memory is about 32 bits times the longest chromosome (about 1 GB for chr1, against 27 MB for samtools); slower than samtools for small one-off regional queries; no gain past about 4 threads; links htslib (C) for decoding.
caveats: The README table lists no hardware, tool versions or commands; tier B would rest on the Bioinformatics 2018 paper, which was not opened (publisher, PMC and bioRxiv blocked; a search snippet confirms the comparison but gives no numbers). Results date from 2017 samtools and htslib. Both mosdepth and samtools decode BAM/CRAM with htslib (C); mosdepth's documented build links htslib with libdeflate, and the htslib build used by samtools in the table is not stated, so part of the gap may be decompression rather than mosdepth's code. By default mosdepth corrects mate overlaps and walks CIGAR operations; --fast-mode (-x) skips both; the README does not say which mode the timing table used, and its accuracy check compared samtools depth defaults with mosdepth without overlap detection. The speedup is algorithmic (difference array against samtools' pileup), not a Nim-versus-C effect; mosdepth uses far more memory (1196 MB vs 27 MB for samtools). Opt levels are not matched if default builds were used (Nim release -O3, samtools Makefile -O2). [retier] The README table lists no hardware, tool versions or commands; the Bioinformatics 2018 paper was not opened. Stale baseline: the 2x is against pileup-based samtools depth (2017; the table predates --fast-mode, v0.2.4 of 2018-11-19). samtools 1.13 (July 2021, PR #1428) rewrote depth without pileup, 3.3x faster than 1.11 on a 30-50x BAM (19.755 s vs 6.049 s) and 33x on deep CRAM, and was never re-compared with mosdepth. Output asymmetry: per-position text vs run-length bgzipped BED plus index. The table predates fixes 0.2.2 (wrong values on same-length chromosomes) and 0.2.5 (full mate-overlap double count). Both tools decode through htslib; mosdepth's documented build links libdeflate. Fast mode counts D/N spans as covered; the median is clamped at 65,535 and the histogram at 400,000; open #268 (CRAM 3.1 static-binary decode failure).
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/bioinformatics?l=nim topic page (brentp/hts-nim ecosystem)
Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts): Nim and D bioinformatics tools that beat C/C++ tools; github.com/brentp/mosdepth README opened on github.com and raw.githubusercontent.com
why_faster: README: depth is kept in an array that is incremented at each read start and decremented at its end, summed cumulatively at output; no extra allocations or objects, whereas samtools depth goes through the pileup machinery.

name: Odin compiler compile throughput vs gcc and g++ in nordlow/compiler-benchmark
baseline: C (gcc 15.3.0 and 16.2.1, clang 23.1.1) and C++ (g++ 15.3.0 and 16.2.1, clang++ 23.1.1) compiling the same generated arithmetic translation unit
workload: nordlow/compiler-benchmark: compile (and run) one massive synthetic translation unit of arithmetic call chains, reported as microseconds per generated function ('Total=Build+Run [us/f]'), untemplated and templated variants.
claimed_speedup: README table (Ryzen AI 7 350), us per generated function, Total=Build+Run. Untemplated: Odin 147 vs C gcc-15 392 (2.7x), C gcc 16.2.1 454 (3.1x), C++ g++-15 303 (2.1x), C++ g++ 16.2.1 486 (3.3x), C++ clang++ 23.1.1 236 (1.6x); Odin is 1.25x slower than C clang 23.1.1 (118). Templated: Odin 98 vs g++-15 600 (6.1x), g++ 16.2.1 566 (5.8x), clang++ 107 (1.09x, near tie). Odin has no link-free Compile cell (the harness runs only check and build for Odin). Check column: Odin 19.1 (47.0 templated) is slower than gcc -fsyntax-only (11.9 and 11.8) and clang (13.5). All ratios derived from page data.
compiler_and_flags: From the public harness script cbench (./benchmark is a symlink to it; the C/C++, C3 and Odin blocks are identical in the 'benchmark' script at the table commit d16d0a5, 2026-10-09): gcc, g++, clang and clang++ get -Wall -Wextra (C) or -Wno-c++11-extensions (C++) and no -O flag, so default -O0; check uses -fsyntax-only, compile uses -c, build links through the driver's default system linker. Odin: check 'odin check <file> -file', build 'odin build <file> -file -build-mode:exe -linker:lld -out:main' with no -o flag, so Odin's default -o:minimal (per odin's help text; separate LLVM build units by default at that level). Versions: odin dev-2026-09:a2fb372b7, gcc/g++ 15.3.0 and 16.2.1, clang/clang++ 23.1.1. Each cell is the minimum of --run-count=10 repetitions (capped at 3 or 2 for steps over 1 s or 3 s) divided by 40,000 generated functions (200 x 200), with tasks run concurrently in a multiprocessing pool and each worker pinned to one core via os.sched_setaffinity.
hardware: AMD Ryzen AI 7 350 (8+8) at 5.09 GHz, Arch Linux; README says 'as of 2026-09', tables last updated in commit d16d0a5 on 2026-10-09
stars_or_usage: 12.1k stars, 1.1k forks (odin-lang/Odin); benchmark repo nordlow/compiler-benchmark 167 stars, 17 forks, MIT
tradeoffs: Odin emits compact code (112.6 B/f, close to gcc's 121.1 B/f); build uses LLVM through the Odin compiler.
caveats: Compile-time claim, not run-time: both sides build unoptimised or minimally optimised code (gcc/g++/clang default -O0, Odin default -o:minimal), so the -O3 rule for run-time baselines and the crippled-baseline precedent do not apply; recorded as a toolchain compile-speed entry. Not a language-level win: clang compiles the C version faster (118 vs 147 us/f), Odin's check (19.1) is slower than gcc -fsyntax-only (11.9), and tcc, cuik, cproc, dmd, ldmd2, Zig and fpc are all faster, so the win is against GCC's -O0 pipeline only. Harness asymmetry: Odin builds link with lld (-linker:lld) while gcc and g++ use the default system linker, and Odin has no link-free Compile cell, so the linker share of the gap cannot be separated; C adds -Wall -Wextra. Synthetic arithmetic call chains in one file with no headers, standard library or modules (the README says real builds differ). Noisy cells: Odin templated (98) is faster than untemplated (147), gcc-15 Total 392 is double its Compile 193.8, and the README prose (odin 92, clang 87, GCC ~418-455) comes from a different run than the tables. The built binaries' results are never checked. Single machine, single sample run by an independent D-community developer.
found_via: GitHub: README of nordlow/compiler-benchmark (found by the sys shootouts search for D; this row and the other systems-language rows of the same table were not recorded there).
why_faster: README: the claim is throughput of the compiler front end and linking against GCC's heavier pipeline; no Odin-specific mechanism is stated in the sections read.

verification.tier_reason: Public harness (cbench in nordlow/compiler-benchmark, MIT) with every command line in code (gcc/g++/clang/clang++ at default -O0 with warning flags; 'odin build <file> -file -build-mode:exe -linker:lld' at Odin's default -o:minimal), compiler versions in the README table (odin dev-2026-09:a2fb372b7, gcc/g++ 15.3.0 and 16.2.1, clang 23.1.1) and the CPU named (AMD Ryzen AI 7 350, Arch Linux), so it meets A; upgraded from B because the flags are in the public script, consistent with the dmd row (batch-66).
verification.notes: Numbers match the README table exactly; flags read from cbench and checked unchanged at the table commit d16d0a5. Odin Zlib, 12.1k stars, last commit 2026-10-11 confirmed. The record's why_faster ('front end') is contradicted by the Check column and is corrected; record as a toolchain compile-speed entry that beats GCC only, with the lld-vs-default-linker asymmetry as its main shortcoming; category is a loose fit, as for the dmd row.

name: rustc compile throughput vs gcc and g++ in nordlow/compiler-benchmark
baseline: C (gcc 15.3.0 and 16.2.1, clang 23.1.1) and C++ (g++ 15.3.0 and 16.2.1, clang++ 23.1.1) compiling the same generated arithmetic translation unit
workload: nordlow/compiler-benchmark: compile (and run) one massive synthetic translation unit of arithmetic call chains, reported as microseconds per generated function ('Total=Build+Run [us/f]'), untemplated and templated variants.
claimed_speedup: README table (AMD Ryzen AI 7 350 run, tables updated 2026-10-09), Total=Build+Run us/f (untemplated / templated): rustc 187 / 238 vs C gcc-15 392, C gcc-16 454, C++ g++-15 303 / 600, C++ g++-16 486 / 566, C++ clang++ 236 / 107, C clang 118. Derived from page data: 2.1x faster than gcc-15 and 2.4x faster than gcc-16 on C, 1.6x faster than g++-15 and 2.6x faster than g++-16 on untemplated C++, 2.5x faster than g++-15 and 2.4x faster than g++-16 templated, 1.26x faster than clang++ untemplated; 1.6x slower than clang C (118) and 2.2x slower than clang++ templated (107). The README highlight says 'rustc (187 µs/f) significantly outpaces GCC-based C/C++ (~450–486 µs/f)'; its Conclusions section, from an earlier run, says rustc (183 µs/f) 'handily outperforms both GCC-based C/C++ front-ends (~418–455 µs/f)'.
compiler_and_flags: Flags are in the public harness cbench (README's ./benchmark is a symlink to it; the same flag code is in benchmark at d16d0a5, the 2026-10-09 commit that updated the README tables): gcc/clang C build = -Wall -Wextra -o <exe> with no -O flag (GCC/Clang default -O0), C++ uses -Wno-c++11-extensions instead of the warning flags; rustc gets no flags (RUSTC_FLAGS = [], so opt-level 0 through LLVM with debug assertions and overflow checks on by default; the cranelift RUSTC_NIGHTLY_FLAGS list is defined but unused); zig build-exe -fno-llvm -fno-lld -fno-clang (Debug mode, Zig's self-hosted x86_64 backend and linker). Versions from the README table: rustc 1.100.0-nightly, zig 0.18.0-dev.35+5e754304d, gcc 15.3.0 and 16.2.1, clang 23.1.1. Defaults: 200 chains x depth 200 = 40,000 functions per file, minimum of up to 10 builds (capped to 2-3 when a build exceeds 1-3 s), constants re-randomised per run to defeat caches.
hardware: AMD Ryzen AI 7 350 (8+8 cores) at 5.09 GHz, Arch Linux, sample run as of 2026-09
tradeoffs: Compile speed only; rustc adds +30% build time for templated (generic) code in this suite.
caveats: Compile-time comparison of unoptimised builds on one synthetic translation unit of 40,000 arithmetic functions with no headers, standard library or module resolution (the README says it does not reflect real builds); not the wave's run-time -O3 comparison. The README does not state flags, but the harness does: gcc/clang get only -Wall -Wextra (default -O0) and rustc gets none (opt-level 0, debug assertions and overflow checks on), so optimisation levels are matched at 'unoptimised'. Not a language win: clang compiles the same C 1.6x faster than rustc (118 vs 187 us/f) and clang++ templated is 2.2x faster (107 vs 238); the margin over GCC comes from GCC's slower -O0 pipeline (gcc-16 compile-only 400 us/f against clang's 78) and a GCC 15 to 16 regression the README itself flags. The templated Rust source omits the per-function constants that the C++ templated source carries (cbench Rust leaf 'x', chain 'x + prev(x)'), so the 2.5x templated ratio compares slightly less code. One sample run with a large run-to-run spread: the README's Conclusions section (an earlier run) gives clang 87, rustc 183 and GCC 418-455 us/f, and in the table the gcc-15 C build (392) is twice its compile-only time (193.8) while the other GCC rows differ by 12-31%. Tasks run concurrently in a multiprocessing pool pinned to cores chosen by cpu_topology.py heuristics on a Zen 5/Zen 5c part, so rows may have run on different core types. GCC and clang skip some C++ semantic checks that rustc performs in full (README note). The sibling record for D (dmd) is from the same table. Independent suite, but a small one (167 stars), one machine.
found_via: GitHub: README of nordlow/compiler-benchmark (found by the sys shootouts search for D; this row and the other systems-language rows of the same table were not recorded there).
why_faster: README: the README says rustc 'handily outperforms' the GCC front ends and notes that GCC and clang skip some C++ semantic checks that Rustc performs in full; no further mechanism is given.

verification.tier_reason: Upgraded B to A: independent public harness (nordlow/compiler-benchmark cbench: bm_Rust, gcc_clang_op_flags, bm_C_and_Cxx_using_gcc/clang) fixes every flag (gcc/clang -Wall -Wextra at default -O0, rustc with no flags at opt-level 0), the README table names every compiler version, and the CPU is stated (AMD Ryzen AI 7 350, Arch Linux). name: sambamba (D tools for SAM/BAM)
baseline: samtools (view, flagstat, markdup, sort, index; C, htslib)
workload: sambamBench-nf (Nextflow) runs flagstat, index, markdup, name sort (-n/-N) and view to /dev/null on the ~4 GB ENCODE BAM ENCFF044SJL with 16 threads and 120 GB (cluster profile; workstation profile 8 CPUs/40 GB), one run per tool version; samtools-1.7 markdup is a name sort, fixmate -m, coordinate sort and markdup pipeline, while sambamba markdup reads the BAM directly.
claimed_speedup: README (quoting the CRG comparison): flagstat 1.4x faster than samtools, index similar, markdup almost 6x, view 4x, sort beaten by samtools but up to 2x faster on 120GB+ machines. The README's linked report (public-docs.crg.es sambamba_ws_report.html) could not be opened. The pipeline's own 16 CPU / 120 GB report gives wall times (realtime) vs samtools 1.7: flagstat 7.7 s (sambamba 0.6.8-pre1) and 11.4 s (0.6.6) vs 11.5 s, 1.49x and 1.00x; index 12.7 s and 14.9 s vs 13.1 s, 1.03x and 0.88x; view 15.9 s (0.6.6) and 52.8 s (0.6.8-pre1) vs 77.8 s, 4.88x and 1.47x; markdup 197.1 s and 244.6 s vs 885.8 s for a four-stage samtools sort/fixmate/sort/markdup pipeline, 4.49x and 3.62x; sort 249.3 s and 327.2 s vs 146.7 s, so samtools 1.7 is 1.70x faster at 120 GB (all ratios derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: sambamba 0.6.6 and 0.6.8-pre1 and samtools 1.3 and 1.7 from grape/<tool>:<version> containers (build flags not published). sambamba's own release build uses ldc2 -O3 -release -enable-inlining -boundscheck=off (test/benchmark/stats.org); samtools 1.7's Makefile defaults to CFLAGS = -g -Wall -O2.
hardware: CRG cluster node, 16 CPUs and 120 GB RAM allocated to each task (CPU model not stated), per the sambamBench-nf README and nextflow.config cluster profile; the README's quoted figures may come from the unopened 'ws' (workstation, 8 CPUs, 40 GB) report.
stars_or_usage: 613 stars; over 1,000 citations (Bioinformatics 2015 paper); 250,000 conda installs
tradeoffs: Implements an important subset of samtools (view, index, sort, markdup, depth); GPL; wins depend on spare cores since parallel reading and writing is the mechanism.
caveats: The markdup baseline is crippled: the samtools-1.7 template does two full sorts plus fixmate before markdup, and its sort and fixmate steps pass '-@{task.cpus}' without the '$', so the thread count is never interpolated; the trace shows 102% CPU for that task versus 658-890% for sambamba. The README's sort claim (up to 2x faster at 120GB+) is contradicted by the 120 GB report, where samtools 1.7 sorts 1.70x faster. The view 4x win holds for sambamba 0.6.6 only (0.6.8-pre1 is 1.47x), and flagstat 1.4x holds for 0.6.8-pre1 only. One run per task, 2018 tool versions (samtools 1.7, sambamba 0.6.x), and the README's linked CRG report does not resolve (getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND public-docs.crg.es). samtools is built at its -O2 default against sambamba's -O3 release build. The README says samtools 1.4 reached parity in many areas and that sambamba's original advantage was parallel BAM I/O; the gains are parallelism and pipeline differences, not D against C. htslib (samtools' library) is listed in wave 8. [retier] The markdup baseline is crippled: the samtools-1.7 template does two full sorts plus fixmate before markdup, and its sort and fixmate steps pass '-@{task.cpus}' without the '$' (the resolved script in report_16_120G.html shows the literal), so samtools ran at 102% CPU against 658-890% for sambamba; the 4.49x and 3.62x markdup wins are against a single-threaded four-stage pipeline. The first task (sambamba 0.6.8-pre1 view) read 4.59 GB cold from disk while every later task read under 4 MB, so its 52.8 s (1.47x) is a cold-cache artefact and the warm 0.6.6 view row (4.88x) has no CPU or I/O counters. The README's sort claim (up to 2x faster at 120GB+) is sambamba against itself (stats.org, 20 GB vs 120 GB) and the 120 GB report has samtools 1.7 sorting 1.70x faster; issue #447: the maintainer recommends samtools sort except on high-RAM machines. samtools 1.7 was built at -O2 with plain zlib (no libdeflate before htslib 1.8). The CRG report behind the README could not be opened.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/bioinformatics?l=d topic page
Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts): Nim and D bioinformatics tools that beat C/C++ tools; github.com/biod/sambamba README and test/benchmark/stats.org opened
WebSearch 'code.dlang.org D library benchmark faster than C++ ... samtools' led to the D ecosystem; opened the biod/sambamba README, test/benchmark/stats.org and guigolab/sambamBench-nf README
why_faster: README: when sambamba started in 2012 its main advantage over samtools was parallelized BAM reading and writing.

verification.tier_reason: Independent measurement: the Guigó lab's public Nextflow pipeline guigolab/sambamBench-nf (templates/<tool>/<version> command scripts, nextflow.config) ran sambamba 0.6.6 and 0.6.8-pre1 against samtools 1.3 and 1.7 in grape Singularity containers, and its 16-CPU/120 GB report (gh-pages report_16_120G.html) carries per-task wall times; CPU model and compiler flags are not stated, so not A. Tier stays B, but the README's headline claims are overstated (see corrections).
verification.notes: README numbers are first-party quotes of a CRG report that no longer resolves; the pipeline's accessible 16-CPU report shows real flagstat (1.49x) and view (1.47-4.88x) wins, parity on index, a samtools win on sort (1.70x), and a markdup win against a crippled single-threaded four-stage samtools pipeline. Downgraded for the overstated markdup and sort claims; tier B kept on the independent pipeline. Record shortcomings: crippled markdup baseline, contradicted sort claim, 2018 versions, single runs, samtools -O2 default against sambamba -O3, parallelism rather than a D language effect.

retier.reason: Enricher: the markdup baseline in guigolab/sambamBench-nf ran single-threaded because the samtools template drops the '$' from '-@{task.cpus}', the sambamba view 1.47x row is a cold-cache artefact and the warm 4.88x row has no counters, and the README's '2x faster at 120GB+' compares sambamba with itself. Crippled-baseline precedent: B to C.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: README: flagstat 1.4x faster than samtools; markdup almost 6x faster; view 4x faster; index similar; sort beaten by samtools in general, but sambamba is up to 2x faster on large-RAM machines (120GB+).
corrected_fields.workload: BAM view, flagstat, markdup, sort and index runs of the sambamBench-nf pipeline (Nextflow, about 4 GB test BAM) on a single node with 16 CPUs and 120 GB RAM.
corrected_fields.compiler_and_flags: LDC (LLVM D compiler) 1.6.1 or later preferred; release build with meson (D_LD=gold CC=gcc meson build --buildtype release); samtools version and build flags in the CRG report not read.
corrected_fields.hardware: CRG cluster node with 16 CPUs and 120 GB RAM (CPU model not stated)
corrected_fields.caveats: The numbers come from an independent CRG comparison pipeline (guigolab/sambamBench-nf) whose report page I could not open, so they are quoted from the README. The README says samtools 1.4 (March 2017) already reached parity in many areas and the original 2012-2015 advantage was parallel BAM I/O. Samtools wins sort in general. Mostly a parallelism effect, not a D-versus-C one.

name: allox (Rust general-purpose allocator)
baseline: glibc malloc (the 'system' column of the Linux table), mimalloc and snmalloc, each driven through a Rust GlobalAlloc wrapper; Rust-native talc and dlmalloc are also compared
workload: 22 direct-call workloads in benches/alloc.rs driven through GlobalAlloc (small, mixed and large size classes at 1 and 8 threads, zeroed allocation, producer/consumer remote free, thread churn, a pthread calibration row, json-ish, request and ECS realloc-growth shapes); ops/s, higher is better. Each allocated block is written at one byte only, so the large and huge rows measure allocator bookkeeping and memory retention rather than memory traffic. A separate process-global String/Vec/HashMap application benchmark (examples/app_workload.rs, scripts/app_bench.sh) runs at 1 and 4 threads.
claimed_speedup: Linux x86-64 (Ryzen 5 1600) direct-call table, ops/s: tight-small 1T 52.52 M/s vs glibc 44.77, mimalloc 48.00, snmalloc 41.54 (1.09x vs best); mixed-small 8T 196.03 M/s vs system 37.17, mimalloc 40.42, snmalloc 57.87 (3.39x vs best); large-only 1T 7.36 M/s vs system 340 K/s, mimalloc 2.52 M/s. The zeroed-large row (86.63x) is struck: a recycled block gets madvise(MADV_DONTNEED) with the memset skipped while the bench touches 1 byte, so the zeroing cost is never paid.
compiler_and_flags: cargo bench; the bench profile inherits [profile.release] opt-level = 3, lto = true, codegen-units = 1 from Cargo.toml; rustc version and RUSTFLAGS not stated (MSRV 1.79). Comparators: mimalloc crate 0.1 and snmalloc-rs 0.7 (build_cc feature) compiled by their build scripts with unlogged C/C++ flags; 'system' is the distro glibc malloc (version unstated); talc 5 and dlmalloc 0.2 are Rust. Every allocator, allox included, is called through a &'static dyn GlobalAlloc, so allox gets no inlining advantage from LTO.
hardware: Linux x86-64 AMD Ryzen 5 1600, taskset -c 0-7, 3 GiB cgroup, BENCH_FRESH=1 BENCH_SAFE_LIVE=1, one fresh process per allocator/workload/repetition, median of 3 x 2 s runs. The Windows x86-64 table names no CPU.
why_faster: README: every fast path is lock-free per thread with sharded class locks touched only by batched slow paths, while single-heap allocators (talc, dlmalloc) serialize on one mutex; no mechanism is given for the glibc/mimalloc/snmalloc gaps on the mixed-size and large rows.
stars_or_usage: 1 star, 0 forks; 1,355 commits, but the latest batch (2026-10-10/11) are docs-only commits that append hidden '<!-- updated: ... -->' comments to README.md; not published on crates.io (API: crate `allox` does not exist) despite the README's `allox = "0.1"` snippet.
tradeoffs: Rust crate with a GlobalAlloc type and allox::malloc/free functions; peak RSS is higher on several rows (93 MiB mixed-small 8T, 118 MiB mixed-all 8T, 300 MiB prodcons 8T). Loses to snmalloc and mimalloc on 8-thread zeroed small allocations.
caveats: Very young single-author repo (1 star), not on crates.io; commit count is inflated by README-comment padding commits. Workloads are the author's own and rows carry a stated ~10% noise floor (median of 3 x 2 s), so the 1.02x-1.12x 'wins' are ties. Each block is touched at one byte: large/huge rows reward allox for keeping arena memory mapped while glibc (mmap threshold) and snmalloc return or decommit it (snmalloc reads 1 K/s on huge-only), and zeroed-large 1T's 86.63x comes from skipping the memset of 5-8 MiB blocks after a madvise discard while the benchmark never faults in more than one page. README size-range labels disagree with the code (big-tail labelled 64K-256K is 262145-524289 in code; big-upper-tail 256K-1M is 524289-1048577; large-only 8T 32K-1M is 32768-262144). mimalloc/snmalloc measured through Rust GlobalAlloc wrappers with unlogged build flags, glibc version unstated, no independent reproduction. The README documents its losses (zeroed-small 8T, 4-thread app workload) and a known telemetry-counter defect rather than hiding them. [retier] The zeroed-large 86.63x is an artefact: a recycled 5-8 MiB block gets madvise(MADV_DONTNEED) and the memset is skipped (alloc_large_ex known_zeroed) while the bench writes 1 byte, so the zeroing becomes page faults that are never triggered; the same 1-byte touch applies to all large rows, and snmalloc's 1-22 K/s implies it zeroes or touches whole blocks. scripts/app_bench.sh's build check is inverted under set -o pipefail, so a failed build counts as built and a stale binary is benchmarked silently. The direct-call harness measures only the Layout-routed sized free; the C ABI allox_free header path is unmeasured.

name: bzip2z (Zig bzip2 with SA-IS block sorting)
baseline: system bzip2 1.0.8 (C); pbzip2 1.1.13 reported as a third column
workload: Compression and decompression throughput of a 1.0 MB mixed-pattern buffer with the bundled bench-bzip2 tool, 3 iterations, single thread and 16 resolved threads.
claimed_speedup: README, mixed pattern, 3 iterations, 1 MB: single thread compress 18.64 vs 10.43 MB/s (1.79x), decompress 67.14 vs 69.38 MB/s (0.97x); threads=auto (16) compress 27.18 vs 10.33 MB/s (2.63x), decompress 0.99x. Across the README's 1-128 MB rows, single-thread compression is 1.72-1.79x faster but decompression is 0.76-0.82x of system bzip2 at 8 MB and above; with 16 threads compression reaches 15.10x at 128 MB (162.74 vs 10.77 MB/s) against single-threaded bzip2, against 115.61 MB/s for pbzip2 (1.41x over pbzip2, derived from page data), and pbzip2 decompresses up to 9.58x faster than bzip2 while bzip2z does not parallelise default single-stream decompression.
compiler_and_flags: bzip2z: Zig 0.15.2, -Doptimize=ReleaseFast; system bzip2 1.0.8 and pbzip2 1.1.13 from a Nix dev shell (build flags not stated; bzip2 1.0.8's own Makefile defaults to -O2).
hardware: Apple M4 Max, Darwin 25.3.0 arm64, threads=auto resolved to 16, run 2026-01-15
tradeoffs: Library with C FFI plus a bzip2-compatible CLI; optional multi-stream (pbzip2-style) mode; clean-room rewrite so conformance is the main risk.
caveats: Harness asymmetry: bench/bench_bzip2.zig times bzip2z as in-memory library calls but times system bzip2 and pbzip2 as subprocesses (process spawn, reading the temp input file and writing the .bz2 or output file), which favours bzip2z; even so its decompression is parity at 1 MB and 18-24% slower at 8-128 MB. The 'mixed' input is synthetic and 75% periodic (a-z cycle, XYXY, byte ramp, then random), a pattern that is bzip2's block-sort worst case and favours linear-time SA-IS. Three iterations of one pattern. Outputs are valid bzip2 but not byte-identical (sizes differ by under 0.2%); only bzip2z's round trip is checked. The threads rows add parallel block compression that stock bzip2 lacks; pbzip2 is the fair parallel comparison (bzip2z 1.41x at 128 MB compress, much slower to decompress). Numbers were recorded 2026-01-15 on Zig 0.15.2, while the current bench source uses the Zig 0.16 std.Io API and the code has changed since (70 commits, last 2026-10-10), so the table predates the current code. bzip2 likely built at -O2 against ReleaseFast. First-party, 1 star. [retier] bench/bench_bzip2.zig's pbzip2 decompress call omits -p, so the 'threads = 1' pbzip2 rows decode on all cores (2.55-9.56x); the 'peak memory' column is a formula (input plus compressed plus decompressed plus 2 MB), identical for 1 and 16 threads, while the real SA-IS scratch is about 15-20 MB per 900 kB block; multi_stream is never set, so its parallel decode is never measured. Numbers predate the Zig 0.16 port and the October decoder changes.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/compression?l=zig topic page
why_faster: README: SA-IS linear-time suffix array construction for the Burrows-Wheeler transform in place of bzip2's original block-sorting logic, plus optional concurrent block compression.

verification.tier_reason: First-party numbers from the repo's own bench/bench_bzip2.zig with Zig 0.15.2 ReleaseFast and an Apple M4 Max stated, but the system bzip2 1.0.8 build flags are not stated and the harness is asymmetric (in-process Zig calls against a spawned bzip2 subprocess with file I/O), so not A.
verification.notes: README numbers match the record's 1 MB rows; the larger rows show decompression 18-24% slower than C bzip2 and the 16-thread compression gain measured against single-threaded bzip2. Keep at C; shortcomings: subprocess against in-process timing, synthetic periodic input that is bzip2's worst case, algorithmic (SA-IS) rather than language win, slower decompression, numbers predate the current code, unknown bzip2 build flags.

baseline: C++ solution of the same suite (clang++ -O3 -std=c++20, nlohmann/json for JSON)
workload: Given posts with tags, compute the top 5 related posts per post by shared tag count (read JSON, tag index, count, sort, write JSON); 5k, 20k and 60k posts; single core; no FFI, unsafe, or single-thread SIMD allowed.
hardware: AWS c7a.xlarge (4 vCPU, 8 GB RAM), Ubuntu 24.04; CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Community-submitted implementations in a prescribed task; each language uses its own JSON library, so results mix language, library and algorithm-variant effects.
found_via: GitHub: kostya-style cross-language suite search; jinyus/related_post_gen README results table.
name: C3 (related_post_gen suite)
claimed_speedup: Single-core total: c3 1.28 s vs C++ 1.57 s (about 1.23x faster, derived from page data); 60k posts 1.13 s vs 1.39 s; 5k posts 10.50 ms vs 12.20 ms.
compiler_and_flags: c3c compile related.c3 json.c3 -O3 (run.sh run_c3; c3c v0.7.9 per dockerfiles/c3.Dockerfile). In c3c v0.7.9 (src/build/builder.c) -O3 means LLVM O2 pipeline, safety checks OFF (no runtime bounds checks), single module, loop/SLP vectorisation on. C++: clang++ -O3 -std=c++20 -I./include main.cpp (run.sh run_cpp), clang from the unpinned Arch Linux base image (dockerfiles/base.Dockerfile), no -march or LTO.
caveats: The README table reports each program's own 'Processing time (w/o IO)' (extract_results.dart pTimeRegex), and both cpp/main.cpp and c3/related.c3 start the clock after the JSON is parsed and stop it before the JSON is written, so JSON parsing (nlohmann/json vs the hand-written json.c3) is NOT in the measured numbers; it only shows in the wall-clock 'total' lines of the raw files (60k posts: C++ about 3.35 s, c3 about 1.76 s). The algorithm is the same on both sides (tag-to-post-index map, uint8 shared-tag counters, 64-byte chunk filter, insertion top-5), and C3 even does extra hashing (has_key/set/get_ref per tag when building the index and a map get per tag per post), while C++ resolves each tag's vector once. The main asymmetry is runtime checks: the C++ solution indexes with std::vector::at() in the counting and top-5 loops (bounds checks kept, as the suite's 'no disabling runtime checks' rule requires), while c3c -O3 turns safety checks off entirely, so the C3 build does not keep the bounds checks the rules ask for. C++ and c3 rows come from separate runs (results committed 2026-02-24 and 2026-02-11) on the same VM type; CPU model (c7a.xlarge) and clang version are not stated. Timers have 1 ms resolution on both sides, so the 5k-post margin (10.50 vs 12.20 ms) is near the timer granularity. Community-written implementations; no plain C solution.

name: cligen/dents (c-blake, Nim fast directory walker behind find, ls and du)
baseline: GNU find, GNU ls -1AUR and GNU du (C); BSD find and fd are also named for find
workload: Recursive tree walk of /usr printing paths (dents find vs GNU find, BSD find and fd), listing with ls -1AUR --color=none and ls -s1AUR --color=none to /dev/null (dents ls1AU -r0, lss1AU -r0), and du totalling st_blocks (bu du vs GNU du).
claimed_speedup: Doc comments in dents.nim: find '2.75-4.5X faster than GNU find /usr; 1.7x faster than BSD find|fd'; ls1AU '-r0 is 1.7-2.25x faster than GNU ls -1AUR --color=none /usr >/dev/null'; lss1AU '1.45-2.0x faster than ls -s1AUR'; bu/doc/du.md: 'my 1.4-2x faster file tree walk' for a mostly compatible GNU du replacement.
stars_or_usage: 584 stars (cligen); used by the c-blake/bu tools
tradeoffs: Linux-oriented (raw getdents64, optional custom kernel batch-syscall module that is not mainline). Not a general find: no expression language; the du clone drops several options and uses PCRE patterns.
caveats: The numbers are one-line source comments with no machine, kernel, file system, cache state, tool versions, Nim build flags or script; ranges are given without raw timings. The ratios date from 2020 and cover only the portable path: commit 2948a0d (2020-06-19) says the optional -d:batch mode (a custom sys_batch kernel module) adds about another 1.25x and that the help ratios were deliberately not updated for it. The '1.7x faster than BSD find|fd' comment means both BSD find and the Rust fd (commit ebb78e9, 2020-10-28: 'Also include slow Rust fd in comparison'). The walk is a different implementation from GNU find's fts traversal: bu/doc/newest.md says GNU find worries about arbitrary file-system depth while the author has never seen a non-artificial depth above 30, so the walker trades generality for speed. Workloads are print-only walks of /usr, not find with predicates. [retier] The numbers are one-line source comments with no machine, kernel, file system, cache state, tool versions, Nim flags or script; ranges without raw timings, dating from 2020 and covering only the portable path (the -d:batch mode adds about 1.25x per commit 2948a0d). Early-EOF shortcut is on by default (eof0=false sets eeof=true): a short getdents read ends the directory, which the source says fails on sshfs and NFS; commit 7559cff (2020-06-28) turned the old opt-in -d:dentsLocalFS into this default, so the benchmarked find and ls runs used it, and bu du hard-codes eof0=false. EMFILE/ENFILE silently ends a subtree (depth capped by ulimit -n). Commit ebb78e9 only added '|fd' to the old '1.7x faster than FreeBSD find' comment with no separate fd number. By code reading: ls1AU and lss1AU print in post-order and lss1AU headers show the parent directory via libc dirname (outputs went to /dev/null); bu du -p uses 1 shl 40, --exclude does not prune, and StatxTs < and <= compare tv_nsec with tv_sec.
found_via: Blogs / talks: c-blake/bu doc/du.md and doc/newest.md claims traced to cligen/dents.nim
why_faster: dents.nim header: raw getdents64 saves one fstat per directory compared with opendir or fdopendir, openat/fstatat remove most full-path handling, and an optimistic open after d_type avoids lstat; the author also notes GNU find's handling of arbitrary filesystem depth.

verification.tier_reason: The ratios are first-party one-line doc comments in cligen/dents.nim (find, ls1AU, lss1AU) and bu/doc/du.md, with no timings, machine, kernel, file system, cache state, tool versions, build flags or script, so C.
verification.notes: All quoted ratios are verbatim in cligen/dents.nim lines 342, 383 and 428 and bu/doc/du.md; ISC licence, 584 stars, last commit 2026-08-26 confirmed. Record shortcomings: no methodology at all, 2020-era ratios, batch-mode speedups excluded from the stated ratios, depth-limited design.

GNU find worries about arbitrary depth, which the author says he has never seen exceed 30, so the walker trades generality for speed. The 'faster than fd' phrasing in the comment is ambiguous.

name: crabz (Rust pigz-style compressor on gzp, pure-Rust deflate backend)
baseline: pigz v2.4 (C, Ubuntu 20 apt package)
workload: Parallel gzip compression at levels 3, 6, 9 with 1 to 32 threads, and gzip decompression, of the bench-data text catted together 100 times, timed with hyperfine.
claimed_speedup: README takeaways: crabz with the rust backend is roughly 5-10% faster than pigz (zlib backend identical, zlib-ng backend 30-50% faster). Rust-backend table (mean seconds): level 3, 1 thread 10.167 vs pigz 11.338 (1.11x, derived from page data); level 3, 32 threads 0.547 vs 0.755 (1.38x); level 9, 1 thread 44.907 vs 53.109 (1.18x); level 9, 32 threads 1.747 vs 2.086 (1.19x); level 6 is a tie (27.064 vs 27.034 at 1 thread, 1.192 vs 1.196 at 32). Decompression 1.599-1.615 s vs pigz 1.696-1.767 s (1.06-1.11x).
compiler_and_flags: cargo build --release --no-default-features --features deflate_rust,libdeflate,snap_default (benchmark.sh; default release profile, no [profile.release] overrides); rustc version for the original run not stated (repo now pins 1.97.1 in rust-toolchain.toml). The README tables use 'crabz -p N -c L < data.txt' while the current benchmark.sh runs 'crabz -p N -l L -f gzip ./data.txt', so the tables came from an earlier script revision. Every build, the deflate_rust one included, installs mimalloc (C) as #[global_allocator] (src/main.rs; also present in the v0.7.0 and v0.10.0 Cargo.toml). pigz is the Ubuntu 20 apt binary with unstated flags. hyperfine --warmup 3 --runs 3. Decompression inputs are made by system gzip -3/-6/-9.
hardware: Ubuntu 20, AMD Ryzen 9 3950X 16-core, 64 GB DDR4, 1 TB NVMe
tradeoffs: The zlib-ng and libdeflate backends are C libraries; only the deflate_rust backend (miniz_oxide) is pure Rust. Level numbers of miniz_oxide and zlib do not mean the same compression effort.
caveats: Not a like-for-like deflate comparison: the deflate_rust backend is miniz_oxide, whose level table (NUM_PROBES = [0,1,6,32,16,32,128,256,512,768,1500], greedy parsing at levels <= 3) searches less than zlib at level 9 (1500 probes vs zlib's max_chain 4096); level 6 settings match and the level-6 result is a tie, so the 1.11x-1.38x level-3/9 wins likely buy speed with compression ratio, and the README reports no compressed sizes. crabz -p 2 at level 9 runs more than twice as fast as its own -p 1 (19.977 s vs 44.907 s), which suggests the two tools count threads differently. The 'all Rust' backend still links the C mimalloc allocator. Numbers are from the Ubuntu 20 era with pigz 2.4, three runs each; the README itself says 'none of this is groundbreaking'. Plain-gzip decompression is single-threaded flate2 MultiGzDecoder over miniz_oxide against pigz -d.

name: fast_rsync (Dropbox, Rust SIMD rsync algorithm)
baseline: librsync (C), legacy MD4 signatures, called through the goffrie/librsync-rs bindings (whole::signature_with_options, whole::delta, whole::patch). The README numbers (commit 'Update README.md with newer benchmarks', 2020-03-01; v0.1.1) used librsync-rs rev ab9c427, which builds mbrt/librsync aed9ab6, a pre-2.0.1 librsync 2.0.x snapshot whose NEWS still lists 2.0.1 as unreleased. That snapshot has search.c and no hashtable.c.
workload: Criterion benchmarks in benches/rsync_bench.rs on random data. Signature: 4 MiB buffer, block_size 4096, strong hash truncated to 8 bytes. Delta: a 4 MiB buffer with a 64 KiB random edit, a fully random 4 MiB buffer, and a pathological case (old data all 0x00, new data all 0x80; 16 KiB for both libraries, 4 MiB for fast_rsync only). Each delta iteration rebuilds the signature index on both sides. Apply: applying the 64 KiB-edit delta to a 4 MiB buffer.
claimed_speedup: Signature of 4 MiB: fast_rsync 1.0696 ms (3.6519 GiB/s) vs librsync 5.8521 ms (683.51 MiB/s), about 5.5x (derived from page data); the README says 6X on this AVX2 CPU and about 3-4X on SSE2-only CPUs. Delta with a 64 KB edit: 7.0596 ms vs 7.4649 ms, about 1.06x (derived from page data). Delta on random data: 38.317 ms vs 42.758 ms, about 1.12x (derived from page data). Pathological delta on 16384 bytes: 6.2550 ms vs 50.185 ms, about 8.0x (derived from page data); the 4 MiB pathological run is listed only for fast_rsync (32.986 ms) because it was too slow for librsync. Apply: 284.20 us vs 400.30 us, about 1.41x (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the README. When the numbers were taken (v0.1.1), rust-toolchain pinned nightly-2020-01-31 with packed_simd. They were run with cargo bench under the default bench profile: opt-level 3, no LTO, no target-cpu, with AVX2 or SSE2 picked at run time. The librsync C sources are compiled by librsync-sys/build.rs through the gcc crate (cc in today's pin), with NDEBUG and no -march. These crates pass the cargo opt-level to the C compiler, so -O3 under the bench profile (inferred from the build scripts; the authors do not state it). C compiler and version not stated.
hardware: Intel Core i7-6820HQ @ 2.70 GHz (AVX2), described by the authors as a noisy laptop
tradeoffs: Only the legacy MD4 signature format is supported, not BLAKE2, and MD4 is insecure, so every applied delta must be verified with another hash. SIMD on x86, x86-64 and aarch64 with runtime detection. In-memory buffers only.
caveats: Stale baseline: the README numbers date from 2020-03-01 and were measured against a pre-2.0.1 librsync snapshot (mbrt/librsync aed9ab6). librsync 2.0.1 (2017-10-17) added an open-addressing hashtable that 'significantly speeds up delta operations' and fixed degenerate behaviour with many duplicate blocks. 2.3.1 added a bloom filter (deltas 20-50% faster) and 2.3.3 made deltas another 5-15% faster (librsync NEWS.md). So the 6% and 12% delta wins may not hold against librsync 2.3.x; this was not measured. The numbers also predate fast_rsync's own 2021 hashmap changes and its 2022 switch from packed_simd to intrinsics, and were not re-run. The pathological rows show different behaviour, not only speed. 4096 bytes of 0x00 and of 0x80 give equal 16-bit rollsum halves (derived), so every offset collides. fast_rsync blacklists a weak checksum after 1024 collisions (MAX_CRC_COLLISIONS in src/diff.rs) and may emit literal data where librsync keeps searching. Only the signature step is a large win; the two realistic delta rows are 6% and 12% and apply is 1.4x. The librsync side also runs through Rust Read/Write stream bindings, which adds a small copy overhead. The win is hand-written SIMD in a library, not a Rust-language effect. Results come from one noisy laptop. No commits since 2024-04-18. [retier] Signature::deserialize and diff() never check block_size > 0, so an untrusted signature with block_size 0 makes diff() panic or loop forever (the fuzzer covers only apply_limited). The pathological 8x is 1,024 versus 12,289 MD4 calls (blacklist), not faster code; single-block MD4 ran about 0.67 GB/s against about 1.0 GB/s for librsync, so SIMD helps signatures only.
found_via: Blogs / talks: Rust ports of C libraries that beat the original; README benchmark section of dropbox/fast_rsync
why_faster: README: SIMD operations (AVX2 gives the 6X on signatures) for the rolling checksum and MD4; delta rows are bound by single-block MD4 and by hash-map lookups where Rust's built-in HashMap gives 'a slight advantage'; pathological inputs are detected instead of degrading.

name: fd
baseline: GNU find (findutils, C)
workload: Search the author's home folder (about 750,000 subdirectories and about 4 million files) for names ending in [0-9].jpg with a warm disk cache, timed with hyperfine. The commands were find ~ -iregex '.*[0-9]\.jpg$', find ~ -iname '*[0-9].jpg' and fd -u '[0-9]\.jpg$' ~ (fd-benchmarks warm-cache-simple-pattern.sh uses fd -HI, 5 warm-up runs, and diffs the outputs). Both tools returned the same 546 files.
claimed_speedup: fd -u '[0-9]\.jpg$' 854.8 ms vs find -iregex 19.922 s (README: approximately 23 times faster) and vs find -iname 11.226 s (about 13 times faster).
tradeoffs: Respects .gitignore and skips hidden files by default (the benchmark needs -u to match find's work); regex search by default instead of glob; parallel traversal uses all cores.
caveats: First-party benchmark on one unnamed machine against the author's own home directory. The README says 'one particular benchmark on one particular machine'. fd, find and compiler versions are not stated, and nor is GNU find's build (distribution packages are usually -O2). fd walks directories in parallel with one thread per core by default, while GNU find is single-threaded. The task is dominated by pattern matching: find -iregex uses gnulib regex on the full path, and -iname uses case-folding fnmatch. Without a pattern the gap disappears. In sharkdp/fd issue #304 (2018, fd 7.0-7.1, Linux source tree, warm cache, no hardware stated), multi-threaded fd -HI -t f only reached parity with 'find . -type f' (69.1 ms vs 68.9 ms after commit 50a2bab), and fd -j1 was 1.49x slower than find. In the reporter's home-directory runs find was 2.15x (warm) and 1.85x (cold) faster than fd 7.0.0. So the README's 13-23x is a parallelism plus regex-engine win on a filtering query, not a codegen win, and single-threaded fd is slower than find on plain traversal. The README credits the regex and ignore crates (shared with ripgrep).
found_via: Checked READMEs of widely used Rust command-line replacements for C tools
GitHub: README of sharkdp/fd (Rust rewrites of C command-line tools); not in KNOWN_LIST.
why_faster: Parallelized directory traversal (README feature list: 'Very fast due to parallelized directory traversal').

verification.tier_reason: The README Benchmark section gives first-party hyperfine results against GNU find (19.922 s, 11.226 s and 854.8 ms; '23 times' and '13 times'). The scripts are public (sharkdp/fd-benchmarks warm-cache-simple-pattern.sh, config.sh, prelude.sh). There is no CPU, no fd or find version, no build flags, and the dataset is the author's own home folder, so it is not reproducible: C. WebSearch found no independent suite.
verification.notes: Numbers and the 546-file equality check match the README verbatim. Metadata is confirmed: MIT OR Apache-2.0, 44.8k stars, last commit 2026-10-06, not archived. Shortcomings to record: first-party, no hardware or versions, private dataset, a parallel versus single-threaded comparison, and issue #304 shows find matching or beating fd on unfiltered listing and fd -j1 1.49x slower than find.

corrected_fields.workload: Search a home directory (about 750,000 subdirectories and 4 million files, warm disk cache) for the 546 files matching [0-9].jpg; hyperfine means; fd runs with -u so it does the same work as find.
corrected_fields.caveats: README itself says this is one particular benchmark on one particular machine. CPU model, find version, filesystem and build flags are not stated, so tier A is not met. The speedup mixes multithreading (fd parallelizes traversal, find is single-threaded) with regex-vs-glob matching, so it is not a per-core efficiency win. Benchmark scripts are in sharkdp/fd-benchmarks (opened: README only, scripts not read or run). GNU find was not confirmed to be built at -O3.

name: hexdump-rs (Rust hexdump -C replacement)
baseline: system hexdump -C (C; implementation and version not stated, likely util-linux or BSD hexdump)
workload: Canonical hex+ASCII dump (hexdump -C) of four files with hyperfine -m 100 --warmup 5: 10 MB from /dev/random, a 7.8 MB semi-random file (test.mca), an 8.5 MB file whose lines all differ (no squeezing) and a 1.1 GB file of zeros.
claimed_speedup: Hyperfine screenshots in the README (img/*.png): dev-random 708.6 ms vs 16.9 ms (42.00x faster); test.mca 617.1 ms vs 16.0 ms (38.62x); no-squeeze.bin 646.3 ms vs 17.1 ms (37.86x); zeros.bin 658.2 ms vs 338.5 ms (1.94x). README text says 'up to a 14x speedup' while the repository description says 'up to 40x faster'.
compiler_and_flags: cargo release build (./target/release/hexdump-rs); Cargo.toml release profile only adds debug = true for flamegraphs; no C build flags (system hexdump binary as installed).
tradeoffs: Implements only hexdump -C, not hexdump's format-string language, and is 'meant as a drop-in replacement for hexdump -C' only.
caveats: Different algorithm: system hexdump drives a generic format-string interpreter while src/main.rs hard-codes the one canonical layout with a hex lookup table and a BufWriter, so the 40x gap is a specialisation effect, not a language effect (inference; the README gives no mechanism). CPU, OS, hexdump implementation and version are not stated; hyperfine discards both tools' output; the numbers exist only as screenshots (which match the claimed figures), and the README text (14x, apparently from before the 2023-08-15 commit 'now ~40x speed difference') disagrees with the screenshots (up to 42x). The zeros.bin row (1.94x) is where both tools squeeze repeated lines. Output is not identical to hexdump -C: render_ascii prints '!' (0x21) and '~' (0x7e) as '.', a run of exactly one repeated line is dropped without the '*' marker, and -n/--length is ignored because end = (i + length).max(usize::MAX); the tests check helpers and two tiny inputs, never output against the real hexdump. These differences do not create a fast path (every line is still formatted), so the numbers stand. Tiny hobby repo (0 stars, 1 fork, 3 commits), last commit 2023-08-15. [retier] Output regressions introduced by the same commit (085158f) as the about 40x screenshots: '!' and '~' print as '.'; a final 9-15-byte line shows stale bytes in the hex column; a single repeated line is dropped without '*'; -n is ignored; offsets wrap at 4 GiB; -s allocates a skip-sized Vec; exit status always 0. hyperfine discards output and nothing checks it. The gap comes from util-linux's printf-per-conversion format interpreter against a hard-coded layout.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Rust rewrite of C tool faster than original C benchmark hyperfine github faster than GNU' surfaced the hexdump-rs README; opened the README, the four screenshots and the commits page.

verification.tier_reason: First-party hyperfine screenshots (img/dev-random.png, test.mca.png, no-squeeze.bin.png, zeros.bin.png) show exactly the claimed means and ratios against system hexdump -C, with the hyperfine command in the README, but no CPU, OS, hexdump implementation/version or C build flags; the test files are generated locally and not published.
verification.notes: Screenshots confirm 42.00x, 38.62x, 37.86x and 1.94x; tier C stands. Shortcomings to record: specialised tool vs generic format interpreter (not a language effect), no hardware/hexdump version, README text says 14x vs 40x in description, output deviates from hexdump -C ('!' and '~' shown as '.', single repeated line dropped without '*', -n ignored), abandoned 0-star repo.

corrected_fields.caveats: Different algorithm: the system hexdump drives a generic format-string interpreter while this tool hard-codes the one canonical layout, so the 40x gap is a specialisation effect, not a language effect (my inference; the README gives no mechanism). CPU, OS, hexdump version and output destination are not stated, the numbers exist only as images, and the README text (14x) disagrees with the screenshots (up to 42x). The zeros.bin row (1.94x) is where both tools squeeze repeated lines. Tiny hobby repo with no stars.

name: Koka (Perceus reference counting): cfold benchmark vs C++ gcc 9.3.0
baseline: C++ port in test/bench/cpp/cfold.cpp (gcc 9.3.0, CMake Release -O3, standard libc allocator): allocates every node with new and never frees anything, and its const_folding only folds the root node (no recursion into children), unlike the recursive Koka cfold.
workload: cfold: constant folding over a large symbolic expression, an allocation-heavy benchmark with little computation.
claimed_speedup: Perceus TR Figure 9 (identical chart in the README, doc/bench-amd3600-nov-2020.png), normalized to Koka = 1.00: cfold execution time C++ 3.33 (Koka about 3.3x faster), peak working set C++ 2.94x. Koka 'no-opt' (reuse analysis and drop/reuse specialization off) is 1.54, so even without reuse Koka is about 2.2x faster than C++ (derived from page data). Other rows of the same figure: deriv C++ 1.33, rbtree C++ 0.92 and nqueens C++ 0.79 (C++ faster), rbtree-ck no C++ version.
compiler_and_flags: Koka 2.0.3 -O2 (test/bench/koka/CMakeLists.txt), which the v2.0.3 compiler (src/Compiler/Options.hs) turns into gcc 9.3.0 '-O2 -flto -DNDEBUG' on the generated C, linked with Koka's bundled mimalloc (KK_MIMALLOC, MI_MAX_ALIGN_SIZE=8; the paper says 'a customized version of the mimalloc allocator'); C++: gcc 9.3.0, C++17, built through test/bench/CMakeLists.txt with CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE Release and no extra flags in cpp/CMakeLists.txt, so CMake's default '-O3 -DNDEBUG', standard libc allocator. Flags are derived from the public build files, not printed with the results. Current Koka (v3.2.x) uses gcc -O2 -DNDEBUG -march=haswell instead.
hardware: 6-core AMD Ryzen 5 3600XT at 3.8 GHz, 64 GiB 3600 MHz memory, Ubuntu 20.04, November 2020; README says averaged over 10 runs, the Perceus tech report says median over 10 runs
tradeoffs: Reference counting with in-place reuse needs no tracing GC but adds refcount work and cannot reclaim cycles; Koka compiles through C so any C toolchain can build it; much smaller ecosystem than C++.
caveats: The paper and README say the results are 'not a direct comparison of absolute performance between systems'. Not like-for-like: the C++ version never reclaims memory (glibc malloc, peak working set 2.94x Koka) while Koka frees and reuses nodes in place with mimalloc, and the C++ const_folding is shallow (does strictly less work than Koka's recursive cfold; the eval checksum is unchanged either way). An arena or pooled C++ version, or C++ linked against mimalloc, was not tried. Numbers are from Koka 2.0.3 and gcc 9.3.0 in November 2020; Koka is now v3.2.9 with different C flags. Koka ints are arbitrary-precision with a small-int fast path, C++ uses long. Mixed results across the suite: C++ wins rbtree (0.92) and nqueens (0.79).
found_via: GitHub: README of koka-lang/koka (benchmark section and chart doc/bench-amd3600-nov-2020.png), listed as a lead without numbers by the sys papers search; I read the values printed on the chart bars.
why_faster: Source (README): precise Perceus reference counting with reuse analysis, compiled to C 'without needing a garbage collector or runtime system'; the README frames the benchmarks as showing reference counting is viable and competitive, not as a direct absolute-speed comparison across languages.

verification.tier_reason: Upgraded C to B: the same Figure 9 (cfold time C++ 3.33, peak working set C++ 2.94, relative to Koka 1.00) is in the Perceus paper (MSR-TR-2020-42 v4, the extended version of the peer-reviewed PLDI 2021 paper, opened), with gcc 9.3.0 and AMD 3600XT stated. Not A: compile flags are not stated with the results (only derivable from CMake's Release default and the v2.0.3 Koka compiler source), and the run is first-party on code since revised.
verification.notes: Numbers verified on the README chart and the Perceus TR figure; same chart, so cfold 3.33x time and 2.94x RSS are correct. Shortcomings to record: C++ baseline leaks every node and its const_folding is non-recursive (different algorithm, same_algorithm false), Koka links mimalloc versus glibc malloc on the C++ side (part of the win belongs to mimalloc, check against the listed mimalloc entry), authors disclaim it as an absolute speed comparison, 2020 Koka 2.0.3 numbers, C++ wins rbtree and nqueens. License Apache-2.0 (LICENSE), 4.1k stars, last commit 2026-10-01 on dev, active.
