name: libbzip2-rs (libbz2-rs-sys, Rust port of libbzip2)
baseline: libbzip2 (C, original bzip2 library)
workload: CPU cycles for compression at levels 1-9 on silesia-small.tar and a small sample file, and decompression of bzip2 test files, comparing the C and Rust builds in one harness (bzip2_benchmarks.json).
claimed_speedup: Latest run in trifectatechfoundation/libbzip2-rs-bench (commit ac73367, 2026-10-06), mean of 20 repetitions per command. Linux x86-64, AMD Ryzen 9 9900X, CPU cycles of Rust vs C: compression of silesia-small.tar at levels 1-9 -10.1% to -12.3% (level 1 -12.28%, level 9 -10.12%), sample3.ref level 1 -5.49%, decompression of six bzip2 test files -3.4% to -7.4%. macOS arm64, Apple M2, user time: compression -3.3% to -4.2%, sample3.ref -5.6%, but decompression is slower in Rust on five of six files (+0.1% to +9.5%), a pattern stable across the 2025-08 to 2026-10 runs (derived from page data). The blog figures in the original record (-14.87% sample3.ref level 1, -14.30% and -9.66% silesia-small levels 1 and 9, 'significant speedups across the board' for decompression) come only from a blocked blog post and do not match any run in the public data (best runs: -12.95% small, -12.51% level 1).
compiler_and_flags: Workflow .github/workflows/bench.yml: Rust side cargo build --release -p test-libbz2-rs-sys --examples with RUSTFLAGS=-Cllvm-args=-enable-dfa-jump-thread (release profile defaults, opt-level 3, no LTO), rustc stable from rustup (version printed only in CI logs). C side: libbzip2 1.0.8 sources from bzip2-sys 0.1.13+1.0.8 (feature static) compiled by its build.rs through the cc crate with CC=clang at the release opt-level (-O3), -D_FILE_OFFSET_BITS=64 -DBZ_NO_STDIO; the extra LLVM DFA jump-threading pass is given to rustc only. Both libraries are linked into the same harness binaries and measured by trifectatechfoundation/benchmarker-action (perf counters, 20 repetitions).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 9900X 12-core (self-hosted runner amd-bench, Linux x86-64; cycles, instructions, task-clock) and Apple M2 (runner mini-bench, macOS arm64; user time).
stars_or_usage: 79 stars; libbz2-rs-sys has 42.7M crates.io downloads and is the default backend of the bzip2 crate since 0.6
tradeoffs: Drop-in libbzip2 C API (cdylib) and Rust crate; memory-safe translation; project page says no further feature development is planned.
caveats: Gains are modest and platform-dependent: about 10-12% fewer cycles for compression and 3-7% for decompression on the Ryzen 9 9900X, but only 3-4% faster compression and up to 9.5% slower decompression on Apple M2. Flag asymmetry: the Rust build gets the LLVM -enable-dfa-jump-thread pass (useful for bzip2's switch-based decoder state machine) while the clang-built C does not, so part of the decompression gain may be the extra pass rather than the port. Whole-process measurement includes reading the input file, equally for both sides. Compiler versions are not in the public data. The port began as a c2rust translation of libbzip2, so the algorithm is the same and the gain comes from implementation changes. The blog numbers quoted earlier were snippet only and do not match the public data. License is the bzip2 and libbzip2 License v1.0.6 (SPDX bzip2-1.0.6), a permissive BSD-style licence that the SPDX list does not mark OSI-approved; usability set to reference for consistency with the wave 9 gitlab.com/bzip2/bzip2 record; no patent grant.

name: Lightpanda
baseline: Headless Google Chrome 143 (Chromium, C++) driven over CDP
workload: Crawler: a Go chromedp program crawls the Amiibo demo site (933 URLs) over the live internet. Chrome runs 1-100 tabs in one browser, while Lightpanda runs 1-100 separate processes (--fork --lpd-path), because Lightpanda cannot open multiple tabs. Each configuration ran once with /usr/bin/time -v, and smem PSS and ps CPU were sampled every 100 ms (watch -n0.1) for peak memory. Campfire: a homemade fake e-commerce page that loads two JSON XHRs, served locally, loaded 100 times via Puppeteer over CDP.
claimed_speedup: README: '16x lighter and 9x faster than Chromium'. Its table is labelled '(100 pages)', but its numbers (123MB vs 2GB, 5s vs 46s) match the BENCHMARKS.md 25-way rows: Lightpanda 25 processes 4.81 s, 123.0M versus Chrome 25 tabs 46.70 s, 2.0G (about 9.7x faster, 16x less memory, derived from page data). Other rows from the same table: 1 process versus 1 tab, 51.68 s, 27.2M versus 1:22.83, 1.3G (1.6x faster, derived from page data). 100 processes versus 100 tabs, 5.23 s, 410.2M versus 1:09.37, 4.2G (about 13x, derived from page data). Best versus best is 4.81 s versus 45.62 s for Chrome at 10 tabs (about 9.5x, derived from page data). Campfire page, 100 local loads via Puppeteer: average 16 ms versus 185 ms (total 1,698 ms versus 18,551 ms, about 11x), peak memory 21.2M versus 402.1M, peak CPU 4.6% versus 158.6%.
compiler_and_flags: Lightpanda commit 7b1f157cf8ccbdded7db6ab47e94577495ee87e4. The build mode is not stated; the README says Zig 0.15.2 and the Campfire section points to the nightly release binary. baseline: GNU find (findutils, C)
workload: Walking a shallow clone of the mainline Linux kernel tree (100,871 entries in 6,201 directories, ~2.1 GB) with a warm page cache; both tools run as subprocesses with output discarded; 100 Criterion samples.

Process startup is included for both; both tools' stdout is captured into a pipe by Command::output() and dropped. The benchmark does not check that the two outputs match; minifind defaults to one filesystem and types d/f/l, plain 'find' lists every type and crosses mounts (equivalent on a kernel clone). GNU find version and build flags (distribution packages are usually -O2) and rustc version are unstated. Numbers come from the 2026-06-19 'full-clock rerun' commit, made the same day the 'fd-anchored parallel walker' landed; warm page cache only, the README says the gap narrows on a cold cache. name: Nim 2.2.10 (ref objects): benchLANG binary trees vs C and C++ at -O3
baseline: C (GCC 16.2.0: gcc -O3 -march=native -flto -funroll-loops -ffp-contract=off) and C++ (g++ -std=c++20, same flags); both malloc/new every node and free (delete) it inside the timed region
workload: CLBG-style binary trees, depths 4 to 18: allocate, check and drop complete binary trees of individually allocated nodes; benchLANG's fifth workload (the others are primes, Fibonacci(45), strings and Mandelbrot).
claimed_speedup: README results table (September 2026, one run per language): Nim 0.809 s vs C 1.010 s and C++ 1.147 s on binary trees, about 1.25x faster than C and 1.42x faster than C++ (derived from page data). Other columns, Nim vs C: primes 2.725 vs 2.725 s, Fibonacci 1.716 vs 1.694 s, strings 2.804 vs 2.132 s, Mandelbrot 2.244 vs 2.201 s; total 10.298 s vs 9.762 s, so C is faster overall.
compiler_and_flags: Nim 2.2.10: nim c --hints:off --nimcache:nimcache -d:danger -d:lto --panics:on --passC:-march=native --passC:-ffp-contract=off --passL:-s; Nim's config/nim.cfg (v2.2.10) adds gcc.options.speed '-O3 -fno-ident -fno-math-errno' and -flto under -d:lto, so the generated C is built at -O3 -march=native -flto (backend gcc from the Nix dev shell, which uses gcc16Stdenv; the exact backend gcc version is not printed). Default Nim 2 memory management (ORC) and Nim's own allocator (no -d:useMalloc). C: gcc -O3 -march=native -flto -funroll-loops -ffp-contract=off -s; C++: g++ -std=c++20 with the same flags (GCC 16.2.0, nixpkgs-unstable).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X locked at 3.5 GHz, 48 GB DDR4-3600 CL16, Arch Linux; one run per language, 3 September 2026
tradeoffs: Peak RSS for the whole process is 51.5 MiB for Nim vs 33.3 MiB for C; Nim loses to C on the strings workload (2.804 s vs 2.132 s).
caveats: One run per language on one machine (run_benchmarks.sh defaults to RUNS=1), so a 0.2 s gap is within plausible run-to-run noise; inputs are compile-time constants. Same algorithm and same work on both sides (C frees each tree inside the timed region, Nim's ORC destructors free at scope exit). The win is allocator behaviour: C and C++ pay glibc malloc/free (new/delete) per 24-byte node, while Nim uses its own runtime allocator; a pooled or arena C version, or C linked with a faster malloc, would likely erase the gap (my inference, not measured). Many other languages also beat C here (Java 0.347 s, Bun 0.816 s, OCaml and Dart 0.865 s, C# 0.931 s, Fortran 0.986 s). C is faster over the whole suite (9.762 s vs Nim 10.298 s); Nim loses strings (2.804 vs 2.132 s). 8-star suite.

compiler_and_flags: At the time of the README table (per-language scripts at commit 80bb306, before the June 2026 move to projects.xml): Nim 'nim c -d:danger -d:lto -d:intpow -d:quake --passC:"-march=native"'; C 'g++ RayTracer.c -x c -O3' (no -march=native, no LTO); C++ 'g++ RayTracer.cpp -O2 -std=c++17 -s'. Compiler versions are not stated, and the table is old (an FX-8120 CPU, Node 15 and PHP 8.0 rows, MSVC rows), so it is not tied to a dated run. Only Nim beats the GCC C and C++ builds; D (LDC) 210 ms, Crystal 190 ms and Rust 220 ms lose to them and beat only the MSVC builds (250 ms). There is no repeat count or variance.

name: procs (c-blake, Nim ps, pgrep and pkill replacement: pd, pf, pk)
baseline: procps ps ('/bin/ps ax'), pgrep and pkill (C)
workload: Listing all processes with a minimal format (pid and command) to /dev/null, and finding a process by name over roughly 200 to 320 processes (pf -e1 vs pgrep -x), measured with the author's tim/tails tools under chrt 99 taskset.
claimed_speedup: README footnote: pd -f%p %c 2.8576 ms +- 0.0070 vs /bin/ps ax 5.0281 ms +- 0.0063 (README says roughly 2X and 'about 57% the run-time'; 1.76x derived from page data); with process typology and highlights on, pd takes 3.9739 ms +- 0.0044, 1.27X faster than stock ps; pgrep and pkill are (5.025 +- 0.015)X and (5.745 +- 0.016)X slower than pf and pk for an 'average process' on a 4-core and a 20-core CPU. bench.sh comments (overhead subtracted): i7-6700K pf -e1 init 1014.1 us, pf -e1 with no match 2060.1 us, pgrep -x init 7724 us; i7-1370P 582.7 us, 1345.7 us and 5539.6 us; bench.sh calls this 'up to' 7.617x and 9.507x. The 'up to' figures compare pf stopping at the first /proc entry (init) with pgrep's full scan; the equal-work full-scan rows (pf with no match vs pgrep) give 3.75x and 4.12x (derived from page data), and the README 5.025X/5.745X figures are pgrep's time divided by the mean of pf's first-hit and no-match times (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the benchmark; README build line is 'nim c -d:release --path:../cligen procs' (C backend compiler version not stated); procps version not stated
hardware: i7-6700K (no HT, 4.7 GHz) and i7-1370P in bench.sh; the machine for the README ps timings is not named
tradeoffs: Linux /proc only. Fewer canned formats than ps (it is a construction toolkit with config files); pd/pf/pk are symlinks to one binary. Author calls it 'a work in progress'.
caveats: The gains come from doing less work, so this is a different, narrower program and not the same algorithm. pd -f%p %c reads only /proc/PID/stat and prints the pid and the 15-character comm. /bin/ps ax prints PID, TTY, STAT, TIME and the full argv (from /proc/PID/cmdline), and procps also parses /proc/PID/status, so the README ps comparison does not produce the same output. In bench.sh, -e1 means --exist --first (exit at the first match with no output). Because init is the first /proc entry, the 'up to 7.617x/9.507x' rows read one process while pgrep scans all of them; the equal-work no-match rows give 3.75x and 4.12x. procps pgrep 3.3.17 with a pattern sets PROC_FILLCOM and PROC_FILLSTATUS, so it reads cmdline and status for every process, while pf reads stat. The author says there are configurations where ps can be faster. The README timing machine and flags are unstated, the Nim/C compiler versions and the procps version are unstated, and bench.sh needs the author's tim and tails tools from c-blake/bu. These are millisecond-scale wins on a single-user tool. The nimble file says 'MIT/ISC' but LICENSE is ISC text. [retier] The gains come from doing less work: pd -f%p %c reads only /proc/PID/stat and prints the pid and the 15-character comm, while /bin/ps ax prints PID, TTY, STAT, TIME and the full argv and procps also parses /proc/PID/status, so the outputs differ. bench.sh never times pkill: the README's '(5.745 +- 0.016)X slower than pk' is the i7-1370P pgrep row over the mean of pf's first-hit and no-match times, and the equal-work ratios are 3.75x (i7-6700K) and 4.12x (i7-1370P). The pgrep side is hard-coded 'pgrep -x init' while pf uses the first /proc entry's comm, so the script breaks on systemd hosts; pf matches with an unanchored PCRE and has no -x mode. In bench.sh -e1 means --exist --first (exit at the first match with no output).
found_via: Blogs / talks: Nim/D/Zig tools with README timings against C utilities (c-blake GitHub projects), after the Nim topic pages gave nothing
why_faster: README: 'tries hard not to make unnecessary system calls', for example only opening /proc/PID/stat for a pid-and-command format while procps ps also opens and parses /proc/PID/status (the author says this makes pd roughly 2X faster).

verification.tier_reason: First-party numbers only: bench.sh (public, names i7-6700K and i7-1370P) times pf against procps pgrep, and the README footnote times pd against /bin/ps ax, but neither states the Nim/C compiler versions, the flags actually used for the benchmarked binaries, or the procps version and build, and the README ps timings name no machine; that falls short of A, and there is no independent measurement.
verification.notes: Real first-party measurements, and the numbers match the README and bench.sh exactly. The win is a narrower program doing less /proc I/O, not the Nim language (language_level_claim false and same_algorithm false are correct; same_opt_level stays unknown because neither side's build flags are stated). The headline 'up to 7.6x/9.5x' pf-vs-pgrep figures compare early exit at the first process with a full scan (equal-work ratio is 3.75x/4.12x, derived), and the README ps comparison prints different columns. name: rasusa (Rust read and alignment subsampler)
baseline: seqtk sample (C) for random read subsampling; filtlong (C++) for target-bases selection
workload: Subsampling a 2.9 GB single FASTQ (379,547 long reads) to 50x coverage of a 4.4 Mbp genome against filtlong, and paired-end 179 MB files (283,590 reads each) down to 140,000 reads against seqtk sample, via hyperfine.
claimed_speedup: rasusa reads ran 34.91 +/- 0.93 times faster than filtlong (0.740 s vs 25.840 s); paired end: 1.19 times faster than seqtk sample one pass (0.950 s vs 1.132 s) and 1.01 times faster than seqtk two pass (0.963 s).
compiler_and_flags: rasusa: cargo build --release with stable Rust (dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable, version unpinned); the release profile sets lto = true, strip = true. filtlong and seqtk come from bioconda through micromamba with unpinned versions; the current bioconda recipes (filtlong 0.3.1, seqtk 1.5) append -O3 in build.sh. hyperfine --warmup 3 --runs 10 (single) and --warmup 10 --runs 100 (paired).
hardware: GitHub Actions runner pinned to ubuntu-24.04 in .github/workflows/benchmark.yaml (the README note says ubuntu-latest); CPU model not stated.
tradeoffs: Subsamples to a coverage or base target without needing a fixed read count; reads and aln modes; supports paired reads.
caveats: First-party, on a shared GitHub Actions runner (CPU model not stated); the tool versions and Rust toolchain are not pinned. The 34.9x over filtlong is not like-for-like: filtlong scores every read by length and windowed quality and keeps the best subset, while rasusa draws a random subset. The rasusa JOSS paper itself says filtlong is a filtering tool, not a subsampler. For the same job, seqtk sample -2 (two-pass random sampling, the mode the README calls analogous), the result is parity: 0.950 s vs 0.963 s, 1.01x. Against seqtk's one-pass reservoir mode it is 1.19 +/- 0.14x. The README's internal v4.1.0 to v5.0.0 table (about 7-8% wall time, 25-74% peak RSS) compares rasusa with itself, not with a C/C++ tool. [retier] Two seqtk processes per hyperfine command against one rasusa process gives rasusa a small fixed edge. Coverage mode uses a u32 index vector (undefined over 2^32 reads); the default modes open the input path twice, so no pipe input; the FASTX path is single-threaded.

The raw files results/raw_results_rust.md and raw_results_cpp.md match the table. At 60k posts their whole-process wall times, including JSON I/O, are 1.27-1.32 s for Rust and 3.35-3.40 s for C++.

Rust: cargo build --release with the rust/Cargo.toml release profile lto = "fat", codegen-units = 1, panic = "abort" (default opt-level 3), plus hashbrown 0.14.3, aligned-vec 0.5 and serde_json. caveats: The suite gives no mechanism. The timed region ('Processing time (w/o IO)') excludes JSON parsing and writing on both sides, so nlohmann/json versus serde_json does not affect the table. It does dominate whole-process time: C++ 3.35 s versus Rust 1.27 s at 60k posts, with 460 MB versus 29 MB RSS. Inside the timed region both programs run the same algorithm: per-tag lists of post indices, uint8 shared-tag counters, a scan in 64-entry chunks with a running minimum, and 5-slot top-k insertion. The tuning differs. Rust zeroes each 64-byte chunk right after scanning it, on a 64-byte-aligned counter buffer padded to a multiple of 64. C++ memsets the whole counter array before each post and uses bounds-checked std::vector::at() for every counter access in the hot loops. The tag index is hashbrown in Rust and std::unordered_map<std::string, unique_ptr<vector<int>>> in C++; Rust re-hashes each tag string per post, while C++ caches per-post pointers. The suite has no C solution. The solutions are community-written and were run on a cloud VM (10 runs at 5k posts, 3 at 20k and 60k) with compiler versions and CPU model unstated. Zig (1.93 s) and Odin (2.00 s) are slower than C++. The Rust HO row (51.55 ms) uses specialised data structures and is excluded. name: sefer-alloc (SeferAlloc, Rust allocator with large-segment cache)
baseline: mimalloc (C, via the Rust mimalloc 0.1 crate as GlobalAlloc) and the Windows System allocator
workload: criterion micro-benchmarks calling SeferAlloc directly through GlobalAlloc: alloc(N)+free round trips of 4, 16 and 64 MiB served by a large-segment cache, realloc growth chains, small-size churn and cold-path tables.
claimed_speedup: README large alloc/free table (lower is better, measured 2026-07-06): 4 MiB ~58.6 ns vs mimalloc ~716 ns (~12.2x) vs System ~17.7 us (~302x); 16 MiB ~61.9 ns vs ~1.13 us (~13.5x); 64 MiB ~60.8 ns vs ~2.58 us (~33x). README 'Why bother' summarises this as ~12-35x faster than mimalloc. realloc_grow_geometric (64 B to 4 MiB) ~238 us vs mimalloc ~431 us (~1.8x; re-measured 2026-08-04 after the earlier '9.67 us / 39.6x' figure was withdrawn as physically impossible); realloc_grow_neighbour_pressure ~400 ns vs ~1.34 ms (~3,350x). The 'Up to ~18x faster than mimalloc on cached large alloc/free' wording is from the GitHub About text, not the README. README also states 0.3.0 loses to mimalloc on the cold path at small sizes (16-64 B, ~1.9-2.7x slower; 2026-07-23 run 16 B 2.37x, 256 B 2.71x slower) and on single-thread larson/mstress at T=1 (1.28-1.36x behind).
compiler_and_flags: cargo bench --features production; Cargo.toml [profile.bench] lto = "thin", codegen-units = 1 (Cargo default opt-level 3 for bench); mimalloc's C core is built by the mimalloc 0.1 crate's build script (Cargo.toml comment: 'at full optimization'); criterion sample_size(10), 1-2 s warm-up, 2-3 s measurement; rustc version not stated (MSRV 1.93).

why_faster: README: the OPT-E large-segment cache keeps pages committed so a same-size re-allocation returns without an OS round trip, while mimalloc and System go back to the OS.

The '~18x' figure appears only in the GitHub About text (README tables give 12.2x-33x). The measured 0.3.0 tree is not on crates.io (latest 0.2.1), although the README install line asks for version 0.3. Sole author, 1 star, heavily agent-driven repo (2,976 commits, CLAUDE.md). The bench's alloc plus free never touches memory; mimalloc's 716 ns is already about 25x below System, so the gap is about 0.65-2.5 us of bookkeeping, around 1% or less of a 2 MiB copy. name: SPARKNaCl
baseline: TweetNaCl (C), compiled into the same binary with the same GNAT compiler at the same -O level
workload: CPU cycles for one Ed25519 Sign operation on a 256-byte message on a SiFive HiFive1 Revision B (32-bit RISC-V); also Curve25519 and SHA512 analysed.
claimed_speedup: Snippet only (two WebSearch result summaries; no page opened): in the February 2021 'Performance analysis and tuning of SPARKNaCl' post, one Ed25519 Sign of a 256-byte message on a HiFive1 Rev B took SPARK 198.03 vs C TweetNaCl 241.83 million cycles at -O0, 98.03 vs 97.65 at -O1 and 93.86 vs 84.99 at -O2 (SPARK slower at -O1 and -O2). After tuning, 'Doubling the Performance of SPARKNaCl (again...)' reports SPARK at 181.74 (-O0), 69.96 (-O1) and 57.82 then 34.94 (-O2) million cycles. A slide deck summary gives final SPARK 24.37 million cycles at -O2 against 84.99 for the original TweetNaCl C and 51.00 for a revised C version, i.e. about 3.5x vs original and about 2.1x vs the revised C (derived from snippet data). The FOSDEM 2022 abstract claims SPARKNaCl outperforms TweetNaCl on Sign by a factor of 3 at all optimization levels. README itself gives no numbers.
compiler_and_flags: GNAT Community 2020/2021 riscv64-elf cross compiler. Since commit e06da81 (2021-02-17) perf/tsign.mk builds the SPARK library with -march=rv32imc plus -falign-functions/-falign-jumps/-falign-loops=4 (and -gnatn at O1 and above) while the TweetNaCl C side gets -march=rv32im with no alignment flags; only the -O level is shared.
hardware: SiFive HiFive1 Revision B board (FE310 32-bit RISC-V SoC, code built for rv32im), cycles read from the mcycle CSR
stars_or_usage: 139 stars, 14 forks; published in the Alire package index
tradeoffs: Full SPARK proof of absence of run-time exceptions (needs CVC4 and Z3), TweetNaCl-compatible API, readable constant-time code; results are for a small RISC-V core and do not transfer to x86.
caveats: Numbers are snippet-only: blog.adacore.com, www.adacore.com and www.slideshare.net returned ENOTFOUND here and archive.fosdem.org was EGRESS_BLOCKED for the search agent, so no cycle table was seen; a verifier with access should read 'Performance analysis and tuning of SPARKNaCl', 'Doubling the Performance of SPARKNaCl (again...)', 'SPARKNaCl with GNAT and SPARK Community 2021' and the FOSDEM 2022 talk. The win is not a language-level codegen effect: both sides run with run-time checks off (-gnatp), and the speedup comes from reworked field arithmetic that the SPARK proofs made safe (Normal_GF limbs bounded to 0..65535, '*' rewritten as a product-scanning multiply on 32-bit limb products U32NL with the carry folded in, fewer carry passes, loop fusion in '+' and '-'), while the C baseline in perf/tweetnacl.c still multiplies i64 limbs (costly on rv32im) followed by two car25519 passes, although it has been given the WireGuard carry and an unrolled inner loop 'as per SPARKNaCl'. The same restructuring could be written in C, so this is a library-versus-library result. Results swing strongly with -O level (SPARK was behind at -O1/-O2 before tuning; README notes the new '*' is slower at -O0). Not an x86 or -O3 measurement; only one embedded 32-bit RISC-V board. README says the latest results are still to be documented. [retier] The two sides use different field arithmetic (32-bit limb products versus i64 limbs); one cold run per side, with SPARK running after Keypair has warmed its code. GNAT 14 -O2 miscompiles SHA-256 (issue #37) and the -fno-tree-vrp workaround applies only when TARGET_ARCH is unspecified.
found_via: GitHub: rod-chapman/SPARKNaCl README; WebSearch snippets of AdaCore blog posts.
why_faster: Per search snippets only ('formal is fast'): the proof of absence of run-time errors lets the code run without run-time checks; README keeps TweetNaCl's constant-time algorithms.

verification.tier_reason: The repo carries a public harness that times SPARKNaCl.Sign against TweetNaCl's crypto_sign in the same binary with mcycle and checks the signatures match (perf/tsign.adb, perf/tweetnacl.c, perf/perf.gpr, perf/tsign.mk), and the compiler, flags and board are known, but the cycle counts exist only in AdaCore blog posts, a FOSDEM 2022 abstract and a slide deck that are all unreachable here (blog.adacore.com, www.adacore.com and www.slideshare.net return ENOTFOUND; archive.fosdem.org was blocked for the search agent), so the numbers are snippet-only and stay at C per the wave-14 snippet rule.
verification.notes: Keep at C with the asymmetric-algorithm shortcoming: harness, flags and board are public (perf/tsign.adb compares SPARKNaCl.Sign with TweetNaCl crypto_sign in one image and checks SM1 = SM2), but cycle counts are snippet-only and the win comes from rewritten GF arithmetic rather than from SPARK codegen; language_level_claim and same_algorithm corrected to false. A paper-access retier could reach A for the harness if the blog tables are read, still capped by the different-algorithm caveat.

name: Supersnappy
baseline: Google Snappy (C++), called through its C API (snappy_compress, snappy_uncompress, snappy_validate_compressed_buffer) from a prebuilt libsnappy.dll loaded by the nimsnappy wrapper (version and build flags unknown; the wrapper says it tracks 1.1.3). Also Andi Kleen's snappy-c (C), compiled from source into the benchmark through the nimsnappyc wrapper's {.compile.} pragma. The pure-Nim status-im/nim-snappy is the fourth column.
workload: Snappy benchmark corpus (alice29.txt, asyoulik.txt, fireworks.jpg, geo.protodata, html, html_x_4, kppkn.gtb, lcet10.txt, paper-100k.pdf, plrabn12.txt, urls.10K). tests/bench.nim times one compress plus one uncompress of the whole file per benchy timeIt sample, with 1000 samples (x1000). The README header's '100 compress-uncompress cycles' does not match the current code.
claimed_speedup: README: 'performs significantly better in all cases than alternatives'. Table, avg ms per compress-plus-uncompress round trip (derived ratios from page data). Against Google Snappy via nimsnappy: alice29.txt 0.513 vs 0.599 (1.17x), asyoulik.txt 0.451 vs 0.529 (1.17x), html_x_4 0.534 vs 0.559 (1.05x), kppkn.gtb 0.435 vs 0.523 (1.20x), lcet10.txt 1.380 vs 1.599 (1.16x), plrabn12.txt 1.898 vs 2.237 (1.18x), urls.10K 1.574 vs 1.842 (1.17x); slower on fireworks.jpg 0.015 vs 0.011, geo.protodata 0.106 vs 0.101 and paper-100k.pdf 0.041 vs 0.017, html 0.128 vs 0.127 (tie). Against snappy-c via nimsnappyc, faster on all 11 files by 1.10x (plrabn12.txt 1.898 vs 2.092) to 1.42x (geo.protodata 0.106 vs 0.150). Against status-im/nim-snappy it is slower on fireworks.jpg (0.015 vs 0.011) and paper-100k.pdf (0.041 vs 0.020). So 'all cases' holds only against snappy-c.
compiler_and_flags: nim c --gc:arc -d:release -r tests/bench.nim (README still says tests/benchmark.nim, which is now 404). Nim's release config compiles both its generated C and the {.compile.}'d snappy-c with the same backend C compiler (gcc/clang -O3, vcc /O2 per Nim's config/nim.cfg), and supersnappy turns checks off in release builds. The backend compiler and version are not stated, and the build of the libsnappy.dll used for Google Snappy is unknown.
hardware: Not stated (a Windows machine, judging by the .\tests path and libsnappy.dll)
tradeoffs: Pure Nim, dependency free, usable at compile time; outputs checked for compatibility with other Snappy implementations.
caveats: Weak entry. Nim compiles to C, so this is a C-versus-C comparison and no language effect. The cleanest comparison is against snappy-c, built by the same C compiler at the same flags, which supersnappy beats on all 11 files by 1.10-1.42x; but the nimsnappyc wrapper calls snappy_init_env/snappy_free_env (allocating the hash table) on every compress, which inflates small-file times. Against Google Snappy the nimsnappy wrapper runs a full snappy_validate_compressed_buffer pass before every uncompress, and newString zero-fills both output buffers, so the C++ baseline does extra work; even so supersnappy wins only 16-20 percent on text, ties html and loses on fireworks.jpg, geo.protodata and paper-100k.pdf (2.4x slower on paper-100k.pdf). The libsnappy.dll version and flags are unknown (the wrapper says it tracks snappy 1.1.3, a 2015 release), no hardware is stated, and the README's 'all cases' claim is contradicted by its own table. The code credits snappy-c as its main influence. [retier] uncompress calls read32 before checking the trailer bytes (checks off in release), so truncated input reads up to 4 bytes out of bounds and can decode instead of failing (issue #7, open); an untrusted varint prefix allocates up to 4 GiB first (issue #8). The fuzzer flips single bytes only; the runtime path is little-endian only; the bench never checks output; the Google path pays an extra validate pass, and Supersnappy allocates a 32 KiB table per compress, so the snappy-c init_env caveat cuts both ways. Table dates from 2022-06-12.

name: tac (neosmart, SIMD-accelerated Rust rewrite of GNU tac)
baseline: GNU Coreutils tac (C)
workload: Reversing the lines of a file (tac FILE); README gives no input size or command.
claimed_speedup: README: 'significantly (2.55x if mitigations disabled, more otherwise) faster than the version of tac that ships with GNU Coreutils'. The author's blog announces the 2.0 release as up to three times faster than GNU tac (WebSearch snippet only; neosmart.net did not resolve here).
why_faster: README: AVX2/NEON SIMD newline detection plus memory-mapped input, which avoids read-syscall cost when speculative-execution mitigations are enabled.
tradeoffs: Fast path needs a seekable file; stdin is buffered in memory up to 4 MiB then spilled to disk, so piped input loses the advantage. NEON needs the nightly compiler.
caveats: One number with no hardware, GNU tac version, input size or command; no benchmark code anywhere in the repo (top level holds only src, .cargo, Makefile; the Makefile bench target runs cargo bench but no benches exist). The blog post (neosmart.net) does not resolve from this environment; its 'up to 3x' wording is from a search snippet only. The win comes from SIMD newline search and mmap input rather than the language; piping input through stdin forces full buffering (disk spill above 4 MiB) and loses the mmap advantage. NEON path needs the nightly feature. No GitHub releases; crates.io 2.1.0 published 2024-01-22, last commit the same day. [retier] AVX2 hot-path bug (code reading plus Python emulation): _mm256_movemask_epi8(..) as u64 sign-extends the i32, so a newline at bit 31 of the lower window sets all upper mask bits and scrambles 32 bytes (162 of 300 random inputs differ from GNU tac in emulation); introduced in ec5f71a (2021-08-31), shipped in crates 2.0.0 and 2.1.0; the README 2.55x predates it but the later +14% was timed on the buggy loop. Piped stdin over 4 MiB is silently truncated; the temp file leaks on a broken pipe; an empty file errors; no -s, -r or -b; no tests.

baseline: Hand-tuned reference implementations in SUPERCOP, compiled with the same C compilers at -O3: Kwan's bitsliced DES (C), Kasper-Schwabe SSSE3 AES-CTR and Kivilinna's AVX AES-CTR (assembly), Dolbeau AVX2, moon AVX/SSSE3 and e/ref ChaCha20, Linux C and avx2-16way/avx-8way/sse2-8way Serpent-CTR, and the Rectangle reference. Secondary: BSC 0.1 (Thomas Pornin's prototype bitslicing compiler, which emits C) on DES in results.org.
metric: throughput (units not stated in the log, probably cycles per byte)
workload: Usuba-generated bitsliced or m-sliced ciphers (DES, AES-CTR, ChaCha20, Serpent-CTR, Rectangle) against hand-tuned references in SUPERCOP crypto_stream (xor_cycles over 4096-byte messages), plus bitsliced DES generated by Usuba against DES generated by BSC 0.1 in experimentations/usuba-vs-bsc (rdtscp cycles per byte, 15 runs).
claimed_speedup: bench/ua-vs-human/human.tex (cycles per byte; SUPERCOP xor_cycles on 4096-byte messages, lower half of samples averaged; speedup = (ref - usuba)/ref). Usuba faster: Rectangle SSE 11.18 vs 14.51 (+22.95%), AVX 4.21 vs 4.92 (+14.43%), AVX2 2.10 vs 2.45 (+14.29%), GP 25.88 vs 28.61 (+9.54%); Serpent GP 25.78 vs 30.37 Linux C (+15.11%), SSE 11.29 vs 11.48 (+1.66%); ChaCha20 SSE 2.31 vs 2.72 moon SSSE3 (+15.07%), AVX2 1.02 vs 1.03, AVX 2.07 vs 2.09; DES GP 11.47 vs 12.01 Kwan (+4.50%). Usuba slower: AES 7.92 vs 7.77 Kasper-Schwabe (-1.93%) and 5.71 vs 5.59 Kivilinna AVX assembly (-2.15%); Serpent AVX2 4.53 vs 4.33 (-4.62%) and AVX 8.66 vs 8.36 (-3.59%); ChaCha20 GP 5.65 vs 5.64. ciphers/des/results.txt also has Usuba behind Kwan on SSE (6.64 vs 6.50) and AVX (3.74 vs 3.63). results.org (main branch): des-usuba 17.086 +-0.121 vs des-bsc 17.419 +-0.142 cycles/byte, about 1.9 percent faster (derived from page data). PLDI 2019 abstract: 'on par with hand-tuned reference implementations' (search snippet only); WPMVP 2018 quoted as about 15 percent faster on DES with 64-bit general-purpose registers depending on the C compiler (search snippet only).
compiler_and_flags: Usuba emits C that is compiled by the same C compilers as the references. DES (ciphers/des/compile.pl): clang -O3 -march=native for both Usuba and Kwan. SUPERCOP rows (bench/ua-vs-human/run.pl): icc or clang with -O3 -fomit-frame-pointer -fwrapv -std=gnu11 plus -march=native, -mssse3, -xSSSE3, -xSSE2 or -msse4.2; several rows pair different compilers or ISA flags per side (Serpent GP: Usuba clang -march=native vs Linux C icc -msse4.2; Serpent AVX: Usuba clang vs reference icc; ChaCha20 GP: Usuba icc -msse4.2 vs e/ref icc -march=native). usuba-vs-bsc (experimentations/usuba-vs-bsc/run.pl): clang -O3 -Wall -Wextra for both, Usuba flags -no-arr -inline-all -no-precalc-tbl -check-tbl -B. Compiler versions not stated.
hardware: Not stated; SUPERCOP data paths name an amd64 host 'dadaubuntu', CPU model unknown.
tradeoffs: Domain-specific language for bitsliced and vector-sliced ciphers; targets x86 SIMD and the generated code is only as good as the C compiler used.
caveats: Win is mixed and small: faster on Rectangle (9.5-23%), Serpent GP (15%), ChaCha20 SSE (15%) and DES GP (4.5%); slower on AES (about 2%), Serpent AVX/AVX2 (3.6-4.6%) and DES SSE/AVX; the paper itself claims 'on par'. The results.org DES comparison is against BSC 0.1, which the experiment's own Readme calls a prototype 'not meant to be an optimizing compiler', so it is not a hand-tuned baseline. The hand-tuned comparison lives only on the old master branch (bench/ua-vs-human/human.tex, ciphers/des/results.txt); the default main branch was restructured and no longer carries bench/, ciphers/ or experimentations/. Numbers are undated author runs on an unstated CPU, and some rows use different compilers or ISA flags for each side. Usuba output is C compiled by the same C compiler, so the gain comes from the Usubac compiler's transformations (scheduling, interleaving, inlining), not from a different backend. results.org also logs broken runs ('No supercop', 'C compilation goes wrong', a stack overflow, 0.00 AVX-512 results). Papers not opened (snippet only).
found_via: WebSearch 'Usuba bitslicing compiler faster than hand-written C ciphers PLDI github usubalang'
why_faster: Compiler-level optimizations specific to bitslicing (inlining, scheduling, interleaving; the repo has bench directories for each).

baseline: C++ (g++ 16.1.0, -std=c++23 -O3 -march=native -flto=auto) 1.097 s; also C/gcc 1.112 s, C/clang 1.136 s and C++/clang++ 1.167 s

Rust 1.008 and D/ldc2 1.078 are also ahead of C++/g++, while Zig 1.327, Nim/gcc 1.171 and V/clang 1.846 are slower. On mandel.b the C++/g++ row (10.143 s) beats V/gcc (17.865 s).
compiler_and_flags: common/commands.mk: COMMON_FLAGS = '-Wall -Wextra -pedantic -Wcast-align -O3 -march=native -flto=auto -Wa,-mbranches-within-32B-boundaries'. V: 'v -prod -no-bounds-checking -prealloc -cflags "-Wno-error=implicit-function-declaration $(COMMON_FLAGS)" -cc gcc'. C++: 'g++ $(COMMON_FLAGS) -std=c++23' (libstdc++); C++/clang++: 'clang++ $(COMMON_FLAGS) -std=c++23 -stdlib=libc++'. C: 'gcc $(COMMON_FLAGS) -std=c23'. Versions: V 0.5.2 (7647ce1), gcc/g++ 16.1.0, clang 22.1.8.
hardware: Intel Xeon E-2324G, Debian forky/sid Docker image, README updated 2026-07-19
tradeoffs: V emits C that gcc compiles, so this reflects V's generated code through the gcc backend; with -no-bounds-checking and -prealloc the safety defaults are off.
caveats: Capped at tier C because the source states no mechanism. V compiles to C, so the V/gcc row is GCC 16.1.0 compiling V-generated C with the same COMMON_FLAGS as the hand-written C and C++. The roughly 10% lead is therefore a difference between two C-level programs, not between compilers, and V adds -prealloc (arena allocator) and -no-bounds-checking. The three programs share the op-tree design but differ in detail: the V Op carries a full []Op array header, the C op is a 16-byte tagged union with a tape_get that returns char, and C++ uses std::vector<Op> with a resize-doubling tape. Only the gcc backend wins: V/clang is 1.846 s, slower than every C and C++ row. On the suite's other brainfuck sample, mandel.b, V/gcc takes 17.865 s against C++/g++ 10.143 s (C++ 1.76x faster, derived from page data), so the bench.b result does not generalise. Single machine (Xeon E-2324G), medians with MAD of about 0.001-0.002 s.

name: verztable
baseline: absl::flat_hash_map/flat_hash_set, boost::unordered_flat_map/unordered_flat_set and ankerl::unordered_dense::map/set (src/cpp_hashtables_wrapper.cpp); integer keys use each library's default hash, string keys use std::string_view with a shared wyhash. The 'std' column is Zig's std.AutoHashMap/StringHashMap, not std::unordered_map.
workload: u32, u64 and random-length (8-64 char) string keys with void, 4-byte and 64-byte values, at 100, 3K and 100K elements (1M appears only in the memory table); 16 operation mixes (random and sequential insert, reserved insert, update, random lookup, high load, lookup miss, tombstone, delete, iteration, churn, mixed, read-heavy, write-heavy, update-heavy, zipfian); ns per operation, 15 iterations; C++ tables called from Zig through per-operation extern "C" wrappers.
claimed_speedup: README: 'outperforms Google's Abseil, Boost, and Ankerl on mixed workloads'. BENCHMARKS.md, 100-element u32 set: Reserved Ins. 5 ns vs Abseil 13 / Boost 14 / Ankerl 9 (but the C++ tables are never reserved, see caveats); Delete 4 vs 13 / 6 / 6; Lookup Miss 1 vs 5 / 2 / 3; Tombstone 5 vs 16 / 6 / 8; losses in the same table: Rand. Lookup 3 vs Boost 2, Write-Heavy 12 vs Ankerl 8. Across all 432 per-configuration rows verztable beats the best of the three C++ tables in 156, ties 37 and loses 239; geometric-mean time ratio C++/verztable is about 1.03 vs Boost, 1.33 vs Abseil and 1.46 vs Ankerl (derived from page data). At 100K integer keys it loses nearly every row to Abseil and Boost (u32 set: 0 wins of 16; geomean 0.61x of Boost's speed); its clearest wins are on string keys (8-10 of 16 rows per configuration) and on 100-element tables. The page's 27-configuration average table shows verztable ahead on 10 of 16 operations and behind on random/sequential insert, lookup miss, iteration and write-heavy.
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.15.2+ with -O ReleaseFast for verztable and the Zig std maps; the C++ wrapper and Abseil sources are compiled by Zig's bundled clang with -std=c++17 -O3 -DNDEBUG -fno-exceptions -fno-rtti (build.zig); native target by default; no LTO configured, so C++ calls are not inlined into the Zig benchmark loop.
tradeoffs: Uses about 25% more memory than the C++ tables (12.0 KB vs 8.0 KB for 1K u32 keys, 12.0 MB vs 8.0 MB at 1M); Zig only.
caveats: Own harness, no CPU model or OS stated. Harness asymmetries: (1) 'Reserved Ins.' calls ensureTotalCapacity for verztable and Zig std, but benchCpp's setup for .insert_reserved does nothing and the wrapper has no reserve function, so the C++ columns in that row are plain un-reserved inserts (verztable 'wins' 22 of 27 such rows); (2) every C++ operation goes through a non-inlined extern "C" call (insert also memcpys the value into a temporary), which adds roughly a call's cost to 1-5 ns operations, the size range where verztable wins most; the README's argument that Ankerl's 0 ns iteration shows minimal FFI overhead does not hold because iteration is a single wrapper call that counts inside C++. The string fast path (keys up to 8 bytes packed into a u64) and stored 64-bit hashes are design features the competitors do not use. Uses about 25% more memory than the competitors by the README's own trade-off note (string sets 3.3 MB vs 1.9-2.0 MB at 100K). Verstable (C) is the algorithmic inspiration, not a benchmark target. 15 stars, single author.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/performance?l=zig description 'faster than the top C++ hash tables'; README and BENCHMARKS.md of ThobiasKnudsen/verztable.
why_faster: README: hash-fragment filtering skips non-matches without touching bucket data; fast path for strings of 8 bytes or fewer; stores full 64-bit hashes for string keys to skip memcmp.

verification.tier_reason: First-party harness is public (src/benchmark.zig, src/cpp_hashtables_wrapper.cpp, C++ flags in build.zig) and BENCHMARKS.md has the quoted numbers, but no CPU model or machine is stated, so not A; tier stays C, and the claim is downgraded because the headline rows are partly harness artifacts and verztable loses most integer-key rows at 3K and 100K elements.
verification.notes: Real table with a public harness, but the claim is overstated: the cited Reserved Ins. win compares reserved verztable against un-reserved C++ tables, all C++ operations pay a non-inlined FFI call, and verztable loses 239 of 432 rows to the best C++ table (beats Boost by only about 3% geomean, loses most integer rows at 3K/100K). Record shortcomings: harness asymmetry (no reserve for C++, per-op FFI), no CPU model, not faster than Boost on integer keys at scale, higher memory use.

name: Zig (kostya/benchmarks base64)
baseline: Hand-written scalar C base64 (no library), gcc and clang, -O3 -march=native -flto
workload: Base64 encode and decode of a 131072-byte string, 8192 tries, into newly allocated buffers; seconds.
claimed_speedup: kostya/benchmarks base64 table (median, Xeon E-2324G, README updated 2026-07-19): Zig 0.703 s vs C/clang 0.918 s and C/gcc 1.117 s, about 1.31x and 1.59x faster (derived from page data); Rust 0.842 s also beats both. The same table has C/clang (aklomp) 0.095 s and C/gcc (aklomp) 0.097 s, about 7.4x faster than Zig, and PHP 0.065 s (its C base64) fastest overall; C++ with libcrypto takes 3.664 s.
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.16.0: zig build-exe -O ReleaseFast -lc (std.base64); C and C++: gcc/g++ 16.1.0 or clang/clang++ 22.1.8 with -O3 -march=native -flto=auto -std=c23 / c++23 -Wa,-mbranches-within-32B-boundaries (common/commands.mk)
caveats: Not the same algorithm: Zig uses std.base64 (checked in lib/std/base64.zig at the 0.15.2 tag and master on the GitHub mirror; the 0.16.0 tag is not on GitHub), whose decoder ORs four 256-entry u32 tables pre-shifted per character position, checks validity once per 4 characters and writes 16 bytes per u128 store, and whose encoder reads 16 bytes as a u128 and emits 16 characters per 12 input bytes; base64/test-nolib.c uses one decode table, branches on every character, scans for \n and \r before each quantum (MIME tolerance Zig's standard decoder does not provide) and stores byte by byte. So the win is a library implementation difference; the SIMD C library (aklomp) is about 7x faster than Zig, and the same four-table technique is available in C (e.g. Chromium modp_b64). Buffers: Zig uses a FixedBufferAllocator and C uses stack VLAs, so 'newly allocated buffers' cost nothing on either side; the Zig input is a comptime constant ("a" ** 131072) and the C input a memset stack array. Zig is built with zig build-exe -O ReleaseFast -lc (native CPU by default), C with -O3 -march=native -flto=auto. Medians with MAD from one machine; the README states no flags in prose (they are in common/commands.mk).
found_via: GitHub: kostya/benchmarks README tables (cross-language suite named in QUEUE.md section E).
tradeoffs: Single task microbenchmark; Zig std.base64 is scalar.

verification.tier_reason: The kostya/benchmarks README (UPDATE 2026-07-19, Intel Xeon E-2324G, Zig 0.16.0, gcc 16.1.0, clang 22.1.8) shows Zig 0.703 s vs C/clang 0.918 s and C/gcc 1.117 s, with code (base64/test.zig, base64/test-nolib.c) and flags (common/commands.mk, base64/Makefile) public, so the harness is A-grade; capped at C because it is not like for like: Zig calls std.base64, which decodes 16 characters per step through four pre-shifted lookup tables with one validity check and a 16-byte store and encodes 12 bytes per u128 load, while the C program is a hand-written per-character decoder with a branch per character and newline skipping (same asymmetric-kernel cap as the kostya matmul D entry in batch-02).
verification.notes: Numbers verified on the README; harness is reproducible (code, flags, CPU, versions) but the win comes from Zig's std.base64 algorithm against a naive hand-written C loop, so it stays C with same_algorithm false; the best C (aklomp/base64, SIMD) is about 7x faster than Zig. Record shortcoming: different algorithm on each side, not a language effect.

Zig uses its standard-library base64 while C is a separate hand-written table-driven implementation, so this compares two implementations, and the best C implementation (aklomp SIMD library) is far faster than Zig. The README states no compiler flags in prose; flags were read from common/commands.mk and the base64 Makefile. Values are medians with MAD from one machine.

name: ziggit (Zig git reimplementation)
baseline: git (C) CLI: status, log -20, branch -a, blame
workload: hyperfine (100 runs, 5 warmups) of small git commands in a test repository on macOS arm64, plus in-process library calls versus spawning git as a subprocess for a bun-style workflow.
claimed_speedup: BENCHMARKS.md (2026-03-31, commit 9b2c398). On macOS arm64 the small repo (51 commits) is 4.9x faster on average (status 8.1 vs 1.0 ms, 8.1x; log -20 5.0x; branch -a 5.6x; blame 1.3x) and the large repo (2,367 commits) 4.4x on average (status 2.1x, show --stat 1.2x, log --oneline all 1.4x, blame 36.0 vs 2.8 ms, 12.6x). On Linux x86_64 the small repo averages 1.2x (log -20 0.8x). On the large Linux repo ziggit is slower on 8 of 10 commands (status 0.7x, diff --stat 0.3x, show --stat 0.3x) and wins only blame (87.9 vs 7.9 ms, 11.1x). End-to-end bun install with the ziggit integration: 0.93-1.39x cold, parity warm. The README's '4-10x' headline mixes small-repo rows with the large-repo blame row and omits the Linux CLI results.
compiler_and_flags: ziggit: Zig 0.15.2, ReleaseFast. git: Apple Git 2.50.1 (macOS) and git 2.43.0 (Linux), build flags not stated. macOS CLI: hyperfine --warmup 5 --runs 100 (small repo) or --runs 50 (large repo). caveats: First-party. The README headline cherry-picks: on Linux x86_64 the CLI averages 1.2x on a small repo, and on a large repo ziggit is slower on 8 of 10 commands (diff --stat and show --stat at 0.3x). The macOS gains are mostly git process launch, about 7-8 ms per invocation according to BENCHMARKS.md itself; the git binary path is not stated. Blame's 11-12.6x comes from in-process memoisation, and src/git/blame_cmd.zig has no rename detection, while git blame follows whole-file renames by default, so the work differs; output equivalence was not shown. The library rows time an in-process call against fork+exec of git; that is overhead, not implementation speed, and libgit2 would be the fair in-process baseline. The end-to-end bun install rows compare a ziggit-integrated bun 1.3.11-canary with stock bun 1.2.10 (different bun versions) and show only 0.93-1.39x. Succinct output is on by default in ziggit, so status/log print less than git. BENCHMARKS.md was removed from master (commit b82fa0c), and the benchmarks/*.zig in the repo do not reproduce the published tables. [retier] Library benchmark shortcut: isLightningFastClean() marks a freshly opened repo clean without reading the worktree ('BENCHMARK OPTIMIZATION ... aggressively assume clean'), so the lib_benchmark.zig status row times a no-op and statusPorcelain()/isClean() miss edits. On Linux cloneBare hardlinks all .git files (HEAD, refs, config) and updateHead rewrites refs in place with truncate, so a library commit or checkout in the clone moves the source's refs, which explains the 34.3x. The macOS 7-8 ms git floor is not fork+exec: the ziggit process itself runs in 1.0-1.4 ms under the same hyperfine.

name: ZLB (Zig Language Benchmark) Mandelbrot SIMD row
baseline: C Mandelbrot with 4-lane SIMD intrinsics, gcc 16.1.1 and clang 22.1.8 at -O3 -march=native -ffp-contract=off (also zig cc)
workload: Mandelbrot set calculation, hyperfine mean of 20 runs after 1 warmup, wall-time ratio against the scalar gcc build (1.00x).
claimed_speedup: Mandelbrot 4000x4000, max_iter 1000, hyperfine mean of 20 runs (results/mandel_*.json): zig_simd_fast 1.922 s and zig_simd_safe 2.249 s vs c_simd_clang 3.261 s, c_simd_gcc 3.302 s, c_simd_zigcc 3.380 s and rust_simd 3.321 s, so the 8-lane Zig kernel is 1.70x to 1.76x faster than the 4-lane C kernels (ReleaseSafe 1.45x to 1.50x) (derived from page data); README ratios vs scalar gcc: 0.16x, 0.18x, 0.26x, 0.27x, 0.27x, 0.27x. Same-algorithm scalar rows are parity: zig_std_fast 12.374 s vs c_std_gcc 12.386 s (1.00x) and c_std_clang 12.631 s (1.02x). Other rows in the same suite (README ratios vs c_std_gcc): sieve zig_static_bitset_fast 0.63x vs c_std_gcc 1.00x but zig_std_fast 1.06x; btree zig_compact_fast 0.19x vs c_arena_gcc 0.21x; log_proc zig_std_fast 0.83x vs c_std_gcc 1.00x; atomics parity (0.97x to 1.00x).
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.16.0 zig build-exe -O ReleaseFast (and ReleaseSafe) with no -target, so the host CPU is targeted (README: all binaries built for native); the SIMD kernel sets @setFloatMode(.strict). C SIMD: gcc 16.1.1 and clang 22.1.8 at -O3 -march=native -ffp-contract=off, zig cc -O3 -ffp-contract=off -march=native. C scalar: gcc/clang -O3 only (no -march=native), zig cc -O3 -ffp-contract=off. Rust 1.97.1: rust_simd rustc -C opt-level=3 -C target-cpu=native (no LTO); rust_std -C opt-level=3 -C lto=yes (Makefile). Measured with hyperfine --warmup 1 --min-runs 20 --output=null (tools/runner.sh); outputs are not checked against an expected checksum during timing.
hardware: Linux 7.1.4-arch; CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Informal suite of five small benchmarks (mandel, sieve, btree, log_proc, atomics) in Zig, C, Rust, Go, Python and Bash.
caveats: Not like-for-like and not a language win. The Zig SIMD kernel (src/mandel/zig_simd/main_simd.zig) iterates an 8-lane @Vector(8, f64) block with u32 counters, which on AVX2 hardware compiles to two interleaved 4-wide chains (or one AVX-512 op if the unnamed CPU has it), while the C and Rust SIMD kernels (c_simd/main_simd.c, rust_simd/main_simd.rs) run a single 4-lane __m256d chain with 64-bit counters; the 1.7x gap is the extra ILP or width of the wider block, which the same C written with 8 lanes (two __m256d chains, AVX-512 intrinsics or GCC vector extensions) would also get. On the same algorithm with the same structure the scalar rows are parity (zig_std_fast 12.374 s vs c_std_gcc 12.386 s) even though the Zig scalar build targets the native CPU and the C scalar builds do not use -march=native. The sieve and btree wins come from different data layouts (a bitset instead of a byte array, 32-bit indices instead of 64-bit pointers), and the log_proc win compares Zig's std.fmt.bufPrint and parseUnsigned against glibc sprintf, strstr and atoi, so they are library and layout effects. Single commit (2026-08-20), 0 stars, CPU model not stated, no correctness check in the timed runs.
found_via: WebSearch: 'written in Zig faster than C library benchmark' (zff.dev mirror of tsukumoakito/zlb), then github.com/topics/benchmark?l=zig
why_faster: Source: Zig's @Vector with 8-lane f64 fills the CPU's execution units better than the 4-lane intrinsics used in C and Rust, and gives LLVM clearer intent.

verification.tier_reason: Public code (src/mandel/{c_simd/main_simd.c,zig_simd/main_simd.zig,rust_simd/main_simd.rs,c_std/main.c,zig_std/main.zig}, Makefile, tools/runner.sh, tools/aggregate.py) with compilers and flags stated and raw hyperfine JSON in results/, but no CPU model anywhere, and it is a single-author, 0-star, one-commit suite written to showcase Zig, so first-party C, not A. verification.notes: Numbers match the README and the raw hyperfine JSON (zig_simd_fast 1.922 s, c_simd_gcc 3.302 s, c_std_gcc 12.386 s). Shortcomings to record: unequal SIMD kernels (8-lane Zig vs 4-lane C/Rust), scalar like-for-like rows at parity, sieve/btree/log_proc wins come from data layout or library differences, CPU model not stated, single-commit 0-star suite, timed runs not checked for correct output; same_algorithm corrected to false, same_opt_level true for the SIMD rows (all three at native with strict FP), rust_simd has no LTO.

name: nom (Rust parser combinator library)
baseline: Handwritten C HTTP parsers Joyent http-parser and h2o picohttpparser (parser_benchmarks/http); the MP4 benchmark compares against hammer (UpstandingHackers), a C parser-combinator library rather than a handwritten parser.
workload: HTTP/1.x request parsing (one small request, the httparse example request, 55 requests in http-requests.txt, 275 requests in bigger.txt) against C parsers; MP4 top-level box parsing against the C combinator library hammer; JSON parsing compared only against Rust and other libraries (no C comparator).
claimed_speedup: nom README: 'just as fast' as handwritten C parsers and 'often outperform ... even handwritten C parsers' (no numbers in nom's README). parser_benchmarks http/README.md (late-2013 MacBook Pro, quad-core 2.3 GHz Core i7): idiomatic nom is slower than Joyent http-parser on every test: 889 vs 606 ns one_test, 59,918 vs 56,385 ns small_test, 333,344 vs 266,254 ns bigger_test, 1,544 vs 1,137 ns httparse_example_test (1.06-1.47x slower, derived from page data). The SIMD 'nom (optimized)' experiment against picohttpparser: 183 vs 170 ns one_test (1.08x slower), 12,253 (+/- 2,473) vs 13,260 (+/- 1,786) ns small_test (1.08x faster), 61,519 (+/- 14,660) vs 65,415 (+/- 5,058) ns bigger_test (1.06x faster), 308 (+/- 48) vs 350 (+/- 76) ns httparse_example_test (1.14x faster) (ratios derived from page data; all within the error bars). mp4/README.md (2015, nom 0.1.6): nom 240 / 195 ns per iteration vs hammer 32,424 / 26,523 ns on small.mp4 / bigbuckbunny.mp4 with optimisations (about 135x, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: HTTP run: compiler versions not stated. Joyent http-parser built with 'gcc -Ofast -O3 -DNDEBUG' (http/joyent_http_parser/Makefile) and timed by its own C clock_gettime loop; nom-http and nom-optimized (nom ^4.0) built with release profile lto = "fat", codegen-units = 1 and timed with the Rust bencher crate; nom-optimized README gives RUSTFLAGS="-C target-feature=+sse2" (labelled SSE4.2; its take_while1_simd path emits PCMPESTRI); picohttpparser called via FFI from pico-sys 0.0.1, whose build.rs runs gcc::compile_library with crate defaults and no -msse4.2, so picohttpparser's __SSE4_2__ path is compiled out unless CFLAGS were set. MP4 run (2015): rustc 1.0.0-dev (522d09dfe 2015-02-19), nom 0.1.6, cargo bench; hammer at commit 4e8d319 built with Apple LLVM 6.0 (clang-600.0.56), scons --variant=opt, -Ofast -DNDEBUG, no -g.
hardware: Late-2013 MacBook Pro, quad-core 2.3 GHz Intel Core i7 (exact CPU model not stated)
why_faster: README lists zero-copy slices, streaming parsing and safe memory handling as design points; it gives no mechanism for beating C.
stars_or_usage: 10.5k stars, 849 forks; about 785 million crates.io downloads (crates.io API, 2026-10-12); latest release 8.0.0 (2025-01-26)
tradeoffs: Rust-only API; parsers are written in combinator style rather than as C state machines.
caveats: The record said no numbers were openable; they are in parser_benchmarks http/README.md and mp4/README.md, and they do not support a win over C. (1) Idiomatic nom loses to Joyent http-parser on all four HTTP tests even though the C harness mallocs and memcpys every header name and value while nom returns borrowed slices; the two sides also use different timing harnesses (Rust bencher vs a C clock_gettime loop that drops the seconds field). (2) The nom-optimized edge over picohttpparser (1.06-1.14x on three tests, 1.08x slower on one_test) is inside the stated error bars and is asymmetric: nom-optimized uses SSE4.2 PCMPESTRI range scans while pico-sys 0.0.1 compiles picohttpparser without -msse4.2, disabling its own SSE4.2 path (crippled baseline by build default). (3) The MP4 135x over hammer is not a handwritten C parser and not the same work: the hammer harness parses every box body as per-byte h_uint8 tokens through h_length_value with arena allocation and treats the MP4 size field (which includes the 8-byte header) as the body length, so it appears to over-read and stop after the first box, while nom slices box bodies; the table comes from nom 0.1.6 on a pre-1.0 rustc (2015) and the checked-in nom-mp4 code is now nom 5 with jemalloc, so the numbers are not reproducible from current code. (4) The README's own wording is parity ('just as fast'). parser_benchmarks last commit 2019-12-10, 128 stars, no LICENSE shown. Kept for notability (10.5k stars, about 785 million crates.io downloads).

The HN queries returned only general Rust/Zig-versus-C discussion threads and projects already catalogued, so this record was found through the GitHub topic page named below after those HN queries. Found while checking Rust library READMEs for explicit comparisons against handwritten C; HN query 'Show HN Rust implementation faster than the C original benchmark' returned only general Rust-vs-C threads.

name: C# NativeAOT minima-sync (HttpArena entry)
baseline: nginx 1.31.4 (C, custom handler module, -O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG) and libreactorng (C, io_uring, gcc -O3 -march=native) implementing the same HttpArena endpoints

The server container is pinned to cpuset 0-31,64-95 (32 cores / 64 threads) and the load generator (gcannon for HTTP/1.1 and WebSocket, wrk for json-tls and static-tls) runs on CPUs 32-63,96-127 of the same machine over loopback (scripts/lib/profiles.sh, scripts/lib/common.sh); each row is the best of 3 runs of 5 s against one container (scripts/benchmark.sh, RUNS=3).

The wins over C are pipelined-4096, which HttpArena marks reference-only (excluded from the composite score), where nginx trails libreactorng 10x, and async-32000 (C++ only except mongoose, which is ahead); the harness notes that the async result depends on the load generator's thread count, so it is not the server's alone (scripts/lib/common.sh). Vert.x writes 62.9 bytes per response vs nginx 135.4, hical 141.1, Drogon 130.7 and libreactorng 106.2 (derived from page data, bandwidth divided by req/s): the entry sends only content-type and content-length (ServerVerticle.java), so part of the pipelined margin is smaller responses. Memory is 4.8 to 8.0 GiB on the HTTP/1.1 and TLS rows and 16.9 GiB on async-32000, against nginx 3.5 GiB, h2o 69 to 308 MiB, libreactorng 105 to 175 MiB and mongoose 178 to 495 MiB (page data). Each row is the best of 3 runs of 5 s against one running container, so JIT warm-up is mostly absorbed by the first run rather than included in the reported number. Rows come from separate runs (vertx.json last written 2026-09-06, nginx.json 2026-08-30, mongoose.json 2026-09-21, per git history). The C and C++ competitor entries are minimal hand-written handlers, not tuned production configurations. The Vert.x README makes no performance claim; BENCHMARKING.md only describes JMH microbenchmarks without numbers. Vert.x runs on Netty (Netty is a separate wave-14 record), and Quarkus (already verified A in wave 14) runs on Vert.x. [retier] HttpArena pipelined responses are exactly 66 bytes with no Date or Server header (validate.sh checks only body and Content-Type) against about 142 bytes for nginx. limited-conn uses only 3,255% CPU against 5,448-6,644% for the C entries (connection setup as the limit, inferred); latency-1m costs 30.3 us per request against 21.0-22.5 for libreactorng, mongoose and hical; latency-500k-8cpu held only rate_ratio 0.75, which the harness flags as not comparable. Memory figures are inflated by -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch with no -Xmx. Open bug #6143: 5-8% HTTP/2 slowdown in 5.1.0; measured 5.1.6, current 5.2.1.

The frameworks/kestrel/README.md claim that JSON is serialized once at startup is stale: Dataset.cs serializes per request and says it keeps no precomputed responses. Kestrel is entered as type 'engine', so it is ranked on the engine board, not against the C++ frameworks. The entry is maintained by the suite owner (MDA2AV), not the ASP.NET team. Each number is the best of 3 runs of 5 s; rows come from different runs on the same machine (kestrel.json 2026-09-05, nginx.json and h2o.json 2026-08-30, drogon.json 2026-09-06, userver.json 2026-09-11 per git history). The TechEmpower plaintext tie is a 10 GbE-limited top group (ranks 1 to 13 within 0.8%, libreactor (C) rank 11 at 6,971,119), so it shows parity, not a win; that ranking is read from a screenshot in panjf2000/illustrations (benchmark/techempower-plaintext-top50-light.jpg), not the live results page. Every HttpArena entry is a minimal hand-written handler for the same endpoint contract (nginx runs a custom C handler module); Drogon is built against the unpinned drogonframework/drogon:latest image. [retier] json-comp: HttpArena requests send 'Accept-Encoding: gzip, br', so Kestrel serves brotli q1 while the C++ rows use their own encoders; Kestrel's responses average 1,582 bytes against Drogon's 1,392 (about 14% more), so the 1.6-3.8x wins compare different compressors and outputs, and engines are not scored on compression profiles. The h2c win is partly HPACK dynamic-table use (25 vs nginx 60 bytes per response). Memory correction: nginx sits at 3.5-3.8 GiB on every profile while Kestrel uses 118-590 MiB on HTTP/1.1 and 3.9-8.1 GiB on HTTP/2. Baseline CPU 5,589% vs nginx 6,444% matches open issue dotnet/aspnetcore#68915 (idle cores under HTTP/1.1 load).

tradeoffs: Strict RFC 6455 compliance (UTF-8 and close handshake validation), which the repo's own benches README contrasts with non-strict libraries; the HttpArena build enables the crate's nightly feature.
caveats: The margin over mongoose is 2 to 6 percent on the non-pipelined rows, and the hand-written C io_uring server ringzero-ws is 3 to 5 percent ahead on every unlimited row and 3.3x ahead on the pipelined rows; mongoose (an embedded general networking library) and proxygen are the only other C/C++ WebSocket entries, and uWebSockets is absent from the suite. Rows are best of 3 runs of 5 s against one container, but come from separate runs months apart: tokio-websockets.json was written 2026-08-28 (#1356), mongoose.json 2026-09-21 (#1489) and ringzero-ws.json no later than 2026-07-24 (per git history), so the 2 to 6 percent margins are cross-run comparisons. The entry was contributed by the author of the Rust wtx library (c410-f3r), not by the tokio-websockets authors; it echoes each message with SinkExt::send, which flushes per frame, which likely explains much of the 3x pipelined deficit. Messages are tiny (about 6.7 bytes of server output per message, derived from page data), so the library's SIMD masking and UTF-8 validation hardly matter here. The project's own benches/README.md (first-party, single-threaded runtime, Ryzen 9 7950X, uWebSockets HEAD built by its default build at -O3 -march=native with clang, load_test client; harness in benches/Dockerfile and run.py) shows chart images only: read approximately from the charts, uWebSockets leads at small payloads (100 connections 0 B about 319k vs 290k msg/s, 100 x 20 B about 318k vs 286k, 10 x 1 KiB about 296k vs 272k) and tokio-websockets leads at 16 KiB payloads (10 connections about 179k vs 120k, 200 about 173k vs 121k, 500 about 164k vs 119k). [retier] The HttpArena server (contributed by the wtx author) echoes with ws_stream.send(msg), one flush per frame, while the crate batches queued frames into one vectored write via SinkExt::feed since 0.12.0, so the 0.30-0.42x pipelined rows reflect the bench code. Non-pipelined rows use about 5-7-byte messages with servers busy on 53-66 of 64 threads, syscall-bound (14.8 us CPU per message vs mongoose 16.4 and ringzero-ws 14.2); the 2-6% margin over mongoose is cross-run and effectively a tie. Issue #128 (poll_close hang with split) is open; no permessage-deflate.

caveats: The json-comp ratios (9.6x over userver, 22x over Drogon) time a response cache: write_json_gzip in main.v keeps complete gzipped responses keyed by (count, m), compresses once on the first miss and appends the cached bytes on every hit, while HttpArena's json-comp rules forbid pre-compressed caches for standard and tuned entries (vanilla is an 'engine' entry, which has no rules) and the C++ rows compress per request. vanilla's rate there is 2.7x the next entry (zix, which compresses per request). No C engine or nginx runs json-comp. The json-tls body is partly pre-serialized: each item's JSON except total is rendered once at startup into a prefix string, so per request vanilla formats one integer per item and copies prefixes, whereas nginx's infrastructure rules require full per-request serialization; TLS is Mbed TLS (C, patched to cache the RSA signing context) with kTLS record offload in the kernel. static-tls and pipelined are reference-only profiles. At baseline-4096 the entry trails libreactorng (0.98x) and is level with libioma (1.01x) and at limited-conn it ties libreactorng and libioma, so on the scored HTTP/1.1 profiles vanilla matches but does not beat the best C engines. The vanilla-epoll entry is slower at baseline-4096 (3,985,550) and at limited-conn-4096 (1,021,750). V compiles to C (gcc -O3 -flto), so this is a V-generated C server against hand-written C servers, not a different code generator. Each number is the best of 3 runs of 5 s with the server limited to 32 cores / 64 threads; results files are undated and rows come from different runs (vanilla-io_uring.json last written 2026-10-02, vanilla-epoll.json 2026-10-11, agensio.json 2026-10-06, libreactorng.json 2026-09-07, per git history). The vanilla entries are maintained by the vanilla author (meta.json maintainers: enghitalo). The vanilla README publishes no throughput numbers against C servers; docs/PERF_GAP_ANALYSIS.md treats libreactorng, zeemo and tokio as the faster reference servers. The Drogon entry builds only its handler against the unpinned drogonframework/drogon:latest image and userver uses a prebuilt v3.2 image, so those ratios are weaker evidence than the nginx, h2o, libreactorng and libioma ratios. [retier] Benchmark-shaped handlers: /pipeline matches the raw prefix 'GET /pipeline ' and copies a constant response without parsing (the 43.7M req/s pipelined row, reference-only), json-tls renders item JSON prefixes at startup, and responses carry no Date header. baseline: lithium (C++) and cinatra (C++) in the TechEmpower Round 22 plaintext leaderboard

compiler_and_flags: TechEmpower frameworks/Rust/faf/faf.dockerfile (HEAD): base image errantmind/debian-faf:v3 (nightly rustc, version not stated), clang-15 and ld.lld-15, RUSTFLAGS -Ctarget-cpu=native -Ztune-cpu=native -Zmutable-noalias=yes -Copt-level=3 -Clto=thin -Ccodegen-units=1 -Cpanic=abort -Coverflow-checks=no -Cdebug-assertions=no, cargo build --release -Zbuild-std; the faf crate is pulled from git HEAD (unpinned). hardware: TechEmpower Round 22 physical environment: Dell R440 servers with an Intel Xeon Gold 5120 (28 HT cores), 32 GB RAM and a dedicated Cisco 10 GbE switch (leaderboard header 'Dell R440 Xeon Gold + 10 GbE' plus the hardware block in the gnet README that embeds the screenshot)
tradeoffs: Linux x86_64 and nightly Rust only, extensive unsafe code (README ranks speed first and memory safety third), bounded response buffer for small and moderate payloads, AGPL-3.0, unsolicited PRs not reviewed.
caveats: At Round 22 faf was listed as Realistic/Platform (IA column 'Rea' on the screenshot); TechEmpower PR #10608 (2026-01-23, under issue #9578 'No more fakes') reclassified it as Stripped because it hardcodes HTTP headers: the TFB src/main.rs copies a constant status line, Server, Content-Type and Content-Length block, then the cached date and the body, after checking only the method and path. lithium (Realistic, Micro) and cinatra (Realistic, Fullstack) run real frameworks, so faf does less work per request. Plaintext at the top of the table is saturated: the first nine rows are within 0.3% and the first 19 within 6%, network and pipelining bound, so the ordering among them is noise, not a language effect. Numbers are read from a screenshot hosted in the gnet author's illustrations repo (the header does not name the round; the gnet README links it to Round 22); techempower.com was unreachable from this environment. The faf README claims design choices were 'meticulously benchmarked' but names no competitors and gives no numbers; the no_std variant is said to be about 1% slower. Last commit 2024-04-14 (stale). Drogon does not appear in the top 50 screenshot. [retier] Security bug (code reading, src/epoll.rs): pipelined responses are appended to a 4,096-byte stack buffer with no bound check and the callback gets no remaining length, so 33 or more short pipelined requests in one packet overflow the stack (about 27 KB per 4 KB packet); the TFB load never hits it. No request-buffer compaction, a len -= i underflow reads past the received bytes, racy static mut Date and counter, partial sendto resets the connection, request bodies not consumed.

why_faster: Single-purpose server tuned for the benchmark: unsafe Rust, no dependencies, optional no_std with about 400 lines of assembly text (README); no profiling analysis given.

It is still classified Realistic/Platform in TFB. The full-codec 'firenio' entry ranks 34 at 5,613,390, 0.80x lithium (derived from page data), so the realistic codec is slower than the C++ baselines. Drogon does not appear in the top 50 screenshot. [retier] The only difference between the two TFB dockerfiles is -Dlite and -Dcachedurl, so building header Strings costs about 20% throughput (lite 7,004,779 vs full 5,613,390). decode_lite never reads GET headers, matches 'Content-Length:' case-sensitively, has no chunked encoding and accepts only GET, POST and HEAD. Epoll falls back to NIO silently, the native library is built without -O, the bind is IPv6-only (issue #57), a JVM crash is open (#66), and it needs sun.misc.Unsafe and JDK internals.

name: grpc-dotnet (gRPC for .NET)
baseline: gRPC C++ (grpc/grpc) servers cpp_grpc_st, cpp_grpc_mt and cpp_asio_grpc in the grpc_bench suite
workload: grpc_bench complex_proto unary SayHello over loopback: 50 client connections, 1000 concurrent requests, unlimited QPS, 120 s with 30 s warmup, ghz client. One run per server-CPU setting: 1 to 4 server CPUs in the 2026-04-22 run (commit c4c93b3, discussion #559) and 1 to 3 in the 2022-04-23 run (commit 14a8435, wiki).
claimed_speedup:
Newest maintainer run (discussion #559, 2026-04-22, commit c4c93b3, .NET 9 with Grpc.AspNetCore 2.66.0): dotnet_grpc is ahead of every C++ server at every CPU count. 1 CPU: 84,809 req/s vs cpp_grpc_mt 57,403, cpp_grpc_st 57,140 and cpp_asio_grpc 56,669 (1.48x, 1.48x, 1.50x). 2 CPUs: 123,609 vs cpp_asio_grpc 74,869 and cpp_grpc_mt 74,574 (1.65x, 1.66x). 3 CPUs: 136,452 vs cpp_grpc_mt 81,581 (1.67x). 4 CPUs: 135,948 vs 85,485 (1.59x).
2022-04-23 wiki run (commit 14a8435, .NET 6): 1 CPU 33,899 vs cpp_grpc_st 26,700, cpp_grpc_mt 26,376 and cpp_asio_grpc 24,926 (1.27x, 1.29x, 1.36x). 2 CPUs: 68,266 vs cpp_grpc_mt 69,882 (0.98x). 3 CPUs: 68,821 vs 71,806 (0.96x).
Third-party run (discussion #547, 2025-12-09, Ryzen 9 5900X, client CPUs equal to server CPUs, 10 s): near tie with cpp_grpc_mt, 0.92x at 1 CPU, 1.01x at 4 and 1.14x at 24.
All ratios derived from page data.
compiler_and_flags: dotnet_grpc in the 2026-04 run (c4c93b3): mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:9.0, net9.0, Grpc.AspNetCore 2.66.0, dotnet build -c Release, Kestrel listener HTTP/2 only (dotnet_grpc_bench/Dockerfile, GreeterServer/GreeterServer.csproj, Program.cs). In the 2022 run (14a8435): sdk:6.0, net6.0, Grpc.AspNetCore 2.41.0 with DOTNET_ReadyToRun=0, DOTNET_TieredPGO=1 and DOTNET_TC_QuickJitForLoops=1. The HEAD Dockerfile now uses sdk:10.0. C++ baselines: cpp_grpc_mt and cpp_grpc_st are built with g++ --std=c++20 -O3 -flto over main.cpp and the generated stubs, linking jemalloc and Debian's prebuilt libgrpc++-dev from the base image (gcc:15.2.0 at c4c93b3, gcc:11 at 14a8435, gcc:16.1.0 at HEAD). The gRPC core's version and build flags are the distro package's and are not stated or pinned. cpp_asio_grpc uses asio-grpc v1.0.0, CMake Release with jemalloc, against the same distro libgrpc++.
hardware: Newest run (discussion #559, posted by maintainer LesnyRumcajs 2026-04-22, commit c4c93b3): Intel Xeon Gold 6548N (16) @ 2.80 GHz, 64 GB RAM, Ubuntu 24.04.3, kernel 6.8.0-71, DigitalOcean dedicated server. Server limited to 1, 2, 3 or 4 CPUs and 4096m RAM; client 11 CPUs. 2022-04-23 wiki run (commit 14a8435): Intel Xeon E5-1650 v3 @ 3.50GHz, 32 GB RAM. Server limited to 1, 2 or 3 CPUs and 512m RAM; client 9 CPUs.
tradeoffs: .NET runtime and JIT required; it sits on Kestrel (ASP.NET Core).
caveats:
The result depends on the run.
- In the newest maintainer run (.NET 9) dotnet_grpc leads every C++ server by 1.48-1.67x at 1-4 CPUs. Its p99 at 1 CPU is worse (54.20 vs 21.81 ms for cpp_grpc_mt), and it uses about 4-6x the memory (127.87 vs 20.59 MiB at 1 CPU, 134.64 vs 31.71 MiB at 4).
- In the 2022 run (.NET 6) it led only at 1 CPU and trailed cpp_grpc_mt by 2-4% at 2 and 3 CPUs.
- In a client-bound third-party run (#547, by the wtx author) the two tie.
- The C++ servers link Debian's prebuilt libgrpc++, which is unpinned and of unstated version and flags, so the -O3 -flto applies only to the server code and stubs. They follow the helloworld async-example pattern: one completion queue and thread per server CPU, with one pre-posted request per queue (cpp_grpc_mt_bench/main.cpp). name: Helidon SE (Nima WebServer)
baseline: nginx 1.31.4 (C, custom handler module, -O3 -march=native) for HTTP/2; Drogon, userver, hical (C++) for the other profiles, all in the HttpArena suite

claimed_speedup: HttpArena (ratios derived from page data): baseline-h2-256 3,612,898 req/s (tuned) vs nginx 3,414,750 (1.06x), production variant 3,502,618 (1.03x); baseline-h2-1024 3,819,721 vs nginx 3,320,285 (1.15x), production 3,761,200 (1.13x); baseline-h2c (cleartext HTTP/2) 4,156,960 / 4,457,541 / 4,497,059 at 256 / 1024 / 4096 connections vs nginx 2,456,329 / 2,490,271 / 2,519,351 (1.69x to 1.79x); json-comp-4096 325,703 vs userver 297,311 (1.10x), proxygen-coro 262,212 (1.24x), hical 261,955 (1.24x), proxygen 243,887 (1.34x), Drogon 127,466 (2.56x), the top C/C++ rows on that profile (nginx, h2o, agensio and mongoose do not run it); pipelined-4096 (reference-only profile) 10,654,871 vs nginx 4,037,345 (2.64x), Drogon 7,801,404 (1.37x).
compiler_and_flags: Helidon: Oracle JDK 27 image (container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk-no-fee-term:27), Maven 3.9.16 package of Helidon SE 27.0.0, run as java -jar app.jar with default JVM options (frameworks/helidon-tuned/Dockerfile); the tuned variant turns off HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 request/response-header and path validation in application.yaml, the production variant keeps it. C/C++ rows: nginx 1.31.4 with a custom handler module, Debian trixie toolchain, --with-cc-opt='-O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG', linked against the system OpenSSL (the Dockerfile's quictls comment has no matching build step); h2o clang CMake Release -march=native -mtune=native (no LTO); userver CMake Release -march=native; hical gcc-14 CMake Release -march=native -mtune=native; proxygen CMake Release from a digest-pinned proxygen base image with mimalloc preloaded; Drogon CMake Release in the unpinned drogonframework/drogon:latest image with jemalloc preloaded (HttpArena frameworks/<name>/Dockerfile).

The server container is pinned to cpuset 0-31,64-95 (32 cores / 64 threads) and the load generator (gcannon for H/1.1, h2load for HTTP/2) to 32-63,96-127 over loopback; 5 s runs, best of 3 (scripts/lib/common.sh, scripts/lib/profiles.sh, scripts/benchmark.sh).
tradeoffs: JVM startup, warm-up and heap are not part of the throughput figure; Helidon 27 needs Java 27 for the virtual-thread server.
caveats: Narrow win. Against nginx, Helidon is ahead only on baseline-h2 (1.06x to 1.15x), baseline-h2c (1.69x to 1.79x) and the reference-only pipelined profile; it is behind nginx on baseline-4096 (0.52x), limited-conn-4096 (605,487 vs 2,626,297, 0.23x), json-tls-4096 (0.53x), json-h2c (1,087,863 vs 1,730,838, 0.63x), static-h2 (0.32x) and static-tls (0.45x). nginx's HTTP/2 path is the slowest C/C++ HTTP/2 stack on the board: at baseline-h2-256 h2o (16,106,978), agensio (14,744,015), proxygen (5,845,844) and proxygen-coro (5,185,268) are all ahead of Helidon (0.22x to 0.70x), and agensio and proxygen also lead on h2c. The json-comp win is over C++ frameworks only; Helidon gzips through java.util.zip GZIPOutputStream, which calls the JDK's native zlib, so compression is C code on both sides. The tuned entry disables header and path validation for the benchmark (the production variant keeps it and still edges nginx on h2). Both Helidon entries are maintained in HttpArena by Helidon developer tomas-langer, so they are vendor-tuned submissions run by the suite. Results files carry no dates; git history shows helidon-tuned.json last changed 2026-10-08/10 (Helidon 27.0.0 upgrade) and nginx.json 2026-08-30, so rows come from separate runs on the same machine. 5 s runs, best of 3, server limited to 32 of 64 cores. The Helidon README states no benchmark numbers. [retier] nginx's h2c rows (2.46-2.52M) sit 25-28% below nginx's own TLS h2 rows (3.32-3.41M) while every other server runs h2c at or above TLS, so the 1.69-1.79x h2c lead is inflated. The production variant (validation on) beats the tuned one on all three h2c rows, so the tuning is noise; quote production 1.03x/1.13x on h2. Memory 10.5-28.2 GiB against nginx's 3.5-3.7; json-comp p99 276 ms against userver's 28.7 ms.
