Drogon 1.9.13: cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=release (CMake release flags), C++17, no LTO; no C++ compiler version pinned in the suite files read (cpp/drogon/config.yaml language version '14/17'); config.json threads_num 0 (auto), log level WARN, Server and Date headers disabled. No server_cpu_cores or server_cpu_saturation metric is recorded for any Dart row.
hardware: data.json hardware field (published 2026-10-06): cpu_name 'M1 Eight-Core Processor', cpus 16, memory 7,733,008 kB, Linux 7.2.7-200.fc44.x86_64 (Fedora). Per-run server_cpu_cores / server_cpu_saturation imply about 4 CPUs allotted to each server container (derived from page data).
tradeoffs: Experimental HTTP/1.1 server for Linux built with Dart FFI and epoll; Linux/WSL only, minimal feature set.
caveats: The suite entry dart/jet_server/server.dart was written by the jet_server author (suite commits b869a75, ac9f6f2 and b3f17f2 by Wdestroier) and is specialised to the benchmark: it returns pre-built response byte arrays, routes by comparing raw bytes, sends no Content-Type header and uses no router, while the Drogon entry runs Drogon's routing (a sync advice for GET /, UserCtrl for the /user routes) and builds HttpResponse objects with Content-Type: text/plain; jet_server averages 62.3 bytes received per request vs 78.3 for Drogon (derived from total_bytes_received / total_requests), so handler work is not equal. The library is pure Dart: lib/src holds buffer_pool, constants, http_parser, jet_server_impl and syscall .dart files and the package depends only on ffi, so the event loop and parser are Dart code calling libc epoll/read/write through dart:ffi; the near-equal AOT and VM rows mean the JIT reaches AOT speed after warmup or both rows hit a common ceiling, not that a native C loop does the work. No Dart row in data.json (jet_server, shelf, relic, spry) carries the suite's server_cpu_saturation / server_cpu_cores validity probe, so whether jet_server was server-bound, or ran under the same 4-CPU allotment as Drogon, cannot be checked. The top rows at 256 connections cluster within 1.5% (morojs-engine 259,617, morojs 259,418, jet_server-vm 256,385, caprese 256,004, jet_server 255,549), consistent with a shared ceiling. name: libxev (HttpArena baseline server)
baseline: libreactorng (C, io_uring) and h2o (C) in the HttpArena suite; also nginx 1.31.4 (C) and Drogon (C++)
workload: HttpArena baseline profile: mixed GET/POST /baseline11 requests with query parsing (sum of query integers plus the body), 4096 keep-alive connections, pipeline depth 1, 5 s runs. Server on 32 cores / 64 threads of a Threadripper PRO 3995WX, gcannon load over loopback. The HTTP/1.1 server is written in Zig on libxev's io_uring backend, with one forked worker per CPU, SO_REUSEPORT and TCP_NODELAY, and parses requests with picohttpparser (C).
claimed_speedup: baseline-4096: 4,381,919 req/s vs libreactorng 4,377,377 (+0.1%, derived from page data, a tie), h2o 3,641,609 (1.20x, derived), nginx 3,284,513 (1.33x, derived) and Drogon 2,022,710 (2.17x, derived). On limited-conn-4096 (connections close after 10 requests) libxev's 2,672,662 is behind libreactorng's 2,685,717 (-0.5%, derived) and level with h2o (2,651,569) and nginx (2,626,297). latency-1m/10k/500k-8cpu are fixed-rate profiles scored on CPU per request, not throughput.
compiler_and_flags: libxev entry: Zig 0.16.0, zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast -Dcpu=native; picohttpparser.c is compiled by zig's C frontend at -O3 (frameworks/libxev/build.zig). libreactorng: Ubuntu 24.04 gcc, library configured with CFLAGS=-O3 -march=native and the server built with gcc -O3 -march=native. nginx 1.31.4: --with-cc-opt=-O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG (Debian trixie gcc). h2o: clang with CMake Release and -march=native -mtune=native, no LTO. Drogon: CMake Release (CMake's default -O3 -DNDEBUG) in the drogonframework/drogon:latest image, without -march=native, with jemalloc LD_PRELOADed.
hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3995WX (Zen 2, 64 cores / 128 threads, 8x DDR4-3200, one NUMA node), per HttpArena site/content/docs/hardware/_index.md. The server is pinned to cpuset 0-31,64-95 (32 cores / 64 threads) and the gcannon load generator to the other half. Traffic goes over loopback with MTU set to 1500, the governor is set to performance, and the sysctls are raised by scripts/lib/system.sh.
tradeoffs: libxev is an event loop (timers, sockets, files) rather than a web server; the measured server is a minimal handler in the HttpArena repo, not part of libxev.
caveats: The libxev README says it will not post benchmark results and claims only that you 'shouldn't notice a slowdown' against other event loops, so the figure here is an HttpArena application, not a library claim. Request parsing is done by picohttpparser (C, compiled at -O3), so the Zig code is the event loop, the glue and the arithmetic. Against the best C entry (libreactorng, also io_uring and SO_REUSEPORT per CPU) the result is a tie on baseline (+0.1%), and libreactorng is 0.5% ahead on limited-conn. The margins over h2o, nginx and Drogon reflect io_uring against epoll engines and minimal handlers against full servers (nginx runs a custom C handler module), not Zig codegen. The libxev server does no routing (every path gets the sum response) while libreactorng dispatches on the path, a small saving for the Zig side. The results JSON files are undated and are rerun by the suite's maintainers; competitor rows come from sibling JSON files in the same directory. HttpArena is a smaller suite (about 128 GitHub stars) than TechEmpower. [retier] Responses are about 86 bytes against libreactorng's about 109 (no Date or Server headers), there is no routing, and the entry is not enrolled in pipelined; best-of-N runs with the top entries clustered at the '~4.4M baseline peak' per profiles.sh, so the +0.1% is noise. The server ignores the write byte count (a short write would truncate) and clamps negative sums to 0 (templates are positive-only). Fixed-rate CPU per request slightly below libreactorng (20.31 vs 21.04 us at 1M). Open io_uring/IOCP/epoll issues #233, #227, #231.

Crow: c++ -O3 -std=c++11 with boost_system and pthread, multithreaded() (benchmarks/crow/run.sh, helloworld.cpp); compiler version not stated (Ubuntu 14.04 toolchain implied). nginx: the OpenResty nginx binary at /usr/local/openresty/nginx/sbin/nginx with the echo module, worker_processes 4 (benchmarks/nginx/run_echo.sh, conf/echo.conf); version and build flags not stated.

tradeoffs: JVM start-up, warm-up and memory are not part of the throughput figure; Netty is a networking toolkit, so the benchmarked server is hand-written on top of it.
caveats: Measured in December 2015 (last results commit 2015-12-22) with the legacy Netty 3 artifact org.jboss.netty:netty resolved through 'latest.integration', so the numbers describe neither Netty 4.x nor the current netty/netty code. The nginx baseline is handicapped: conf/echo.conf sets worker_processes 4 on a 6-core/12-thread Xeon while Netty 3's NioServerSocketChannelFactory uses a cached thread pool with its default worker count, and nginx is the OpenResty build with the echo module, not a tuned stock nginx; its 24.24 ms p99 against Netty's 4.08 ms points to worker saturation. Load generator (wrk, 12 threads) shares the host. JVM, Netty, Crow, OpenResty and compiler versions are not stated; the README table matches single runs (netty_04, nginx_echo_01). Crow is the 2015 ipkn/crow submodule, built -O3 and multithreaded, which is the fairer comparison. Netty loses to all three C servers (Kore, libmicrohttpd, Onion), so it is not faster than C servers in general. Single-author suite with 53 stars, not a well-known third-party benchmark. [retier] The measured jar is org.jboss.netty 3.2.10.Final per the Maven metadata. The handler omits the Date header the benchmark spec requires (bytes per response: Netty 100, nginx echo 119 chunked, Crow 128); nginx is capped at 4 workers with bimodal latency; the README picks the best of 4 runs. Current Netty 4.2 has open adaptive-allocator memory issues (#15691, #15850) and the HttpServerCodec pipelining advisory GHSA-pvjx-v7vp-62vq (High).

name: ntex
baseline: Drogon (C++) in the HttpArena baseline profile; lithium and cinatra (C++) in the TechEmpower Round 22 plaintext leaderboard
workload: HttpArena baseline profile (mixed GET/POST with query parsing, 4096 connections) with ntex 2 on its tokio-backed runtime; and TechEmpower Round 22 plaintext (ntex [raw]).
claimed_speedup: HttpArena baseline-4096: 2,168,712 req/s vs Drogon 2,022,710 (1.07x, derived from page data) and Cutelyst 2,153,860 (1.007x, a tie), behind nginx 3,284,513, h2o 3,641,609 and libreactorng 4,377,377. limited-conn-4096: ntex 1,449,176 is slower than Drogon 1,694,883 (0.86x, derived) and Cutelyst 1,736,401 (0.83x, derived). Workload profiles where ntex leads Drogon: async-32000 963,884 vs 143,001 (6.7x, derived) and Cutelyst 761,563 (1.27x); json-comp-4096 589,934 vs 127,466 (4.6x, derived); json-tls-4096 1,254,763 vs Drogon 253,055 (4.96x, derived), level with h2o 1,229,462 and behind nginx 1,313,755. TechEmpower Round 22 plaintext screenshot: ntex [raw] 7,000,539 vs cinatra 6,998,076, lithium 6,993,976 (+0.1%, a tie) and userver[bare] 5,974,256 (1.17x, derived).
compiler_and_flags: HttpArena: ntex built in the rust:1.94 image with cargo build --release, Cargo profile.release opt-level=3 and codegen-units=1, and no target-cpu=native and no LTO (the Dockerfile comment cites rustc SIGSEGV and GCC ICE history). Drogon: CMake Release (CMake's default -O3 -DNDEBUG) in the drogonframework/drogon:latest image, without -march=native, with jemalloc LD_PRELOADed. Cutelyst: CMake Release with Ubuntu 26.04 g++. TechEmpower Round 22: build flags not verified. The current FrameworkBenchmarks ntex.dockerfile (rust:1.93, RUSTFLAGS=-C target-cpu=native) postdates Round 22 (2023), and its benchmark_config.json no longer has an 'ntex [raw]' variant, so it does not describe the run that produced 7,000,539.
hardware: HttpArena: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3995WX (Zen 2, 64 cores / 128 threads), with the server pinned to cpuset 0-31,64-95 (32 cores / 64 threads) and gcannon on the other half over loopback (MTU 1500), per site/content/docs/hardware/_index.md. TechEmpower Round 22: Dell R440 Xeon Gold + 10 GbE, as printed on the leaderboard image; the gnet README describing that environment gives 28 HT cores of Intel Xeon Gold 5120, 32 GB RAM and Debian 12.
tradeoffs: Composable networking framework with its own runtimes (tokio, neon, compio); the README gives no benchmark figures.
caveats: The win over C++ is mixed and small where the work is equal. On baseline ntex is level with Cutelyst and 7% over Drogon, behind nginx, h2o and libreactorng (C), and on limited-conn it is 14-17% slower than both C++ frameworks. The large json-comp, json-tls and async margins are over Drogon only: its JSON path deep-copies jsoncpp Values per item (a library choice), and Drogon's gzip level was not checked against ntex's flate2 level 1. ntex is built without target-cpu=native, while nginx and h2o use -march=native and Drogon does not. The TechEmpower margin over lithium and cinatra is 0.1%, noise on a saturated plaintext test: the first 19 rows are within 6% of each other and the first nine within 0.3%, which is network and pipelining bound. Those numbers come from a screenshot of the Round 22 leaderboard hosted in the gnet author's illustrations repo (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/panjf2000/illustrations/master/benchmark/techempower-plaintext-top50-light.jpg), since the primary results site was not reachable. The ntex README itself makes no performance claim. The HttpArena results JSON files are undated and are rerun by the suite's maintainers. [retier] async-32000 6.7x: the Drogon entry puts every delay on app().getLoop() (a single main event loop at 812% CPU) while ntex's sleep rounds to a 16 ms tick, so a 10 ms delay averages 30.63 ms; json-comp 4.6x: ntex gzips at level 1 against Drogon's level 6 (about 1,718 vs 1,393 bytes per response). The entry runs Logger middleware on every request with no logger installed, so baseline and limited-conn likely understate ntex. Measured ntex 2.18 on tokio; current 4.2.0.
found_via: WebSearch 'comparative performance study web frameworks Rust actix-web Go Java Spring C++ Drogon' led to the-benchmarker/web-frameworks; HttpArena (github.com/MDA2AV/HttpArena) found by following the TechEmpower-style suites; per-entry JSON in site/data/results opened via raw.githubusercontent.com; TechEmpower plaintext screenshot via the gnet README

name: PowPow
baseline: Drogon 1.9.13 (C++, trantor event loop; the-benchmarker cpp/drogon, cmake release build); also agoo-c 0.7 (C) in the same table
workload: the-benchmarker/web-frameworks minimal HTTP contract (GET /, GET /user/:id, POST /user on port 3000), total_requests_per_s at 64, 256 and 512 connections, each framework in its own container.
claimed_speedup: powpow 0.2 in data.json updated 2026-10-06: 237,033 / 248,309 / 238,538 req/s at 64 / 256 / 512 connections vs Drogon 177,005 / 178,341 / 171,358 (1.34x / 1.39x / 1.39x, derived from page data); vs agoo-c (C) 1.65x at 64, 1.16x at 256, 1.19x at 512, and vs cwist 3.9 (C, best C row at 64, 186,252) 1.27x (derived from page data). Per busy server core: powpow 106.6k / 116.5k / 112.4k vs Drogon 69.9k / 71.8k / 69.3k req/s (derived from total_requests_per_s / server_cpu_cores). The win appears in this one snapshot only: the 2026-10-02 snapshot (commit 8657397), after the suite's 2026-09-30 commit 4cce691 'ensure powpow is running multithreaded', has powpow at 100,905 / 93,959 / 91,689 req/s with 13% CPU saturation (0.56x / 0.53x / 0.53x Drogon), and the 2026-09-24 snapshot (commit f673364) has it on one core at 0.63x / 0.55x / 0.55x (derived from page data). README 'Dummy Benchmarks' (first-party, no baseline, wrk 4 threads / 100 connections / 5 s run via GitHub Actions, hardware not stated): 202,743 req/s multi-threaded (4 workers, SO_REUSEPORT) keep-alive and 97,965 req/s single-threaded keep-alive.
compiler_and_flags: Suite nim/Dockerfile: every Nim entry built with --passC:-flto --passL:-flto --assertions:off (nimlang/nim:2.2 on bookworm); -d:powpowPewPew is read only in powpow's own config.nims, which the suite's server.nim build does not use, so it is most likely a no-op. Drogon: plain cmake release without LTO on debian:trixie-slim.
hardware: data.json hardware field (published 2026-10-06): cpu_name 'M1 Eight-Core Processor', cpus 16, memory 7,733,008 kB, Linux 7.2.7-200.fc44.x86_64 (Fedora). Per-run server_cpu_cores / server_cpu_saturation imply about 4 CPUs allotted to each server container (derived from page data).
tradeoffs: Event-notification library (alternative to libuv and libevent) with a built-in HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 server, epoll/kqueue/IOCP and an io_uring option; no router, so the suite entry hand-matches paths.
caveats: The README says 'not production-ready and may contain bugs and security vulnerabilities' and claims 'Pow Pow is the #1 fastest HTTP server' from the same benchmark site, a first-party reading of this table. The suite entry nim/powpow was written by the powpow author (georgelemon commits, including 4cce691 on 2026-09-30); it has no router and dispatches on method and path by hand, while the Drogon entry runs Drogon's routing and HttpResponse path; powpow averages 99.3 bytes received per request vs 78.3 for Drogon (derived from total_bytes_received / total_requests). The win over Drogon is in one published snapshot only: on 2026-10-02 (after the multithreading fix) powpow ran at 13% CPU saturation and 0.53-0.56x Drogon, on 2026-09-24 at one core and 0.55-0.63x. The build flag -d:powpowPewPew does not appear in src/powpow.nim, src/powpow/{loop,net,types,proto}.nim or src/powpow/proto/{http,httpserver,multithread}.nim at HEAD, so its effect was not found (possibly a no-op). The README footer says 'All rights reserved' beside an MIT LICENSE file (2026 OpenPeeps); the LICENSE file governs. The README 'Dummy Benchmarks' (wrk -t4 -c100, 5 s) ran on a GitHub Actions runner with client and server on the same machine and no baseline. 20 stars. Suite-level weaknesses: published snapshots move a lot between runs (Drogon 101,282-179,279 req/s across the 2026-09-15 to 2026-10-06 snapshots) and a snapshot gives no repeat spread; the suite README says a run is server-bound only above 75% CPU saturation and invalid below 50%, and in the 2026-10-06 snapshot the 60 fastest rows sit at 49-63% (Drogon 62-63%), so the ceiling for the fastest servers may be the load generator or the box rather than the server; the presence of the server_cpu_saturation / server_cpu_cores probe places this snapshot in the README's current zrk --closed keep-alive revision, although the README's contract paragraph still describes oha with keep-alive disabled; the workload is three trivial routes (GET /, GET /user/:id, POST /user) with near-empty bodies. The C/C++ rows are only Drogon 1.9.13 (cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=release, threads_num 0 = auto, Server and Date headers disabled, no LTO), oatpp 1.3, agoo-c 0.7 and cwist 3.9 (C); cwist is the best C row at 64 connections (186,252) and agoo-c at 256 and 512; nginx, h2o and lithium are not rows in this suite. Same table, losers to Drogon at 256 connections: Crystal toro 166,910, Go fasthttp 166,243, C# aspnet-minimal-api 147,805 vs Drogon 178,341. The CPU string 'M1 Eight-Core Processor' on an x86_64 Fedora kernel is not a recognisable CPU model, and no C++ compiler version is pinned in the suite files read (cpp/drogon/config.yaml language version '14/17'), which is why this is B and not A. [retier] Build asymmetry: the Nim entry gets LTO and assertions off while Drogon is a plain release without LTO, on different distro GCCs. p99 is 7.6/15.9/21.3 ms against cwist's 0.50/1.84/3.68 ms (a throughput-only win); single-threaded until suite commit 4cce691 (2026-09-30); issue #2 reports an 8x regression (138k to 16-30k req/s); the multithreaded server does not run on Windows; the README says not production-ready.
found_via: the-benchmarker/web-frameworks data.json (raw.githubusercontent.com HEAD) ranked by total_requests_per_s; followed by WebSearch 'TechEmpower Round 23 results Rust may-minihttp xitca-web faster than drogon' (TechEmpower pages are egress-blocked) and the repo README at github.com/the-benchmarker/web-frameworks
why_faster: Event loop built directly on epoll with one worker per core and SO_REUSEPORT (README, suite entry).

name: Quarkus (Vert.x/Netty, JDK 21)
baseline: nginx (C, hand-written handler module compiled -O3 -march=native, per HttpArena frameworks.json) in the HttpArena suite; h2o, Drogon, Mongoose, libreactorng and other C/C++ rows come from the same results directory
workload: HttpArena request throughput on one 64-core machine (mixed GET/POST with query parsing at 4096 connections, plus pipelined, HTTP/2 and h2c baseline profiles as listed). Entry is Quarkus with RESTEasy Reactive on Vert.x/Netty, JDK 21, 'optimized JVM tuning' (HttpArena tuned mode).
claimed_speedup: Rows measured with the current entry (commit 029e5d6, 2026-08-21) against nginx rows from commit df1a679 (2026-08-20): baseline-h2-256 (h2 over TLS) 4,668,449 req/s vs nginx 3,414,750 (1.37x) but h2o 16,106,978 (0.29x); pipelined-4096 (16x pipelining, reference-only, excluded from the composite) 7,858,636 vs nginx 4,037,345 (1.95x), h2o 4,938,603 (1.59x), Drogon 7,801,404 (1.01x). Slower than nginx on the scored HTTP/1.1 and TLS profiles: baseline-4096 1,818,132 vs nginx 3,284,513 (0.55x), h2o 3,641,609 (0.50x), Drogon 2,022,710 (0.90x); limited-conn-4096 564,503 vs nginx 2,626,297 (0.21x); json-tls-4096 588,855 vs nginx 1,313,755 (0.45x) and h2o 1,229,462 (0.48x), though 2.33x Drogon's 253,055; static-h2-256 173,987 vs nginx 802,090 (0.22x); static-tls-1024 339,193 vs nginx 720,869 (0.47x); json-comp-4096 301,675 vs Drogon 127,466 (2.37x). The baseline-h2c-256 row (6,188,551 vs nginx 2,456,329, 2.52x) is stale and not valid evidence. All ratios derived from page data.
compiler_and_flags: Quarkus 3.17.8 (RESTEasy Reactive, quarkus-rest) compiled for Java 21, run on the eclipse-temurin:25-jre image; quarkus.vertx.prefer-native-transport=true is set but pom.xml lacks netty-transport-native-epoll, which Quarkus 3.17.8 requires, so the runs almost certainly used Java NIO (inferred).
hardware: HttpArena dedicated machine: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3995WX (Zen 2, 64 cores / 128 threads, one NUMA node, 8x DDR4-3200), 251 GiB RAM, Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS, kernel 6.17.0-22-generic, Docker 29.3.0 (runc), performance governor (site/data/current.json, site/content/docs/hardware/_index.md); server pinned to cpuset 0-31,64-95 for these profiles (scripts/lib/profiles.sh), load generator (gcannon, h2load for HTTP/2) on the same machine over loopback.
tradeoffs: JVM start-up and warm-up cost and memory footprint are not part of the throughput figure; Netty/Vert.x event loop under a full framework.
caveats: The baseline-h2c rows in quarkus-jvm.json (and its json-h2c and unary-grpc rows) were last written no later than the 2026-07-24 migration commit 5698fa8 and cannot come from the current entry: its Dockerfile has passed -Dvertx.disableH2c=true since at least 2026-03-28, application.properties opens no port 8082 (the h2c prior-knowledge port), and meta.json no longer subscribes to baseline-h2c, json-h2c or grpc; every h2c row also reports p99 equal to the mean, unlike nginx's h2c rows measured on 2026-08-20, so the 2.52x h2c ratio is a cross-run comparison against stale data. The remaining wins are on pipelining (reference-only in the HttpArena README) and h2 over TLS, where nginx's HTTP/2 path trails h2o by 4.7x on the same profile; on the scored HTTP/1.1 baseline, limited-conn, json-tls and static profiles Quarkus is 0.21x to 0.55x of nginx. Uses 6.8 to 10.7 GiB of memory against nginx's 3.5 GiB. The entry's meta.json and README say JDK 21 but the Dockerfile runs Temurin 25. nginx is a custom C handler module, not a stock config; every entry is a minimal hand-written handler, so this measures server-engine overhead, not static-file serving. Results are 5 s runs on one machine, rerun per framework by the maintainers. [retier] json-comp runs gzip level 1 at about 1,580 bytes per response against Drogon's 1,392, and HttpArena's size-squared scoring cuts the 2.37x to about 1.84x. baseline-h2 is one constant GET /baseline2?a=1&b=1 with 100 streams per connection, Quarkus about 27 bytes per response against nginx's 82; h2o is 3.45x Quarkus. The entry pins 3.17.8 (latest 3.40.1).

name: Tako (per-thread server)
baseline: Drogon 1.9.13 (C++, trantor event loop; the-benchmarker cpp/drogon, cmake release build); also agoo-c 0.7 (C) in the same table
workload: the-benchmarker/web-frameworks minimal HTTP contract (GET /, GET /user/:id, POST /user on port 3000), total_requests_per_s at 64, 256 and 512 connections, each framework in its own container.
claimed_speedup: the-benchmarker data.json (updated 2026-10-06): tako 2.4 219,732 / 200,361 / 193,822 req/s at 64 / 256 / 512 connections vs Drogon 1.9.13 177,005 / 178,341 / 171,358 (1.24x / 1.12x / 1.13x, derived from page data); vs agoo-c 0.7 (C) 143,753 / 214,704 / 200,748 (1.53x at 64, 0.93x at 256, 0.97x at 512, derived); vs CWIST 3.9 (C) 186,252 / 166,573 / 162,101 (1.18x / 1.20x / 1.20x, derived). Corroborated in HttpArena (MDA2AV/HttpArena site/data/results/tako.json and drogon.json, Threadripper PRO 3995WX): baseline-4096 3,258,564 vs Drogon 2,022,710 (1.61x), limited-conn-4096 2,474,910 vs 1,694,883 (1.46x), pipelined-4096 22,082,892 vs 7,801,404 (2.83x), json-comp-4096 212,739 vs 127,466 (1.67x), json-tls-4096 904,303 vs 253,055 (3.57x), latency-500k-8cpu 470,285 vs 374,962 (1.25x), 8gbit-512 48,998 vs 49,360 (0.99x), all derived from page data.
compiler_and_flags: the-benchmarker: tako built in rust:1.98-slim with cargo build --release, Cargo.toml release profile opt-level 3, lto = true, codegen-units = 1, panic = abort (the Dockerfile repeats lto/panic/codegen-units via --config), tako-rs 2.4 with feature per-thread, no target-cpu. Drogon v1.9.13 built in debian:trixie-slim with build-essential (GCC 14 from Debian trixie, inferred from the image) via cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=release (CMake's Release flags -O3 -DNDEBUG), C++17, no LTO, no -march; config.json threads_num 0 (one IO thread per core). HttpArena: tako built in rust:1.99-trixie with RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native', lto = 'fat', codegen-units = 1; Drogon built from drogonframework/drogon:latest with CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (no -march=native, compiler version not stated) and run with LD_PRELOAD jemalloc.
hardware: the-benchmarker data.json hardware field: cpu_name 'M1 Eight-Core Processor' (does not name a recognisable CPU model), 16 logical CPUs, 7,733,008 kB RAM, Linux 7.2.7-200.fc44.x86_64; per-run server_cpu_cores / server_cpu_saturation imply about 4 CPUs allotted to each server container (derived from page data). HttpArena current.json: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3995WX (64 cores, 128 threads), 251 GiB, Ubuntu 24.04.4, kernel 6.17.0-22, governor performance.
stars_or_usage: 163 stars; tako-rs crate 5,186 downloads (crates.io API, 2026-10-12; latest 2.4.1)
tradeoffs: Multi-transport Rust framework (HTTP/1.1, h2, h3, WebSocket, SSE, gRPC) on Tokio or Compio; the fast path is the thread-per-core 'per-thread' server with current-thread runtimes and SO_REUSEPORT listeners.
caveats: The suite win is architectural (thread-per-core runtime with SO_REUSEPORT listeners), not a Rust language effect, and margins are small (1.12-1.24x over Drogon; agoo-c (C) beats tako at 256 and 512 connections). The README's own benchmark compares only against Actix Web, ntex and Axum on a 24 vCPU EPYC 9655P container (not C or C++). the-benchmarker weaknesses: one published snapshot (data.json updated 2026-10-06, no repeat spread); the suite README says above 75% server CPU saturation the number is the framework's and below 50% it is not, and tako (56-57%) and Drogon (62-63%) both sit in the band between; the 57 of the 60 fastest rows at 256 connections that carry a saturation value range 49-69% (suite median 71%), so the fastest servers may be generator-bound; the README describes the current method as zrk --closed keep-alive (saturation fields exist only in that method, so this snapshot is probably that revision, inferred) but an older paragraph still describes oha with keep-alive disabled; three trivial routes with near-empty bodies. Flags differ: Rust side uses LTO and codegen-units 1, Drogon has no LTO; in HttpArena the Rust side is built with target-cpu=native and Drogon generically, and the HttpArena tako entry is maintained by the tako author (meta.json maintainers dancixx). HttpArena does not generalise the win to nginx: level on baseline-4096 (3,258,564 vs nginx 3,284,513, 0.99x) and far behind on HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 (baseline-h2-256 741,740 vs 3,414,750; baseline-h3-64 534,205 vs 4,849,624) and static TLS (142,858 vs 720,869). nginx, h2o and lithium are not rows in the-benchmarker; same-table losers to Drogon at 256 connections include Crystal toro, Go fasthttp and C# aspnet-minimal-api.
found_via: the-benchmarker/web-frameworks data.json (raw.githubusercontent.com HEAD) ranked by total_requests_per_s; followed by WebSearch 'TechEmpower Round 23 results Rust may-minihttp xitca-web faster than drogon' (TechEmpower pages are egress-blocked) and the repo README at github.com/the-benchmarker/web-frameworks
why_faster: Thread-per-core design with one current-thread runtime per CPU and SO_REUSEPORT listeners (from the HttpArena entry description and the README).

verification.tier_reason: Independent, well-known suite (the-benchmarker/web-frameworks, 7.1k stars): data.json rows tako 2.4 (id 3313) 219,732 / 200,361 / 193,822 req/s and drogon 1.9 (id 55) 177,005 / 178,341 / 171,358 at 64/256/512 match the record; build files (rust/tako/Cargo.toml, rust/Dockerfile, cpp/drogon/config.yaml, cpp/Dockerfile) are public, but the published cpu_name 'M1 Eight-Core Processor' does not identify a CPU model, the C++ compiler version is only implied by the debian:trixie-slim build-essential image, and both servers ran at 57-62% CPU saturation, inside the band the suite's README calls neither valid nor invalid, so not A.
verification.notes: Numbers verified in the-benchmarker data.json and corroborated by HttpArena, where tako also beats Drogon by 1.25-3.57x on most shared tests (8gbit tie), though HttpArena builds tako with target-cpu=native against a generic Drogon build. Shortcomings: architectural not language-level win, 1.12-1.24x margins, saturation in the suite's grey zone, unidentifiable CPU string, LTO/native-flag asymmetry, loses to agoo-c (C) at 256/512 and to nginx on HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and static TLS in HttpArena.

name: Thruster (Rust, thruster-grpc)
baseline: gRPC C++ (grpc/grpc) servers cpp_grpc_st, cpp_grpc_mt and cpp_asio_grpc in the grpc_bench suite
workload: grpc_bench complex_proto unary SayHello echo: 50 client connections, 1000 concurrent requests, unlimited QPS, 120 s with 30 s warmup; server capped by docker --cpus at 1-4 CPUs (2026 run, 4096m RAM) or 1-3 CPUs (2022 run, 512m RAM).
claimed_speedup: grpc_bench complex_proto unary, ratios derived from page data. Latest run (discussion 559, 2026-04-23, commit c4c93b3): 1 server CPU rust_thruster_st 98,464 req/s and rust_thruster_mt 88,443 vs cpp_grpc_st 57,140, cpp_grpc_mt 57,403, cpp_asio_grpc 56,669 (st vs st 1.72x, mt vs mt 1.54x); 2 CPUs rust_thruster_mt 134,859 vs cpp_grpc_mt 74,574 (1.81x) and cpp_asio_grpc 74,869; 3 CPUs 138,576 vs 81,581 (1.70x); 4 CPUs 135,989 vs 85,485 (1.59x). Older run (wiki 2022-04-23, commit 14a8435): 1 CPU rust_thruster_st 41,334 (23.88 ms avg) vs cpp_grpc_st 26,700, cpp_grpc_mt 26,376, cpp_asio_grpc 24,926 (1.55x, 1.57x, 1.66x), rust_thruster_mt 36,793 (1.39x vs cpp_grpc_mt); at 2 CPUs rust_thruster_mt 56,740 vs cpp_grpc_mt 69,882 (0.81x) and at 3 CPUs 65,903 vs 71,806 (0.92x).
compiler_and_flags: 2026-04 run at c4c93b3: rust_thruster_st/mt on the rust:1.94 image, cargo build --release --locked with opt-level 3, codegen-units 1, lto true, jemallocator; thruster 1.3.10 (hyper_server feature) plus thruster-grpc 0.2.3 on hyper 0.14 and prost 0.11; st runs tokio current_thread, mt a multi-thread runtime with GRPC_SERVER_CPUS workers. cpp_grpc_st/mt on the gcc:15.2.0 image: g++ -O3 -flto (mt adds --std=c++20) on main.cpp and the generated stubs, linked against Debian's prebuilt libgrpc++-dev and jemalloc (apt-get, unpinned; Debian's grpc package is 1.51.1, search snippet only), so the -O3 -flto flags never reach the gRPC core. 2022 run at 14a8435: rust:1.59 with thruster 1.2.2, thruster-grpc from git and hyper 0.13, same release profile; C++ on gcc:11 with the then-current Debian libgrpc++-dev (version not checked). HEAD has since moved the C++ images to gcc:16.1.0.
hardware: 2026-04-23 run (discussion 559): Intel Xeon Gold 6548N @ 2.80 GHz (16 cores shown), 64 GB RAM; server limited to 1-4 CPUs and 4096m RAM, ghz client on 11 CPUs, 120 s with 30 s warmup, 50 connections, 1000 concurrency. 2022-04-23 run (wiki): Intel Xeon E5-1650 v3 @ 3.50 GHz, 32 GB RAM; server limited to 1, 2 or 3 CPUs and 512m RAM, client 9 CPUs.
tradeoffs: Rust middleware web framework; the gRPC server is the separate thruster-grpc crate; the repository's last commit is October 2024.
caveats: The Thruster README gives no benchmark numbers, only 'Runs fast'. The measured server is thruster plus the separate thruster-rs/thruster-grpc crate on hyper's HTTP/2 stack and tokio, the same hyper/h2 base as tonic, so the result largely measures hyper/h2 rather than Thruster's own code. In the 2022 run the win was single-CPU only (cpp_grpc_mt led at 2 and 3 CPUs); the 2026 run shows rust_thruster_mt ahead of cpp_grpc_mt at 1-4 CPUs (1.54x to 1.81x), but java_vertx_grpc beats it at 2-4 CPUs and rust_tonic_st beats it at 1 CPU. The C++ baseline is Debian's distro libgrpc++ (1.51.1 per Debian's tracker, a December 2022 release; search snippet only), not an upstream gRPC built with the harness's -O3 -flto, so it is both older and built with distro flags. Server CPU limits use docker --cpus quotas, which penalise gRPC C++'s extra internal threads. Thruster's last commit is 2024-10-16 (stale).
found_via: WebFetch github.com/LesnyRumcajs/grpc_bench wiki 2022-04-23 results; Cargo.toml and src/main.rs of rust_thruster_st_bench read via raw.githubusercontent.com
why_faster: Single-threaded tokio current_thread runtime on hyper with jemalloc at a 1-CPU limit (inference from the benchmark setup; no source claim).

name: tokio-uring (HttpArena minimal HTTP/1.1 server)
baseline: nginx 1.31.4 (C, custom handler module, -O3 -march=native) in the HttpArena suite; h2o, mongoose, libreactorng, libioma (C) and Drogon, Cutelyst, hical, agensio, userver (C++) rows alongside
workload: HttpArena H/1.1 profiles (baseline with 4096 connections, pipelined, limited-conn) on one 64-core machine; the entry is a hand-written HTTP/1.1 parser on tokio-uring (io_uring completion API, owned buffers), one runtime per core with SO_REUSEPORT, no HTTP framework.
claimed_speedup: baseline-4096: 3,565,878 req/s vs nginx 3,284,513 (1.09x, derived from page data), Drogon 2,022,710 (1.76x), hical 3,228,043 (1.10x), agensio 3,558,559 (1.00x); level with or behind h2o 3,641,609 (0.98x), mongoose 3,707,598 (0.96x). pipelined-4096: 48,876,057 vs nginx 4,037,345 (12.1x), Drogon 7,801,404 (6.27x) and libreactorng (C, io_uring) 43,424,448 (1.13x). limited-conn-4096: 2,636,459 vs nginx 2,626,297 (1.00x, a tie).
compiler_and_flags: tokio-uring entry: rust:1.95 image, RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native' cargo build --release with opt-level 3, codegen-units 1, thin LTO, panic=abort, tokio-uring 0.5 (frameworks/tokio-uring/Dockerfile and Cargo.toml). C/C++ rows: nginx 1.31.4 with a custom handler module, Debian trixie toolchain, --with-cc-opt='-O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG'; h2o clang CMake Release -march=native -mtune=native (no LTO); mongoose gcc-14 -O3 -march=native -flto; Drogon CMake Release in the unpinned drogonframework/drogon:latest image with jemalloc preloaded; hical gcc-14 CMake Release -march=native -mtune=native; libreactorng -O3 -march=native (HttpArena frameworks/<name>/Dockerfile).
hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3995WX (Zen 2, 64 cores / 128 threads, one NUMA node), 251 GiB RAM, Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS, kernel 6.17.0-22-generic, Docker 29.3.0 (runc), performance governor (HttpArena site/data/current.json and site/content/docs/hardware/_index.md). The server container is pinned to cpuset 0-31,64-95 (32 cores / 64 threads) and the load generator (gcannon for H/1.1, h2load for HTTP/2) to 32-63,96-127 over loopback; 5 s runs, best of 3 (scripts/lib/common.sh, scripts/lib/profiles.sh, scripts/benchmark.sh).
stars_or_usage: 1.5k stars (tokio-uring); the server itself is an HttpArena entry
tradeoffs: tokio-uring needs Linux with io_uring and is still described by its README as very young (filesystem and network operations); the HttpArena server is a minimal hand-rolled parser, not a framework; the repo's last commit is from July 2025.
caveats: Not an io_uring win: the suite's plain tokio entry (epoll, same hand-rolled parser design, same Rust flags) is faster than tokio-uring on every shared profile (baseline-4096 4,187,085 vs 3,565,878; limited-conn-4096 2,721,455 vs 2,636,459; pipelined-4096 54,755,795 vs 48,876,057). The entry is a minimal hand-rolled server written for HttpArena (no maintainer listed, not the tokio-uring project's own code): it routes only /pipeline and answers every other path with the a+b sum, and sends about 63 bytes per response against about 135 for nginx (Date and Server headers; derived from page data, bandwidth over req/s), so the per-request work is not the same. At baseline-4096 it is behind libreactorng (4,377,377), libioma (4,255,834), mongoose (3,707,598) and h2o (3,641,609) and level with agensio; at limited-conn-4096 it ties nginx (1.00x) and is behind libioma, mongoose, libreactorng and h2o. The large pipelined ratio is on a reference-only profile (pipeline depth 16) and mostly reflects nginx's pipelining cost. 5 s runs, best of 3, server limited to 32 of 64 cores; results files are undated. The tokio-uring README states no benchmark numbers and calls the project 'still very young'; last commit 2025-07-07.
found_via: WebFetch of github.com/MDA2AV/HttpArena/tree/main/site/data/results (file list) and /frameworks (meta.json, Dockerfile, README); per-entry JSON read via raw.githubusercontent.com and compared with every C/C++ row in the same directory; frameworks/tokio-uring/meta.json names the tokio-rs/tokio-uring repo
why_faster: io_uring completion-based I/O with owned buffers and one runtime per core sharding accepts through SO_REUSEPORT, against nginx on epoll (HttpArena entry description; the repo gives no claim).

verification.tier_reason: Upgraded B to A on the HttpArena precedent: every quoted number matches site/data/results/tokio-uring.json and the sibling nginx/drogon/hical/agensio/h2o/mongoose/libreactorng JSON files; the code is public (frameworks/tokio-uring/{Dockerfile,Cargo.toml,src/main.rs}, frameworks/nginx/{Dockerfile,nginx.conf}, scripts/benchmark.sh, scripts/lib/profiles.sh), Rust and nginx flags are in the Dockerfiles and Cargo.toml, and the CPU model (Threadripper PRO 3995WX) is in site/data/current.json.
verification.notes: All quoted numbers verified; tier raised to A on the HttpArena precedent. Shortcomings to record: the record's why_faster (io_uring) is contradicted by the suite's own epoll tokio entry, which beats tokio-uring 1.17x at baseline-4096; minimal hand-rolled handler sending about half nginx's response bytes (same_algorithm false); behind four C servers at baseline and limited-conn; pipelined is reference-only. Metadata confirmed: MIT, 1.5k stars, last commit 2025-07-07 (stale), not a fork, not archived.

name: tonic (Rust gRPC)
baseline: gRPC C++ (grpc/grpc) servers cpp_grpc_st, cpp_grpc_mt and cpp_asio_grpc in the grpc_bench suite
workload: grpc_bench 'complex_proto' unary scenario: 50 client connections, 1000 concurrent requests, unlimited QPS, 120 s with 30 s warmup, server RAM 512m, commit 14a8435 (2022-04-22); server limited to 1, 2 or 3 CPUs.
claimed_speedup: 1-CPU server (req/s, avg latency): rust_tonic_st 41,546 (23.77 ms) vs cpp_grpc_st 26,700 (37.33 ms), cpp_grpc_mt 26,376 and cpp_asio_grpc 24,926 (1.56x, 1.58x, 1.67x, derived from page data); rust_tonic_mt 35,443 (1.33x vs cpp_grpc_st). At 2 CPUs rust_tonic_st 42,072 vs cpp_grpc_st 26,229 (1.60x) but cpp_grpc_mt 69,882 and rust_tonic_mt 53,832 (0.77x); at 3 CPUs cpp_grpc_mt 71,806 vs rust_tonic_mt 64,091 (0.89x).
compiler_and_flags: 2022-04-23 run at grpc_bench commit 14a8435. rust_tonic_st: rust:1.59 image, cargo build --release --locked, [profile.release] opt-level 3, codegen-units 1, lto true; jemallocator 0.3.2, tonic 0.7, prost 0.10, tokio 1.17 current_thread. cpp_grpc_st: gcc:11 image, g++ -O3 -flto on main.cpp and the protoc-generated stubs, linked with -lgrpc++ -lprotobuf -lgrpc -ljemalloc from the distro packages (apt libgrpc++-dev). cpp_grpc_mt: the same plus --std=c++20 and -lpthread, one completion queue and thread per GRPC_SERVER_CPUS. cpp_asio_grpc: asio-grpc 1.0.0, CMake Release, the same distro libgrpc++. The gcc:11 image was presumably Debian bullseye, whose libgrpc++-dev is gRPC 1.30.2-3 (Debian package listing, search snippet only); that library was built with Debian's flags, not the benchmark's -O3 -flto.
hardware: Intel(R) Xeon(R) CPU E5-1650 v3 @ 3.50GHz, 32G RAM (grpc_bench wiki page 2022-04-23; server limited to 1, 2 or 3 CPUs, client 9 CPUs)
tradeoffs: Rust async gRPC on tokio and hyper; the winning variant is single-threaded, so it cannot use more than one core per process; calling it from C++ needs a separate process.
caveats: The win appears only with the server limited to 1 CPU. There, all three C++ servers (cpp_grpc_st 26,700, cpp_grpc_mt 26,376, cpp_asio_grpc 24,926 req/s) trail rust_tonic_st (41,546) and rust_tonic_mt (35,443). With 2 and 3 CPUs, cpp_grpc_mt (69,882 and 71,806) and cpp_asio_grpc (66,828 and 71,296) lead rust_tonic_mt (53,832 and 64,091). The wiki page states no compiler versions or flags; they come from the Dockerfiles at commit 14a8435, and the repo's current Dockerfiles (gcc 16.1, Rust 1.94) are newer than the run. The C++ servers link the distro libgrpc++ package (probably gRPC 1.30.2 from Debian bullseye, a 2020 release, against tonic 0.7 from 2022). That library is built with distribution flags, while the Rust stack is compiled whole with opt-level 3 and LTO. At 1 CPU, rust_grpcio, which compiles the gRPC C core from source, reached 31,035 req/s, also above every C++ server, so part of the gap may come from the distro build or the old gRPC version rather than from tonic. go_vtgrpc (44,074) topped the 1-CPU table. Both servers do the same echo work (copy the request string into the reply). It is a single run with no variance reported. The tonic README makes no performance claim; the evidence is the third-party grpc_bench suite, whose latest wiki results page is this 2022-04-23 run. [retier] All three grpc_bench C++ servers post exactly one RequestSayHello per completion queue against 1,000 in-flight requests, which gRPC's performance guide calls essentially serial request processing (grpc_bench issue #490, open since 2024-11-04; same code at c4c93b3), so the C++ baseline is untuned. The 'win only at 1 CPU' caveat is outdated: discussion #559 (2026-04-23, Xeon Gold 6548N) has rust_tonic_mt beating the best C++ at 2/3/4 CPUs (130,370 vs 74,869; 139,886 vs 81,581; 136,638 vs 85,485). The repo is now grpc/grpc-rust.

name: bladebench Rust raw TCP server
baseline: the same minimal blocking TCP/HTTP server in C (gcc -O2) and C++ (g++ -O2) from the same repo
workload: Single-threaded blocking accept loop that reads once, writes a fixed 'HTTP/1.1 200 OK' response and closes the connection, load-tested with wrk -t8 -c1000 -d10s over loopback.
claimed_speedup: wrk 8 threads, 1000 connections, 10 s: Rust 49,388 req/s vs C++ 40,715 (1.21x, derived from page data) and C 32,976 (1.50x, derived), ~0 socket errors.
compiler_and_flags: Makefile: gcc -O2 blade_core.c, g++ -O2 blade_core.cpp, 'rustc blade_core.rs' with no -O or opt-level (an unoptimised debug build), and 'zig build-exe blade_core.zig' (Debug by default). No compiler versions. The C/C++ side is not -O3, and the optimisation levels are not matched.
tradeoffs: Toy micro-benchmark, not a usable server library.
caveats: Not a valid language comparison. The Rust build has no optimisation flag while C and C++ use -O2. All four servers are the same single-threaded blocking loop (accept, one read, write a fixed 'HTTP/1.1 200 OK ... OK' response, close), so the time goes to kernel accept/close and the wrk client, not to language codegen. The C and C++ servers are functionally identical yet differ by 23% (32,976 vs 40,715 req/s), which shows the run-to-run noise exceeds the claimed Rust margin. There is one 10 s run per server and no repetitions, and CPU, kernel and compiler versions are not stated. Minor asymmetries: the Rust server binds 127.0.0.1 while C and C++ bind INADDR_ANY (wrk connects to 127.0.0.1 in every case); Rust uses write_all and unwrap() (a reset would abort the server) where C and C++ do a single write; C reads 1023 bytes and C++ 1024. The listen backlog is 128 in C, C++ and Rust std alike. The Zig row (80,700 req/s) came with 701k write errors. The repo has 0 stars and a single commit (2025-07-12).

Each server got one 10 s wrk run with no hardware or compiler versions stated, and the byte-for-byte equivalent C and C++ servers differ by 23%. That is the degenerate-benchmark precedent (ThreadPool, hop) for D.

name: bladebench Zig raw TCP server
baseline: the same minimal blocking TCP/HTTP server in C (gcc -O2) and C++ (g++ -O2) from the same repo
workload: Single-threaded blocking accept loop that reads once, writes a fixed 'HTTP/1.1 200 OK' response and closes the connection, load-tested with wrk -t8 -c1000 -d10s over loopback.
claimed_speedup: wrk -t8 -c1000 -d10s on loopback (first-party, single run): Zig 80,700 req/s vs C++ 40,715 (1.98x, derived from page data) and C 32,976 (2.45x, derived from page data); the same table marks the Zig row '701k write errors (buffer overrun)' and the C/C++ rows 0 errors. Not a like-for-like measurement (the Zig server skips the request read).
compiler_and_flags: Makefile: gcc -O2 and g++ -O2 for C and C++; 'zig build-exe blade_core.zig' with no optimize flag (default Debug mode, Zig 0.12 per source banner). Not -O3 and not matched.
tradeoffs: Toy micro-benchmark, not a usable server library.
caveats: Not a valid language comparison. blade_core.zig accepts, writes the fixed response and closes without ever reading the request, whereas blade_core.c and blade_core.cpp read() once before writing; closing a socket with unread data makes the kernel reset the connection, which fits the 701k write errors the page reports for Zig (the page blames a 'buffer overrun'), so the Zig row measures less work and an abortive close rather than codegen. The Makefile builds Zig with a bare 'zig build-exe blade_core.zig' (Debug mode, Zig 0.12 per the source banner) and Rust with plain rustc (no -O), against gcc -O2 / g++ -O2 for C and C++; none is -O3. Each server is a single-threaded blocking accept loop that closes every connection, while wrk keeps HTTP/1.1 keep-alive and must reconnect after every response, so throughput is dominated by connection setup and teardown. Ports differ (8080, 8081, 8083) and only the Zig server sets SO_REUSEADDR. CPU, kernel, compiler and wrk versions are not stated; single run. The C and C++ servers are functionally identical yet differ by 23% (32,976 vs 40,715), which shows the noise. The README itself recommends 'Zig (if tuned)'. One commit, 0 stars.

name: Caddy
baseline: nginx (C), HTTPS reverse proxy
workload: Claim: HTTPS reverse proxying (HN title only). Opened benchmark: Vegeta open-loop attack at 500 req/s for 10 s against https://localhost/ through Caddy or nginx in Docker, proxying to patrickdappollonio/hello-docker (20-byte reply) or to docker-http-server serving a 256K data.bin; metric is latency at a fixed rate, not throughput. Cross-check: HttpArena HTTP/1.1, TLS, h2 and h3 origin-serving profiles with custom Go handler modules in Caddy and a custom C module in nginx.
claimed_speedup: No verified win. 'Caddy Outperforms Nginx 4x' is the title of HN item 33725154 (snippet only; the post at https://manishrjain.com/reverse-proxy-caddy-nginx, which the benchmark README credits as its inspiration, could not be opened: getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND). patrickdappollonio/nginx-vs-caddy-benchmark (Vegeta, fixed rate 500 req/s for 10 s, HTTPS reverse proxy to a local container): hello-docker response mean latency nginx 337.36 us vs Caddy 385.502 us (nginx 14% faster per the README); 256K file first run Caddy 1.310211 ms vs nginx 1.536594 ms (Caddy 1.17x, derived from page data) with an untuned nginx.conf; after commit 7cb9315c tuned nginx, nginx 1.192198 ms vs Caddy 1.471049 ms (nginx 23% faster per the README). HttpArena (Caddy v2.8.4 serving directly, not proxying): baseline-4096 431,894 vs nginx 3,284,513 req/s (0.13x), limited-conn-4096 237,689 vs 2,626,297 (0.09x), pipelined-4096 761,137 vs 4,037,345 (0.19x), json-tls-4096 321,964 vs 1,313,755 (0.25x), static-tls-1024 159,177 vs 720,869 (0.22x), baseline-h3-64 360,511 vs 4,849,624 (0.07x); ratios derived from page data.
compiler_and_flags: patrickdappollonio benchmark: unpinned caddy:latest and nginx:latest images, no versions or build flags stated. HttpArena cross-check: Caddy v2.8.4 built with xcaddy on golang:1.22-bookworm with the httparena and httparena_json handler modules; nginx 1.31.4 built with --with-cc-opt='-O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG'.
hardware: patrickdappollonio benchmark: laptop, 6-core Intel Core i7-10710U, 15.7 GB RAM, Pop!_OS 22.04 LTS, kernel 6.0.6. HttpArena: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3995WX (64 cores, 128 threads), server container pinned to cpuset 0-31,64-95 (32 cores, 64 threads) per scripts/lib/profiles.sh.
tradeoffs: Automatic HTTPS and a Go module system; higher CPU and memory per request than nginx; garbage-collected runtime.
caveats: Recorded as an unsupported and contradicted claim. The 4x figure is only an HN submission title; the post could not be opened, so its method, versions and configs are unknown. In the opened benchmark (11 stars, no license, 'quick-and-dirty' by its own description) the first nginx.conf had worker_connections 1024 and no sendfile, access_log or upstream HTTP/1.1 settings, so nginx logged every request and proxied over HTTP/1.0 while Caddy ran with its defaults; the author's commit 7cb9315c tuned nginx (worker_connections 4000, access_log off, sendfile, proxy_http_version 1.1) and nginx then won the 256K test by 23% on mean, 13% on p95 and 11% on p99; nginx had already won the hello test by 14% before tuning. The tuned config still has no upstream keepalive directive. Images are unpinned :latest, single runs at a fixed 500 req/s. HttpArena shows Caddy 4x to 14x slower than nginx on every shared row, but it tests Caddy v2.8.4 (2024, Go 1.22) as an origin server with custom handler modules rather than as a reverse proxy, and the Caddy rows (commit 0a18672, 2026-08-15) and nginx rows (commit df1a679, 2026-08-20) come from different runs; the nginx rows at 0a18672 are within about 2% of the later ones on baseline, limited-conn and pipelined and 9% higher on json-tls, so the gap holds either way. The Caddy README makes no performance claim against nginx. [retier] Recorded as an unsupported and contradicted claim. The 4x figure is only an HN submission title; the post could not be opened, so its method, versions and configs are unknown. In the opened benchmark (11 stars, no license, 'quick-and-dirty' by its own description) the first nginx.conf had worker_connections 1024 and no sendfile, access_log or upstream HTTP/1.1 settings; in every run Vegeta sent HTTP/2 to Caddy (offered by ALPN) and HTTP/1.1 to nginx ('listen 443 ssl' without http2), and the nginx upstream block has no keepalive directive, so nginx opened a new backend TCP connection per request while Caddy reused pooled ones. Both asymmetries favour Caddy, and the tuned nginx still won.

name: cblt
baseline: nginx (Docker image nginx:latest per benchmark/nginx/Dockerfile)
workload: Apache Benchmark, 3000 requests at 1000 concurrent connections, downloading a 23 KB logo.png from 127.0.0.1; response-time percentiles.
claimed_speedup: README percentile table for 'ab -c 1000 -n 3000 http://127.0.0.1/logo.png' (23,911-byte file; ab reports ms): 50%: 179 vs nginx 1209 (6.75x lower, derived from page data); 75%: 194 vs 1655 (8.53x); 100%: 200 vs 2146 (10.73x). Feature list: '10 times faster than Nginx for small content under 100KB'. The table was added on 10 Nov 2024 (commit 3fb9fa5, version 0.1.5) and replaced an earlier 5 MB test (ab -c 100 -n 300, logo_huge.png) whose medians were cblt 1956 ms, nginx 1941 ms, Caddy 1768 ms.
compiler_and_flags: Cargo release profile with lto = true (opt-level 3 by default); benchmark/cblt/Dockerfile runs the Docker image ievkz/cblt:0.1.2 (Alpine, cargo build --release) and overwrites its config with a Cbltfile for host 'example.com'; nginx is the nginx:latest Docker image with its default configuration; both run in Docker.
hardware: Not stated for the 23 KB table; the earlier README revision with the 5 MB test shows the runs were made from a Windows MINGW64 shell on a Lenovo machine with Docker containers.
tradeoffs: Minimal file server and reverse proxy with load balancing, Docker label integration and TLS; far fewer features than nginx.
caveats: Single first-party run of one 23 KB file with no raw ab output, so it cannot be checked that cblt actually returned the file: the repo's benchmark/cblt/Cbltfile (last changed in PR #4 'Highload', merged the same day the table appeared) defines only host 'example.com', and cblt 0.1.x returns 403 Forbidden when no '*' host exists and the Host header (here 127.0.0.1) does not match; only the root Cbltfile ('*:80', ./assets) would have served logo.png, and the README does not say which was used. The previous README benchmark (5 MB file, same week) showed cblt at parity with nginx (median 1956 vs 1941 ms) and slower than Caddy, and was removed rather than kept beside the new table. Medians above one second for nginx at 1000 concurrent connections for 3000 requests suggest connection queueing (listen-backlog overflow and SYN retransmission are a plausible cause, not verified) rather than per-request serving cost. Hardware, OS, Docker networking mode and the nginx config are not stated; the '10x faster for content under 100KB' headline rests on this one file. The benchmarked build was cblt 0.1.x (November 2024); the current crate is 0.6.2 (December 2024) and the last commit is June 2025. [retier] Harness flaw (inferred from source): tokio/mio listens with backlog 1024 while nginx's Linux default is 511, so at ab -c 1000 nginx's accept queue overflows and its about 1.2 s median fits the 1 s SYN retransmit rather than serving cost. Correctness bug at HEAD: when Accept-Encoding has gzip the file body is gzip-compressed but the Content-Encoding header line has been commented out since e5861b5 (2024-11-10) and Content-Length stays the uncompressed size. No timeouts, unbounded buffering. An older 5 MB run in article-en.md shows parity with nginx.

name: D (LDC, betterC) port of the C epoll raw HTTP responder (httpbench)
baseline: the C epoll raw HTTP responder in the same suite (c/epoll/http_epoll.c, gcc -O3), same fixed 'Hello, World!' reply, prefork over 2 CPUs
workload: Fixed-response HTTP/1.1 keep-alive responder (no parsing, no routing) under wrk for 30 s at 2, 8, 64, 128 and 256 connections, plus 256 connections with pipeline depth 10; level-triggered and edge-triggered variants, prefork over 2 pinned CPUs.
claimed_speedup: No claim in the README; the tables show parity. Level-triggered D vs C RPS: 43752 vs 39886 (2 clients), 93942 vs 88906 (8), 176532 vs 187141 (64), 232039 vs 226433 (128), 276433 vs 261440 (256), 2075254 vs 2132917 (pipelined); edge-triggered D vs C: 43096 vs 39911, 86692 vs 85850, 166672 vs 173116, 234975 vs 216984, 261737 vs 258486, 1938169 vs 2005563. Ratios 0.94x to 1.10x (derived from page data); D ahead in 8 of 10 non-pipelined cells (behind at 64 clients) and about 3% behind in both pipelined cells.
compiler_and_flags: D: ldc2 1.29.0 via dub, DFLAGS '--betterC' from dlang/epoll/meta.json with the runner default '--release -O3 --boundscheck=off --ffast-math --mcpu=native' appended (_suite/runner.d applyDefaultBuildEnv); C: gcc -Wall -O3 -D_GNU_SOURCE (plus -D EDGE for the edge variant) from c/epoll/Makefile, gcc version not stated (build-essential in an unpinned debian:testing Docker image, _suite/Dockerfile).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3700X (8 cores, 16 threads) host, Fedora 36, kernel 5.17.9; server in a KVM VM with 2 pinned CPUs and load generator (wrk 4.1.0) in a KVM VM with 14 pinned CPUs, both Ubuntu 22.04 (bridged network)
tradeoffs: betterC @nogc D, i.e. D used as a C replacement without druntime, GC or exceptions; a micro benchmark that does not parse HTTP, so it says nothing about a real server.
caveats: This is a parity data point, not a win: counting the 10 non-pipelined cells, D is ahead in 8 and behind in 2 (64 clients, both variants) by at most 10%, and about 3% behind in both pipelined cells (0.97x); single 30 s runs with no variance reported, so the differences are probably noise. The D build adds --mcpu=native and --ffast-math while the C build is plain -O3 without -march=native, so the flags are not matched (likely irrelevant for a syscall-bound loop). The C file is frevib's epoll echo server slightly modified; the D file is a near line-by-line port calling the same libc functions, but it is not identical: epoll_wait takes 256 events per call in D versus 128 in C, D keeps each client's 2048-byte buffer inline in a static array while C mallocs a 4096-byte buffer on every accept, and D skips C's send-length checks and partial-request handling (asserts instead). The suite's own C README says the D variants exist to test performance issues of the during library, and the main README presents the C servers as the reference ceiling, so neither source claims D is faster. Benchmark code, flags, ldc2 1.29.0 and the CPU are public; only the gcc version is missing. Unlicense is a public-domain dedication with no patent grant. Last commit 2022-05-30.

name: during (D io_uring wrapper)
baseline: C liburing echo server (MarkReedZ/mrloop) and C++ epoll echo server (methane/echoserver), both built with -O3; in the httpbench suite also the C liburing HTTP-reply server
workload: Single-threaded echo server, 50 clients, 512-byte messages, 10 s, best of 3, driven by haraldh/rust_echo_bench on loopback; second data set is a fixed-reply HTTP responder under wrk at 2 to 256 connections in tchaloupka/httpbench.
claimed_speedup: echo_server README: during 131090 req/s vs C liburing server 95894 req/s vs C++ epoll server 45063 req/s (1.37x and 2.91x, derived from page data). httpbench README (separate harness, D port of the C liburing server, RPS from the tables): during/raw vs C io_uring raw is 41404 vs 37872 (2 clients), 86500 vs 75711 (8), 150752 vs 155627 (64), 221916 vs 185000 (128), 253256 vs 246812 (256), 2012380 vs 1898736 (256 clients, pipeline depth 10), i.e. 0.97x to 1.20x (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: during echo server: dub build -b release --compiler=ldc2, ldc2-1.18.0. Baselines: built with -O3 and no -g (compiler name and version not stated). httpbench D builds: ldc2 1.29.0 with --betterC --release -O3 --boundscheck=off --ffast-math --mcpu=native; C baseline gcc -Wall -O3 -D_GNU_SOURCE -luring (gcc version not stated, liburing cloned from axboe/liburing at build time).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3700X 8-Core, Fedora 31 Linux 5.3.12 (echo_server README); httpbench: AMD Ryzen 7 3700X (8 cores, 16 threads) host, Fedora 36, kernel 5.17.9; server in a KVM VM with 2 pinned CPUs and load generator (wrk 4.1.0) in a KVM VM with 14 pinned CPUs, both Ubuntu 22.04 (bridged network)
tradeoffs: D library (druntime or betterC), Linux 5.7+ io_uring only; the echo example preallocates fixed io buffers registered with io_uring and can exceed the memlock limit; the library does not use liburing, so it reimplements the ring handling in D.
caveats: First-party numbers from the library author. The echo baselines are different programs, not ports: mrloop is a generic C event-loop library using liburing and methane/echoserver a generic C++ epoll echo server, whereas the during example uses a preallocated mempooled buffer pool registered with io_uring and swaps read/write buffers, so the echo comparison is not same-algorithm. The echo numbers date from 2019 (ldc2-1.18.0, Fedora 31, Linux 5.3.12), are best-of-3 on loopback with the load tool on the same machine, and the baselines' compiler and version are not stated (only -O3 without -g); the library has since been rewritten for Linux 6.x and released as 0.6.0 (2026-10-09) without new measurements. The httpbench rows compare a D port (dlang/during/raw/app.d) of the C liburing HTTP responder (c/io_uring/http_uring.c) with the same provided-buffer design (D uses 1024-byte buffers, C 2048): single 30 s runs per cell on a 2-vCPU server VM, D ahead in 5 of 6 cells (up to 1.20x at 128 clients) and 3% behind at 64 clients, within plausible single-run noise, and the D build adds --mcpu=native --ffast-math while the C build is plain -O3. The httpbench C README says the D variants exist to test performance issues of the during library, not to claim a win, and the during README makes no performance claim beyond pointing to the echo example. An echo server is a socket event loop rather than an HTTP server, so the category fits loosely.

corrected_fields.caveats: First-party numbers from the library author. The baselines are different programs, not a port: mrloop is an event-loop library and the C++ epoll echo server is a generic echo server, whereas the during example uses a fixed memory pool and buffer swapping, so the echo comparison is not same-algorithm. The echo README numbers come from 2019-era tools (ldc2-1.18.0, Linux 5.3.12, io_uring just introduced) and best-of-3 on loopback with one client machine; compiler versions of the baselines are missing. The httpbench rows are single 30 s runs per cell on a 2-vCPU server VM; the D port beats the C port in 5 of 6 cells (up to 1.20x) and loses by 3% at 64 clients, which is within plausible run-to-run noise for single runs, and the D build adds --mcpu=native while the C build does not. The httpbench README itself says the D variants exist to test performance issues of the during library, not to claim a win. The during README makes no performance claim and only points to the echo example. The echo-server category fits 'serving' loosely: it is a socket event loop, not an HTTP server.

name: fib
baseline: Sogou workflow (C++ HTTP server) and uSockets (C, BoringSSL) in the lesismal go-*-benchmark repositories; nginx (C) in HttpArena
workload: HTTP/1.1 echo, pipelined, TLS 1.3 echo and WebSocket echo benchmarks, 10,000 connections, 1 KiB payload, GitHub-hosted ubuntu-24.04 runners with 4 vCPUs (2 for server, 2 for client), single run each.

First-party go-http1-benchmark (single GitHub Actions run, 10,000 connections, 1 KiB): fib 194,671 TPS vs Sogou workflow (C++) 150,407 (1.29x), memory 32 MB vs 14 MB.
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.27; HttpArena entry built with CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -ldflags='-s -w' (frameworks/fib/Dockerfile). Baselines: workflow v1.1.0 built from source with CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release and its server main.cc with c++ -std=c++11 -O3 -DNDEBUG (go-http1-benchmark frameworks/workflow/build.sh); uSockets server.c with cc -std=c11 -O3 -DNDEBUG on pinned uSockets and BoringSSL (go-tls-benchmark frameworks/usockets/build.sh); nginx 1.31.4 with a custom handler module at -O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG (HttpArena frameworks/nginx/Dockerfile). Compiler versions not stated.
hardware: HttpArena: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3995WX (site/data/current.json). First-party rows: GitHub Actions ubuntu-24.04 runner (the container got 4 vCPUs instead of the wanted 8).
tradeoffs: Event-loop networking library for Go that keeps the net/http handler model; no LICENSE file found in the repo, so reference only; uses far more memory than workflow (32 MB vs 14 MB) and TLS 1.3 pipelining uses 180 MB vs 51 MB for uSockets.
caveats: First-party single runs on noisy shared GitHub runners (the README says read differences of a few percent as ties); 2 vCPUs for the server, where workflow keeps its default 20 handler threads plus pollers. It loses to axum on HTTP/1 echo (236,244 vs 194,671), to uSockets on TLS pipelining (690,000 vs 735,000) and to the Go servers uws_std, fnet and uws_events on WebSocket pipelining; the workflow pipeline row is missing because workflow does not support pipelining. 'uws_events'/'uws_std' are Go servers on UIO, not uWebSockets; the C++ uWebSockets entry of go-websocket-benchmark is not shown in fib's table. In HttpArena (fib entry maintained by lesismal, CPU model not stated) it is slightly behind nginx at baseline-4096 (3,164,504 vs 3,284,513) and far ahead of nginx on h2c (12,891,491 at 256 connections vs 2,456,329), but agensio (C++) beats it on h2c (15,185,367) and h2 (14,744,015 vs 5,634,126 at 256), libreactorng (C) beats it on pipelined-4096 (43,424,448 vs 20,397,414) and mongoose (C) on most WebSocket profiles; fib leads static-tls-1024 (1,229,892 vs agensio 1,191,970 and nginx 720,869). No LICENSE file in the repo. [retier] HttpArena rows are cross-run against nginx's (different dates) and agensio is ahead; the entry runs prefork with 32 child processes (GOMAXPROCS=2 each) because one process with 64 Ps stalls on Go's shared heap lock and GC. First-party rows are single runs on a shared 4-vCPU runner with client and server on one VM, workflow at its stock 2 pollers plus 20 handler threads with strftime Date per response, and the TLS pipeline rate-driven. No LICENSE; the author says not production-proven (issue #1); object reuse is on by default (fasthttp rule); no http.Hijacker.

name: ioxide
baseline: nginx 1.31.4 (C) and h2o (C) in the HttpArena suite; also libreactorng and libioma (C, io_uring), mongoose (C) and agensio (C++)
workload: HttpArena baseline (mixed GET/POST with query parsing, 4096 connections), pipelined and HTTP/2 profiles for a hand-written HTTP/1.1 handler on ioxide, a shared-nothing io_uring runtime for .NET (one ring per reactor thread, raw syscalls without liburing).
claimed_speedup: baseline-4096: 4,111,381 req/s vs nginx 3,284,513 (1.25x, derived from page data), h2o 3,641,609 (1.13x), mongoose 3,707,598 (1.11x), agensio 3,558,559 (1.16x). pipelined-4096: 53,376,982 vs nginx 4,037,345 and libreactorng 43,424,448. baseline-h2-1024: 12,235,767 vs nginx 3,320,285 (3.7x).
compiler_and_flags: .NET SDK 11.0.100-preview.7 / runtime 11.0.0-preview.7, dotnet publish -c Release with ServerGarbageCollection and runtime-async=on (HttpArena frameworks/ioxide/Dockerfile and ioxide-arena.csproj, ioxide NuGet 0.7.211); nginx 1.31.4 configured with --with-cc-opt='-O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG' on debian:trixie (frameworks/nginx/Dockerfile); h2o built with clang, CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release and -march=native.
hardware: HttpArena dedicated 64-core machine, containers per entry (README says '64-core dedicated hardware'; CPU model, RAM, NIC and kernel not stated)
tradeoffs: Linux-only (io_uring, seccomp must be unconfined), needs a preview .NET 11 runtime; HTTP/3 uses ngtcp2/nghttp3 and TLS uses OpenSSL (C libraries).
caveats: The ioxide repo is owned by the same GitHub account as the HttpArena suite (MDA2AV), so tier is C rather than B even though every entry runs through one public harness. The ioxide Dockerfile notes that moving from .NET 11 preview.6 to preview.7 took baseline-4096 from 4.11M to 3.90M with no change to the entry; the saved 4,111,381 is the preview.6 figure, and at the 3.90M the currently pinned preview.7 gives, the lead shrinks to about 1.19x nginx, 1.07x h2o, 1.05x mongoose and 1.10x agensio (derived from page data). It is behind libreactorng (4,377,377) and libioma (4,255,834), both C io_uring servers, at baseline-4096, so the win over nginx comes from io_uring against nginx's epoll rather than from C#; behind nginx at limited-conn-4096 (2,543,314 vs 2,626,297); and on baseline-h2-1024 the 3.7x over nginx is against nginx's slow h2 path, while h2o (15,633,023) and agensio (C++, 14,210,433) both beat ioxide's 12,235,767, and agensio also leads static-h2-1024 (1,420,432 vs 950,009). The h2 path uses pure-C# ioxide.http2 with OpenSSL encrypting in userspace; h1 TLS uses OpenSSL handshake plus kernel kTLS; h3 rides the bundled C libraries ngtcp2 and nghttp3. The repo README gives no throughput numbers against C servers. Results JSON files are undated and the suite is rerun by its maintainers; entries are minimal hand-written handlers (nginx is a custom C handler module, ngx_http_httparena_module.c), and the baseline-4096 profile mixes GET and POST with query parsing, not static files. CPU model not stated, so not tier A. The .NET build uses Server GC and the runtime-async preview feature; README marks ioxide experimental. [retier] Correction: the stored 4,111,381 baseline-4096 is the final saved run of HttpArena PR #1372 (results commit 048221e), already on the pinned .NET preview.7 with runtime-async=on (3,896,541 was preview.7 before runtime-async), so the 1.25x over nginx stands. The benchmarked ioxide 0.7.211 carries issue #221 (severity high: a recycled write slab lets one client receive another client's response bytes), fixed only in 0.15.251 (2026-09-27); keep-alive rows are probably unaffected. The entry's h2/h3 static cache (Multiplexed.cs) is built in the entry and never refreshed, breaking HttpArena's engine rule, so the static-h2 and static-h3 wins are suspect. The HTTP/1.1 handler sends no Date or Server header (about 63 vs 135 bytes per response) and uses unbounded buffers; nginx rows 2026-08-15/20, ioxide 2026-08-29 (cross-run).

name: kawipiko
baseline: NGINX (distribution package; configuration in the kawipiko examples/nginx folder), also darkhttpd
workload: Static 'Hello World!' file served from a CDB archive held in memory (kawipiko) or from tmpfs (NGINX), wrk over loopback with keep-alive, 512 to 16384 connections; plus a 250k-file OpenStreetMap tile set at 16384 connections.
claimed_speedup: Hello World over loopback, 2 server threads, 2 wrk threads: kawipiko 106,698.89 / 100,296.65 / 95,628.34 / 53,548.52 req/s at 512 / 2048 / 4096 / 16384 connections (section 'Last updated in August 2018') vs NGinx 79,816.08 / 78,211.46 / 75,970.82 / 43,909.67 (section 'Last updated in August 2019'), 1.34x / 1.28x / 1.26x / 1.22x (derived from page data, pairing the two separately dated sections). OpenStreetMap tile run (one section, August 2019, i7 4770, 8 threads, 16384 connections, 2 minutes): kawipiko --archive-inmem 238,499.86 req/s, --archive-mmap 237,239.35, 8 processes mmap 248,266.83 vs NGinx 8 workers 188,255.32 (1.27x / 1.26x / 1.32x, derived); the author states ~25% more requests/s, ~29% lower average latency, ~40% lower p90 latency, ~25% less CPU per request, while NGinx used the least RAM and kawipiko about 1 GiB. The summary (December 2021) calls kawipiko 'at least on-par with NGinx'.
compiler_and_flags: Go build of kawipiko (version and flags not stated); NGINX from distribution packages (version and build flags not stated); server run with --archive-inmem, --security-headers-disable and --timeout-disable.
hardware: Laptop with Intel Core i7 3667U (2 physical cores, 4 threads), 8 GiB RAM for the Hello World runs; desktop Intel Core i7 4770 (4 cores, 8 threads), 32 GiB for the tile run; wrk and server pinned to separate physical cores, tmpfs.
tradeoffs: Serves only a prebuilt CDB archive, so content changes need a rebuild; HTTP/2 is about 6 times slower than its HTTP/1 path (Go net/http), where the author says NGINX is much better; kawipiko used about 1 GiB RAM in the tile run while NGINX used the least; AGPL licence.
caveats: First-party, measured on 2013-era CPUs (i7 3667U laptop, i7 4770 desktop) with an older kawipiko version (the author says the current one is at least 10% more efficient). The Hello World kawipiko rows (August 2018) and NGinx rows (August 2019) are in separately dated sections, so the 1.22-1.34x ratios compare runs a year apart; only the tile run is a same-session comparison. kawipiko was requested at '/' and NGinx at '/index.txt' (the author chose the path he says favours NGinx). NGinx is a distribution package with an author-tuned config (examples/nginx); kawipiko ran with --archive-inmem, --security-headers-disable and --timeout-disable (the author says timeouts cost 10-15%). wrk reports socket errors for kawipiko at every row from 512 connections (timeouts 86 / 4,449 / 2,288 at 2048 / 4096 / 16384, versus NGinx 11 / 187 / 1,121) and in both tile runs (kawipiko 7,032 timeouts, NGinx 16,833). The tile CDB was deduplicated to ~100k of ~250k files, and the wrk command shown targets a single URL, so how the tile list was driven is not shown. The author says kawipiko over HTTP/2 is about 6x slower than its own HTTPS over HTTP/1, where NGinx is not. The author says the real advantage is deployment simplicity. The win comes from the CDB in-memory design on fasthttp, not from Go versus C codegen.
found_via: WebSearch 'static file web server written in Rust OR Zig OR Go "faster than nginx" benchmark wrk requests/sec README comparison h2o lwan' (github.com, gitlab.com, codeberg.org filter)
why_faster: Content pre-indexed in a CDB archive held in memory with a compact lookup (no per-request file system calls), on Go fasthttp; the README says the advantage grows for many small files accessed in random patterns.

name: linkerd2-proxy (Rust) vs Envoy as service-mesh sidecars
baseline: Envoy (C++), as the Istio sidecar proxy
workload: Kinvolk service-mesh-benchmark harness (wrk2 load against emojivoto-style microservices, mTLS on, metrics on, no retries or tracing) at 20, 200 and 2,000 RPS, 10-minute runs, 5 kept runs per level after discarding outliers, reporting the maximum memory and CPU time of any single data-plane proxy plus client-side latency percentiles; the 2020 figures come from an internal run at 4,000 RPS.
claimed_speedup: Buoyant posts on linkerd.io (source markdown in linkerd/website): (1) 'Why Linkerd doesn't use Envoy' (2020-12-03), internal benchmark on Kinvolk's harness at 4,000 RPS: Linkerd2-proxy 14-15 MB vs Istio's Envoy 135-175 MB ('ten times the size'), CPU 15 ms per instance vs 22-156 ms ('from 50% more to 10x more'), called 'not an entirely fair comparison'. (2) 'Benchmarking Linkerd and Istio' (2021-05-27, Linkerd 2.10.2 vs Istio 1.10.0 minimal, 2,000 RPS): max data-plane proxy memory 17.8 MB vs 154.6 MB (8.7x, derived from page data), max proxy CPU time 10 ms vs 88 ms; added latency 9 ms vs 15 ms at the median and 47 ms vs ~253 ms at the max (Istio 438% more at the max, derived from page data). The Buoyant press release's '36% more median latency' is snippet only and does not match the post's data (67% more, derived from page data). (3) 2021 Redux (2021-11-29, Linkerd 2.11.1 vs Istio 1.12.0, 2,000 RPS): 26.3 MB vs 156.2 MB memory (5.9x, derived from page data), 36 ms vs 67 ms CPU (1.86x), added latency 6 ms vs 17 ms median and 42 ms vs ~350 ms max. name: monolake

Plain HTTP: nginx ahead or equal everywhere, 16 threads about 707k vs about 688k (monolake about 0.97x), 4 threads about 194k vs about 168k (about 0.87x), 512 B about 186k vs about 168k (monolake about 0.91x), equal at 32768 and 65536 B. name: Orion Proxy
baseline: Envoy Proxy (C++)
workload: HTTP reverse proxy to an nginx upstream, wrk at 2048 and 16384 connections, 1 to 48 cores assigned to the proxy.
claimed_speedup: README: '2x-4x better throughput and latency than Envoy Proxy'. HTTP chart (docs/pics/performance/baseline/wrk-reqsec.png), requests/s orion-mr-st vs envoy: 2048 connections, 1 core 46,593 vs 12,819 (3.63x, derived from page data), 48 cores 1,881,522 vs 310,231 (6.06x, derived); 16384 connections, 1 core 38,573 vs 17,059 (2.26x, derived), 48 cores 1,410,611 vs 514,254 (2.74x, derived). HTTPS chart (tls/wrk-reqsec.png): 2048 connections, 1 core 30,398 vs 11,268 (2.7x, derived), 48 cores 1,478,634 vs 324,135 (4.56x, derived); 16384 connections, 1 core 26,354 vs 14,096 (1.87x, derived), 48 cores 738,429 vs 483,069 (1.53x, derived). The latency chart (baseline/wrk-latency.png, microseconds, percentile not stated, lower is better) does not support a 2x-4x latency win across the board: with 2048 connections Orion's latency is higher than Envoy's at 2, 8, 16, 24, 32 and 48 cores (e.g. 48 cores 251,325 vs 201,636; 16 cores 193,495 vs 85,659) and lower only at 1 core (280,347 vs 323,953), about equal at 4; with 16384 connections Orion is worse at 1, 2 and 4 cores (1,879,395 vs 1,789,400; 1,944,476 vs 1,769,852; 971,338 vs 633,244) and better at 8-48 cores (e.g. 270,335 vs 1,815,855 at 16 cores).
hardware: Two-host testbed: DUT proxy host and tester host with wrk on NUMA 0 and nginx upstream on NUMA 1, 25 Gbps Mellanox and Intel NICs, IRQ affinity tuned (CPU model not stated)

caveats: First-party; the numbers exist only as chart images, and the repo carries no benchmark scripts, wrk invocation, Envoy or Orion configuration (docs/performance holds only performance.md; tools/ has no bench files). The methodology lists 'Envoy, Ng-proxy, and Nginx' as compared proxies and scaling at 1-32 cores, but the charts show only Orion (series 'orion-mr-st', a runtime mode the page does not explain) and Envoy, at 1-48 cores. Envoy version, build and config, Orion build flags and the CPU model are not stated, so tier C. The README's 2x-4x is lower than the 6x seen in the 2048-connection HTTP chart at 48 cores and does not hold for latency: the latency chart is mixed (with 2048 connections Orion's latency is higher than Envoy's at 2 and 8-48 cores; with 16384 connections it is worse at 1-4 cores and better at 8-48 cores). [retier] In the TCP chart Envoy does 53/47 req/s on 1-2 cores and 0 on 1-4 cores at 16,384 connections, with no Envoy configuration or circuit-breaker settings published; the latency charts plot an unstated tail value, not a mean (Little's law gives about 1.1 ms against the chart's 251,325 us at 48 cores) and do not back the README's latency claim; the top core counts are capped by the testbed (L4 plateaus at 2.3M near nginx's 2.6M limit).
