name: routez
baseline: nginx 1.30.5 (C) and HAProxy 3.2.23 (C)
workload: nginx-style edge server in Zig 0.17 measured with wrk, keep-alive, 256 connections, 3 workers each, median of 3 x 10 s runs, on Docker Desktop on an Apple M-series Mac (10 cores).
claimed_speedup: requests/s routez vs nginx: fixed response 627k vs 529k (1.19x, derived from page data), reverse proxy to keep-alive upstream 262k vs 208k (1.26x), TLS fixed response 582k vs 324k (1.8x), TLS 10 KB static file 208k vs 152k (1.4x), TLS new connection per request 17k vs 13k; p99 at a held 208k req/s fixed response 3.6 ms vs nginx 21.2 ms.
compiler_and_flags: routez: zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast -Dcpu=native (native+aes+sha2 on arm64) with Zig 0.17.0 inside an ubuntu:26.04 container (bench/lib.sh, bench/Dockerfile); nginx 1.30.5 is the nginx.org stable Ubuntu package and HAProxy 3.2 comes from the vbernat PPA, both on OpenSSL 3.5, with compile flags not stated. nginx config (bench/conf/nginx.conf) is tuned: reuseport, keepalive_requests 100000, open_file_cache, sendfile, TLS 1.3 pinned to AES-128-GCM and X25519.
hardware: Apple M-series Mac, 10 cores, Docker Desktop VM (the author writes 'a VM is not a benchmark machine'), 20 Sep 2026
tradeoffs: Pure Zig edge server with HTTP/1.1, HTTP/3, TLS 1.3, ACME, reverse proxy and load balancing; no license file found, so reference only.
caveats: The author's own table is mixed: 10 KB static file 308k vs nginx 312k (a tie); full RSA-2048 TLS handshakes 1.0k/s vs nginx 3.6k/s; HTTP/3 10 KB static file 94k/s vs 247k/s; gzip on the fly through the proxy 5.5k/s vs HAProxy 15k/s; a new connection per request 187k/s vs nginx 231k/s; p99 at a held rate proxied 4.30 ms vs HAProxy 1.79 ms; at the held 208k req/s fixed-response row HAProxy's p99 (3.2 ms) beats routez's 3.6 ms; a reload every 2 s under load fails 74 requests vs HAProxy 0. Rows come from different passes: the 10 KB static row reads 308k (tie) in the main table but '343k/s, 10% ahead' in the 'rows that have come off this list' table. The README itself says two runs of one build on a busy Mac differed by 90% and that a VM is not a benchmark machine; numbers are a median of 3 x 10 s runs on Docker Desktop on an unnamed Apple M-series Mac. routez is built with -Dcpu=native while nginx and HAProxy are generic distribution packages. The build needs a sibling checkout of endel/quic-zig (public, MIT). No LICENSE file in the repo (LICENSE returns 404, GitHub shows no license), so usability is reference. Harness strengths: a correctness gate checks byte-identical responses and identical TLS parameters before each row, servers are measured one at a time with rotated order and pinned cores, and nginx gets its best settings. [retier] Both sides use epoll (quic-zig picks libxev Epoll on Linux, not io_uring). bench.sh's gate compares status and body only, rate.sh checks status 200 only, and the held rate is 0.5x the slowest server's peak from a separate 4 s wrk pass. quic-zig's README says 'Not production-ready'.
found_via: WebSearch '"faster than nginx" Rust OR Zig OR Go reverse proxy web server benchmark wrk results README' (github.com filter)
why_faster: Worker threads with SO_REUSEPORT on libxev, an open-file cache and sendfile for plain-HTTP static files (README feature list); no profile attribution for the wins.

name: rproxy
baseline: nginx as a reverse proxy (version and config not stated); HAProxy 2.8.5 (vendored build) as a second row
workload: HTTP/1.1 reverse proxy in front of an nginx backend answering '200 OK' with a 2-byte body, wrk -t4 -c100 -d10s keep-alive, two proxy workers each for rproxy and nginx on two pinned cores, loopback.
claimed_speedup: June run (bench/BENCHMARK_RESULTS.md, 2026-06-27, median of 3 after warmup, proxies pinned to cores 2-3 with 2 workers each): rproxy 189,810.00 req/s (557 us) vs nginx reverse proxy 153,484.52 (662 us) = 1.24x; rproxy before its hot-path optimisation 135,700.79 (0.88x); backend ceiling 362,163.20. August run (README, measured 2026-08-16 with bench/haproxy_baseline.sh, labelled median of 3 but the script keeps the best of 3): rproxy 323,035 (352 us) vs nginx reverse proxy 282,032 (400 us) = 1.15x and HAProxy 2.8.5 266,603 (395 us) = 1.21x; ceiling 632,175. rproxy with TLS 134,168 req/s (no TLS comparison against nginx).
compiler_and_flags: Cargo release profile: lto = 'fat', codegen-units = 1, panic = 'abort', opt-level = 3, debug = true; monoio 0.2.4 with io_uring. nginx version and build flags not stated (installed from the system, per the script's 'command -v nginx'); HAProxy 2.8.5 vendored build, flags not stated.
hardware: 12th Gen Intel Core i5-12450H, 12 logical cores; June run: wrk on cores 4-7, backend nginx on cores 0-1, proxy on cores 2-3. The August script does no pinning: backend nginx and the nginx proxy each run worker_processes 4, HAProxy and rproxy use their defaults, all on the same box.
tradeoffs: Not a general reverse proxy: the author positions it as a filtering layer (JWT, rate limiting, ACL and canonicalization checks) behind nginx; Linux with io_uring (kernel 5.6+); rate limit and cache state are per worker; TLS rate 134,168 req/s vs ceiling 629,459.
caveats: First-party; both runs (2026-06-27 and 2026-08-16) predate the repo's first public commit (2026-08-18), so the measured revisions are not in public history. The August three-proxy run's script (bench/haproxy_baseline.sh) labels its result 'median-of-3' but keeps the best of 3 runs, pins no cores, gives the nginx proxy worker_processes 4 and reads rproxy's worker count from bench_config.yml, which is not in the repo, so the equal-core claim holds only for the June run; that also explains the ceiling jump from 362k (2 pinned backend cores) to 632k (4 unpinned workers). The June nginx proxy config is not published and its upstream keep-alive is not stated (bench/nginx_proxy.conf in the repo listens on 8081 and proxies to 8081, so it is not the config used). The README is internally inconsistent about HAProxy: it shows a measured HAProxy row and then says 'HAProxy was not measured on the current rig' and no HAProxy comparison is claimed. Tiny 2-byte keep-alive body, same box, no TLS comparison; larger bodies, no keep-alive or TLS may differ. No LICENSE file, so reference. 0 stars, 2 commits. The README positions rproxy as a filter behind nginx, not a replacement. The win is architectural (prefork thread-per-core monoio workers on io_uring, coalesced head+body writes), not a Rust language effect. [retier] bench/haproxy_baseline.sh labels best-of-3 as 'median-of-3' and pins no cores; the backend nginx and nginx proxy each get worker_processes 4; HAProxy runs default threads; rproxy reads its worker count from a missing bench_config.yml, and under 12 CPUs its cpu_affinity auto pins its workers while nginx stays unpinned, so the August 1.15x/1.21x is not equal-resource. The script needs an unpublished root haproxy.cfg and haproxy-2.8.5/; the June run had a system nginx already running; bench/rproxy.yaml (log_level debug) is not the measured config.

name: Spire
baseline: HAProxy 2.7.3 (C) and Envoy 1.22.8 (C++) reverse proxies; nginx 1.23.3 in the same table is faster than Spire
workload: hey -n 100000 -c 250 GET through each reverse proxy to one echo-server backend under docker-compose, with the proxy and backend each limited to 4 CPUs and 8 GB. The hey container's limit differs between runs in the checked-in compose files: 12 CPUs for Spire and nginx, 4 CPUs for HAProxy, Envoy, Traefik and Caddy. The Traefik run used the jmalloc/echo-server backend; the others used ghcr.io/lsk569937453/echo-server:0.0.5. Each proxy had one run of about 1 s. Harness adapted from NickMRamirez/Proxy-Benchmarks; configs are in benchmarks/{spires,haproxy,envoy,nginx,traefik,caddy}/.
claimed_speedup: Page (2025-06-13 run): Spire 114,512 req/s (avg 2.2 ms, p99 11.8 ms) vs HAProxy 2.7.3 85,406 (1.34x, derived from page data), Envoy 1.22.8 48,040 (2.38x, derived from page data), Traefik 2.9.8 59,487 (1.93x, derived from page data; this Traefik row is copied unchanged from the 2023 run) and Caddy 2.6.4 13,168 (8.70x, derived from page data). nginx 1.23.3 reached 148,677 req/s, so Spire is 0.77x of nginx (derived from page data). In the 2023 run, where hey had 4 CPUs for every proxy, Silverwind (Spire's old name) reached 66,370 req/s vs HAProxy 81,674 (0.81x, derived from page data) and Envoy 61,847 (1.07x, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for any side. All proxies ran as prebuilt Docker images: lsk569937453/spire:0.0.24 (jemalloc via JEMALLOC_SYS_WITH_MALLOC_CONF), haproxytech/haproxy-ubuntu:2.7.3, envoyproxy/envoy:v1.22.8, nginx:1.23.3, traefik:v2.9.8 and caddy:2.6.4. The README's source build is cargo build --release.
hardware: 13th Gen Intel Core i5-13600K PC, 32 GB RAM (benchmarks.md); services limited to 4 cores and 8 GB
tradeoffs: Rust reverse proxy and gateway on Tokio and Hyper (HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, gRPC, TCP/TLS) with rate limiting, circuit breaking, ACME and hot reload; about 7 MB binary and 4 MB start-up memory per README.
caveats: Crippled baseline harness. The compose files committed with the 2025 numbers give the hey load generator 12 CPUs for the Spire and nginx runs but 4 CPUs for the HAProxy, Envoy, Traefik and Caddy runs, while benchmarks.md says every service was limited to 4 cores. Only the two 12-CPU rows jumped between runs (Spire 66,370 to 114,512 req/s, nginx 42,388 to 148,677); HAProxy stayed at 81,674 to 85,406. In the 2023 equal-CPU run Spire (then Silverwind) was 0.81x HAProxy. The Traefik row is copied byte-for-byte from the 2023 run and used a different backend (jmalloc/echo-server). Configs differ: nginx is tuned (4 workers, upstream keepalive 100), HAProxy has a minimal config with no timeouts, and Envoy's concurrency is not set. Envoy also adds headers that the echo backend returns, so its response is 294 bytes vs Spire's 155. Even so, Spire is slower than nginx in its own table (114,512 vs 148,677 req/s; p99 11.8 ms vs 4.9 ms). Each proxy had one hey run of about 1 s on the same PC as the load generator, with old HAProxy and Envoy releases and unstated build flags. The checked-in Spire compose sets CONFIG_FILE_PATH to /temp/app_config.yaml but mounts the file at /tmp/app_config.yaml, and app_config.yaml uses an older schema than the README, so the published harness may not run as checked in. The README headline 'Exceptional Performance' is not backed by a like-for-like win over any C or C++ proxy. [retier] docker cpus: 4.0 is a CFS quota, so the defaults give HAProxy 2.7 nbthread and Envoy 1.22.8 --concurrency about 20 host threads inside a 4-CPU quota while nginx is pinned to 4 workers and Tokio honours the cgroup quota (inferred, fits the 40-51 ms tail clusters). The compose JEMALLOC_SYS_WITH_MALLOC_CONF is a no-op; the global allocator is mimalloc (also at 0cac057). Third-party holmofy/proxy-benchmark (2024-09): Silverwind 19,352 vs HAProxy 17,826 req/s (1.09x) with a different echo backend image (80 vs 169 bytes per response) and 280 MB vs HAProxy's 85 MB.

why_faster: README attributes it to the Tokio async runtime and the Hyper HTTP library; no mechanism analysis is given.

name: statico
baseline: nginx (static in-memory 'return' response)
workload: Synthetic static in-memory HTTP response served to 1024 connections at 1, 2 and 4 server threads, comparing statico runtimes with nginx, HAProxy, Go net/http, fasthttp, Axum and actix-web.
claimed_speedup: README table, requests/s at 1 / 4 threads: statico (tokio) 399,025 / 1,071,433 vs nginx (return) 286,960 / 832,082 (1.39x / 1.29x) and statico (monoio) 656,517 / 1,436,420 (2.29x / 1.73x), but the nginx rows are from an earlier run (2025-12-31) than the statico rows (2026-03-28). In the original same-run table standard statico was 279,842 vs nginx 286,960 req/s at 1 thread (nginx 2.5% faster) and 966,248 vs 832,082 at 4 threads (1.16x, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: cargo build --release with per-runtime feature flags; Cargo.toml [profile.release] is opt-level 3, lto fat, codegen-units 1, panic abort, mimalloc as default allocator (profile added in the 2026-09-12 commit 'Optimize release build for performance', after the table was last updated on 2026-04-25 'Benchmarks updated.'). nginx build and flags not stated.
tradeoffs: Designed strictly for benchmarking: returns a fixed response from memory, no routing, no logging; Linux-only io_uring runtimes.
caveats: First-party; no CPU model, load generator (or whether it pipelines requests), nginx configuration or nginx build is published, so tier C. The table was last updated 2026-04-25, before the current release profile (2026-09-12) and the removal of the tokio-local runtime (2026-08-20). The README's key observations disagree with its own table: they list tokio-uring leading at 1.39M, monoio 1.36M and compio 1.27M at four threads, while the table gives monoio 1,436,420, compio 1,395,047 and tokio-uring 1,393,573, so the prose and table come from different runs. The io_uring runtimes write a response pre-encoded once per connection (src/response.rs build_response; any Date header frozen at connection start), while nginx builds its headers per request, so the io_uring rows do less work per response. statico is a benchmarking stub that returns one configured response, not a general web server. Actix-web (798,809) is slower than nginx (832,082) at four threads in the same table, and the README does not say whether nginx used tuned worker settings. src/monoio.rs builds a Vec with Vec::from_raw_parts pointing into the middle of another Vec's allocation (forgotten after the read), an unsound pattern. [retier] First-party; no CPU model, load generator, nginx configuration or nginx build is published. Cross-run baseline: the nginx, HAProxy, Go, Axum and actix-web rows are unchanged since the table first appeared on 2025-12-31 (commit 5e044f0) while the statico rows were re-measured by 2026-03-28, so the 'about 40% faster single-threaded' claim compares different runs; the only same-run table had nginx 2.5% faster at 1 thread and statico 1.16x at 4 threads. The table (2026-04-25) predates the current release profile (2026-09-12) and the removal of the tokio-local runtime (2026-08-20), and the README's key observations disagree with its own table.

why_faster: Pre-built responses held in memory, HTTP pipelining, thread-per-core io_uring runtimes (tokio-uring, monoio, glommio, compio) with CPU pinning for glommio and compio (README).

name: swerver
baseline: nginx (openresty/openresty:alpine Docker image, unpinned tag; tuned nginx.conf with worker_processes auto, reuseport, 'return 200' for /health and content_by_lua for /echo)
workload: swerver-benchmarks: k6 scenarios against minimal endpoints (/health, /echo, /blob) in Docker with 2 CPUs and 512 MB per container, swerver vs nginx, actix, http-zig and APISIX.
claimed_speedup: GET /health, 100 VUs, 30 s: swerver 147,435 req/s vs nginx 118,061 (1.25x, derived from page data), actix 133,691; no keep-alive connections/s 90,657 vs nginx 19,206 (4.7x); rapid-fire 143,437 vs nginx 125,346; error handling 114,455 vs nginx 80,053; TLS /health h2 161,781 vs nginx 107,741.
compiler_and_flags: swerver (April 2026 results, harness commit f5eb7c1): Zig 0.16.0-dev.3133+5ec8e45f3 aarch64-linux, zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast (servers/swerver/Dockerfile); HEAD now builds a bench app with .ReleaseFast hard-coded in servers/swerver/app/build.zig on Zig 0.16.0. nginx: openresty/openresty:alpine image, whose OpenResty configure adds -O2 by default (util/configure) and whose Dockerfile passes only -D/-I cc-opts, so nginx is built at -O2, not -O3.
hardware: Docker Desktop VM on macOS Apple Silicon (chip not stated), 2 CPUs and 512 MB per server container via docker-compose limits, k6 load generator in an unconstrained container on the same VM, April 2026
tradeoffs: Alpha release; library API will change; HTTP/3 first version runs at 16.5K req/s.
caveats: First-party benchmark by the swerver author, single run reported (no medians or repeat counts). Hot endpoints (/health, /plaintext, /json) are served from a per-second-refreshed pre-encoded response cache that skips the router, middleware and encoder, and the HEAD bench config sets disable_middleware: true; nginx answers /health with 'return 200' and /echo through content_by_lua. swerver container runs with seccomp unconfined so io_uring is used; nginx uses epoll. nginx is built at -O2 (OpenResty default), not -O3. Worker counts are not pinned equal (nginx worker_processes auto; swerver --workers defaults to 1 per its README, April image ran it without a config). Hardware is an unnamed Apple Silicon chip under Docker Desktop's VM. Results are mixed: mixed workload 36,929 vs nginx 36,969 (tie), /echo latency scenario nginx 8,659 vs swerver 8,517, actix-web ahead of swerver on TLS throughput (171,726 vs 161,781), h2 throughput (129,428 vs 111,698) and error handling (141,755 vs 114,455). The native wrk table (274,617 req/s on /health) has no nginx row. swerver's own README concedes feature-stripped reference servers edge it by 1-2% on raw HTTP/1.1 HttpArena tests. The harness has changed since the April results (Jul 2026 commit 'serve the benchmark endpoints + unbreak the baseline build'), so HEAD does not reproduce the measured build exactly. [retier] The k6 suite is one closed-loop run on Docker Desktop, so all five servers land at 91K-147K req/s on /health while native wrk on one swerver process hit 274,617; nginx's worker_processes auto counts VM CPUs, not the 2-CPU quota; /health came from the pre-encoded cache; the 4.7x connection-churn win vanishes on HttpArena limited-conn (2,629,113 vs 2,626,297, a tie). HttpArena (Threadripper PRO 3995WX, nginx -O3 -march=native, preencoded off): baseline-4096 1.12x, json-tls 1.15x, h2-256 1.18x over nginx, but 0.18x on baseline-h3 and 0.25x of h2o on h2; nginx rows date from Aug 15-20 and swerver rows from Aug 25-Sep 25 (cross-run). The README's json-tls 1,950,310 is stale (file now 1,510,149).

name: Traefik (Go reverse proxy; TLS latency vs Nginx and HAProxy)
baseline: Nginx 1.28.3 (C, official nginx:1.28.3 image) and HAProxy 3.3.6 (C, official haproxy:3.3.6 image) in Docker. Configs read: nginx worker_processes auto, epoll, multi_accept, upstream keepalive 64, TLSv1.2/1.3 with ECDHE AES-GCM ciphers, no ssl_session_cache, proxy_buffers 8 4k; HAProxy maxconn 20000, no-tls-tickets, http-reuse always, alpn h2,http/1.1. All proxies use the same self-signed RSA-4096 certificate.
workload: Fixed-rate Vegeta v12.13.0 load of 5,000 req/s for 20 s (5 s warmup per proxy/protocol, shuffled run order) for GET /data.json (~20 KB static JSON served by an nginx 1.28.3 backend) through each proxy; load generator, proxies and backend share one Docker host. -connections=64 sets only Vegeta's max idle connections per host (MaxIdleConnsPerHost), not the connection count. Both TLS scenarios negotiate HTTP/2 via ALPN (vegeta's -http2 flag defaults to true; nginx listens 'ssl http2', HAProxy advertises 'alpn h2,http/1.1', Go servers advertise h2), so requests are multiplexed over few TLS connections; the plain-HTTP scenario is HTTP/1.1. Run twice: unrestricted and restricted (cpus 2.0, mem_limit 4G per proxy via docker-compose.restricted.yml).
claimed_speedup: README Key Findings (approximate best-per-scenario values, 0% errors for all four proxies at 5,000 req/s): HTTPS/1.1 Traefik best mean about 0.48 ms and best P99 about 1.47 ms, Nginx P99 about 24 ms; HTTPS/2 Traefik best mean about 0.46 ms and P99 about 1.37 ms, HAProxy next at about 1.79 ms P99. Plain HTTP/1.1: all four within about 5%, Caddy/HAProxy best mean (about 0.41 ms), HAProxy best P99 (about 1.09 ms), so no Traefik win. The only committed chart (assets/local-results/benchmark.png, generated 2026-04-10) shows mean latency and throughput only: unrestricted HTTPS means are all near or below about 2 ms; in the 2-core restricted run Nginx means are about 32 ms (HTTPS/1.1) and 34 ms (HTTPS/2) against about 1.3 ms for Traefik on HTTPS/1.1 (read from chart, approximate). Per-proxy P99 tables are not published. Note: the 'HTTPS/1.1' row is really HTTP/2 (vegeta -http2 defaults to true and the harness never passes -http2=false).
compiler_and_flags: Official container images: Nginx 1.28.3, Caddy 2.11.2, Traefik 3.6.13, HAProxy 3.3.6; Vegeta v12.13.0; no compiler flags (prebuilt images)
hardware: Chart footer: host with 24 cores, 29.0 GB RAM, Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS (CPU model not stated); all containers on the same host; optional restricted run limits each proxy to 2 CPUs (CFS quota) and 4 GB.
tradeoffs: The benchmark records latency percentiles and success rate only; CPU and memory use are not reported. The author states that Nginx wins plaintext throughput and recommends running the suite on one's own hardware.
caveats: Benchmark repo (fabianwimberger/reverse-proxy-benchmark) is a third-party suite but a 0-star personal repo the owner archived on 2026-07-17; hardware lacks a CPU model and the proxies are prebuilt images with unknown build flags on both sides. Fixed-rate latency test at 5,000 req/s, not saturation throughput; all four proxies sustain the rate with 100% success, so differences are sub-millisecond except tails. Harness flaw: the 'HTTPS/1.1' scenario is actually HTTP/2 because vegeta's -http2 flag defaults to true (attack.go v12.13.0) and the harness only passes -insecure, so both TLS rows measure HTTP/2 over a few multiplexed connections; Nginx serves each connection from a single worker process, which plausibly explains its tail latency more than any language effect. The P99 values exist only as approximate README prose; the committed chart shows means only and raw vegeta JSON is not committed. Restricted-run asymmetry: nginx worker_processes auto counts the host's 24 CPUs under a 2-CPU CFS quota, whereas Traefik v3.6.13 (go.mod go 1.25.0) gets Go 1.25's container-aware GOMAXPROCS (likely cause of Nginx's ~32 ms restricted means; not tested). No HTTP/1.1 win: the author credits Nginx with plaintext throughput and calls HTTP/1.1 'extremely tight'. Not a same-algorithm comparison: different proxy designs and TLS stacks (Go crypto/tls vs OpenSSL).

It is a fixed-rate latency test at 5,000 req/s, not a saturation throughput test. The Nginx TLS P99 of about 24 ms probably reflects configuration (session cache, buffer sizes) rather than the language gap, and the configs were not read; the README itself says 'in this environment'. No HTTP/1.1 win: the author calls plain HTTP 'extremely tight' and credits Nginx with plaintext throughput. Tier C: partial methodology, hardware missing.

name: wut-server
baseline: nginx (C; own build with all optimization options, LTO, static OpenSSL, ngx_headers_more; 1 worker, 1024 worker connections, HTTP/2, TLS 1.3 only)
workload: wrk, 10 s, 6 threads, 1000 connections (from the wrk output header), against https://ip.erix.dev (nginx, port 443) and https://ip.erix.dev:11313 (wut-server) on the same host. Both servers terminate TLS and return the caller's IP address as the body; wrk speaks HTTP/1.1.
claimed_speedup: 38,110.60 requests/s (382,057 requests in 10 s) vs nginx 25,650.31 (257,322), about 49% more per the page (1.49x, derived from page data); transfer 3.27 MB/s vs 2.79 MB/s; max latency 279.57 ms vs 520.46 ms; nginx had connect 95 and read 17 socket errors.
compiler_and_flags: wut-server: Cargo.toml [profile.release] lto = true, codegen-units = 1, strip = true (default opt-level 3); hyper 0.14 with hyper-rustls 0.24, rustls 0.21 and tokio 1.34; rustc version not stated. nginx: 'all optimization options enabled', LTO, static OpenSSL and ngx_headers_more; version, compiler and exact flags not stated.
hardware: Server: single-core AMD EPYC 7302P, 1 GB ECC RAM, 1 Gbit/s uplink; client: AMD Ryzen 5600, 32 GB ECC RAM, 250 Mbit/s uplink; OS not stated; network benchmark, not loopback.
tradeoffs: Single-purpose server that returns the caller's public IP over HTTP and HTTP/2; not a general web server.
caveats: First-party single run per server, with no variance, no wrk command line, no versions, and the two runs were not interleaved. The author calls it a 'non-scientific comparison'. Both servers use TLS 1.3 over HTTPS (the wut-server wrk URL is https://...:11313, and the binary requires --cert-path and --key-path), but the TLS stacks differ: rustls 0.21 with ring on the Rust side, statically linked OpenSSL in nginx. Average latency is higher for wut-server (45.00 ms vs 28.07 ms), while max latency is lower (279.57 ms vs 520.46 ms). nginx logged 95 connect and 17 read socket errors, so it served fewer than the 1000 connections. wut-server formats the client IP once per connection, while nginx evaluates $remote_addr per request. The benchmark harness is not in the repo. The repo has 2 commits and 0 stars. [retier] The wut-server wrk output fails Little's law: 38,110.60 req/s at 45.00 ms average latency needs about 1,715 requests in flight, but wrk opened 996 connections, so about 22,100 req/s is the maximum at that latency; either an unshown pipelining script or not one plain run. The nginx run is consistent (about 720 in flight); bytes per response check out (90 vs 114). The server log counts connections, not requests. Cargo.lock pins h2 0.3.24 (RUSTSEC-2024-0332).
